synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Regime selection depends on relative depth, wave steepness, Ursell and Froude numbers, surf similarity, current-to-wave speed, relative bathymetric or boundary amplitude, bandwidth, sediment mobility and fall-velocity scaling, and ratios among forcing, dissipation and adjustment scales.
synthesis.disagreements: Alternative closures can share conservation laws yet predict different asymptotes; exactness under idealized boundaries does not imply field accuracy; fitted empirical coefficients can outperform theory locally while transferring less reliably; formally higher order is not always better outside its scaling regime.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: The reviewed evidence connects theory to finite-depth crest and setup measurements, truncated-beach overtopping experiments, estuarine fetch/depth wave observations, and coastal wave or morphology datasets used to constrain asymptotic regimes.
synthesis.governing_physics: Mass, momentum, energy and sediment conservation are closed with gravity, pressure, dispersion, nonlinearity, friction, turbulence or transport parameterizations and boundary conditions for the bed, shoreline, free surface, currents and structures.
synthesis.limitations: Tractability usually requires simplified geometry, weak nonlinearity or dispersion, scale separation, prescribed closures, narrow spectra, uniform sediment or currents, and idealized boundaries; breaking, turbulence, three-dimensionality and stochastic forcing often enter indirectly.
synthesis.major_equations: Core families include potential-flow and free-surface boundary conditions, shallow-water and Boussinesq-type equations, wave-action and spectral balances, radiation-stress or momentum balances, Exner continuity, transport energetics, eigenvalue/scattering systems and perturbation expansions.
synthesis.numerical_models: Analytical solutions serve as standalone reduced-order models and verification benchmarks for spectral wave, shallow-water, Boussinesq, morphodynamic, scattering, wave-current and fluid-structure solvers.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities are analytical hierarchies for compound forcing, irregular directional waves, nonlinear breaking, mixed sediments, porous and deformable boundaries, coupled morphology, nonstationarity, uncertainty propagation and explicit transition criteria between model orders.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent analytical work increasingly couples currents, complex or compliant boundaries, partial reflections and morphology, and uses observations plus high-fidelity computation to map validity rather than presenting a closed form without an error regime.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Classical linear and nonlinear wave theories, shallow-water characteristics, perturbation and multiple-scale methods, radiation stress, spectral balances and sediment-continuity reductions established the analytical vocabulary used by coastal engineering.
synthesis.typical_methods: Methods nondimensionalize the governing problem, identify small or large parameters, impose idealized initial and boundary conditions, derive exact or asymptotic solutions, test limiting behavior, and compare with laboratory, field or converged numerical evidence.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Examples span weakly nonlinear finite-depth waves, fetch- and depth-limited basins, long waves over gently varying or corrugated beds, idealized planar beaches, partial reflection, deformable boundaries and energetics-based sandy shoreface adjustment.
synthesis.well_established: Analytical coastal models reduce conservation laws and boundary conditions to exact, approximate, asymptotic, similarity, perturbation, spectral, or reduced-order relations whose assumptions remain visible and testable.

claims.text: Reanalysis of fully developed wind seas relates asymptotic integral spectral limits to the source-term balances used to validate operational wave models.
claims.regime: Revisiting the Pierson–Moskowitz Asymptotic Limits for Fully Developed Wind Waves

claims.text: An energetics-based cross-shore sediment-transport formulation yields a mechanistic morphodynamic depth of closure rather than prescribing one solely from wave statistics.
claims.regime: Exploring shoreface dynamics and a mechanistic explanation for a morphodynamic depth of closure

claims.text: Second-order three-dimensional finite-depth theory explains setup and surface-elevation and crest statistics when evaluated against controlled experimental data.
claims.regime: Second-Order Theory and Setup in Surface Gravity Waves: A Comparison with Experimental Data

claims.text: Fetch- and depth-limited estuarine wind waves can be organized by nondimensional scaling that distinguishes growth constrained by basin geometry and water depth.
claims.regime: Wind Wave Behavior in Fetch and Depth Limited Estuaries

claims.text: Weakly dispersive surface and internal waves admit reduced analytical descriptions of interacting long-wave structures, with applicability bounded by the asymptotic assumptions.
claims.regime: Analytical behavior of weakly dispersive surface and internal waves in the ocean

claims.text: Theory and experiments for a truncated planar beach relate an individual incident wave to overtopped volume and identify the limits of idealized run-up representations.
claims.regime: Overtopping a truncated planar beach

claims.text: An asymptotic solution describes Bragg scattering by variable bathymetry with a uniform current and floating membrane, exposing how current, depth variation, and compliance modify resonance.
claims.regime: Bragg scattering of gravity waves by a sea bed of varying depth in the presence of uniform current covered by a floating membrane

claims.text: A nonlinear shallow-water formulation coupled to an elastic sheet on a viscoelastic foundation describes wave propagation over a deformable seabed.
claims.regime: Nonlinear waves propagating over a deformable seafloor

claims.text: A free-long-wave framework with partial reflections resolves nearshore transformation relevant to inundation and shoreline or dune erosion.
claims.regime: Free Long-Wave Transformation in the Nearshore Zone through Partial Reflections

claims.text: Perturbation analysis shows how a wavy bed modifies currents induced by long waves approaching a beach, including nearshore and swash-zone circulation effects.
claims.regime: Currents induced by long waves propagating towards a beach over a wavy bed

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Key regime controls include relative depth kh, H/h, wave steepness, Ursell number, bed slope, directional spread and topographic length relative to wavelength.
synthesis.disagreements: A model can match bulk wave height while scattering more in setup or second-order statistics, and horizontal-bottom kinematics can fail near a slope even when horizontal velocity remains little affected. Accuracy therefore depends on the diagnostic, not merely the model label.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Reviewed evidence includes storm observations over a 2-degree nearshore slope, three laboratory cases including a fringing reef and barred beach, laboratory topographic-scattering observations, and six regional operational-model applications.
synthesis.governing_physics: Core physics are gravity-restored free-surface motion, depth-dependent dispersion, conservation of energy or wave action, bathymetric refraction and diffraction, and slope-dependent vertical structure.
synthesis.limitations: Linearization omits finite-amplitude harmonic coupling, breaking, strongly nonlinear runup and some current interactions. Forward-scattering, hydrostatic structure, spectral closure and abstract-only evidence impose additional source-specific limits.
synthesis.major_equations: Common formulations include the Airy dispersion relation, linear velocity-transfer functions, shoaling and group-velocity relations, mild-slope and coupled-mode equations, and spectral wave-action balance.
synthesis.numerical_models: Models include sloping-bed linear transfer theory, forward-scattering stochastic coupled modes, a two-layer non-hydrostatic solver benchmarked against linear dispersion, and SWAN driven by WAM, WW3 or buoy observations.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities include quantified switching criteria between linear and nonlinear models, uncertainty propagation from bathymetry and forcing, efficient wide-angle scattering, and common benchmarks spanning kinematics, spectra, setup and extremes.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent developments improve dispersion through layered non-hydrostatic pressure structure, retain coherent interference in stochastic coupled modes, and integrate increasingly resolved coastal domains into operational spectral systems.
synthesis.seminal_papers: The branch rests on classical Airy dispersion and kinematics, energy-flux shoaling, mild-slope transformation and action-balance modeling; the current review slice validates selected descendants rather than establishing a complete historical canon.
synthesis.typical_methods: Methods compare analytical solutions with field velocity profiles, laboratory transformation data, stochastic moment equations, non-hydrostatic solvers and operational spectral hindcast-nowcast-forecast systems.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Explicit abstract-level bounds include H/h<0.3 and Ursell number<0.6 on a 2-degree slope, and improved two-layer dispersion and shoaling through kh=4 compared with a one-layer shallow-water range kh<1.
synthesis.well_established: Linear wave theory remains the reference model for small-amplitude surface-gravity-wave dispersion, kinematics, energy flux, shoaling, refraction and diffraction. Its usefulness depends on stating depth, slope, amplitude, directionality and scattering assumptions.

claims.text: For observed nearshore waves on a 2-degree bed slope with H/h below 0.3 and Ursell number below 0.6, sloping-bed linear theory reproduced near-bed vertical-velocity magnitude and phase substantially better than horizontal-bottom theory, while horizontal velocity was comparatively insensitive to slope.
claims.regime: Near-bed observations on a 2-degree slope for H/h below 0.3 and Ursell number below 0.6 during two storm intervals.

claims.text: Against linear-wave dispersion and shoaling benchmarks, the two-layer non-hydrostatic model extended useful behavior from the one-layer model's shallow-water range kh<1 to shallow and intermediate depths through kh=4, though setup and second-order statistics showed more scatter than bulk and spectral wave height.
claims.regime: Shallow to intermediate water through kh=4, with validation cases including a fringing reef and barred beach.

claims.text: For the tested two-dimensional topographies, a stochastic coupled-mode model based on forward scattering reproduced coherent interference and the combined wide-angle refraction-diffraction effects in agreement with analytical solutions and laboratory observations within its linear-interaction focus.
claims.regime: Random directionally spread waves over fully two-dimensional coastal topography under a forward-scattering approximation; the reported paper focuses on linear topographic interaction.

claims.text: Across six ocean and coastal applications, SWAN-based hindcast, nowcast, and forecast schemes provided an effective wave-prediction framework when forced by WAM, WW3, or buoy observations, but the abstract does not establish universal accuracy or isolate linear-theory error.
claims.regime: SWAN applications from high-resolution coastal domains to quasi-oceanic scales in Portugal, Madeira, Sardinia, and the Black Sea.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Approximation choice is organized by wave steepness, relative depth kh, Ursell number, relative amplitude H/h, dispersion and nonlinearity orders, surf similarity, Froude number, Shields parameter, suspension number, settling-to-advection time ratio, and morphology relaxation time.
synthesis.disagreements: A reduced model may solve its parent equations accurately yet omit decisive physics. Linear or weakly nonlinear wavemaker theory fails at higher steepness; nonlinear shallow-water theory cannot reproduce dispersive or post-breaking behavior; local linear wavelengths can misinterpret free-bound spatial beating.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Theory has been checked against transient-wave flumes, Tainan nonlinear shoaling tests, Synolakis plane-beach and Briggs conical-island runup, Monai valley inundation, current-wave suspended-transport measurements, and multi-year shoreline or inlet observations.
synthesis.governing_physics: Key mechanisms are finite-amplitude kinematics and dynamic boundary conditions, weak dispersion, quadratic and higher-order harmonic coupling, free-bound interference, nonlinear shoaling and runup, moving wet-dry boundaries, wave-current diffusion, settling lag, and feedback toward or away from morphological equilibrium.
synthesis.limitations: Asymptotic truncation, idealized geometry, inviscid or hydrostatic assumptions, weak dispersion, prescribed profile shape, unidirectionality, nonbreaking conditions, friction closure, and scale separation constrain transfer. Mathematical existence alone does not establish coastal relevance.
synthesis.major_equations: Principal frameworks include nonlinear shallow-water equations, Boussinesq and extended mild-slope equations, Stokes and perturbation expansions, eigenfunction wavemaker solutions, asymptotic convection-diffusion reductions, exact Lagrangian seiche solutions, stochastic half-cycle transport, and dynamic-equilibrium profile laws.
synthesis.numerical_models: Reviewed implementations include semi-analytical eigenfunction-FFT wavemakers, higher-order Boussinesq solvers, nonlinear shallow-water inundation models, SWAN phase-decoupled diffraction, quasi-3-D transport, exact seiche benchmarks, stochastic bedload models, and dynamic-equilibrium shoreline models.
synthesis.open_questions: Needs include uniform theories across shoaling, breaking and runup; multidirectional and current-coupled nonlinear interactions; error bounds for truncation and closure; efficient stochastic extremes; sediment and morphology coupling; and principled switching among reduced and process-resolving models.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent work combines free-bound harmonic separation, nonlinear spectral diagnostics, stochastic transport, benchmark-driven model hierarchies, and dynamic-equilibrium reduced models to retain essential physics while remaining efficient enough for design or forecasting.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Within the reviewed corpus, exact shallow-water shoreline benchmarks, Boussinesq runup validation, mild-slope-derived diffraction, quasi-3-D transport asymptotics, and nonlinear wavemaker theory form reusable analytical foundations across coastal applications.
synthesis.typical_methods: Methods derive ordered reduced equations, exact or semi-analytical solutions, matched or regular perturbation expansions, spectral/eigenfunction decompositions, stochastic averaging, equilibrium stability analysis, and comparisons with laboratory, field, or higher-dimensional numerical solutions.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Examples include Tainan H=0.05-0.40 m and T=2-5 s, plane-beach H/d=0.021-0.626 with breaking above 0.045 on a 1:19.85 slope, conical-island H/d=0.10 and 0.20, narrow-band second-order random waves, and source-specific low-to-steep wavemaker tests.
synthesis.well_established: Nonlinear coastal theory is useful when finite amplitude, shallow depth, moving shorelines, wave asymmetry, harmonic coupling, dispersion, or morphology feedback invalidate linear superposition. Its value depends on explicit ordering assumptions and validation inside the retained regime.

claims.text: Sine-Gordon and generalized Kudryashov methods yield soliton solutions of the Boussinesq equation used for weakly nonlinear long waves in harbors and shallow seas.
claims.regime: Soliton solutions to the Boussinesq equation through sine-Gordon method and Kudryashov method

claims.text: Nonlinear WKB and perturbation analyses show a convex non-reflecting beach generates higher harmonics during wave propagation.
claims.regime: Nonlinear wave effects at the non-reflecting beach

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Reviewed controls include slide Froude number, relative slide thickness and mass, grain Reynolds number, Cauchy and WFSI parameters, fence porosity and relative thickness, and stage-specific power ratios.
synthesis.disagreements: Rigid landslide blocks do not necessarily generate larger waves than granular slides, and a scaling law adequate for nonbreaking loads can fail badly for breaking pressure or flexible response. Apparent disagreement reflects unmatched secondary physics and response choice.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Evidence includes 144 block-slide tests, factor-four granular-slide tests in a 6 m apparatus, plate-impact models up to 40 times smaller, 1:5 wooden-fence tests, and three WEC PTO case studies.
synthesis.governing_physics: Froude scaling preserves gravity-inertia balance, Reynolds scaling represents viscous effects, Cauchy-type controls represent elastic-fluid interaction, and power similarity governs energy-conversion stages; exact simultaneous similitude is often impossible.
synthesis.limitations: Abstract-level evidence, laboratory confinement, finite scale range, unscaled air or fluid properties, particle stiffness, material substitution, simplified PTO behavior, and incomplete prototype validation bound transfer.
synthesis.major_equations: Core tools are Buckingham-Pi dimensional analysis and model-prototype scale ratios for length, time, velocity, force, pressure, stiffness, power, Froude number, Reynolds number, Cauchy number, and process-specific relative geometry.
synthesis.numerical_models: Numerical support includes discrete-element slide simulations, prototype/model wave-flexible-plate simulations, SWASH fence upscaling, and process-decomposed WEC scaling frameworks.
synthesis.open_questions: Needs include optimal multi-physics scale selection, principled distortion correction, uncertainty propagation to prototypes, shared multi-scale benchmarks, and field validation for breaking impacts, nature-based structures, slides, and energy devices.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent work uses paired numerical and physical models to quantify rather than merely note scale effects, proposes partial-parameter WFSI scaling, orchestrates similarity across energy-conversion stages, and separates scale bias from design-variable effects.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Classical Froude similitude and Buckingham-Pi analysis provide the foundation; the reviewed corpus demonstrates why Reynolds, elasticity, grain-air, porosity, and power constraints must be added for specific coastal processes.
synthesis.typical_methods: Methods combine multi-scale flume tests, systematic parameter variation, prototype-model numerical comparison, discrete-element or hydrodynamic simulation, calibration, uncertainty/error estimation, and mechanism-by-mechanism scaling orchestration.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Reported bounds include wave-height effects up to a factor two from block-slide parameters, granular velocity and runout effects of 35% and 26%, breaking-pressure errors to 132%, displacement errors to 98%, new WFSI deviations below 4.3%, and fence scale bias near 5%.
synthesis.well_established: Physical-model similarity requires matching dominant nondimensional controls; geometric resemblance alone does not guarantee dynamic similarity when gravity, viscosity, elasticity, air entrainment, granular drag, structural response, or power conversion compete.

claims.text: Across 144 Froude-model block-slide tests, slide Froude number, relative thickness, and relative mass changed wave amplitude and height by as much as a factor of two, and rigid blocks did not systematically generate larger waves than deformable granular slides.
claims.regime: Systematic variation of slide Froude number, relative thickness, and relative mass in physical landslide-tsunami models.

claims.text: For wave impacts on plates modeled at scales down to 1:40, precise Froude scaling removed detectable scale effects, whereas unscaled fluid properties produced breaking-pressure errors up to 132% and traditional Froude scaling underestimated displacement by up to 98%; a new WFSI approach kept validated peak deviations below 4.3%.
claims.regime: Rigid and flexible plates under breaking and non-breaking regular and solitary waves, with models up to 40 times smaller.

claims.text: A review of wave-energy-converter power-take-off experiments found that credible small-scale reproduction requires explicit setup enhancement, calibration, and error estimation, with some recommendations transferable across technologies despite device-specific scaling choices.
claims.regime: Small-scale wave-energy-converter PTO experiments across technology-dependent configurations.

claims.text: For oscillating-buoy wave-energy-converter model tests, the proposed orchestration applies Froude similarity to the water-contacting capture stage and power similarity to later conversion stages without requiring their geometric similitude.
claims.regime: Oscillating-buoy WEC model tests decomposed into capture and downstream conversion stages.

claims.text: For porosity-0.81 wooden fences, a SWASH model validated against 1:5 tests with 4.7% transmitted-height RMSE predicted model-scale reflection and transmission about 5% above full-scale values, smaller than the effects of fence thickness and porosity.
claims.regime: Wooden fence porosity 0.81 with varied thickness, comparing 1:5 and full-scale simulations.

claims.text: Across factor-four Froude-scaled dry granular-slide models, nondimensional surface velocity increased up to 35% and runout up to 26% from smallest to largest scale; correlation with grain Reynolds number and air-free DEM comparisons implicated particle-air drag.
claims.regime: Dry granular slides in a 6 m apparatus across a factor-four scale range.

claims.text: For Froude-scaled dry granular slides in 0.25-1.00 m channels at grain Reynolds numbers of order 10^2-10^3, experiments showed significant velocity and runout scale effects that the discrete-element model did not capture at the smaller scale.
claims.regime: Dry granular slides in channels 0.25-1.00 m wide with grain Reynolds numbers of order 10^2-10^3.

claims.text: Similarity criteria relate turbulent vertical-displacement time scales to phytoplankton photoadaptation time scales, identifying regimes in which vertical mixing alters light exposure and production response.
claims.regime: Relationships between vertical mixing and photoadaptation of phytoplankton: similarity criteria

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Controls include wave steepness and direction, relative water level, surf similarity, fall-velocity parameter, closure depth, profile slope, sediment size, transport-gradient and recovery time scales, compartment leakage and sediment-input/transport-capacity ratios.
synthesis.disagreements: A shoreline line alone may indicate retreat while subaerial volume or profile storage behaves differently; equilibrium models are efficient but miss pathways and memory; local trends may reflect basin climate rather than secular forcing; fixed cells may leak sediment.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Evidence includes Australia-wide Landsat coastlines, global satellite shorelines, the Elwha dam-removal coast, West African and Ebro sediment systems, Shoalhaven compartments and modeled shelf-ridge/shoreline coupling.
synthesis.governing_physics: Wave and current stresses move sediment; water level controls where energy is delivered; gradients in longshore transport change planform; cross-shore exchange reshapes profiles; rivers, cliffs, shelf stores, dunes and engineering alter the budget; morphology feeds back on forcing.
synthesis.limitations: Shoreline proxies and tidal correction introduce error; bathymetric records are sparse; sediment budgets rarely close; recovery may exceed monitoring duration; intervention histories are incomplete; model parameters are nonstationary and scale-dependent.
synthesis.major_equations: Core formulations are Exner sediment continuity, one-line shoreline continuity, equilibrium-profile and disequilibrium response, cross-/longshore transport laws, sediment-budget mass balance, state-space/data assimilation and coupled shelf–shoreline models.
synthesis.numerical_models: Represented tools include shoreline trend clustering, satellite-assimilative dynamic shoreline models, sediment-budget calculators, coupled cross-/longshore and shelf–shoreline models, equilibrium response, mesoscale multi-model frameworks and climate-driver attribution.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities include profile–planform coupling, shelf exchange, event recovery and memory, mixed sediment, compound water levels, human intervention attribution, dynamic compartment boundaries and probabilistic multi-decadal forecasting.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent work uses decades of satellite shorelines, data assimilation, cluster-based reaches, global climate attribution, intervention natural experiments, coupled shelf–shoreline models and hierarchical management compartments.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Profile and one-line shoreline models established reduced beach evolution, while sediment budgets and littoral-cell concepts established source–pathway–sink management.
synthesis.typical_methods: Methods combine repeated topobathymetry, satellite shorelines, lidar/UAS, sediment tracing and budgets, wave/water-level records, trend segmentation, equilibrium and process models, multi-model frameworks, data assimilation and scenario analysis.
synthesis.validated_ranges: The corpus spans sandy open coasts and barriers, adjacent managed compartments, river- and port-modified littoral cells, low-gradient deltas, seasonal through multi-decadal records, national mapping and global climate variability.
synthesis.well_established: Beaches are open sediment systems whose shoreline and profile evolve through coupled cross-shore and longshore transport, changing water levels, sediment sources and sinks, antecedent morphology and human interventions.

claims.text: Three decades of Landsat observations provide consistent mean-sea-level coastline mapping for measuring Australia-wide dynamic shoreline change.
claims.regime: Mapping Australia's dynamic coastline at mean sea level using three decades of Landsat imagery

claims.text: Cluster-based segmentation improves shoreline-trend analysis by identifying spatially coherent change regimes rather than imposing arbitrary reaches.
claims.regime: Understanding coastal change using shoreline trend analysis supported by cluster-based segmentation

claims.text: Removal of a large dam restored fluvial sediment supply and reversed coastal erosion, demonstrating direct sediment-budget control of shoreline trajectory.
claims.regime: World’s largest dam removal reverses coastal erosion

claims.text: Assimilating satellite-derived shorelines into a dynamic model enables fine-scale wave- and sea-level-driven predictions across large coastal regions.
claims.regime: A Model Integrating Satellite‐Derived Shoreline Observations for Predicting Fine‐Scale Shoreline Response to Waves and Sea‐Level Rise Across Large Coastal Regions

claims.text: A quantitative West African sediment budget separates river regulation, port interception, natural transport and climate effects on a connected coastal barrier.
claims.regime: A quantitative assessment of human interventions and climate change on the West African sediment budget

claims.text: Integrated analysis of the Ebro Delta links storms, morphology, climate change, river regulation and development to combined flooding and erosion.

claims.text: A mesoscale framework combines complementary models to represent interacting shoreline processes for decadal-to-centennial coastal management.
claims.regime: Simulating mesoscale coastal evolution for decadal coastal management: A new framework integrating multiple, complementary modelling approaches

claims.text: Global satellite shorelines show El Niño reorganizes shoreline-position variability through basin-scale changes in waves and water levels.
claims.regime: Influence of El Niño on the variability of global shoreline position

claims.text: Intra-seasonal sea-level anomalies exacerbate beach erosion independently of named storms, showing water-level history modifies morphological response.
claims.regime: Sea level anomalies exacerbate beach erosion

claims.text: A review frames coastal morphodynamics as coupled feedback among waves, water levels, sediment, morphology and climate across scales.
claims.regime: Coastal Morphodynamics and Climate Change: A Review of Recent Advances

claims.text: Coastal compartments provide a hierarchical management unit in which sediment supply and local morphodynamics explain differing behavior of adjacent beaches.
claims.regime: Coastal compartments: the role of sediment supply and morphodynamics in a beach management context

claims.text: A coupled shelf–shoreline model shows waves and tides link kilometer-scale shelf sand ridges to long-term shoreline morphodynamics.
claims.regime: Long‐Term Morphodynamics of a Coupled Shelf‐Shoreline System Forced by Waves and Tides, a Model Approach

claims.text: Nearly five years of Torrey Pines observations show an approximately 40 m seasonal shoreline retreat associated with incident wave-energy changes and support an equilibrium shoreline-response model.
claims.regime: Equilibrium shoreline response: Observations and modeling

claims.text: Geologically controlled beaches differ systematically from unconstrained beaches because headlands, rock platforms and coral or bedrock controls set accommodation, wave shadows, rip circulation, sediment-budget closure, rotation and storm response along both cross-shore and longshore gradients.
claims.regime: Sandy beaches constrained by headlands, rock platforms, coral formations or other basement geology.

claims.text: Multivariate analysis of 92 English and Welsh beaches identifies nine morphodynamic types: dimensionless fall velocity and relative tide range separate groups, but absolute wave-energy flux is additionally needed to distinguish intermediate beaches with three-dimensional bar-rip morphology.
claims.regime: Gravel, sand, embayed, exposed, macro- and mesotidal beaches across England and Wales under their mean wave, tide, sediment, and morphological conditions.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Controls include shoreline displacement relative to positional uncertainty, observation duration relative to storm and recovery cycles, beach width normalized by wave runup, sediment-budget imbalance, closure-depth ratio, wave obliquity, nourishment volume per shoreline length and erosion/accretion cluster significance.
synthesis.disagreements: Different shoreline proxies—instantaneous waterline, wet/dry line, vegetation line or modeled datum contour—can yield different trends. Linear rates can conceal episodic storms, recovery and interventions, and apparent accretion need not imply positive subaqueous sediment volume.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Reviewed evidence includes 769 Haikou images from 1986-2023, Iztuzu transects and clusters for 2013-2022, national cross-mission remote sensing, northwest Ireland waterlines from 1999-2024 and fuzzy-classified northern Java change from 1994-2000.
synthesis.governing_physics: Cross-shore storm erosion and recovery redistribute profile sediment, alongshore transport gradients rotate or translate shorelines, inlets and headlands reorganize cells, and nourishment or construction alters sediment budgets; waterline position also moves instantaneously with tide, runup and setup.
synthesis.limitations: Clouds, pixel size, georegistration, tidal stage, runup, datum mismatch, proxy migration, sparse ground truth, short or uneven sampling, anthropogenic confounding and absent profile volume limit attribution. Random positional error does not capture all systematic bias.
synthesis.major_equations: Change metrics fit shoreline position versus time for endpoint or linear-regression rates and uncertainty, compute transect displacement and area or volume budgets, and relate gradients in alongshore transport to shoreline movement through one-line continuity; probabilistic methods characterize indicator and classification error.
synthesis.numerical_models: The reviewed set emphasizes satellite classification and statistical change analysis, including fuzzy c-means and spatial clustering. Hybrid two-dimensional/one-line, moment and climate-response shoreline models remain in the lawful-full-text queue.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities include globally consistent uncertainty-aware shoreline products, separation of waterline and morphology, profile-volume assimilation, intervention causal inference, storm-recovery memory, sediment-cell closure, compound drivers and forecast validation under nonstationary climate and management.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent advances combine cross-mission optical and SAR imagery, subpixel and probabilistic classification, lidar and video validation, cloud-scale transect analysis, Bayesian change points, physics-informed shoreline models and explicit propagation of waterline and geolocation uncertainty.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Repeated beach profiles and aerial-photo transects established quantitative shoreline monitoring; sediment-budget and one-line theory linked transport gradients to movement, while satellite archives and automated extraction enabled dense regional and global time series.
synthesis.typical_methods: Workflows define a repeatable shoreline proxy, harmonize imagery and datums, correct tide or waterline effects, quantify georeferencing and classification uncertainty, cast stable transects, calculate rates and confidence intervals, detect clusters or change points, validate against surveys and interpret results with forcing and interventions.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Findings cover selected urban, nourished, storm-affected, dissipative, reflective and deltaic coasts over years to decades. Reported rates and intervention associations are site-, proxy-, resolution- and interval-specific.
synthesis.well_established: Beach change is spatially and temporally variable: shoreline indicators respond to waves, water level, sediment supply, morphology and engineering, while erosion at one interval or transect can coexist with accretion nearby or later.

claims.text: Between 2013 and 2022, Iztuzu Zones II-IV were predominantly erosional, whereas Zones I and V contained the strongest accretion, with substantial variation among subperiods.
claims.regime: Manually digitized Google Earth shorelines at 18 dates along Iztuzu Beach; shoreline-position uncertainty from water level and image timing remains.

claims.text: Of 819 Iztuzu shoreline transects, 287 points (35%) belonged to statistically significant erosion or deposition clusters, with erosion clusters concentrated mainly in Zone II and deposition clusters in Zone V.
claims.regime: 2013-2022 NSM-based hotspot analysis at 5 m transect spacing; results depend on manual shoreline extraction and neighborhood definition.

claims.text: Fuzzy c-means shoreline classification at the northern Java site achieved kappa values of 0.86-0.96 and represented both boundary position and pixel-level change uncertainty, including 739 ha converted to water in 1994-2000.
claims.regime: The 1994-2015 optical images, t=0.5 membership threshold, and northern Java class definitions.

claims.text: Across 769 Haikou images from 1986-2023, artificial-island construction and five nourishment projects were mainly associated with accretion, with a 4.9 m random waterline-position error.
claims.regime: Haikou Beach, its engineering chronology, and satellite mean-waterline proxy; association is not universal causation.

claims.text: Over 1999-2024, two broad dissipative northwest Ireland beaches remained comparatively stable or accreting under consistent extreme-waterline trends, whereas the narrower reflective beach showed the greatest variability and landward retreat.
claims.regime: The three undisturbed northwest Ireland beaches and their satellite waterline proxies.

claims.text: In an 18-year Tairua blind test, 19 process and machine-learning shoreline models lost skill on unseen 2014–2017 data and fast extremes; an ensemble outperformed individual models and exposed architecture uncertainty.
claims.regime: Blind testing of shoreline evolution models

claims.text: Satellite analysis for 1984–2016 estimates sandy beaches comprise 31% of ice-free shoreline; 24% erode faster than 0.5 m/yr, 28% accrete and 48% are stable.
claims.regime: The State of the World’s Beaches

claims.text: Mekong delta shoreline analysis links rapid erosion to human-driven reductions and redistribution of river sediment rather than coastal forcing alone.
claims.regime: Linking rapid erosion of the Mekong River delta to human activities

claims.text: A shoreline-prediction review identifies nonstationary forcing, multiscale processes, data limitations and model uncertainty as central barriers to reliable coastal forecasts.
claims.regime: Challenges and Opportunities in Coastal Shoreline Prediction

claims.text: Multitemporal remote sensing at Sayung documents spatially variable shoreline erosion and accretion suitable for diagnosing coastal change and management priorities.
claims.regime: Dynamics of shoreline changes in the coastal region of Sayung, Indonesia

claims.text: Global long-term satellite observations quantify coastal erosion and accretion patterns and demonstrate that shoreline change is geographically heterogeneous rather than uniformly erosional.

claims.regime: Mechanisms, volumetric assessment, and prognosis for rapid coastal erosion of Tuktoyaktuk Island, an important natural barrier for the harbour and community

claims.text: Across 54 river deltas, multi-decadal shoreline response to diminished fluvial sediment supply was heterogeneous and often delayed, but eroding deltas experienced roughly twice the sediment-load reduction of stable or advancing deltas, indicating that sediment supply chiefly sustains resilience to marine forcing, subsidence, and sea-level rise rather than guaranteeing immediate shoreline advance.
claims.regime: Subaerial shorelines of 54 large and small river deltas worldwide, evaluated mainly from 1972-2015 satellite imagery and pre-/post-1970 river sediment-load evidence.

claims.text: Integrated 1947-2018 shoreline, elevation, stratigraphic, and ground-ice evidence shows that exposed-shore recession at Tuktoyaktuk Island accelerated from 1.58±0.05 to 1.80±0.02 m/year; erosion comprises 88% of island volume change (about 9,200 m3/year), and post-2000 rates project breach of the natural harbour barrier by 2044 or sooner.
claims.regime: Ice-rich permafrost barrier island protecting Tuktoyaktuk Harbour, western Canadian Arctic, with thermo-abrasional cliff undercutting, block failure, storm waves and surge, rising relative sea level, and an expanding open-water season.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Transferable regime descriptors include water level and runup relative to dune toe and crest, freeboard normalized by wave height, surf similarity, storm duration relative to profile-adjustment time, berm and dune volume normalized by active-profile scales, and erosion or overwash volume relative to initial dune volume.
synthesis.disagreements: Forcing-only thresholds can separate weak and severe impacts in some datasets, while intermediate cases require morphology; process-based profile models explain sediment redistribution but do not by themselves establish universal damage classes. These are complementary scales, not interchangeable predictors.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: The New Jersey Beach Profile Network supported profile-based erosion analysis for eighteen historical storms selected from a 1980-2013 erosion-potential climatology.
synthesis.governing_physics: In the reviewed New Jersey study, peak joint wave-water-level forcing was the dominant tested predictor of dune loss, while berm and dune morphology modulated how much forcing reached and removed the dune.
synthesis.limitations: The available reviewed evidence is geographically narrow; its data-driven thresholds and performance should not be transferred outside New Jersey or beyond the reported storm and morphology ranges without retraining or increased uncertainty.
synthesis.major_equations: Dune impact was quantified as 100 times the difference between pre- and post-storm area inside the pre-storm dune footprint divided by the pre-storm area.
synthesis.numerical_models: A 260-tree bootstrap ensemble predicted Minor, Moderate, and Major dune-volume-loss classes with reported within-dataset accuracies of 92%, 84%, and 98%, respectively; this was not external regional validation.
synthesis.open_questions: Unresolved needs include representing the timing and duration of peak erosion intensity, adding rare severe impacts, testing other beach regimes, and externally validating the model.
synthesis.recent_advances: For this dataset, PEI below 69 generally separated Minor impacts and PEI above 102 generally separated Moderate/Major impacts; morphology was necessary between those thresholds.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Early storm-surge profile models established offshore redistribution of eroded dune sand under elevated water levels; later impact-regime concepts organized collision, overwash and inundation, and modern data-driven work quantifies how storm intensity and morphology jointly classify loss.
synthesis.typical_methods: One demonstrated workflow combines repeated pre/post-storm beach profiles, hindcast wave and water-level intensity indices, correlation analysis, and classification-tree ensembles with held-out testing.
synthesis.validated_ranges: The model was trained and tested for New Jersey profiles with berm volume 1.8-420.1 m3/m, dune volume 1.5-281.7 m3/m, median grain size 0.16-2.19 mm, crest elevation 2.2-7.8 m NAVD, toe elevation 1.0-4.8 m NAVD, SEI 55-3871, and PEI 24.3-163.3.
synthesis.well_established: Storm waves and elevated water levels erode dune faces and redistribute sediment toward the beach and nearshore; whether impact remains collision and scarping or progresses to overwash and inundation depends jointly on forcing intensity and pre-storm berm–dune geometry.

claims.text: Among the seven tested predictors, Peak Erosion Intensity was the most important predictor of storm-induced dune damage.
claims.regime: Compiled New Jersey beach-profile observations for eighteen storms, using the seven reported predictors and PEI range 24.3-163.3.

claims.text: PEI below 69 generally identified Minor dune damage, whereas PEI above 102 generally identified Moderate or Major damage in the study data.
claims.regime: New Jersey training observations; damage defined by dune-volume loss (<5% Minor, 5-40% Moderate, >40% Major); high-PEI branch based on only 33 observations.

claims.text: For intermediate storm intensity, beach-dune morphology was needed in addition to PEI to distinguish dune-damage outcomes.
claims.regime: New Jersey observations and the reported morphology ranges; derived from the fitted tree and ensemble, not a universal physical threshold.

claims.text: Larger berm volume was associated with lower percent dune loss under comparable storm intensities in the compiled observations.
claims.regime: New Jersey profile/storm data, particularly PEI 69-82; association within the fitted data does not alone establish universal causality.

claims.text: Under the modeled storm-surge process, eroded dune sand was transported offshore and deposited on the beach as the profile adjusted to the elevated water level.
claims.regime: Sandy beach-dune profiles subjected to the study's storm-surge and random-wave conditions.

claims.text: Pre- and post-Sandy LiDAR across more than 800 profiles found dune faces steepened 43% without becoming vertical and only half the dune toes followed the assumed foreshore-slope trajectory, challenging common erosion-model assumptions.
claims.regime: Testing model parameters for wave‐induced dune erosion using observations from Hurricane Sandy

claims.text: Nine months of hourly Greenwich Dunes monitoring show that moderate 8-12 m/s winds delivered much of the foredune sediment, whereas only 1 of 15 large wind events produced large deposition and the strongest storms instead caused wave scarping; wind angle, fetch, moisture and snow/ice governed event effectiveness.
claims.regime: Greenwich Dunes, Prince Edward Island, across nine months of wind, beach and seasonal conditions.

claims.text: A two-step meso-scale dune-supply model improved nine-month sediment-input predictions by first filtering winds that fail supply thresholds and then reducing potential transport for fetch and moisture; predictions matched measured deposition order of magnitude while coarse surveys missed erosion between events.
claims.regime: Greenwich Dunes, Prince Edward Island, with hourly wind and supply controls over nine months.

claims.text: Across 861 Hurricane Sandy lidar profiles, dune faces steepened by 43% on average but never became vertical, half of dune toes retreated downward opposite the commonly assumed foreshore-slope trajectory, and dunes lost 41% of their volume on average, demonstrating that standard wave-impact erosion assumptions can overestimate dune stability.
claims.regime: Undeveloped sandy dunes in Maryland, New Jersey, and New York exposed to Hurricane Sandy collision-regime forcing, evaluated with pre/post-storm airborne lidar and a COAWST-derived total-water-level hindcast.

equations.name: Dune volume loss percentage
equations.regime: Profile-based storm impact classification used in this study; Minor <5%, Moderate 5-40%, Major >40% loss.
equations.variables: {"A_pre": "pre-storm cross-sectional area within the pre-storm dune footprint", "A_post": "post-storm cross-sectional area within the pre-storm dune footprint"}

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Transferable controls include relative grain size, relative fill width and length, profile-scale and equilibrium-shape parameters, wave-energy disequilibrium, relative notch position within the active swash zone, and normalized crest rise under sea-level change.
synthesis.disagreements: Multi-year subaerial persistence in southern California and no net width gain after decades at Nice are conditional outcomes, not a universal contradiction: sediment size, shoreface steepness, canyon proximity, wave exposure, monitoring metric, and boundary flux differ. Likewise, statistical model fit does not establish physically credible lifecycle prediction.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: The screened evidence spans four southern California fills monitored for 4-16 years, an 1100 m Florida fill through its first calm and hurricane periods, thirty years at Nice, two years of daily video in Barcelona, nine UAS surveys at Deal, and volume histories at two South Carolina barrier beaches.
synthesis.governing_physics: Constructed shoreline gradients drive alongshore diffusion even in calm conditions, wave-energy disequilibrium drives cross-shore profile response, storms accelerate redistribution, and steep shorefaces, canyons, inlets, and groins create sinks or transfers that a local control volume may register as loss.
synthesis.limitations: Evidence remains site-limited, monitoring often misses subaqueous or cross-boundary flux, storms confound early equilibration, ecological and groundwater impacts are sparse, and reduced models omit inlet, barrier, and structure interactions. Success metrics based only on dry-beach width can therefore be misleading.
synthesis.major_equations: Common reduced descriptions include the Dean equilibrium profile h=A x^(2/3), dynamic shoreline relaxation proportional to wave-energy disequilibrium, one-line shoreline diffusion, empirical linear or exponential volume-loss curves, and sediment control-volume balances.
synthesis.numerical_models: One-parameter dynamic-equilibrium models can match more parameterized shoreline models at a calibrated site, while one-line volume models can retain more credible parameters than statistically adequate empirical decay curves; neither result removes the need to represent inlets, structures, or open sediment boundaries where relevant.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities are prospective multi-site validation, full littoral-cell sediment budgets, predictive grain-size and profile design, coupled inlet and structure effects, ecological and groundwater thresholds, adaptive monitoring triggers, and lifecycle optimization under uncertain storms and sea-level rise.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent advances use parsimonious dynamic-equilibrium prediction, multi-year regional sediment accounting, UAS-SfM diagnosis of nourishment-structure interaction, and scenario-based crest and volume design under sea-level rise.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Within this screened branch, the 2006 Upham field study establishes simultaneous immediate planform and profile adjustment, while the 2011 Nice record provides a rare multi-decadal test of nourishment efficiency.
synthesis.typical_methods: Robust evaluations combine repeated topographic and bathymetric profiles, shoreline or daily video observations, wave records, UAS-SfM elevation differencing, placed-volume histories, open-boundary sediment budgets, and calibration-validation that checks parameter physics as well as fit.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Directly tested ranges include 500-1500 m by about 50 m southern California pads integrated to 8 m depth, an 1100 m Florida project with 45 calm days before strong storms, 558,000 m3 placed along 4.5 km at Nice, two years of daily video at Nova Icaria, nine surveys of eight groins including three notches, and 1-5 m sea-level-rise scenarios at four gravel defenses.
synthesis.well_established: Nourishment creates a deliberately nonequilibrium sediment body that begins adjusting cross-shore and alongshore immediately; persistence, protection, and adverse effects depend on grain size, constructed geometry, waves, shoreface and inlet connectivity, structures, and the boundaries used for accounting.

claims.text: At four southern California nourishments, coarse subaerial pads persisted for years but redistributed across open control-volume boundaries; Torrey Pines lost about 300,000 m3 over 16 years, and Imperial Beach drift contributed to the 2016 Tijuana River mouth closure.
claims.regime: The four surveyed southern California fills; natural variability and open boundaries limit attribution.

claims.text: At the 1100 m Upham Beach project, planform adjustment began during calm conditions immediately after construction, and a subsequent strong storm caused a substantial portion of total profile equilibration, demonstrating simultaneous longshore and cross-shore adjustment.
claims.regime: Low-energy west Florida nourishment with strong constructed-width gradients and hurricane-influenced early months.

claims.text: At Nice's 4.5 km gravel beach, 558,000 m3 placed from 1976-2005 produced no significant net width increase across 50 transects and 87 surveys, implying chronic offshore loss promoted by the steep shoreface and seasonal profile flattening.
claims.regime: Steep reflective, almost tideless gravel beach beside narrow shoreface and canyon heads; offshore pathways were inferred.

claims.text: At Deal, New Jersey, three identically notched groins stabilized adjacent shoreline but only the notch remaining near the seaward swash-zone edge promoted bidirectional bypassing; notches buried by post-nourishment widening behaved like traditional groins.
claims.regime: The monitored eight-groin field under northward net transport and evolving 2016 nourishment morphology.

claims.text: At Folly Beach and Hunting Island, four nourishment-loss models all fit observed volumes statistically, but only the wave-linked One-Line model retained physically credible parameters at both sites; inlet and barrier-island processes remained unresolved.
claims.regime: Two South Carolina barrier-beach projects with measured volume time series and wave information.

claims.text: Nineteen Dutch shoreface nourishments supplied sediment landward for years, while energetic breaking waves and cross-shore transport dominated initial nourishment erosion.
claims.regime: Observations and Modelling of Shoreface Nourishment Behaviour

claims.text: Fine sediment in a beach nourishment briefly elevated local surf-zone fecal indicator bacteria, followed by rapid inactivation and wave-current dispersal.
claims.regime: Beach Nourishment Impacts on Bacteriological Water Quality and Phytoplankton Bloom Dynamics

claims.text: Monitoring of the 2014 Dunkirk nourishment shows rapid initial adjustment and predominantly eastward wave-driven redistribution rather than simple loss, benefiting the downdrift recreational beach while erosion weakened during the second year.
claims.regime: Dredged-sand nourishment fronting the Digue des Allies at Dunkirk on a tide-dominated northern French coast.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: The foundational reviewed scaling parameter is relative fall velocity H/(Tw), combining wave height, period, and sediment settling velocity. Correlation, explained skill, and return probability are statistical rather than universal physical similarity parameters and must retain their site/sample definition.
synthesis.disagreements: Water level appears minor in the 2024 wave-dominated Narrabeen event regression, whereas storm-surge elevation is fundamental to Vellinga's dune-attack experiments. This is a regime difference, not evidence that water level is generally unimportant. Likewise, positive energy-erosion relations at exposed sectors coexist with deposition at sheltered or sediment-supplied Iztuzu sectors.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Reviewed datasets include random-wave Delta Flume mobile-bed tests up to Hs=2 m, 276 monitored Narrabeen-Collaroy storms, 48 years of five Narrabeen profiles plus six high-resolution storm responses, and 18 Iztuzu shorelines at 819 transects paired with a modeled 2013-2022 storm record.
synthesis.governing_physics: Integrated wave energy and duration organize storm demand, while direction controls longshore-current forcing and antecedent width/profile controls available sediment and exposure. Local refraction, wave focusing, rips, river input, and reefs can amplify erosion or produce adjacent deposition.
synthesis.limitations: The evidence is dominated by Dutch, Narrabeen, and Iztuzu cases. Sparse profiles can miss 3D hotspots, sparse images weaken correlation inference, abstract-only model records hide calibration ranges, and site-trained regressions may not extrapolate to surge-dominated, different-sediment, or differently oriented coasts.
synthesis.major_equations: Reviewed formulations range from Vellinga's fall-velocity similitude H/(Tw), through Leont'yev's zone-dependent q=qW+qR transport decomposition, to storm indices SPI=Hs^2 t and TSWE=integral(Pw dt), shoreline rates NSM/EPR/LRR, and empirical multilinear or extreme-value response models.
synthesis.numerical_models: The reviewed model spectrum spans Vellinga's equilibrium-profile safety method, Leont'yev's cross-shore qW/qR process decomposition, site-specific multilinear forecasting, nested SWAN diagnostics, DSAS shoreline statistics, and empirical extreme-value/amplification curves; these models answer different temporal and spatial questions.
synthesis.open_questions: Major needs are transferable event models with uncertainty, simultaneous waves-water levels-currents-sediment observations, prediction of localized 3D amplification, separation of storm clusters from single events, field validation at data-poor coasts, and recovery-aware forecasting after erosion.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent advances combine high-frequency morphology with fast site-specific forecasting, direction-resolved satellite/model attribution, and full-beach 3D amplification analysis that exposes erosion maxima missed by conventional sparse transects.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Vellinga (1982) is the foundational reviewed journal study in this slice, establishing large-scale mobile-bed storm-dune experiments and fall-velocity similitude for Dutch dune safety assessment.
synthesis.typical_methods: Current evidence combines mobile-bed flumes, process-based cross-shore transport models, high-frequency video or profile monitoring, satellite/DSAS shoreline analysis, spectral wave downscaling, regression forecasting, extreme-value analysis, and event-scale 3D morphology mapping.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Quantitative skill is currently site-bound: the 2024 Narrabeen multilinear forecast reports RMSE 3.7-6.4 m over 276 events; the 2026 Narrabeen analysis spans 48 years but only six high-resolution events; Iztuzu uses 18 images over ten years and explicitly reports broad confidence intervals; Vellinga's large-scale waves reached Hs=2 m.
synthesis.well_established: Storm beach response is a redistribution problem governed jointly by hydrodynamic forcing and antecedent/local morphology: elevated waves erode the subaerial beach or dune and move sediment, but the magnitude and even sign of local shoreline change vary with exposure, orientation, reefs, currents, and sediment supply.

claims.text: At Iztuzu Zones III-V, southern-storm duration, storm power index, and total storm wave energy correlated above 0.8 with end-point shoreline-change rate and above 0.7 with linear-regression rate.
claims.regime: Five-zone Iztuzu analysis over 2013-2022 using 18 manually digitized images and modeled storms; many 95% confidence intervals were wide because sample size was small.

claims.text: Storms from the southern sector were more strongly associated with erosion of Iztuzu's southwest-facing central zones than storms from the south-southwest sector.
claims.regime: Iztuzu Zones II-IV, their reported orientations, modeled storm directions, and 2013-2022 shoreline record; sediment transport was inferred rather than measured.

claims.text: A stronger storm metric did not imply erosion everywhere at Iztuzu: reef- and river-outlet-influenced sectors showed negative correlations consistent with local wave-energy sheltering or sediment deposition.
claims.regime: Specific northern and reef-adjacent Iztuzu transects; causal sediment supply and transport were proposed but not directly observed.

claims.text: The Iztuzu near-annual correlations often lacked significance at the 95% level because only a small number of high-resolution image intervals were available.
claims.regime: This study's 18-image, ten-year correlation design; absence of significance does not establish absence of storm influence.

claims.text: Vellinga's large-scale Delta Flume tests used random waves up to 2 m significant height and supported mobile-bed similitude based on the dimensionless fall-velocity parameter H/(T w).
claims.regime: The paper's sandy mobile-bed 2D/3D program and Delta Flume storm-surge tests; transfer outside the tested sediment and profile regimes is not established here.

claims.text: Across 276 Narrabeen-Collaroy storm events, cumulative storm wave energy was the dominant erosion predictor, followed by pre-storm beach width and wave direction; water level contributed only weakly at this site.
claims.regime: Wave-dominated Narrabeen-Collaroy Beach and the observed 276-event predictor domain; the ranking is not universal for surge-dominated coasts.

claims.text: During the 2016 Narrabeen-Collaroy storm, the measured local maximum erosion reached 235 m3/m above mean sea level and 58.3 m of shoreline retreat.
claims.regime: June 2016 event and the paper's above-MSL volume/shoreline definitions at Narrabeen-Collaroy.

claims.text: Localized reef-related wave focusing and a migrating rip current produced erosion hotspots that were not represented by the five fixed historical profile locations.
claims.regime: The six high-resolution Narrabeen-Collaroy storm datasets and site-specific reef/rip morphology.

claims.text: After the 2013/14 winter, 38 southwest England beaches showed mechanism-dependent recovery: more than 200 m³/m offshore loss at exposed sand beaches, overwash loss at gravel barriers, and rotation at obliquely forced sites.

climate.label: Sea-level rise and climate adaptation
climate.description: Long-term change and adaptation of coasts.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Useful controls include sea-level increment relative to local extreme-level scale, flood-frequency amplification, exposed-population fraction, vulnerability indices normalized to 0–1, accommodation-space ratio, defense freeboard relative to projected total water level and adaptation benefit-cost or avoided-loss ratios.
synthesis.disagreements: Magnitude and timing differ across emissions, ice-sheet, vertical-motion, storm, wave, demographic and adaptation assumptions. Static exposure can seriously understate dynamic flooding, while unconstrained global assessments can overstate realized impacts if protection or migration is ignored.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Reviewed evidence includes global coastal populations and elevation models, probabilistic extreme-level projections, national US 30 m compound-flood maps, Mediterranean heritage sites, California dynamic exposure, Bangladesh cyclone records, Australian blue-carbon inventories and Grenada reef and shoreline observations.
synthesis.governing_physics: Ocean thermal expansion and land-ice loss raise mean sea level; regional circulation, gravity, vertical land motion and tides alter local change. Storms, waves, runoff, erosion, sediment accretion, wetland migration and reef condition govern how that baseline becomes flooding or shoreline impact.
synthesis.limitations: Elevation bias, incomplete hazard dependence, coarse coastal grids, uncertain ice response, socioeconomic pathways, autonomous adaptation, protection failure, ecosystem feedbacks and distributional inequity limit inference. Global rankings identify hotspots but do not replace local design analysis.
synthesis.major_equations: Assessment combines sea-level projections with extreme-value or joint-probability distributions, dynamic inundation and erosion models, exposure overlays and risk as a function of hazard, exposure and vulnerability. Carbon accounts quantify stored stock and avoided emissions; adaptation comparisons modify hazards, assets or response capacity.
synthesis.numerical_models: Models range from probabilistic sea-level and extreme-value ensembles to global or local hydrodynamic flooding, GIS exposure and vulnerability overlays, wetland accommodation models, shoreline equilibrium or erosion models and coupled demographic scenarios. Static bathtub mapping omits important dynamic pathways.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities include local vertical-motion integration, joint compound extremes, dynamic morphology, cascading infrastructure failure, ecosystem adaptation limits, migration and development feedbacks, equitable financing, adaptation effectiveness and transparent deep-uncertainty decisions.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent advances correct coastal elevation with machine learning, couple waves, surge, tides, rainfall and rivers, represent erosion and cliff retreat dynamically, quantify blue carbon and wetland accommodation, and compare flexible adaptation pathways with explicit equity and ecosystem services.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Detection and attribution established climate-driven sea-level rise; scenario and extreme-value studies translated it into changing flood frequency, and integrated vulnerability frameworks joined physical exposure with social capacity. Dynamic and nature-based approaches subsequently broadened assessment beyond static inundation.
synthesis.typical_methods: Workflows combine tide gauges, altimetry, elevation and socioeconomic data with emissions and sea-level scenarios, tide-surge-wave or compound-flood models, dynamic shoreline response, ecosystem and carbon inventories, vulnerability indices and participatory adaptation assessment. Uncertainty should be propagated across all layers.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Reported evidence spans site, city, national and global scales and scenarios through 2100. Quantitative values are conditional on emissions, elevation, population, protection and process assumptions; the US compound model reports map-validation CSI of 0.69–0.82, not universal predictive skill.
synthesis.well_established: Climate-driven mean sea-level rise shifts the baseline on which tides, waves, surge and river or rainfall flooding act. Small mean changes can strongly amplify threshold exceedance, while exposure, vulnerability, geomorphic response, ecosystems and adaptation determine consequences.

claims.text: Coastal climate assessment must connect observed and projected sea-level rise and its causes to physical and societal impacts and feasible response options.
claims.regime: Cross-cutting global and Japanese sea-level-rise assessment.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Useful controls include sea-level rise relative to freeboard, benefit-cost ratio, residual-risk fraction, adaptation lifetime relative to hazard-change timescale, lead-time-to-threshold ratio, avoided-loss fraction, robustness across scenarios and ecological recovery relative to disturbance interval.
synthesis.disagreements: Protection can reduce near-term risk but induce lock-in and residual catastrophe; retreat avoids exposure but faces social and political barriers. Nature-based measures add co-benefits and adaptability yet have uncertain extreme-event and long-term performance; hybrid portfolios often manage these tradeoffs.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Reviewed evidence includes a global coastal-adaptation literature synthesis, Bay County building-level Monte Carlo damage and dynamic-programming analysis under four sea-level projections, and a review of living-shoreline utility under changing climatic conditions.
synthesis.governing_physics: Relative sea-level rise raises baseline water levels and shifts wave, surge, erosion, groundwater and drainage hazards; compound events and geomorphic or ecosystem response determine local exposure, while intervention performance depends on deterioration, recovery and sediment or ecological feedbacks.
synthesis.limitations: Deep climate uncertainty, incomplete compound hazards, uncertain damage and behavior, discounting, omitted distributional effects, institutional fragmentation, funding and maintenance gaps, path dependence and ecological nonstationarity can dominate apparently precise rankings.
synthesis.major_equations: Decision analysis combines probabilistic hazard and damage functions, discounted life-cycle cost and benefit, dynamic programming or real-options logic, and robustness across scenarios. Adaptive pathways encode actions, thresholds, lead times and transfer points when objectives are no longer met.
synthesis.numerical_models: The set includes scenario-based hazard and pathway frameworks, building-level Monte Carlo damage simulation and dynamic programming. Nature-based evidence emphasizes forward-looking performance, maintenance and adaptive intervention rather than a single fixed design model.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities include equitable pathway design, endogenous development and migration, compound hazard and cascading infrastructure risk, finance and governance experiments, monitoring thresholds, adaptation effectiveness audits and comparable long-term evidence for hybrid and nature-based portfolios.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent advances integrate high-resolution exposure, probabilistic projections, adaptation tipping points, building-level digital twins, participatory pathway tools, natural-capital accounting, climate services and evaluation of implementation, maintenance and distributional outcomes.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Protect–accommodate–retreat frameworks organized response options; robust decision making, real options and dynamic adaptive policy pathways shifted planning from fixed forecasts toward sequences that remain adjustable under uncertainty.
synthesis.typical_methods: Workflows co-produce objectives, map compound hazards and vulnerability, evaluate portfolios under multiple projections, include capital and maintenance costs and distributional impacts, identify thresholds and lead times, stress-test pathways, monitor indicators and pre-authorize adjustment or retreat options.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Bay County findings apply to its building inventory and four projections; global and living-shoreline reviews support principles rather than universal local benefit-cost rankings. Transfer requires local hazards, institutions, ecosystems, costs and stakeholder objectives.
synthesis.well_established: Coastal adaptation is a continuing risk-management process rather than a one-time project; effective strategies combine protection, accommodation, ecosystem measures and retreat with monitoring, maintenance, finance, governance and triggers for adjustment as hazards and information change.

claims.text: A 2025 review concludes that durable living-shoreline performance under climate change requires forward-looking design, coordinated holistic planning, and maintenance and adaptive interventions, because present-day success does not establish resistance or recovery under future extremes.
claims.regime: Conceptual guidance across nature-based and hybrid shoreline types; no universal quantitative threshold is claimed.

claims.text: A global coastal-adaptation review concludes that long-term plans must combine locally relevant sea-level projections with compound hazards, agreed action thresholds, stakeholder priorities, finance, and maintenance capacity; construction alone does not establish durable adaptation.
claims.regime: Strategic planning across diverse coasts; local design values require site-specific analysis.

claims.text: Australian vegetated coastal ecosystems store an estimated 70–185 Tg C above ground and 1,055–1,540 Tg C in the upper metre of soil; ongoing losses could emit 2.1–3.1 Tg CO2-e per year.
claims.regime: Australian vegetated coastal ecosystems as global hotspots for climate change mitigation

claims.text: Projected global coastal-wetland loss by 2100 ranges from 0 to 30% without added accommodation space; resilience is governed primarily by space for landward migration, which infrastructure can constrain and adaptation can restore.
claims.regime: Future response of global coastal wetlands to sea-level rise

claims.text: Coastal climate-risk practice should replace stationary, single-hazard assumptions with multidimensional probabilistic frameworks that represent changing hazards, exposure, vulnerability, and uncertainty, and connect risk assessment to flexible, monitoring-supported adaptation pathways.
claims.regime: Coastal flood, erosion, infrastructure, ecosystem, and socioeconomic risks under long-term climate change, including compound drivers and deep uncertainty beyond 2050.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Useful controls include relative sea-level rise to freeboard, relative wave height and steepness, exceedance probability, return-period ratio, groundwater depth normalized by relief, rainfall-to-drainage-capacity ratio, recession normalized by active-profile width, benefit-cost ratio and fractional avoided loss.
synthesis.disagreements: The literature differs less on whether impacts grow than on representation and response: static area accounting versus ecological function, autonomous optimization versus governance feasibility, equilibrium shoreline rules versus process-rich morphology, and generic technical planning versus sovereign community-grounded adaptation.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: This branch is dominated by field-derived and scenario datasets rather than laboratory experiments: the 2007 Walcott flood, Oakland topography/groundwater/rainfall data, 13 Indian port-adjacent beach segments, UK habitat-compensation records, Chinese coastal economic/geographic inputs and reviewed Australian and Tribal adaptation evidence.
synthesis.governing_physics: Rising mean water level reduces structure freeboard, shifts groundwater upward, increases boundary head on drainage, exposes shorelines to profile adjustment and intensifies coastal squeeze where landward habitat migration is blocked. Coincident tide, waves, rainfall and groundwater make impacts nonlinear and spatially heterogeneous.
synthesis.limitations: Recurring limitations are climate and socioeconomic scenario uncertainty, static exposure, omitted compound drivers, simplified groundwater or morphology, empirical overtopping, discounting and valuation choices, incomplete monitoring, publication bias, qualitative causal chains and transfer of governance conclusions across communities.
synthesis.major_equations: Core formulations include joint extreme-value probability for waves and water levels, overtopping discharge as a nonlinear function of relative freeboard, two-dimensional shallow-water continuity and momentum, Bruun-rule equilibrium shoreline translation, and discounted impact-adaptation objective functions that combine damage and intervention cost.
synthesis.numerical_models: Extracted models include an integrated offshore-to-overtopping chain using EurOtop, HEC-RAS 5.0.7 2D, GCM ensembles coupled to Bruun-rule/GIS translation, and pyCIAM. Conceptual and review frameworks cover indirect impacts, WAMPUM, habitat-compensation robustness and institutional barriers.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities include coupled groundwater-surface-coastal validation, dynamic morphology and habitat succession, correlated extremes, adaptation tipping points, distributional and indirect losses, Indigenous data sovereignty, monitoring of compensation performance, governance implementation and transparent propagation of deep uncertainty.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent work couples groundwater emergence with urban rainfall flooding, evaluates flexible adaptation portfolios at national scale, tests ecological compensation against robustness principles, centers Tribal sovereignty and water security, and systematically diagnoses institutional barriers rather than treating adaptation as an unconstrained model choice.
synthesis.seminal_papers: The 2012 Walcott analysis demonstrated how modest freeboard loss can radically change overtopping recurrence, while the UK indirect-impact study broadened coastal assessment beyond direct local damage. Together they frame physical amplification and cross-border propagation.
synthesis.typical_methods: Methods span climate-model ensembles, downscaling, joint probability and extreme-value analysis, HEC-RAS 2D inundation, GIS exposure mapping, equilibrium-profile rules, integrated assessment and optimization, systematic reviews, policy robustness assessment and Indigenous community-centered adaptation frameworks.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Quantitative findings are bounded to their sources: Walcott 0.35–1 m SLR cases; Oakland 1 m SLR, 1.94 m high tide and 2-year rainfall; Indian RCP4.5/RCP8.5 projections through 2100; and pyCIAM strategies along China's segmented coast. These ranges are scenarios, not universal thresholds.
synthesis.well_established: Coastal climate impacts arise through interacting changes in mean sea level, extremes, waves, rainfall and groundwater, then propagate through shoreline position, overtopping, drainage, habitats, assets, economies, water security and institutions. Adaptation materially changes outcomes but is itself constrained by governance and local context.
