synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Useful controls include exceedance probability, relative sea-level change normalized by freeboard or crest height, crest-rise amplification, relative wave height and runup, discount and maintenance fractions, and ensemble weights or scenario probabilities.
synthesis.disagreements: Differences among design outcomes often reflect scenario choice, localization, impact model, asset lifetime, discounting, and adaptation objective rather than disagreement about whether sea level is rising. A deterministic high scenario can stress-test feasibility but is not itself a probabilistic forecast.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: The screened engineering evidence uses Adelaide annual maxima, four southeast England beach profiles and a 2014 validation storm, a Bay County building and flood inventory, and more than three decades of multi-mission altimetry; these datasets support different links in the projection-to-decision chain.
synthesis.governing_physics: Thermal expansion and land-ice loss drive global mean rise, while ocean circulation, gravitational fingerprints, tides, vertical land motion, waves, surge, sediment response, and groundwater processes shape local relative level and impact.
synthesis.limitations: The branch lacks a full primary projection ensemble and ice-sheet synthesis. Local vertical land motion, changing surge and wave climatology, datum consistency, compound flooding, sediment supply, model structural error, socioeconomic change, and deep uncertainty remain incompletely propagated into most engineering decisions.
synthesis.major_equations: Engineering translations include products of time-varying annual-maximum distributions, scenario crest-rise ratios, runup and barrier-stability relations, depth-damage functions, Monte Carlo expectation, and Bellman recursion for sequential adaptation.
synthesis.numerical_models: Models include multi-distribution nonstationary extremes, the Shingle Beach Run-up Tool, Barrier Inertia Model, stochastic depth-damage simulation, and dynamic adaptation optimization; they are consequence translators rather than interchangeable sea-level projection generators.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities include traceable global-to-local probabilistic workflows, nonstationary extremes beyond simple location shifts, compound-hazard projections, observational signposts for adaptive pathways, equitable financing, sediment-aware defense adaptation, and validation of decisions as sea level and exposure evolve.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent engineering work couples multiple SLR trajectories to stochastic damages and revisable actions, while coastal design studies resolve how local wave transformation and morphology can amplify physical requirements beyond the imposed mean rise.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Within this screened slice, the 1990 paper is seminal for replacing stationary return-period logic with time-varying annual distributions, providing an early direct bridge from projected mean rise to future design extremes.
synthesis.typical_methods: Methods span tide gauges and satellite altimetry, process-based or scenario projections, localization with land motion, nonstationary extreme-value analysis, profile and runup models, GIS exposure inventories, Monte Carlo damage simulation, cost-benefit optimization, and adaptive-pathway planning.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Reported applications include four southeast England beaches under 1-5 m scenarios with crest rise up to 1.26 times SLR, a 200-year joint wave-water-level standard, four SLR trajectories in Bay County, and a location-shift extreme model demonstrated for Adelaide; none constitutes a universal design factor.
synthesis.well_established: Coastal engineering must treat mean sea level as nonstationary over asset lifetimes. Global trajectories require localization for land motion and regional ocean effects, then combination with tides, surge, waves, morphology, exposure, and vulnerability before they become design criteria.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Useful normalized controls include subsidence-to-eustatic-rate ratio, vertical-motion uncertainty relative to trend, record duration relative to climate oscillations, compaction relative to sediment thickness and projected subsidence relative to defense freeboard.
synthesis.disagreements: Linear trends can obscure changing extraction, postseismic transients and compaction, while short records can misidentify climate variability as acceleration. Different geodetic products and reference frames can yield conflicting vertical-motion estimates.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Reviewed evidence covers Galveston Pier 21 since 1909, five long-record Oceania gauges plus Tuvalu and Adelaide cases, incomplete Chinese gauge records, and 50 Southeast Asian sites with overlapping 1993–2020 tide-gauge and altimetry observations.
synthesis.governing_physics: Coastal land moves through groundwater and hydrocarbon withdrawal, sediment compaction, loading, tectonic and postseismic deformation, glacial isostatic adjustment and shallow infrastructure settlement, while steric and mass changes move the sea surface.
synthesis.limitations: Sparse colocated GNSS, datum changes, gauge relocation, altimetry coastal contamination, InSAR reference choices, nonlinear motion, short records and uncertain causal attribution limit projections; abstract-level values also require full-text methodological audit.
synthesis.major_equations: With upward-positive land motion, relative sea-level rate is approximately absolute sea-level rate minus vertical land-motion rate; time-varying analyses add acceleration, periodic variability, datum offsets and correlated error terms.
synthesis.numerical_models: Methods range from segmented and nonlinear tide-gauge regressions to differencing relative tide-gauge and absolute altimetry signals; hydromechanical aquifer or sediment-compaction models can test causal attribution but are not represented directly in this reviewed set.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities include forecasting nonlinear subsidence under changing water management, separating shallow from deep motion, reconciling geodetic frames, propagating local motion into probabilistic extremes and sustaining dense observations in rapidly subsiding deltas and cities.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent work fuses tide gauges, GNSS, altimetry and InSAR, resolves nonlinear site histories, maps aquifer and sediment compaction, and incorporates time-varying vertical motion into local sea-level and flood-risk projections.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Tide-gauge geodesy established that relative records combine ocean and crustal motion; leveling and later continuous GNSS enabled correction, while satellite altimetry and InSAR expanded regional separation and spatial mapping.
synthesis.typical_methods: Studies combine long tide-gauge records with colocated GNSS, satellite altimetry or InSAR, homogenize datum and offsets, estimate nonlinear trends and accelerations, compare independent geodetic products and attribute mechanisms using extraction, geology and earthquake histories.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Evidence spans individual gauges and regional networks over multi-decadal periods. Rates are site- and interval-specific and should not be transferred without colocated vertical-motion observations and consistent reference frames.
synthesis.well_established: Relative sea-level change combines ocean-surface change with vertical land motion; subsidence can equal or exceed the climatic ocean component and therefore must be estimated locally.

design.label: Coastal engineering design
design.description: Design criteria, performance, and lifecycle decisions.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Important controls include reliability index, utilization and safety factors, return-period and exceedance probability, damage and serviceability indices, relative freeboard, wave steepness and surf similarity, armor stability numbers, corrosion or fatigue life ratios, redundancy, recovery time and benefit-cost ratios.
synthesis.disagreements: Deterministic factors and probabilistic reliability encode uncertainty differently; least first cost can conflict with lifecycle reliability and environmental benefit; hard protection can reduce one failure mode while shifting erosion or ecological impacts; robust near-term actions may differ from expected-value optima.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Evidence comes from material and component tests, hydraulic model tests, prototype storm and damage records, long-term defence and structure monitoring, inspection and maintenance histories, failure databases, environmental performance, and infrastructure risk inventories.
synthesis.governing_physics: Design actions arise from waves, currents, tides, surge, overtopping, flooding, erosion and geotechnical change; resistance evolves through structural response, soil interaction, fatigue, corrosion, wear, settlement, ecological succession and cumulative damage.
synthesis.limitations: Joint hazard tails, deterioration, hidden defects, failure dependence, construction quality, maintenance behavior, ecosystem trajectories, indirect losses and future climate remain weakly observed; standards may lag nonstationarity and institutional responsibilities can fragment system performance.
synthesis.major_equations: Core formulations include action–resistance limit states, partial-factor or reliability equations, joint-probability load combinations, hydraulic and structural response relations, deterioration and condition-transition models, lifecycle cost or utility, benefit-cost and risk integrals, and adaptation decision rules.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Controls include reliability index, return-period-to-design-life ratio, freeboard relative to wave/runup scale, demand-to-capacity ratio, partial safety factors, crest deficit, attenuation or damage threshold and layout-uniformity parameters such as Sr.
synthesis.disagreements: Stationary return periods are familiar but can misstate future magnitude under changing baselines. Prescriptive geometry is auditable but may not capture system response, while performance-based criteria are flexible yet depend on models, uncertainty and validation.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Reviewed evidence includes changing annual sea-level extreme distributions, airborne-LiDAR profiles of federal levees in south Louisiana and four flexible-vegetation layouts tested for spatial wave-attenuation uniformity.
synthesis.governing_physics: Waves, water levels, currents, erosion and material or ecosystem response combine nonlinearly, while sea-level rise shifts baseline hazards and deterioration changes capacity. Spatial nonuniformity and weak points can govern failure even when average performance is acceptable.
synthesis.limitations: Hazard nonstationarity, dependence, model and survey error, undocumented weak points, construction tolerance, deterioration, maintenance, climate scenario spread and unmodeled failure modes can undermine nominal compliance. Evidence is heterogeneous and sparse for cross-system transfer.
synthesis.major_equations: Criteria use extreme-value quantiles, load and resistance factors, reliability or exceedance probability, freeboard and crest checks and response functions for overtopping, stability or attenuation. Under nonstationarity, annual distributions shift through time and lifecycle failure integrates yearly exceedance.
synthesis.numerical_models: The set includes a multi-distributional nonstationary extreme-value model, geospatial crest-compliance analysis and a layout-response criterion for vegetation attenuation. Direct intermediate-depth design-wave selection remains pending full-text review.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities include joint nonstationary hazards, lifecycle and adaptive reliability targets, system-versus-component criteria, nature-based durability, cascading failure, equity and consequence classes, digital compliance monitoring and transparent treatment of deep uncertainty.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent advances combine nonstationary extremes, Bayesian joint hazards, lidar and digital twins for as-built compliance, real-time condition monitoring, probabilistic fragility and adaptive criteria that trigger staged upgrades as observations and projections change.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Return-period design and factor-of-safety methods established prescriptive criteria; reliability-based design introduced probabilistic load–resistance balance, followed by performance-based, lifecycle and adaptive approaches under nonstationary climate.
synthesis.typical_methods: Workflows define limit states and consequences, estimate joint and nonstationary hazards, propagate uncertainty, select target reliability, evaluate alternatives and failure modes, audit constructed geometry with surveys, test response across representative conditions and specify inspection, maintenance and adaptation triggers.
synthesis.validated_ranges: The levee audit found about 5% of evaluated points met the stated 100-year minimum; the vegetation Sr threshold was derived from four tested layouts; the sea-level method addresses shifting annual distributions. None supplies universal criteria across asset classes.
synthesis.well_established: Coastal design criteria translate probabilistic hazards, performance objectives, consequence classes and physical response into verifiable elevations, loads, geometry and maintenance requirements; compliance with a nominal return period alone does not establish lifecycle reliability.

synthesis.governing_physics: Guidance must connect waves, water levels, tsunami, erosion, scour, overtopping, structural resistance, ecological response, human use, deterioration, and adaptation because performance and failure emerge from interacting loads and systems.
synthesis.limitations: Guidance can lag climate, technology, and evidence; transfer across morphology and governance can fail. Sparse extremes, correlated loads, uncertain deterioration, ecological dynamics, maintenance, informal development, and inconsistent indicators constrain standardization.
synthesis.major_equations: Common design frameworks combine joint probability and return levels, limit states and partial factors, runup and overtopping relations, stability and scour formulae, reliability or risk integrals, lifecycle cost, multi-criteria decisions, and adaptive pathways.
synthesis.numerical_models: Guidance-supporting tools include joint-probability extreme-level models, spectral wave and overtopping models, XBeach with multilevel Monte Carlo, performance-indicator frameworks, and multi-hazard risk models.
synthesis.open_questions: Needs include climate-adjusted and adaptive standards, transparent hybrid indicators, multi-hazard sequences, lifecycle reliability, monitored performance, equitable consequences, update triggers, and machine-readable provenance for every recommendation.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent guidance emphasizes portfolios, nature-based and hybrid infrastructure, uncertainty-efficient ensembles, integrated earthquake-tsunami assessment, broader performance indicators, and explicit links between structural and evacuation measures.
synthesis.seminal_papers: The branch rests on probabilistic coastal levels, empirical structure manuals, reliability and limit-state design, risk-based planning, and field-forensic learning; current sources extend these toward NNBF, hybrid, and multi-hazard guidance.
synthesis.typical_methods: Methods synthesize codes, field failures, laboratory and numerical models, expert judgment, probabilistic analysis, consequence assessment, lifecycle and cost-benefit methods, multi-criteria analysis, monitoring, and periodic revision.
synthesis.validated_ranges: This abstract-bounded slice supports no universal coefficient range. Quantitative adjacent evidence includes 40-fold-or-greater MLMC speedups and a 187-study hybrid assessment base; every formula must retain its source-specific validity limits.
synthesis.well_established: Coastal design guidance converts hazard and performance evidence into repeatable decisions. synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Decision controls include inspection interval/service life, transition and failure probabilities, false-positive/false-negative rates, intervention effectiveness, discount rate, cost ratios, reliability index and value-of-information ratios.
synthesis.disagreements: Constant transition rates are convenient but may misstate aging and environment changes; fixed inspection schedules are simple but can waste resources; condition thresholds alone may omit consequences, while cost-only policies may violate reliability or sustainability goals.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: The retained abstract evidence uses long-term condition and maintenance records for generic civil infrastructure, concrete bridges and pavements; direct breakwater, seawall and coastal-bridge records remain lawful-access targets.
synthesis.governing_physics: Assets transition among condition states as loading and exposure accumulate damage. Inspections observe state imperfectly; maintenance changes condition or transition rate; delayed action increases future failure and repair consequences.
synthesis.limitations: Coastal validation is presently weak in the lawful corpus; storm shocks, armor rearrangement, chloride and corrosion, scour, sea-level rise and adaptation are not captured by generic gradual-deterioration models; action-effect data are sparse.
synthesis.major_equations: Core tools include Markov transition matrices, partially observable or sequential decision processes, reliability and hazard functions, Bayesian state updating, discounted/average life-cycle cost, and constrained or multiobjective policy optimization.
synthesis.numerical_models: Models include homogeneous and time-varying Markov chains, continuous two-stage deterioration, partially observed maintenance decisions, data-driven condition curves, life-cycle-cost calculators and optimal preventive-timing frameworks.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities include coastal condition-state standards, event-driven deterioration, spatial dependence, remote inspection error, climate nonstationarity, adaptation flexibility, residual value, embodied carbon, ecological co-benefits and robust decision-making.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent work uses data-calibrated and time-varying deterioration, explicit two-dimensional inspection error, timing-sensitive preventive maintenance, and integrated cost, environmental and reliability objectives.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Markov inspection–maintenance–replacement scheduling established sequential lifecycle decisions; later reliability and partially observable formulations incorporated safety and imperfect information.
synthesis.typical_methods: Methods use periodic condition surveys, deterioration-curve calibration, Markov simulation, inspection-error models, maintenance-action matrices, dynamic or linear programming, reliability constraints, cost–benefit analysis and scenario sensitivity.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Evidence spans component and network decisions, discrete and continuous deterioration, perfect and imperfect inspection, fixed and changing transition rates, preventive and reactive actions, and short inspection intervals through multi-decade horizons.
synthesis.well_established: Lifecycle management links condition inspection, deterioration prediction, safety or reliability targets, maintenance and repair actions, replacement, and discounted whole-life cost rather than treating each decision independently.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Useful controls include demand-to-capacity and reliability indices, annual exceedance probability, relative crest elevation or submergence, response normalized by allowable limit, adaptation increment relative to sea-level rise, lifecycle utilization and expected loss or downtime ratios.
synthesis.disagreements: Prescriptive event-based design is simpler and transparent, whereas response-based probabilistic design better represents nonlinear response and joint uncertainty but requires more data and computation. Nature-based performance also changes biologically and morphologically, challenging fixed resistance assumptions.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: The reviewed evidence includes four southeast England mixed sand–gravel defenses evaluated under 1–5 m sea-level-rise scenarios and a Virginia restored-oyster field experiment comparing two substrates, reef elevation, water level and marsh-edge response.
synthesis.governing_physics: Performance emerges from interaction of waves, water levels, currents, sediment and ecological or structural geometry; changing submergence, depth, exposure, material state and morphology alter loads, attenuation, erosion, overtopping and failure pathways.
synthesis.limitations: The evidence slice is small; objectives and acceptable consequences are context dependent; hazard dependence and nonstationarity are difficult to estimate; model and deterioration uncertainty can dominate tails; ecological functions and cascading systems lack common metrics; and monitoring may not match design variables.
synthesis.major_equations: Core formulations combine hazard exceedance with conditional response and limit-state probability, reliability or fragility functions, lifecycle accumulation and consequence integration; system-specific equations relate crest or reef elevation, water depth, wave transformation, sediment volume and load resistance.
synthesis.numerical_models: Current evidence combines scenario-based beach-defense crest and volume design with observed reef wave-attenuation performance; broader response-based, reliability and consequence models are represented only by title-screened records and are not treated as extracted evidence.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities include multi-hazard joint probability, response-based versus event-based calibration, time-dependent deterioration and climate adaptation, system fragility and cascading failure, nature-based lifecycle reliability, equity-weighted consequences, observation updating and transferable verification datasets.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent advances use environmental contours, stochastic response simulation, time-dependent climate scenarios, lifecycle reliability, adaptive pathways, digital monitoring, coupled consequence assessment and performance objectives for hybrid and nature-based coastal systems.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Reliability-based and limit-state structural design established probabilistic performance checks; coastal work extended them to overtopping, sliding, erosion, flood consequences and lifecycle adaptation, while performance-based earthquake engineering supplied hazard–response–damage–loss integration concepts.
synthesis.typical_methods: Workflows define stakeholders and objectives, identify hazards and failure modes, select measurable performance metrics and thresholds, propagate joint forcing through response models, validate component behavior, quantify epistemic and aleatory uncertainty, compare alternatives and monitor triggers for adaptation.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Direct support is limited to four mixed sand–gravel sites and one restored-oyster setting with two substrates. It does not establish transferable performance targets, fragilities, design lives or reliability levels for caissons, levees, pumps or other systems.
synthesis.well_established: Performance-based coastal design begins with explicit functional objectives and limit states, maps uncertain hazards to response and consequences, and verifies that structural, hydraulic, morphological and operational performance remains acceptable over stated conditions and time horizons.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Controls include Reynolds and Froude numbers, Keulegan–Carpenter number, submergence, frontal-area density, solid-volume fraction, Cauchy or flexibility number, wave transmission and attenuation coefficients, Shields stress, Rouse number, hydroperiod fraction and relative sea-level/accretion rate.
synthesis.disagreements: Aboveground biomass can strongly attenuate waves yet showed no mean winter erosion benefit in one soil-controlled test, indicating that wave attenuation, bed reinforcement and breach erosion are distinct services. Gray–green comparisons also depend on whether success means local velocity reduction, system change or ecological value.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Reviewed datasets include a 410 ha controlled-tide Ramsar restoration monitored for eight years, real-morphology Typha channel profiles, 1:20 marsh–dyke basin tests, winter marsh erosion flumes, Phragmites wave tests, an Oregon Inlet model and in-situ high-velocity marsh erodibility tests.
synthesis.governing_physics: Vegetation drag extracts wave and current momentum; flexibility, buoyancy and reconfiguration change drag. Canopy shear layers and wakes redistribute turbulence and sediment, roots reinforce soil, and tidal inundation controls oxygen, salinity and habitat zonation. Morphodynamic and ecological responses feed back on flow geometry.
synthesis.limitations: Surrogate fidelity, scale effects, plant reconfiguration, seasonal biomass, mortality, patch fragmentation, uncertain drag, limited extreme-event data, evolving topography and mismatch between patch observations and landscape decisions constrain prediction.
synthesis.major_equations: Models couple mass and momentum conservation to vegetation drag, wave-energy dissipation, turbulent diffusivity, sediment advection–diffusion and erosion/deposition, then link inundation or stress to habitat response. Drag and bulk dissipation closures must retain the scale and morphology assumptions of their calibration.
synthesis.numerical_models: Approaches range from cylinder-array drag and diffusivity closures to phase-averaged wave–vegetation, 2D wetland hydrodynamics, inlet circulation and coupled hydro-ecological or morphodynamic models. High-resolution ecological detail is usually limited to small domains; landscape models require aggregation.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities include multiscale upscaling, mixed-species and fragmented canopies, failure thresholds under extremes, long-term adaptation to sea-level rise, sediment–vegetation feedback, standardized attenuation metrics, ecological trade-offs and monitored performance of hybrid defenses.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent work uses real plant morphology, automated eco-hydrological restoration, in-situ failure testing, cross-disciplinary vegetation taxonomies, gray-to-green system comparisons and nested high-resolution/landscape models with more explicit ecological variability.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Foundational canopy-flow and vegetation-drag studies established momentum extraction and wake turbulence; wetland biogeomorphology connected inundation and sediment accretion to habitat persistence. Nature-based engineering later framed these processes as quantifiable protection services.
synthesis.typical_methods: Evidence combines flumes with live or surrogate plants, field velocity/wave/sediment and vegetation surveys, erosion tests, remote sensing, calibrated hydrodynamic or morphodynamic models and before–after restoration monitoring. Comparative designs vary density, height, flexibility, patch geometry and water level.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Findings are regime-specific: artificial Phragmites reduced wave height 6–25% at canopy entry; marsh erodibility tests exceeded 0.5 m/s; the restoration covered 410 ha. These values cannot be transferred across species, season, scale or geometry without similarity and uncertainty checks.
synthesis.well_established: Coastal organisms alter waves, currents, turbulence and sediment transport, while hydroperiod, salinity, bed change and disturbance control organism survival and morphology. These two-way feedbacks create habitat and can provide flood, erosion, water-quality and carbon benefits.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Useful nondimensional measures include relative elevation and inundation, porosity and relative structural dimensions, habitat or vegetation fraction, standardized effect size, classification agreement, survival or recruitment ratios, carbon additionality and permanence factors, and quality-adjusted habitat units normalized by cost.
synthesis.disagreements: Stable or advancing hybrid shorelines and failed decade-scale oyster persistence are conditional, contrasting outcomes rather than a universal verdict on living shorelines. Similar mean fish density in restored and natural sites also does not prove equal fisheries production, because abundance, ontogenetic use, trophic export, and harvest occur at different scales.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Evidence includes a 3.5-year created-wetland colonization series at Mugu Lagoon, four years at three paired hybrid-shoreline sites, six Louisiana oyster reefs revisited after ten years, restored reef and living-shoreline fish observations, 133 Gulf restoration projects, and 42 wetland-fisheries studies with 15 suitable for meta-analysis.
synthesis.governing_physics: Waves, wakes, tides, inundation, sediment moisture and grain size, erosion and accretion, elevation, and structural porosity or complexity set the physical template; colonization, recruitment, trophic subsidy, growth, mortality, dispersal, and succession determine whether that template becomes functioning habitat.
synthesis.limitations: Most evidence covers few sites, taxa, designs, and years; reference sites can be non-equivalent; direct production and trophic subsidy are rare; restoration area is often substituted for quality; physical protection may outlast biological function or vice versa; and carbon and economic valuation require uncertain boundaries and permanence assumptions.
synthesis.major_equations: Common formulations include sediment and habitat-state balances, species-density and occupancy models, dispersal-distance relationships, random-effects standardized mean difference, shoreline-rate comparison, vegetation spectral regressions, carbon accounting, and cost per average annual habitat unit.
synthesis.numerical_models: Models include habitat-suitability and colonization regressions, random-effects meta-analysis and moderator tests, spatial conservation prioritization, vegetation biomass regression, point-cloud and habitat classifiers, blue-carbon accounting, and cost-effectiveness per quality-adjusted habitat outcome.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities are function-specific design rules, seascape connectivity and trophic-subsidy measurement, demographic and fisheries-production outcomes, multi-decadal persistence, adaptive maintenance thresholds, cross-habitat tradeoffs, standardized quality-adjusted metrics, and coupled ecological-hydrodynamic-economic optimization under climate change.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent work shifts from acreage and simple abundance toward life-stage habitat function, decade-scale persistence, remote high-resolution habitat condition, systematic evidence synthesis, spatial recovery prioritization, blue-carbon finance, and quality-adjusted restoration cost.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Within this screened branch, the 2004 Mugu Lagoon study demonstrates that habitat suitability and dispersal jointly limit colonization, while the 2018 boulder synthesis frames structural complexity and stability as explicit ecological-engineering design variables.
synthesis.typical_methods: Robust assessment uses BACI or restored-natural-disturbed comparisons, replicated physical and biological surveys, shoreline and elevation monitoring, sediment and water measurements, abundance plus demographic and diet metrics, remote sensing, long-term maintenance records, meta-analysis, spatial prioritization, and lifecycle cost and service accounting.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Observed regimes include 3.5 years of wetland colonization; four-year shoreline trends from roughly 1 m/y advance to nearly 2 m/y retreat; ten-year oyster density falling below 60 individuals/m2 from early values above 1000/m2; project extents of 0.04-364 ha; and a 42-study review yielding only 15 quantitatively compatible studies.
synthesis.well_established: Building or protecting habitat does not by itself establish ecological function. Outcomes depend on environmental suitability, hydrodynamics and sediment, connectivity and dispersal, structural complexity, target species and life stage, unresolved stressors, restoration age, maintenance, and the reference and metric used to define success.

claims.text: Modeled tidal-wetland restoration shows tidal amplitude, floodgates, and creek microtopography control inundation, velocity, and hydrologic connectivity.
claims.regime: Assessing hydrodynamic effects of ecological restoration scenarios for a tidal-dominated wetland in Liaodong Bay (China)

claims.text: Physical coral-canopy experiments identify interception, settlement, and wake accumulation as microplastic-trapping mechanisms governed by flow and canopy density.
claims.regime: Microplastic trapping efficiency and hydrodynamics in model coral reefs: A physical experimental investigation

claims.text: A northeast Atlantic synthesis identifies threats, evidence gaps, and ecosystem services associated with kelp forests along temperate and polar coasts.
claims.regime: Threats and knowledge gaps for ecosystem services provided by kelp forests: a northeast A tlantic perspective

claims.text: Sustainable estuarine restoration requires ecoengineering to recreate or reconnect site-specific hydrographic and sedimentary processes, while adding direct planting or restocking when physical habitat recovery alone cannot restore ecological function.
claims.regime: Human-modified estuaries and coastal wetlands undergoing managed realignment, tidal reconnection, flow alteration, habitat creation, mangrove or seagrass restoration, or shoreline intervention.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Key quantities include drag coefficient, vegetation and root Reynolds numbers, relative submergence, frontal-area density, porosity, blockage, forest-width-to-wavelength scale, applied bed stress, and sediment availability.
synthesis.disagreements: Mangroves do not uniformly attenuate every hazard: short waves are more consistently reduced than long surge, low-drag channels can eliminate forest-scale attenuation, foreshore breaking can exceed forest contribution, and poorly located patches can amplify water elsewhere.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Accessible cases include Pearl River typhoons, Hurricane Andrew/Ike/Harvey, Typhoon Mangkhut, New Zealand creek systems, Australian temperate mangroves, Mumbai waves, natural pneumatophore turbulence, and Rhizophora flumes.
synthesis.governing_physics: Controls include submerged frontal area, stem/root density and diameter, porosity, flexibility, vertical leaf distribution, relative water depth, Reynolds regime, forest width, channels, bathymetry, and sediment feedback.
synthesis.limitations: Drag coefficients and frontal areas depend on measurement method, species, age, water depth, damage, flexibility, scale, and event. Many studies remain model- or site-specific, and vertical structure and channel networks are often simplified.
synthesis.major_equations: Models use vegetation drag and wave-energy sinks, porous-canopy momentum exchange, turbulence closures, frontal-area and bulk-drag relations, surge-wave coupling, and bio-morphodynamic sediment conservation.
synthesis.numerical_models: CH3D-SWAN, SWAN-type vegetation dissipation, 3-D vegetation-resolving surge models, porous-root flow models, delta-scale hydrodynamics, and bio-morphodynamic models span event to sea-level-rise scales.
synthesis.open_questions: Needs include extreme-event drag and failure, flexible and broken vegetation, channel-forest exchange, wave-surge-tide interaction, evolving bathymetry, sediment budgets, species transfer, uncertainty, and coupled ecological persistence.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent work quantifies prototype drag, geometry-measurement uncertainty, nonlinear low-cover erosion benefits, age-dependent failure, field-calibrated Rhizophora coefficients, delta-wide placement effects, and climate-driven morphology.
synthesis.seminal_papers: The branch develops from mangrove wave-propagation and vegetation-drag theory toward parameterized-tree experiments, vegetation-resolving storm models, field turbulence, drag scaling, and bio-morphodynamic design.
synthesis.typical_methods: Evidence spans natural-forest velocity arrays, storm and erosion surveys, prototype and reduced flumes, detailed geometry scanning, field-calibrated drag, coupled surge-wave models, and long-term bio-morphodynamics.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Case results include about 20% transmission through a 75 m Rhizophora forest, 77% reduction over 100 m during Mangkhut, nearly 70% over 100 m temperate forest, high-water gradients of 12-36 cm/km, and drag formulations with explicit Reynolds bounds.
synthesis.well_established: Mangroves dissipate waves and alter currents through form drag, turbulence, blockage, sheltering, and bed friction, while creeks can bypass forest resistance and redistribute water levels.

claims.text: A mangrove-specific wave framework established vegetation resistance as a control on surface-wave propagation through forests.
claims.regime: Mangrove geometry and resistance alter wave propagation and couple water motion to forest processes.

claims.text: Wetlands attenuate short-period storm waves more reliably than long-period storm surges, whose response depends on event, vegetation, and landscape geometry.
claims.regime: Wetlands consistently attenuate short-period storm waves, while long-period surge attenuation is weaker or absent depending on storm, wetland, and landscape geometry.

claims.text: Mangrove protection from tsunamis and cyclones is conditional on forest structure, width, bathymetry, event characteristics, and evidence quality.
claims.regime: Protection varies with forest width, density, structure, bathymetry, hazard, and evidence quality; mangroves are not an absolute shield.

claims.text: Permeable-dam restoration on mangrove-mud coasts requires adequate sediment supply, system-scale diagnosis, maintenance, and governance rather than structure placement alone.
claims.regime: Permeable structures can restore sediment balance only when embedded in system understanding, maintenance, governance, and suitable sediment supply.

claims.text: Engineering with mangroves requires joint assessment of flood attenuation, ecological persistence, uncertainty, and integration with conventional defenses.
claims.regime: Implementation must jointly evaluate hydraulic functionality, ecosystem persistence, uncertainty, and compatibility with conventional defenses.

claims.text: Pearl River Delta simulations showed that forest width, drag, and location control local and nonlocal typhoon water levels, including possible amplification elsewhere.
claims.regime: Wide, high-drag forests increased local attenuation; narrow upper-estuary patches could attenuate upstream levels but could amplify water elsewhere if poorly placed.

claims.text: Parameterized Rhizophora tests found about 20% transmission through a 75 m prototype-equivalent forest, with foreshore breaking important and solitary-wave drag coefficient near 1.5.
claims.regime: Foreshore breaking contributed strongly; a prototype-equivalent 75 m forest transmitted about 20%, and solitary-wave drag was approximately 1.5.

claims.text: Contrasting field sites showed that channels can bypass forest drag and eliminate measurable long-wave attenuation, making landscape routing decisive.
claims.regime: One site attenuated long waves, while another showed no measurable flood-tide attenuation because flow bypassed vegetation through low-drag channels.

claims.text: Prototype-scale Rhizophora tests proposed CD=0.6+3×10^4/Re_D​BH for Re_D​BH 5×10^3-1.9×10^5, with stated uncertainty 0.69.
claims.regime: Combined scaled datasets yielded CD=0.6+3e4/Re_D​BH over Re_D​BH 5e3-1.9e5, with uncertainty about 0.69.

claims.text: Bio-morphodynamic simulations found mangrove accretion can accelerate under sea-level rise, with nonlinear dependence on sediment supply, waves, slope, tidal range, and forest-edge distance.
claims.regime: Forest accretion could accelerate under SLR, but timing and magnitude varied nonlinearly with coastal conditions and distance from the seaward edge.

claims.text: Hurricane Harvey plots showed up to 196 m² erosion without mangroves and up to 9 m bank retreat with decreasing cover, with nonlinear benefits at low cover.
claims.regime: The zero-cover plot lost 196 m2 and banks retreated up to 9 m as cover decreased; protection was nonlinear and low cover supplied much of the benefit.

claims.text: A modeled intermediate mangrove-root porosity minimized near-bed fluctuations through a vorticity sink and inhibited sediment transport through dominant viscous dissipation.
claims.regime: An intermediate porosity created a vorticity sink; viscous dissipation exceeded turbulence production and obstructed sediment transport.

claims.text: Dense-array experiments showed that blockage, sheltering, reflection, orientation, and water depth control wave dissipation relevant to mangrove-restoration structures.
claims.regime: Element orientation, blockage, sheltering, and reflection controlled dissipation; a conceptual model reproduced arrangement effects.

claims.text: Mangrove-creek observations measured high-water attenuation up to 12 cm/km in the creek and 36 cm/km in forest and identified creek-platform exchange as a tidal-asymmetry control.
claims.regime: High water fell up to 12 cm/km in the creek and 36 cm/km in forest; creek-sheet-flow interaction controlled asymmetry and attenuation.

claims.text: During Typhoon Mangkhut, a roughly 100 m planted mangrove forest reduced wave height by 77%, avoided uprooting/lethal stem breakage, and showed sedimentation.
claims.regime: A roughly 100 m, six-year-old forest reduced wave height 77%, survived without uprooting or lethal stem breakage, and accumulated sediment.

claims.text: Natural pneumatophore canopies produced Reynolds stress up to 5.3×10^-3 m²/s², eddy viscosity up to 1.9×10^-3 m²/s, and near-bed drag up to an order above unvegetated expectations.
claims.regime: Reynolds stresses reached 5.3e-3 m2/s2, eddy viscosity 1.9e-3 m2/s, and near-bed drag was up to an order above unvegetated expectation.

claims.text: A field-validated Hurricane Andrew model found vegetation removal greatly increased inundation, while buffering depended on vertical wetted and frontal leaf-area profiles.
claims.regime: Removing vegetation greatly increased inundation volume and area; buffering depended on vertical wetted and frontal leaf-area structure.

claims.text: For Hurricane Ike, physics-based 3-D vegetation-resolving modelling captured surge dynamics more accurately than a 2-D Manning approach and represented onshore sediment transport.
claims.regime: A physics-based 3-D vegetation treatment captured complex surge dynamics more accurately than a 2-D Manning representation while resolving onshore sediment transport.

claims.text: Mangrove design modelling found Sonneratia wave attenuation peaked near age 10, while canopy emergence after age 20 shifted drag and increased wind-failure exposure.
claims.regime: Sonneratia attenuation peaked near age 10; after age 20 canopy emergence shifted attenuation to trunks/roots and increased cyclone wind-failure exposure.

claims.text: A field-calibrated Rhizophora formulation uses root diameter as characteristic length for bulk drag in wave-attenuation models.
claims.regime: An integrated bulk-drag formulation used root diameter as characteristic length to improve wave-attenuation inputs for complex Rhizophora geometry.

claims.text: Mumbai modelling and measurements found 49-55% attenuation for 0.175 stems/m², 0.3 m diameter, and drag coefficient 0.4-1.5.
claims.regime: For density 0.175/m2, 0.3 m stems, and CD 0.4-1.5, modeled attenuation was 49-55% and agreed reasonably with measurements.

claims.text: Woody-vegetation frontal-area methods produced inferred bulk drag coefficients from 0.94 to 1.70, demonstrating measurement-driven wave-attenuation uncertainty.
claims.regime: Alternative frontal-area methods yielded bulk drag coefficients 0.94-1.70; TLS shadowing required correction.

claims.text: An Australian temperate mangrove belt 100 m wide reduced ordinary wave heights by nearly 70%, with attenuation decreasing as water depth increased.
claims.regime: A 100 m belt reduced ordinary incoming waves by nearly 70%; efficiency decreased with depth and UAV data under-resolved near-bed obstacles.

claims.text: Homogenized long-wave analysis represents emergent coastal forests as cylinder arrays and quantifies frictional and turbulence-mediated attenuation.
claims.regime: Long waves through emergent coastal vegetation

claims.text: Submerged mangrove canopies materially increase regular-wave attenuation, and a hydraulic submerged volume index collapses damping across no-, sparse- and dense-canopy configurations; drag also varies with Reynolds, Keulegan-Carpenter and Ursell regimes.
claims.regime: Regular waves through the tested 1:10 young/short-mangrove patch with no, sparse and dense canopies over submerged to emergent states.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Useful controls include relative water level and platform elevation, wave-to-current velocity ratio, relative submergence, drag and frontal-area density, settling-to-advection time, sediment supply relative to accommodation, and SLR relative to accretion.
synthesis.disagreements: Vegetation does not universally increase deposition: trapping can be offset by flow buffering, small mown plots showed no local effect, and vegetation simultaneously promotes channelization through drag and channel infilling through enhanced platform accretion.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Evidence includes Venice and Massachusetts networks, confined-estuary scenarios, true-scale surge surfaces, Wax Lake floods, restored marshes, microtidal storm delivery, paired vegetation plots, and cross-marsh topographic signatures.
synthesis.governing_physics: Controls include tidal prism and asymmetry, surge level, wind waves, creek-edge exchange, sediment concentration and settling, plant frontal area and flexibility, platform elevation, edge geometry, sediment supply, subsidence, and relative sea-level rise.
synthesis.limitations: Marsh response is scale-, species-, season-, and event-dependent. Sparse storm observations, uncertain belowground and edge processes, simplified plant mechanics, incomplete sediment budgets, and transfer across tidal regimes constrain forecasts.
synthesis.major_equations: Frameworks combine shallow-water and wave-current flow, vegetation drag, suspended-sediment conservation, erosion/deposition, Exner-type morphology, tidal storage, edge retreat, plant response, and elevation-dependent accretion.
synthesis.numerical_models: Three-dimensional routing models, estuary storage models, delta sediment models, decadal edge and channel models, restoration biogeomorphology, pond-growth models, and wave-current plant models address complementary scales.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities include storm versus fair-weather budgets, creek-edge pathway partitioning, edge failure distributions, vegetation trait and damage dynamics, pond thresholds, subsidence, sediment diversion, restoration geometry, and uncertainty under accelerating SLR.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent studies resolve competing density effects, surge-enabled sediment delivery, tide-wave import switches, topographic storm signatures, creek-complexity resilience, pond intervention windows, and restoration design controls.
synthesis.seminal_papers: The branch progresses from marsh-surface flux and vegetation-routing concepts to network efficiency, flexible-plant damping, field-calibrated sediment budgets, and coupled restoration and climate-response models.
synthesis.typical_methods: Methods span flux stations, erosion and elevation surveys, channel-network metrics, true-scale surge tests, mown-plot experiments, storm reconstructions, remote topography, and coupled hydro-biogeomorphic modelling.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Reported cases include less than 0.6 cm mean storm-surface lowering, roughly 0.5 cm extra accretion per 60-day flood with stronger tides, doubled marsh flux during a moderate surge, and effects that can reverse sign with sediment supply or scale.
synthesis.well_established: Salt marshes are coupled biogeomorphic systems: vegetation changes drag and routing, which alters sediment delivery and channel form, while elevation and morphology feed back on inundation and plant survival.

claims.text: Three-dimensional modelling showed vegetation organizes unvegetated channels and vegetated levee-basin platforms by shifting flow routing and sedimentation with water level.
claims.regime: Vegetation routed low-stage flow into unvegetated channels and created levee-basin deposition; overtopping produced more homogeneous sheet-flow sedimentation.

claims.text: Salt-marsh persistence under climate change depends jointly on vertical accretion, vegetation feedbacks, edge erosion, sediment supply, and accelerating sea-level rise.
claims.regime: Marsh response reflects interacting mineral and organic accretion, vegetation, edge dynamics, sea-level rise, warming, CO2, and sediment supply.

claims.text: Cross-system comparisons found vegetation promotes more efficient tidal-channel networks by altering channel branching and meandering.
claims.regime: Vegetated Massachusetts and Venice marshes had more efficient networks than unvegetated arid systems through vegetation-related branching and meandering.

claims.text: Salt-marsh budgets require simultaneous high-frequency measurement of water, sediment, organic matter, nutrients, and silica exchange across tidal boundaries.
claims.regime: Marsh exchange spans tidal water and sediment plus particulate, dissolved, and biogenic compounds, requiring high-frequency, long-duration measurements.

claims.text: Tidal-flat–marsh flood defense is a dynamic biogeomorphic service whose performance changes as morphology and vegetation adjust to forcing and intervention.
claims.regime: Dynamic morphology and vegetation adjust to forcing and can strengthen or weaken defense; interventions can accelerate favorable natural processes.

claims.text: Confined-estuary modelling found diminishing attenuation beyond a wetland-size threshold and stronger upstream benefit when the same wetland area was located farther landward.
claims.regime: Attenuation increased with wetland area to a threshold, and equal-area wetlands farther upstream stored more local flood volume and reduced upstream high water more.

claims.text: Salt-marsh edge erosion increased with wind-wave exposure, while rare large failures produced long-tailed local erosion even under low-wave-energy conditions.
claims.regime: Erosion related significantly to wind-wave exposure; low-energy conditions still produced rare large failures and long-tailed local rates.

claims.text: Deltaic-marsh modelling showed vegetation density has competing trapping and flow-buffering effects, while resuspension extends and homogenizes sediment delivery.
claims.regime: Vegetation both trapped sediment and buffered delivery; with resuspension sediment penetrated farther and deposited more uniformly.

claims.text: True-scale storm-surge tests produced less than 0.6 cm mean surface lowering, with organic matter and plant species controlling soil stability and canopy damage.
claims.regime: Repeated simulated surges lowered surfaces less than 0.6 cm on average; organic matter and species controlled stability and damage.

claims.text: Biogeomorphic modelling showed restoration inlet geometry can steer marsh development, with larger breach-width contrast increasing habitat diversity.
claims.regime: Inlet-width asymmetry changed development and greater breach-width contrast increased restored-habitat diversity.

claims.text: A decadal model found sediment supply can reverse wave-driven marsh-edge retreat into expansion, with outcome also controlled by vegetation response time.
claims.regime: Higher waves lowered and retreated the edge, but sufficient sediment supply could reverse a wave-stressed marsh from retreat to expansion.

claims.text: Wax Lake simulations found vegetation enhances sedimentation only when trapping exceeds flow buffering, while larger tides added about 0.5 cm accretion per 60-day high-discharge flood.
claims.regime: Vegetation increased retention only when trapping exceeded flow buffering; larger tides at high discharge added about 0.5 cm accretion per 60-day flood.

claims.text: Marsh plant-flow prediction requires direct measurement of drag-relevant geometry and mechanics, including frontal area, density, stiffness, and reconfiguration.
claims.regime: Drag-relevant properties depend on density, frontal area, stiffness, reconfiguration, and measurement method rather than biomass or cover alone.

claims.text: Restored-marsh observations and modelling linked channel morphology and vegetation to tidal asymmetry, accretion, and possible sea-level-rise amplification of ebb-driven sediment export.
claims.regime: Ebb dominance and sediment export interact with channels and vegetation and may intensify with sea-level rise, reducing resilience.

claims.text: Wind-wave power controls marsh-margin form, while halophyte colonization reduces lateral erosion and shifts edges toward gentler, irregular morphology.
claims.regime: Vegetation reduced lateral erosion; high cliffs and smooth edges marked rapid erosion, whereas low-energy shallow-flat margins were gentler and irregular.

claims.text: Flexible-marsh-plant experiments and modelling showed weak current can reduce wave damping while strong current increases it through reconfiguration and wave-current kinematics.
claims.regime: Weak currents reduced wave dissipation whereas strong currents increased it through reconfiguration, group velocity, and canopy velocity changes.

claims.text: Microtidal-bay simulations found wind waves resuspend sediment but surge water levels govern marsh delivery; a moderate surge doubled flux to most marshes.
claims.regime: Waves controlled flat resuspension, but surge inundation controlled marsh deposition; a moderate surge doubled flux to most marshes and deposition rose linearly with surge intensity.

claims.text: Vegetation has competing effects on tidal channels—drag promotes channelization while platform accretion reduces tidal prism and infills channels—with dominance set by platform elevation and sediment/SLR regime.
claims.regime: Vegetation can enhance channelization through drag yet shrink tidal prism through platform accretion and infilling; platform elevation determines which effect dominates.

claims.text: Field-calibrated models linked pond expansion to sea-level-rise drowning and used a power-law growth relation to identify a finite intervention window before widespread merging.
claims.regime: Pond growth mechanisms were consistent with SLR-driven drowning and could be summarized by a power law that bounds intervention time before merging.

claims.text: Paired 4 m² marsh plots found no deposition difference between mown and vegetated patches, showing vegetation does not automatically enhance sedimentation at small scales.
claims.regime: At 4 m2 scale mowing did not change flow or deposition, and vegetation presence did not automatically increase local sedimentation.

claims.text: Biogeomorphic modelling and real networks showed greater creek-network complexity enhances flow concentration, sediment deposition, and marsh resilience to rising water levels.
claims.regime: Drainage complexity concentrated flow and increased sediment transport/deposition, improving resilience alongside vegetation traits.

claims.text: Marsh topography preserves a detectable signature of surge-enabled, wave-driven sediment delivery across the tidal-flat–marsh transition.
claims.regime: Surge water levels enabled wave-driven cross-edge delivery and left a detectable topographic signature consistent across marshes with differing tide and wave regimes.

claims.text: Salt-marsh sediment supply can switch between net import and export depending on the joint tide-wave regime and pathway through creeks versus edges.
claims.regime: Net import or export through creeks and across edges depended on the joint tidal and wave regime and varied among estuaries and marshes.

claims.text: In 1:20 marsh–dyke basin tests, vegetation reduced waves and overtopping across varied forcing; for a fixed marsh width, taller and denser surrogate marshes produced stronger attenuation.
claims.regime: Experimental Study of Wave Attenuation Across an Artificial Salt Marsh

claims.text: Winter flume tests found no significant mean-erosion effect of aboveground biomass or difference between two marsh species with comparable root biomass and soil density, suggesting persistent belowground protection in the tested patches.
claims.regime: Erosion protection by winter state of salt marsh vegetation

claims.text: A Wadden Sea review concludes that salt-marsh flood and erosion management must integrate site initial conditions, conservation aims, biogeomorphology and climate adaptation; marshes can adapt to sea-level rise under suitable management.
claims.regime: Management of Wadden Sea Salt Marshes in the Context of Nature Conservation, Coastal Flooding and Erosion Risks: A Review

claims.text: In-situ tests above 0.5 m/s found a mature tidal marsh highly erosion resistant; for comparable soil and vegetation, breach-flow surface erosion may be negligible relative to headcut erosion, but transfer requires further testing.
claims.regime: Assessment of in-situ tidal marsh erodibility under high flow velocities

claims.text: Hydrodynamic attenuation changes wetting, drying, and inundation depth and can increase modeled coastal-wetland vulnerability to sea-level rise.
claims.regime: Potential increase in coastal wetland vulnerability to sea-level rise suggested by considering hydrodynamic attenuation effects

claims.text: Emergent-plant morphology controls vertical velocity and turbulent-kinetic-energy profiles, enabling canopy turbulence prediction from frontal-area structure.
claims.regime: Measured and Predicted Turbulent Kinetic Energy in Flow Through Emergent Vegetation With Real Plant Morphology

claims.text: Wider salt marshes and higher foreshores reduced storm wave run-up at Dutch Wadden Sea dikes, but marshes were least likely to form where protection was most needed.
claims.regime: Using salt marshes for coastal protection: Effective but hard to get where needed most

claims.text: Established marsh topsoil resisted fast-flow erosion better than bare tidal flats, with cohesive layers and fine-root density governing resistance after disturbance.
claims.regime: The importance of marshes providing soil stabilization to resist fast‐flow erosion in case of a dike breach

claims.text: Across eight modeled estuaries, salt marshes reduced storm flooding and damages, with the strongest benefits during high-intensity events.
claims.regime: Coastal wetlands mitigate storm flooding and associated costs in estuaries

claims.text: Eco-geomorphic scenarios indicate that accelerated sea-level rise can expand newly colonized wetland area while reducing its soil-carbon accumulation opportunity, so vegetation-area conservation does not guarantee maximum carbon storage.
claims.regime: Accelerated Sea‐Level Rise Limits Vegetation Capacity to Sequester Soil Carbon in Coastal Wetlands: A Study Case in Southeastern Australia

claims.text: Seasonal tests of 418 Elymus specimens and resin surrogates spanning 8.45-1708.42 MPa Young's modulus produced bending angles from 0 to 77.4 degrees under 0.4-1.2 m/s currents, supporting Cauchy-scaled plant analogues.
claims.regime: From seasonal field study to surrogate modeling: Investigating the biomechanical dynamics of Elymus sp. in salt marshes

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Controls include submergence, canopy height/depth, wave excursion/shoot spacing, Cauchy number, blade stiffness and buoyancy, Reynolds and Keulegan–Carpenter numbers, frontal-area density, meadow length/wavelength, gap/patch size, current/wave velocity ratio, and Shields stress.
synthesis.disagreements: Rigid-canopy drag can overpredict attenuation when blades move with water, yet flexible canopies may generate different turbulence rather than uniformly less effect; vegetation can both shelter the bed and add wake stress; shoot density alone is insufficient when flexibility, morphology, patch length and gaps vary.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: The evidence includes Posidonia and Zostera field meadows, natural and transplanted canopies, storm before/after surveys, oscillatory and combined-flow flumes, flexible/stiff mimics, fragmented and gapped patches, particle capture/deposition, streaming observations, and spectral wave dissipation.
synthesis.governing_physics: Relative blade–water velocity sets drag; flexibility reduces projected area and changes phase; cumulative drag dissipates waves; canopy shear generates coherent vortices and vertical exchange; sheltering lowers bed stress while wakes add turbulence; sediment–light feedback can create bistability.
synthesis.limitations: Mimic materials and geometric scaling distort reconfiguration; many studies isolate waves or currents; field morphology is seasonal and heterogeneous; storm breakage, cohesive sediment, root effects, species mixtures, meadow recovery, and full-scale sediment budgets remain underrepresented.
synthesis.major_equations: Models use Morison/drag force with effective frontal area and relative velocity, beam or blade dynamics, wave-energy decay, Reynolds-averaged canopy momentum, turbulent kinetic-energy budgets, advection–diffusion–settling, critical Shields stress, and coupled sediment–light–biomass equations.
synthesis.numerical_models: Models include relative-velocity blade dynamics, eelgrass–flow coupling, meadow-scale attenuation, digital twins for surge scenarios, subgrid canopy closures, SPH–finite-element stem interaction, sediment–light bistability, and spatial particle-deposition models.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities include spectral dissipation across changing morphology, combined wave–current–tide forcing, patch-edge networks, breakage and uprooting, cohesive sediment and carbon, sediment–light thresholds, restoration trajectories, and uncertainty-aware upscaling to coastal protection.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent work directly measures frequency-dependent meadow dissipation, combined-flow resuspension thresholds, turbulence and bedload, carbon-accretion heterogeneity, storm-surge digital twins, transplanted-meadow attenuation, and stem-scale SPH–FE interaction.
synthesis.seminal_papers: The branch progresses from eelgrass flow and transport observations and relative-blade-velocity drag to flexible blade models, canopy vortex and streaming measurements, fragmented-patch hydraulics, sediment feedback, spectral budgets, and coupled fluid–structure simulation.
synthesis.typical_methods: Methods span wave/current flumes with flexible mimics or live plants, ADV velocity and turbulence, wave gauges, force and blade-motion imaging, PIV, sediment traps and optical backscatter, field meadow transects and storms, spectral budgets, coupled CFD–structure models, and ecosystem feedback models.
synthesis.validated_ranges: The corpus covers low-energy through storm waves, steady, oscillatory and combined flow, submerged and near-emergent canopies, rigid-to-flexible blades, single- and multispecies meadows, intact-to-fragmented patches, and blade-to-barrier-coast scales; detailed numeric ranges remain source-specific.
synthesis.well_established: Seagrass modifies waves, currents, turbulence and sediment through distributed drag, flexible reconfiguration, canopy-interface shear, wave streaming, near-bed sheltering, and particle interception; these physical changes feed back on light, accretion and meadow persistence.

estuaries.label: Estuaries and tidal inlets
estuaries.description: Hydrodynamics, mixing, and exchange in estuaries and inlets.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Controls include tidal-excursion-to-intrusion-length, estuarine Richardson, Froude and Simpson numbers, freshwater and tidal-volume ratios, mixing and dispersion parameters, convergence length, stratification, Rossby number, settling and Shields measures.
synthesis.disagreements: Classical steady gravitational-circulation scaling works in long estuaries but can fail in short tidally dominated systems. Convergence may enhance residual flow under constant viscosity yet weaken or reverse tidal-straining circulation when mixing varies over the tide.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Evidence includes the Merrimack and Hudson contrast, low-flow Willapa Bay, the 2014 Changjiang intrusion, 2015 Sebou supermoon observations, lower Meghna irrigation sampling, idealized funnel estuaries and marsh–farmland surge scenarios.
synthesis.governing_physics: Longitudinal density gradients drive baroclinic exchange, tides advect and mix salinity fronts, and river discharge opposes landward salt transport. Wind and coastal-ocean density anomalies alter boundary conditions; convergence, rotation and evolving bathymetry modify residual circulation and sediment pathways.
synthesis.limitations: Sparse vertical and lateral sampling, uncertain bathymetry and diffusivity, rapidly changing discharge and coastal boundaries, unresolved turbulence, wetland and groundwater coupling, morphology feedback and limited extreme-event records constrain transfer.
synthesis.major_equations: Models solve hydrostatic mass, momentum, salt and sediment conservation with turbulence closure and free-surface forcing. Knudsen bulk relations and isohaline coordinates diagnose exchange; analytical intrusion laws balance advection and dispersion, and morphodynamic systems add bed evolution.
synthesis.numerical_models: Reviewed systems include validated unstructured hydrodynamics, isohaline-coordinate diagnostics, Savenije intrusion theory, HEC-RAS salinity transport, coupled surface–subsurface variable-density flow and COAWST-like three-dimensional sediment morphodynamics.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities include compound drought–surge–wind intrusion, shelf–estuary exchange, wetland migration, oxygen and sediment feedbacks, data assimilation, climate-driven regime shifts and scalable predictors spanning short and long estuaries.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent advances use isohaline coordinates across contrasting regimes, resolve episodic wind-driven intrusion, couple surface and subsurface salinization, embed baroclinicity in long-term morphology and quantify counterintuitive convergence–mixing interactions.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Classical salt-balance, Knudsen and gravitational-circulation theories established exchange and intrusion scaling; later tidal-straining, pumping and estuarine-classification frameworks explained time-dependent mixing and residual transport.
synthesis.typical_methods: Studies combine salinity, velocity and water-level moorings, hydrographic transects, shelf observations and water sampling with unstructured-grid circulation, HEC-RAS, analytical intrusion, isohaline-budget, coupled groundwater and three-dimensional morphodynamic models.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Examples include 17.6 m/s Changjiang wind and 23-day intake interruption, near-10 cm/s Willapa intrusion, 1.3 dS/m lower-Meghna salinity, and conditional agricultural protection by 200–400 m marsh migration under at least 3 m surge on a 0.1% slope.
synthesis.well_established: Estuaries exchange freshwater, salt, sediment and tracers under interacting river, tidal and density forcing. Stratification and mixing set salinity intrusion; gravitational circulation, tidal pumping and straining control exchange, while geometry and adjacent-shelf variability can reorganize these balances.

claims.text: For the validated 2006-2012 Delaware Bay hindcast, shelf waves were predominantly remote swell, bathymetric and tidal-current refraction controlled entrance energy, and energetic in-bay waves were mainly locally wind driven with fetch set by wind direction.
claims.regime: Delaware Bay and adjacent shelf, 2006-2012, validated at three buoys.

claims.text: Mangrove vegetation alters lagoon-wide tidal propagation rather than only local forest flow: vegetation drag preferentially attenuates semidiurnal constituents, enhances the M4 overtide and tidal asymmetry, and produces stronger and longer ebb flow, especially during spring tides.
claims.regime: Microtidal, shallow Somone Coastal Lagoon, Senegal, during two lunar months in the 2020 dry season, with negligible river discharge and both creek and sheet flow through mangroves.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Controls include estuarine Froude and Richardson numbers, tidal and freshwater velocity ratio, Simpson and Wedderburn-type straining measures, salinity difference, mixing efficiency, depth/width and convergence, tidal excursion/length, river flow/tidal prism, wind stress/baroclinic pressure, and flushing-time/tidal-period.
synthesis.disagreements: Classical two-layer gravitational circulation is useful but incomplete: tidal rectification can generate exchange in well-mixed water, lateral advection can rival longitudinal dynamics, wind can reverse the expected pattern, and flushing/residence estimates depend on diagnostic definition and temporal averaging.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: The corpus spans Hudson and San Francisco systems, Galveston and Capibaribe bays, Wadden and German Bight estuaries, macrotidal and narrow idealized channels, along-coast coupled estuaries, glacial fjords, and the segmented multi-basin Salish Sea.
synthesis.governing_physics: Density gradients drive gravitational circulation; tidal straining and periodic stratification modulate shear; covariance of eddy viscosity and shear rectifies tides; lateral advection and bathymetry redistribute exchange; wind can reinforce, weaken or reverse flow; mixing entrains salt and transforms water masses.
synthesis.limitations: Sparse sections miss lateral recirculation; residuals depend on averaging; salinity-coordinate transport can hide geography; model mixing is resolution/closure sensitive; residence time is not unique; open-boundary shelf properties and episodic winds are uncertain; constituent transformation complicates tracer closure.
synthesis.major_equations: Core formulations include along-channel momentum and salt balance, Knudsen relations, residual/tidal decomposition, exchange in salinity coordinates (TEF), salinity variance and mixing budgets, eddy-viscosity–shear covariance, box/flushing models, water-age transport, and nondimensional estuarine scaling.
synthesis.numerical_models: Models include idealized 1DV/2DV and three-dimensional circulation systems, Hudson and urban-channel configurations, TEF diagnostics, salinity-variance budgets, eddy-viscosity–shear covariance, unsteady flushing models, shelf-source particle tracking, plume/coastal forcing experiments, and tracer budgets.
synthesis.open_questions: Needs include unified TEF and water-age diagnostics, lateral and multi-inlet exchange, event-to-climate variability, morphology/deepening and sea-level effects, compound wind–river–shelf forcing, exchange–biogeochemistry coupling, and observation-based mixing closure.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent advances use salinity-coordinate TEF, variance budgets tying exchange to mixing, shelf-source tracing, segmented-estuary diagnostics, plume-versus-coastal attribution in fjords, multiple closed tracer budgets, and explicit tests of remote-ocean forcing limits.
synthesis.seminal_papers: The branch evolves from partially mixed momentum/salt balances and tidal rectification toward lateral-advection models, mixing covariance, wind reversal, salinity-variance links, TEF, shelf-source attribution, seasonal segmentation, and multi-tracer budgets.
synthesis.typical_methods: Methods combine moored velocity/salinity sections, ship surveys and tracers, residual harmonic and covariance analysis, primitive-equation models, idealized channels, TEF salinity-coordinate integration, variance/mixing budgets, particle or age tracers, flushing boxes, sensitivity experiments, and shelf-source tracking.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Evidence covers well-mixed to partially and periodically stratified estuaries, weakly to strongly tidal and macrotidal settings, narrow to wide channels, seasonal segmentation, spring–neap variability, local and remote winds, channel deepening, glacial plume forcing, and connected shelf–estuary systems.
synthesis.well_established: Estuarine exchange is compensating inflow and outflow driven by baroclinic pressure but strongly modified by tides, mixing, wind, river discharge, lateral circulation, geometry and shelf conditions; net volume transport alone conceals this renewal.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: No universal dimensionless stability parameter is established by this reviewed slice. Tide-wave dominance, transport-capacity ratios, and geometry-normalized relations are regime descriptors whose coefficients depend on inlet population and units.
synthesis.disagreements: Simple prism-area relations imply a compact equilibrium geometry, whereas the empirical morphology study found limited classification improvement from tidal prism alone. These results address different outputs but jointly warn against treating prism as a sufficient universal predictor.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Key reviewed evidence includes the summer 1995 Wilson Inlet field campaign, historical Frisian Inlet adjustment before and after basin reduction, a Snowy River observed/design case, and an 89-inlet United States database paired with 20-year wave hindcasts.
synthesis.governing_physics: Tidal prism and entrance geometry set exchange velocities, while waves, littoral drift, ebb transport, river flow, storms, and antecedent morphology control sediment import and export; feedback between area, velocity, and transport creates stable, unstable, or closed states.
synthesis.limitations: The reviewed studies simplify sediment supply, geometry, or transient forcing; two extractions are abstract-limited, field cases are geographically sparse, empirical correlations omit geology and engineering controls, and reduced rules are unsuitable as stand-alone final design models.
synthesis.major_equations: Common reduced formulations include the O'Brien prism-area relation, the Escoffier area-velocity stability diagram, Bruun sediment-capacity criteria, and nonlinear attractor equations; the 2004 Frisian formulation adds a physical ebb-transport balance to the Escoffier construction.
synthesis.numerical_models: Wilson Inlet uses coupled cross-shore/longshore morphodynamics to isolate closure mechanisms; reduced engineering tools include O'Brien, Escoffier, Bruun, and an attractor map, each with distinct sediment and hydrodynamic simplifications.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities include transferable stability criteria under nonstationary sea level and wave climate, transient closure/reopening prediction, multi-inlet interaction, uncertainty-aware sediment budgets, and independent validation across geological and engineered inlet classes.
synthesis.recent_advances: The 2012 multi-inlet database quantifies limits of classical morphology classification, while the 2018 attractor comparison unifies long-term tidal and river-controlled states and clarifies how reduced tools should support preliminary design.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Within this screened branch, Wilson Inlet (1999) supplies a process-resolving closure case and the Frisian Inlet study (2004) gives Escoffier stability a sediment-balance basis; earlier O'Brien, Escoffier, and Bruun works remain seminal but were not directly extracted here.
synthesis.typical_methods: Methods combine field wave-current-bed observations, coupled morphodynamic simulation, analytical sediment balances, equilibrium/stability diagrams, nonlinear dynamical systems, aerial or chart morphology mapping, hindcast climatologies, and multi-inlet empirical correlation.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Evidence is regime-bound: Wilson Inlet is a microtidal wave-dominated seasonal inlet; Frisian results address basin reduction; the attractor comparison uses Snowy River; and morphology correlations span 89 United States inlets but perform poorly in the moderate-wave-exposure group.
synthesis.well_established: A sandy tidal inlet remains open when current-driven sediment export and scour can balance marine or littoral sediment delivery; closure or cross-sectional adjustment occurs when that balance is persistently shifted.

claims.text: At Wilson Inlet, persistent summer swell drove onshore sediment transport that exceeded removal by weak inlet currents and formed the entrance bar responsible for seasonal closure.
claims.regime: Wilson Inlet and comparable microtidal, wave-dominated, seasonally open sandy inlets under persistent summer swell.

claims.text: The influence of summer streamflow and storm events on inlet open duration depended on both event intensity and timing.
claims.regime: The Wilson Inlet model scenarios; event-response direction is not universal outside the modeled sequence and sediment state.

claims.text: For the Frisian Inlet framework, annual-mean entrance area is an equilibrium in which ebb currents restore cross-section losses caused by seasonal storm deposition.
claims.regime: The paper's sandy inlet schematization with annually averaged littoral input and separable entrance/interior sections.

claims.text: An inlet equilibrium is stable only when a perturbation in cross-sectional area drives the section back toward its equilibrium value; the allowable reduction before closure measures its stability margin.
claims.regime: The extended Escoffier construction applied to basin reduction.

claims.text: O'Brien, Escoffier, Bruun, and attractor methods can provide rapid preliminary stability checks, but the authors advise that final inlet design use more sophisticated models.
claims.regime: Sandy barrier estuaries and tidal inlets consistent with each reduced method's assumptions.

claims.text: The attractor formulation generalizes prism-area, Escoffier, and Bruun concepts by representing long-term tidal and river-controlled entrance states within one nonlinear dynamical framework.
claims.regime: Barrier estuaries with erodible entrances and the model's reduced sediment and hydrodynamic balances.

claims.text: In idealized COAWST inlet simulations, ebb-shoal bathymetry was the dominant control on outflow-jet structure, while incident waves increased lateral spreading and limited seaward reach through momentum conversion, friction, and Stokes-drift interaction, with regime-dependent return-current effects.

claims.text: Analysis of 89 U.S. tidal inlets using tidal prism and a 20-year wave hindcast found limited support for the Hayes tide-range/wave-height morphology classification; ebb-delta seaward and downdrift extents correlate best after stratifying by wave exposure, remaining nearly constant below an approximately 10^8 m3 tidal-prism threshold and increasing roughly linearly above it.
