claims.text: Microstructure and velocity transects in a curved, weakly stratified Wadden Sea inlet show that differential advection creates a lateral buoyancy gradient which reinforces curvature-driven single-cell circulation and late-flood stratification during flood, suppresses cross-channel exchange during ebb, and thereby drives a residual longitudinal estuarine exchange flow.
claims.regime: Well-mixed to weakly stratified, curved tidal channel in the German Wadden Sea, with channel-shoal bathymetry and reversing flood-ebb currents.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Key controls include internal Froude, Kelvin/source-width-to-deformation-radius, Rossby and Richardson numbers, discharge and buoyancy flux, tidal excursion/source width, wind stress/buoyancy forcing, plume depth/shelf depth and Ekman transport.
synthesis.disagreements: Classical surface-trapped coastal-current theory does not encompass bottom-trapped plumes sustained by tidal mixing, upstream spreading, or wind-driven supercritical export; apparent plume boundaries also differ among salinity, temperature and optical tracers.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Evidence includes Columbia, Fraser, Changjiang, Rhine, Gironde and Winyah Bay plumes; Great Barrier Reef floods; Oregon and Kochi coastal currents; small Southern California streams; and northern Adriatic flood-plume interactions.
synthesis.governing_physics: Freshwater spreads radially near the mouth, adjusts geostrophically over a deformation radius and commonly turns into a coastally trapped current. Supercritical outflow forms leading fronts; tides strain and mix the plume; wind-driven Ekman transport compresses, deepens or exports it.
synthesis.limitations: Fronts and mixing are intermittent and undersampled, discharge data can be uncertain, satellite proxies are not unique salinity measures, turbulence closures differ, nested boundaries affect transport and idealized theories simplify source geometry and ambient currents.
synthesis.major_equations: Models use reduced-gravity shallow-water or hydrostatic primitive equations with salinity buoyancy, Coriolis, turbulence closure and surface/bottom stress. Integral salt, volume and freshwater budgets estimate entrainment, flushing and transport.
synthesis.numerical_models: The corpus spans reduced-gravity theory, idealized rotating plume models, FVCOM and other primitive-equation shelf models, Lagrangian discharge inversion, front-resolving Rhine simulations and wave–current models for small nearshore outflows.
synthesis.open_questions: Needs include predictive mixing closure, submesoscale frontal instability, wave effects, multiple interacting plumes, sediment and biogeochemical feedback, flood extremes, data assimilation, and robust transfer among source-width, rotation and tidal regimes.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent work resolves bottom-generated tidal mixing, bottom trapping, wind-driven supercritical export, small-creek sensitivity, high-resolution frontal instability, satellite–Lagrangian discharge inversion and coupled radar/glider/model attribution.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Foundational theory framed radial spreading versus rotational trapping; long river-mouth records and Columbia/Fraser studies then established tidal pulsing, supercritical fronts, bulges and multi-timescale estuarine forcing.
synthesis.typical_methods: Approaches combine ship and ferry salinity transects, gliders, moorings, HF radar, microstructure, drifters, satellite color/temperature/turbidity, Lagrangian inversion, idealized theory and nested three-dimensional coastal models.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Studies cover small creeks to major rivers, weakly rotating to rotational plumes, tidal and nontidal shelves, surface- and bottom-trapped structures, downwelling and upwelling winds, flood pulses to four-year records and near-field to regional scales.
synthesis.well_established: River discharge forms buoyant bulges, fronts and coastal currents whose fate reflects competition among inertia, buoyancy, rotation, tides, wind, waves, mixing and shelf geometry.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Controls include estuarine Froude and Richardson numbers, tidal excursion/estuary length, freshwater Froude, mixing/stratification parameters, Simpson number, discharge/tidal prism, convergence length, drag, X2 position, sea-level/depth ratio and wind stress.
synthesis.disagreements: One-dimensional effective dispersion can predict intrusion length but obscures lateral and temporal mechanisms; equilibrium formulas miss transient memory; greater depth from sea-level rise can either enhance intrusion or alter tides/mixing enough to offset it, depending on geometry.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Evidence spans Willapa, Puget/Salish, Pearl, Mekong, Sumjin, San Francisco, Hudson, Yarra, Strymon and Rhine–Meuse systems, plus idealized barrier/constriction cases and a global estuary ensemble.
synthesis.governing_physics: Longitudinal density gradients drive landward bottom flow and seaward surface flow; tides alternately strain and mix salinity; river discharge advects salt seaward; wind, waves, ocean salinity, sea level, branching and constrictions alter circulation and mixing.
synthesis.limitations: Sparse cross-channel observations limit lateral-flux closure; mixing is intermittent; bathymetry and roughness evolve; discharge and ocean salinity boundaries are uncertain; empirical coefficients are site-dependent; global projections simplify local structures and operations.
synthesis.major_equations: The salt budget uses advection–diffusion conservation with resolved or effective dispersion. Exchange decompositions separate mean, tidal oscillatory and shear transports; intrusion models link length to discharge, tidal velocity, convergence and dispersion; tracer-variance decay diagnoses irreversible mixing.
synthesis.numerical_models: Models include UnTRIM, FVCOM, coupled ocean–wave systems, primitive-equation estuary models, time-dependent box models, integrated coastal–inland delta models, effective-dispersion salt-wedge models and global scenario frameworks.
synthesis.open_questions: Needs include transient memory and hysteresis, branching deltas, lateral transport, barrier operations, morphology feedback, compound drought–surge–sea-level forcing, ocean salinity change, data assimilation and probabilistic freshwater thresholds.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent work uses tracer-variance mixing, lateral transport theory, sub-estuary networks, drought observations, coupled wind–wave effects, integrated delta models and global attribution of compounding future salt intrusion.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Classical adjustment, salt-flux and effective-dispersion studies established river–tide control and gravitational exchange; long field records then revealed unsteadiness, lateral circulation and intermittent stratification.
synthesis.typical_methods: Methods include longitudinal and cross-channel CTD/ADCP surveys, fixed salinity and microstructure time series, tracer variance, box and one-dimensional models, three-dimensional hydrostatic models, empirical intrusion equations, scenario ensembles and global forcing attribution.
synthesis.validated_ranges: The corpus covers well-mixed, partially mixed, periodically stratified and salt-wedge regimes; microtidal to macrotidal systems; single and branching channels; normal flow, drought and near-zero discharge; storm barriers, constrictions and future sea level.
synthesis.well_established: Estuarine salinity reflects a dynamic balance between landward ocean salt transport and seaward river flushing, mediated by gravitational exchange, tidal oscillatory transport, stratification-dependent mixing, dispersion and geometry.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Observational adequacy depends on sampling-to-process frequency, record-length-to-event scale, spatial spacing relative to wavelength or morphology, signal-to-noise ratio, platform speed and footprint, relative water depth, wave and current regime, sediment size, calibration range, data return and uncertainty ratios.
synthesis.disagreements: Point instruments resolve time but may miss spatial structure; remote sensors resolve area but infer rather than directly sample variables; Eulerian and Lagrangian views differ; proxy shorelines and concentrations are algorithm-dependent; denser sampling can still be biased if placement or duration misses the governing process.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: The reviewed evidence includes a nine-station barred-beach array, multi-site European storm morphology, Willapa Bay wave–current observations, reef-to-island flooding transects, barrier-reef networks, autonomous sandbank plume surveys, multibeam sediment calibration and satellite wind-wave-current products.
synthesis.governing_physics: Instruments sample coupled waves, currents, water levels, turbulence, sediment, bathymetry and morphology through mechanical, pressure, acoustic, optical, electromagnetic or satellite interactions, each filtered by platform motion, geometry, propagation, scattering and environmental interference.
synthesis.limitations: Energetic events cause sensor loss and saturation; biofouling, bubbles, turbidity and bed mobility corrupt signals; datums and clocks drift; platforms disturb or move with the flow; calibration may not span field conditions; short records alias extremes and morphology; access and maintenance constrain continuity.
synthesis.major_equations: Core relations include sensor transfer and calibration functions, wave spectra and directional moments, velocity and discharge transformations, acoustic or optical backscatter inversion, sediment and volume budgets, datum and coordinate transformations, sampling and aliasing criteria, and uncertainty propagation or data-assimilation observation operators.
synthesis.numerical_models: Field data support retrieval and inversion algorithms, quality-control systems, spectral and directional estimators, observation operators, data assimilation, process-model calibration and validation, uncertainty models, adaptive sampling and digital observing-system design.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities include event-resilient and low-cost sustained arrays, seamless land–water topobathymetry, direct sediment-flux sensing, uncertainty covariance across platforms, compound-hazard measurements, adaptive sampling, autonomous calibration, reproducible retrievals and equitable long-term observing networks.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent advances integrate satellite winds, waves and currents; autonomous underwater and surface vehicles; calibrated multibeam concentration mapping; dense cross-shore arrays; rapid repeat topobathymetry; cloud-ready standards; and observation-model fusion with explicit uncertainty.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Early coastal field programs established pressure and current arrays, sediment concentration sampling, profile surveys, spectral analysis and wave–current boundary-layer observations; satellite altimetry, imaging, acoustics and autonomous platforms later expanded coverage and repeatability.
synthesis.typical_methods: Methods combine fixed gauges and profilers, pressure and velocity arrays, tide gauges, GNSS and survey control, lidar and photogrammetry, multibeam and sidescan acoustics, sediment traps and optical sensors, drifters, autonomous vehicles, satellites, repeat topobathymetry and coordinated multi-platform campaigns.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Examples span beaches, tidal bays, coral and barrier reefs, shallow sandbanks and regional-to-global satellite coverage, from intra-wave sensing through tidal and storm campaigns to multi-year morphology; each dataset remains bounded by its platform and site regime.
synthesis.well_established: Coastal field measurement requires simultaneous attention to the process, decision variable, spatial and temporal scales, platform response, calibration, datum, sampling design, uncertainty, metadata and survivability; a sensor record is not automatically a representative observation.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Important controls include Froude number, wave steepness, relative freeboard, barrier inertia, Shields mobility, relative depth, directional angle, spectral bimodality, structure or vegetation density, normalized surge, and model skill or uncertainty metrics.
synthesis.disagreements: The CERC longshore formula alternated between over- and underprediction during storms. A surfbeat-resolving model was not superior during TC Olwyn because locally generated wind waves dominated. Hard structures can shield locally yet divert and concentrate damaging flow elsewhere.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Key datasets include a 340 km post-Tohoku survey, multi-instrument Tohoku waveforms, five Duck storm sediment transects, two Lake Michigan storm-current campaigns, 2 Hz Loe Bar overwash scans, Upham hurricane nourishment surveys and Ningaloo cyclone reef-lagoon observations.
synthesis.governing_physics: Observed response is governed by tsunami momentum and Froude regime, wave-current interaction, spectral period and bimodality, breaking and setup, runup and overwash, vegetation drag, structure diversion, undertow, longshore currents, sediment suspension and antecedent morphology.
synthesis.limitations: Extreme measurements are sparse, dangerous and often opportunistic; instruments fail or perturb flow, post-event marks mix processes, bedload may be unmeasured, pier effects and changing morphology bias transects, and event-calibrated models may not transfer to different spectra or sites.
synthesis.major_equations: Field interpretation couples nonlinear shallow-water or surfbeat equations, wave-action models, sediment-flux integration, Froude scaling, overtopping and runup thresholds, vegetation drag and moment, XBeach-G wave-by-wave physics, and nonlinear data-driven waveform transfer.
synthesis.numerical_models: Models include modified depth-integrated tsunami equations, regularized extreme learning machines, XBeach-G, SWAN and XBeach surfbeat configurations, direct suspended-flux integration, and event-specific shoreline or nourishment analyses.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities include redundant interoperable sensors, rapid bathymetry updates, bedload measurement during storms, uncertainty-aware real-time assimilation, compound-event observations, standardized post-event protocols, and validation across events larger than the calibration record.
synthesis.recent_advances: High-frequency laser scanning now resolves overwash hydraulics and morphology, nonlinear machine learning accelerates near-field tsunami waveform forecasts, and coupled observations reveal when local wind waves, vegetation, structures or antecedent morphology dominate expected hazard response.
synthesis.seminal_papers: The 1981 barred-beach storms and 1999 Duck transport campaign established quasi-synoptic and flux-resolving storm observations; the 2011 Tohoku event enabled unprecedented regional surveys and multi-gauge tsunami reconstruction.
synthesis.typical_methods: Methods include post-event transects, video velocimetry, pressure and tide gauges, offshore pressure sensors, GPS buoys, movable instrument sleds, laser scanning, repeated profiles, sediment concentration arrays, remote sensing, numerical reconstruction and real-time assimilation.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Explicit regimes include Sendai U=6.2 m/s and Fr=1.14-1.4; Duck Hm0 to 3.5 m and transport to 1780 m3/h; Loe Bar Hs=4 m, Hmax=8 m and Tp=10-15 s with under-5% hydrodynamic error; and barred-beach currents to 1.8 m/s.
synthesis.well_established: Extreme coastal events require direct observations because storm and tsunami response depends on time-varying waves, water levels, currents, sediment, bathymetry, structures and ecosystems in combinations not captured by single bulk forcing metrics.

claims.text: For 2011 Great East Japan tsunami evidence along about 340 km, modeling identified the vegetated dune as the primary mitigation at Misawa and showed that straight versus crooked access roads changed velocity; at Hachinohe, seawall diversion kept vegetation moments below 0.2 kNm behind the wall but produced 2-4 kNm in exposed areas, while Sendai video implied 6.2 m/s flow 1 km inland and Fr about 1.14-1.4.
claims.regime: Twenty-five locations over about 340 km; detailed Misawa vegetated-dune and Hachinohe seawall/forest cases; Sendai video evidence.

claims.text: Across five Duck storm transects with waves up to Hm0=3.5 m, directly integrated suspended-load longshore transport reached 1780 m3/h and usually peaked near breaking at the bar and beach; CERC estimates were sometimes high and sometimes low, indicating missing short-term storm controls.
claims.regime: At least nine cross-shore positions over five storms; Hm0 up to 3.5 m; SIS operable above Hs=3 m, wind 20 m/s, and currents 2 m/s.

claims.text: For 2011 Tohoku records from ocean-bottom pressure, GPS buoy, wave, and tide gauges, a regularized nonlinear extreme-learning-machine forecast outperformed standard linear waveform inversion without materially increasing computing time, and consecutive random-weight runs showed insignificant variability.
claims.regime: 2011 Tohoku waveforms from four OBP gauges plus GPS buoys, wave gauges and tide gauges; example inversion window 35 min.

claims.text: During the 1 February 2014 Loe Bar storm (Hs=4 m, Hmax=8 m, Tp=10-15 s), 2 Hz laser observations validated XBeach-G overwash hydrodynamics to less than 5% error; simulations showed that long-period or strongly bimodal spectra reduce overtopping and overwash thresholds by enhancing runup.
claims.regime: Loe Bar D50=2-4 mm; offshore Hs=4 m, Hmax=8 m, Tp=10-15 s, spring high tide 2.45 m and surge about 0.15 m.

claims.text: During two Lake Michigan storms sampled every approximately 3 h for 24 and 28 h, incident angles near 30 degrees and Hrms breaker heights no greater than 1.5 m produced time-averaged longshore currents up to 1.8 m/s that were often nearly uniform across the surf zone despite barred bathymetry.
claims.regime: Profiles every about 3 h for 24 and 28 h; incident angle about 30 degrees; Hrms breaker height <=1.5 m; bar about 30 m offshore and 0.75 m deep in calm conditions.

claims.text: Force-balanced dynamically scaled tank experiments showed that storm waves can form the characteristic features of imbricated coastal boulder deposits, so even megagravel deposits cannot be treated as de facto tsunami indicators.
claims.regime: Dynamically scaled storm-wave interaction with imbricated coastal boulders.

claims.text: During 6–8 m Atlantic storms, cliff-top vertical ground motion exceeded 50–100 μm and two-week cliff loss was two orders of magnitude above the long-term rate, showing strongly episodic erosion.
claims.regime: Coastal cliff ground motions and response to extreme storm waves

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Controls include Shields and mobility numbers, Rouse number, sediment fall velocity relative to orbital velocity, wave-current ratio, suspension height relative to boundary-layer thickness, sampling duration relative to waves and events, gross-to-net flux ratio and closure error relative to measured transport.
synthesis.disagreements: Optical sensors offer high frequency but depend on grain size and bubbles; pumped samples are direct but intrusive and sparse; traps can disturb flow and mix deposition with resuspension. Gross flux, suspended concentration and morphological change answer different questions.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Reviewed evidence includes 65 seven-level concentration profiles in about 1.5 m depth, paired two-way flux trays at four sites on two turbid Great Barrier Reef systems and seasonal entrance-bar observations at Wilson Inlet.
synthesis.governing_physics: Waves mobilize grains, asymmetric orbital motion, undertow and currents advect them, turbulence suspends sediment and settling plus bed exchange controls concentration. At inlets and reefs, persistent directional forcing and local trapping or flushing integrate these processes over larger scales.
synthesis.limitations: Spatial aliasing, sensor calibration drift, biofouling, bubbles, uncertain sampling efficiency, unmeasured bedload, short deployments, storm gaps, tracer recovery, changing bathymetry and open control-volume boundaries can prevent sediment-budget closure.
synthesis.major_equations: Suspended flux is the time and depth integral of concentration times velocity, bed change follows sediment continuity, and settling–diffusion balances describe mean concentration profiles. Trap or tray mass rates measure gross directional exchange, while surveys close net volume budgets.
synthesis.numerical_models: The reviewed set is observation-centered. Interpretation uses suspension-profile, flux and sediment-continuity concepts; direct process-model calibration is not established for this node, and instrument-comparison and fluorescent-tracer papers await full-text review.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities include co-located bedload and suspension, event-resolving vertical flux, tracer recovery and mixing depth, autonomous calibration, cohesive–sand mixtures, reef and vegetation interactions, cross-shore/alongshore integration and open standardized field benchmarks.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent advances combine acoustic/optical arrays, fluorescent and RFID tracers, sediment-imaging velocimetry, autonomous platforms, UAV and sonar morphology, Bayesian sensor fusion and real-time sediment-budget assimilation.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Pump and bottle sampling established concentration profiles; optical and acoustic backscatter enabled high-frequency suspension records, tracers revealed pathways, and synchronized velocity–concentration measurements advanced direct flux estimation.
synthesis.typical_methods: Campaigns pair concentration samplers, optical or acoustic sensors, pumps or pressure-difference collectors, velocity profilers, bed-level surveys, sediment traps/trays and tracers; synchronize sampling, calibrate grain and turbidity response, resolve vertical profiles and waves, estimate uncertainty and close gross and net budgets.
synthesis.validated_ranges: The pressure-difference sampler resolved roughly three-minute profiles from 1 cm above bed upward; reef trays measured gross flux of 34 to over 640 g/m2/d while net sedimentation stayed below 122 g/m2/d. Results are method- and site-specific.
synthesis.well_established: Field sediment transport is intermittent, vertically structured and often strongly two-way; concentration or delivery alone does not determine net accumulation because advection, resuspension, settling and export must be measured within a sediment budget.

claims.text: At four sites on two turbid Great Barrier Reef systems, paired trays measured two-way sediment flux from 34 to more than 640 g/m2/d while mean net sedimentation remained below 122 g/m2/d, demonstrating that high delivery need not imply high accumulation.
claims.regime: Shallow turbid inshore reefs; tray and site-specific limitations apply.

claims.text: A pump-free pressure-difference sampler collected seven suspended-sand samples simultaneously from about 1 cm above the bed upward during approximately 3 min intervals in roughly 1.5 m depth, yielding 65 field concentration profiles with hydraulic and sediment metadata.
claims.regime: Sixty-five profiles; seven simultaneous elevations starting about 1 cm above bed; approximately 3 min samples in about 1.5 m water depth.

claims.text: A quantitative Venice Lagoon assessment maps cumulative human disturbance of shallow coastal seabeds and associated geomorphic footprints.
claims.regime: Assessing the human footprint on the sea-floor of coastal systems: the case of the Venice Lagoon, Italy

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Relevant controls include excursion relative to domain scale, release duration relative to tide, inertial and windage response, horizontal/vertical diffusivity, sampling interval relative to decorrelation time, and observation duration relative to residence time.
synthesis.disagreements: SF6/tracer models and drifter/particle models predicted different larval fate in the same lagoon experiment, showing that apparent validation depends on tracer type, vertical sampling, biological spread, and the transport quantity compared.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Accessible observations include an eight-day lagoon cohort/SF6/drifter comparison, centimetre-accuracy 10 Hz shallow-water drifters, three UAV dye campaigns, and three nine-probe estuary plume releases.
synthesis.governing_physics: Observed transport reflects mean currents, tides, wind and Ekman flow, waves and surf-zone currents, fronts, vertical shear, turbulence, bathymetry, shoreline interaction, and particle buoyancy or behavior.
synthesis.limitations: Surface windage, drogue slip, positioning error, dye photochemistry, finite release duration, sparse recovery, vertical motion, shoreline loss, imperfect concentration calibration, model resolution, and ambiguous timescale definitions bias inference.
synthesis.major_equations: Core tools include advection-diffusion, single- and pair-particle statistics, residence/flushing/age/transit definitions, trajectory integration, coherent structures, mass balance, and model-observation skill metrics.
synthesis.numerical_models: Trajectory and tracer models range from local lagoon and shoreline-release simulations to coupled wave-current shelf models and climatological coherent structures; model particles require observational checks against scalar and drifter behavior.
synthesis.open_questions: Needs include vertical and three-dimensional dispersion, intermittent fronts and rip exchange, storm sampling, shoreline/beaching processes, multi-tracer intercomparison, source attribution, adaptive releases, and uncertainty propagation into residence and connectivity metrics.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent advances include centimetre RTK positioning, low-cost open electronics, UAV tracer concentration maps, multiscale wave-current tracer models, and climatological coherent pathways for persistent transport diagnosis.
synthesis.seminal_papers: The branch connects classical dye and inert-gas dispersion, Lagrangian drifters, diagnostic timescales, biological cohort tracking, particle trajectories, and coherent-structure analysis.
synthesis.typical_methods: Methods include soluble fluorescent or SF6 releases, GPS/RTK surface and subsurface drifters, introduced biological cohorts, conductivity plume probes, UAV concentration imaging, Eulerian co-observations, particle models, and Lagrangian coherent structures.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Reported capabilities include 10 Hz centimetre positioning, motion resolved to 1 Hz, UAV concentration grids of 2×2 m, three releases of nine probes, and basin-scale attraction attribution of 44% to the Black Sea Rim Current.
synthesis.well_established: Tracers and drifters reveal coastal advection, dispersion, retention, and exchange, but scalar parcels, surface drifters, subsurface drogues, organisms, and numerical particles can follow different pathways.

claims.text: Coastal residence, flushing, age, and transit times must be explicitly defined because they answer different transport questions and depend on the chosen Lagrangian or Eulerian framework.
claims.regime: Lagrangian, Eulerian, field, model, and algebraic timescales are not interchangeable and require explicit definitions and process scope.

claims.text: An eight-day lagoon experiment found SF6/tracer-model and drifter/particle predictions disagreed and observed larval spreading along the advective path that the models omitted.
claims.regime: SF6/tracer-model fate disagreed with drifter/particle predictions and observed larvae spread along the advective path, exposing missing dispersion mechanisms.

claims.text: Gulf transport synthesis identifies coupled river, wind, wave, tide, front, inlet, shelf, and open-ocean processes as controls on tracer fate, with storm fluxes and multiscale coupling unresolved.
claims.regime: Winds, waves, tides, river inputs, fronts, shelf-deep-ocean exchange, and multiscale advection jointly control constituent fate; storm fluxes and scale coupling remain uncertain.

claims.text: A 10 Hz centimetre-accuracy RTK-GNSS shallow-water drifter resolved motion to 1 Hz and yielded dispersion coefficients comparable to dye-tracer studies.
claims.regime: The low-windage drifter resolved motion to 1 Hz, captured tidal elevation, and produced shallow-estuary dispersion estimates comparable to dye studies.

claims.text: A shoreline-dye simulation attributed alongshore transport to wave breaking and pressure gradients and offshore exchange to wind-driven Ekman flow and submesoscale frontogenesis rather than tides.
claims.regime: Wave breaking and pressure gradients drove alongshore transport; wind-driven Ekman and submesoscale frontogenesis contributed cross-shelf exchange, while tides did not explain it.

claims.text: UAV visible imagery calibrated against a fluorometer mapped fluorescent-tracer concentration on a 2×2 m grid across three measurement campaigns.
claims.regime: Visible-camera imagery produced georeferenced fluorescein and Rhodamine WT concentration maps on a 2×2 m grid.

claims.text: HF-radar Lagrangian diagnostics at 3.5–25 km scales link attracting fronts and negative divergence to phytoplankton clustering, while positive-divergence filaments indicate upward nutrient injection and high chlorophyll.

claims.text: A 250 m triangular oxygen-control volume on a Hawaiian reef produced Eulerian net-production estimates agreeing with dye-based Lagrangian estimates at r²=0.81; drifters moved 30–100% faster than dye and depth-mean currents.
claims.regime: Continuous measurements of net production over a shallow reef community using a modified Eulerian approach

claims.text: Validation with 4,130 drifter–radar pairs gave X-band radar near-surface current RMSE of 4 cm/s and direction error of 12°, resolving roughly 500 m currents to 3 km range.
claims.regime: Near-Surface Current Mapping by Shipboard Marine X-Band Radar: A Validation

claims.text: Marine population connectivity cannot be inferred from circulation alone: resolving larval pathways requires coordinated Lagrangian physical observations and biological evidence because fronts, stratification, vertical behavior, tides, mortality, and spawning timing jointly shape dispersal.
claims.regime: Coastal, shelf, bay and estuarine transport of weakly swimming marine early life stages, with source-specific hydrodynamic and biological controls.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Controls include relative depth, wave steepness, surf-similarity, directional spread, transmission coefficient, vegetation or reef submergence, fetch, current-to-wave celerity ratio, sensor separation relative to wavelength and error normalized by wave height.
synthesis.disagreements: Buoys provide reliable point spectra but sparse spatial sampling; altimeters broaden coverage yet degrade nearshore and may miss extrema; HF radar maps coastal fields but requires local validation. Aggregated height and period can conceal materially different multimodal spectra.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Reviewed evidence spans ten natural-beach setup/runup campaigns, 90 days of SandyDuck setup, living-shoreline and oyster sites, tropical-storm marsh records, a seasonal saltmarsh dataset, 40 years of harbor spectra, Iberian HF-radar/buoy/altimetry comparisons and northeastern US multi-mission altimetry.
synthesis.governing_physics: Wind-sea and swell propagate, refract, shoal, break, reflect and interact with currents, bottom stress, vegetation and structures; resulting spectra, setup, runup and attenuation depend on bathymetry, water level, directional partitions and local morphology.
synthesis.limitations: Mooring motion, pressure attenuation, sidelobes, currents, breaking, biofouling, gaps, clock or datum error, land contamination, satellite revisit, short campaigns and changing bathymetry create bias. Extreme-event sampling and directional validation are especially sparse.
synthesis.major_equations: Wave observations are summarized by spectral moments, significant height, periods and directions; energy-flux and radiation-stress balances connect transformation to setup, while transmission ratios compare incident and lee energy. Validation uses bias, RMSE, correlation, scatter and distributional or spectral scores.
synthesis.numerical_models: Field evidence evaluates empirical setup/runup parameterizations, roller and bottom-stress setup models, porous-transmission theory, vegetation-aware MIKE SW, harbor spectral reconstruction and remote-sensing retrieval algorithms. Models remain conditional on sensor and site coverage.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities include seamless multisensor fusion, coastal altimetry and SAR calibration, directional and infragravity retrieval, uncertainty-aware extremes, affordable dense arrays, autonomous quality control, changing-bathymetry correction and standardized open benchmark campaigns.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent advances combine new coastal altimeters and SAR, compact directional buoys, distributed acoustic sensing, video and radar, autonomous vehicles, cloud-based spectral partitioning and assimilation of heterogeneous observations into operational wave models.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Pressure and buoy spectra established field wave statistics; array methods enabled direction, radiation-stress studies tied waves to setup, and satellite altimetry plus HF radar extended spatial coverage. Long-term coastal observatories connected these methods.
synthesis.typical_methods: Campaigns collocate buoys, pressure sensors, ADCPs, wave staffs, HF radar, altimetry and shoreline measurements; synchronize clocks and datums, apply response and depth corrections, partition spectra, quality-control breaking and land contamination, quantify sampling uncertainty and validate derived quantities across sea states.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Iberian Sentinel-3 comparisons achieved correlations above 0.94, bias below 0.19 m and RMSE 0.17-0.42 m; SandyDuck setup agreed within about 30% to 6 m depth; other results cover their stated beaches, structures, vegetation and harbor regimes only.
synthesis.well_established: Field wave observations require complementary in situ and remote sensors because no platform simultaneously resolves nearshore transformation, directional spectra, extremes and broad spatial coverage; uncertainty grows near land, shallow water, breaking and vegetation or structures.

claims.text: Against Iberian buoys, Sentinel-3 significant-wave-height observations achieved correlations above 0.94, biases below 0.19 m, and RMSE of 0.17-0.42 m, enabling spatial validation of HF-radar wave retrievals.
claims.regime: West Iberian Sentinel-3/buoy collocations from 2017-2019; nearshore sampling and sea-state limits apply.

claims.text: Spotter real-time buoy bulk wave statistics were within 10% of a Datawell reference across stand and field tests, enabling multi-buoy measurements of decorrelation, speed and directional spread.
claims.regime: Performance Characteristics of “Spotter,” a Newly Developed Real-Time Wave Measurement Buoy

inundation.label: Flood mapping and inundation
inundation.description: Prediction and representation of flood extent and depth.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Useful controls include Froude number, relative depth, friction and slope ratios, Courant number, grid spacing relative to hydraulic controls, DEM error relative to flood depth, compound-driver dependence, validation overlap and depth-error metrics, and computational speedup.
synthesis.disagreements: Fast terrain-based or learned models can support large-domain warning but may miss momentum, inter-catchment exchange or compound pathways; high-resolution hydrodynamics represents these processes but costs more and remains sensitive to terrain and friction. Extent-only agreement can conceal depth or timing error.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Reviewed evidence includes the 2010 Kabul flood, historical dam-break test cases, MERIT/SRTM ensembles benchmarked against lidar, the 2016 Brazos Landsat extent, southwest Florida climate ensembles, Cork compound scenarios, the 2000 Langat flood and sparse-observation mapping applications.
synthesis.governing_physics: Flood waves spread according to pressure gradients, inertia, friction and topographic connectivity; rainfall, runoff, river discharge, tide, surge, waves and failures can interact. Small elevation errors can open or close flow paths, while defenses and drainage create thresholds and discontinuities.
synthesis.limitations: DEM bias, unresolved buildings and defenses, uncertain roughness and drainage, sparse extreme observations, boundary dependence, climate and downscaling spread, numerical wetting/drying choices and inconsistent validation metrics limit confidence. Static maps do not demonstrate event forecasting skill.
synthesis.major_equations: Models solve shallow-water or diffusion-wave mass and momentum equations, sometimes coupled to rainfall–runoff and coastal boundary models. Reduced approaches use HAND or storage/connectivity rules; surrogates emulate depth and extent, while probabilistic maps integrate hazard frequency and uncertain inputs.
synthesis.numerical_models: Representations include coupled rainfall–runoff–inundation diffusion waves, full shallow-water solvers on structured or unstructured grids, HAND, MIKE11 GIS, MSN_Flood, Gaussian-process/EOF surrogates and physics-aware classifiers. Model choice trades process fidelity, data needs and forecast speed.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities include dynamic defense and drainage failure, compound dependence, urban microtopography, transparent DEM ensembles, rapid depth-and-velocity surrogates, transfer under nonstationarity, observation assimilation and common multi-variable validation benchmarks.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent advances simulate spatial DEM error, learn physics-aware maps from sparse data, emulate unstructured high-resolution models, integrate pluvial–fluvial–coastal drivers and translate climate ensembles into changing inundation magnitude and recurrence.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Early storage-cell and shallow-water models established dynamic floodplain routing; GIS and DEM methods enabled regional mapping, and satellite observations supported extent validation. Modern work combines high-resolution solvers, ensembles and emulators for operational and climate-scale analysis.
synthesis.typical_methods: Workflows assemble conditioned terrain, roughness, drainage and defenses; generate rainfall, river and coastal boundaries; solve 1D/2D hydraulics or surrogates; validate against satellite extent, lidar, gauges, water marks and arrival times; and propagate forcing, parameter, DEM and model-structure uncertainty.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Reported performance is case-specific: Brazos extent overlap ranged 56–70%, Langat sampled-map agreement was 70%, and one hybrid surrogate was 12 times faster than its high-resolution model. These metrics use different observations and cannot be directly ranked as universal skill.
synthesis.well_established: Inundation is controlled by conservation of water across connected terrain, with wetting and drying, storage, friction, drainage, defenses and boundary forcing determining extent, depth, velocity and arrival time. Reliable maps require both hydraulic realism and defensible terrain and forcing data.

claims.text: Coastal inundation assessment must jointly represent changing storm forcing, sea-level rise, precipitation and their probabilistic dependence because their combined effects can alter both flood magnitude and recurrence nonlinearly.
claims.regime: Large southwest Florida coastal floodplain and the study's climate/downscaling scenarios.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Important nondimensional controls include relative tsunami amplitude H/d, Froude and friction measures, relative terrain and building scale, ensemble exceedance probability, normalized error metrics, and ratios of wave, surge, tide, rainfall, and river contributions to total water level.
synthesis.disagreements: The evidence does not support one universally preferred representation of urban form: explicit high-resolution geometry can improve routing and visualization, while subgrid directional drag can capture building effects more efficiently. Their relative accuracy and cost remain configuration-dependent.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Validation evidence includes Synolakis plane-beach and Briggs conical-island runup tests, the 1:250 HyTOFU Onagawa urban-tsunami experiment, NOAA and USGS Hurricane Ike records, Colombian Hurricane Iota profiles and flood maps, surveyed Haiyan inundation limits, and observed Korean coastal-city flood extent.
synthesis.governing_physics: The reviewed models combine long-wave or reduced shallow-water propagation, surge, wave setup and runup, rainfall-runoff and river inflow, bed and building drag, topographic control, urban blockage, and moving shorelines. Which mechanisms are retained materially changes predicted extent and depth.
synthesis.limitations: Common limitations are uncertain topography and bathymetry, forcing and dependence assumptions, friction and building closure, omitted waves or compound drivers, limited field observations, resolution sensitivity, computational cost, and validation against only one or a few historical events.
synthesis.major_equations: Core formulations include nonlinear Boussinesq or shallow-water continuity and momentum equations, bottom-friction and directional building-drag source terms, wet-dry algorithms, nonstationary extreme-value and joint-probability models, raster depth-damage functions, and ensemble exceedance probabilities.
synthesis.numerical_models: Reviewed models include a higher-order Boussinesq inundation model, coupled MIKE 21 and XBeach configurations, an RDM plus Zero-Point Boundary method, a distributed hydrologic-GIS damage chain, an urban Drag Force Model, SFINCS compound-flood ensembles, and explicit high-precision 3D urban simulation.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities include transferable urban roughness and blockage closures, multi-event and multi-site benchmarks, explicit wave-pluvial-fluvial-surge coupling, nonstationary ensemble generation, terrain and friction uncertainty propagation, probabilistic spatial validation, and operational accuracy-cost criteria.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent advances pair reduced-complexity coastal solvers with large forcing ensembles, retain useful multi-day forecast skill, parameterize unresolved buildings directionally, resolve cities with LiDAR and drone-derived geometry, and report omission warnings when computational constraints remove wave effects.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Within this screened branch, the 2015 higher-order Boussinesq application established explicit regional tsunami inundation with laboratory runup validation, while the 2017 Manhattan study linked nonstationary compound forcing to mapped damage.
synthesis.typical_methods: Typical methods couple terrain and bathymetry preprocessing with depth-averaged or reduced-complexity solvers, deterministic hindcasts, probabilistic forcing ensembles, laboratory or gage validation, observed-extent comparison, sensitivity analysis, and GIS exposure or damage overlays.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Reported validation regimes span solitary-wave plane beaches and conical islands with H/d of 0.10-0.20, a 1:250 idealized Onagawa city, Hurricane Iota in the Colombian archipelago, a 5 m Haiyan terrain model with 81% surveyed-limit accuracy, and Hurricane Ike ensembles of 81-1000 members at one- to three-day lead times.
synthesis.well_established: Coastal inundation prediction requires explicit wetting and drying plus defensible marine and terrestrial forcing. Validation must be process- and site-specific: agreement for one tsunami geometry, hurricane, city, resolution, or water-level metric does not establish universal model skill.

claims.text: For Manhattan, incorporating nonstationarity increased modeled coastal floodplain extent and damage, whereas defining scenarios with the joint probability of rainfall and water level reduced them relative to combinations that did not account for dependence.
claims.regime: Manhattan rainfall and coastal water-level records, the study's three scenarios, distributed model, DEM, land-use, and depth-damage functions.

claims.text: A drag-force inundation model represented unresolved urban structures with characteristic height and directional projected areas and was validated against the 1:250 HyTOFU idealization of Onagawa.
claims.regime: Tsunami inundation through building fields representable by the three DFM parameters; validation is bounded by the 1:250 idealized Onagawa experiment.

claims.text: For Hurricane Ike on the Texas Gulf Coast, SFINCS ensemble means reduced average station errors by 16% versus a deterministic case, and a roughly 100-member ensemble ran in under four hours on one CPU while retaining useful one- to three-day flood guidance.
claims.regime: Hurricane Ike, the modeled Texas Gulf Coast domain, 81-1000 members, one- to three-day lead times, stated forcing and terrain data, and SFINCS assumptions.

claims.text: In a Korean coastal-city case, a high-precision 3D urban inundation model reasonably matched observed flood extent and indicated that explicit building geometry matters for routing and visualization, although quantitative skill was not reported in the accessible record.
claims.regime: The studied Korean coastal city and the available high-definition maps, LiDAR, drone imagery, and 3D city representation.

claims.text: A coupled rainfall–runoff–inundation model using 2D diffusion-wave equations reproduced the MODIS-derived large-scale 2010 Kabul River flood extent and identified flash-flood damage areas across a 92,605 km² basin.
claims.regime: Rainfall–runoff–inundation analysis of the 2010 Pakistan flood in the Kabul River basin

claims.text: Historical dam-break validation data are most useful when breach geometry, maximum depths, arrival times, water marks, flood extent, topography and scenario inputs are sufficiently documented; the review separates complete from partial test cases.
claims.regime: Review of Historical Dam-Break Events and Laboratory Tests on Real Topography for the Validation of Numerical Models

claims.text: For ungauged Hurghada, an integrated GIS, remote-sensing, 2D rainfall–runoff–inundation and multicriteria workflow mapped hazard and seven-component vulnerability for 5-, 10- and 50-year return periods.
claims.regime: Integrated Methodology for Urban Flood Risk Mapping at the Microscale in Ungauged Regions: A Case Study of Hurghada, Egypt
