nature_based.reefs.label: Reefs and living shorelines
nature_based.reefs.description: Oyster, coral, and constructed reef protection.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Important nondimensional controls are relative crest or reef height, relative submergence, porosity, transmission coefficient, friction and resistance coefficients, relative wave height and depth, and ratios separating wave, infragravity, and locally generated lagoon energy.
synthesis.disagreements: Short-term hybrid success and decade-scale native-reef failure are not universal contradictions: structure, exposure, recruitment, salinity, maintenance, and monitoring horizon differ. Likewise, wave-height amplification over a submerged reef need not imply increased energy flux, so performance metrics must match the erosion mechanism.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Key datasets include nearly 1000 boat wakes at two Florida breakwalls, a four-year three-site hybrid intervention, six Louisiana reefs revisited after ten years, four paired-tray sites on two Great Barrier Reef systems, a steep-faced reef-platform experiment, and comparative restored-oyster substrates in Virginia.
synthesis.governing_physics: Breaking on reef rims creates setup and cross-reef pressure gradients; porous and rough reef material dissipates energy; emergence, submergence, wave breaking, bottom friction, lagoon wind-wave generation, and bidirectional sediment resuspension determine the realized response.
synthesis.limitations: Most studies cover few sites, narrow structural designs, boat wakes or ordinary wind waves rather than extremes, and limited design lives. Geometry, biology, water quality, sea-level rise, material degradation, and maintenance covary, preventing simple transfer of one attenuation coefficient.
synthesis.major_equations: Core formulations include radiation-stress/setup balances, open-channel reef-top and reef-rim control, energy-flux transmission Kt=sqrt(Ft/Fi), Darcy-Forchheimer porous resistance, shallow-water breaking and friction balances, and paired-tray sediment mass balance.
synthesis.numerical_models: The screened evidence uses analytical reef-control and porous-transmission models plus phase-averaged SWAN and surfbeat-resolving XBeach; model choice must preserve locally generated wind waves when they dominate reef-lagoon storm energy.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities are storm-scale multi-site validation, coupled ecology-hydraulics-morphology prediction, lifecycle performance under recruitment failure and sea-level rise, metric choice for height versus energy flux, maintainable porous materials, and adaptive thresholds for intervention.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent work shifts from proving short-term attenuation toward optimizing substrate and elevation, testing decade-scale ecological persistence, resolving cyclone-specific model physics, and embedding future conditions, maintenance, and adaptive action into design.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Within this screened slice, the 2005 steep-faced reef study establishes coupled setup-flow control, while the 2020 paired breakwall studies connect porous-transmission physics to measured shoreline and habitat response.
synthesis.typical_methods: Evidence combines reef-platform flumes, pressure and velocity arrays across porous structures, paired treatment-control shoreline experiments, oyster demographic and topographic surveys, sediment mass balances, spectral and surfbeat models, and multi-year lifecycle monitoring.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Observed regimes include 0.7-porosity branch barriers with mean energy transmission 53%, 0.9-porosity barriers with 83%, relative breakwall height about 0.5-1 for clear tidal modulation, four-year shoreline trends from about 1 m/y advance to nearly 2 m/y retreat, and ten-year oyster density below 60 individuals/m2 with erosion near 1 m/y.
synthesis.well_established: Reefs and reef-like living shorelines can reduce wave energy, currents, and shoreline erosion, but protection is conditional on crest elevation relative to water level, porosity and roughness, reef width and morphology, incident forcing, sediment setting, biological persistence, and maintenance.

claims.text: For a laboratory steep-faced horizontal reef, wave-generated flow was organized into reef-top-control and reef-rim-control regimes, and coupled open-channel setup-flow relationships reproduced most measured values with reasonable accuracy.
claims.regime: Two-dimensional horizontal reef tops with steep faces under wave-driven quasi-steady flow.

claims.text: Ten years after construction of six Louisiana oyster reefs, oyster density was below 60 individuals/m2 versus above 1000/m2 during 2009-2011, and both reef and reference shorelines continued eroding at about 1 m/y.
claims.regime: Sister Lake native-shell fringing reefs exposed to highly variable salinity; results do not imply all oyster defenses fail.

claims.text: A restored-oyster field study found that coastal-protection performance depends jointly on reef elevation, substrate type, and adjacent marsh-edge morphology, with wave dissipation effective primarily when water depth is near or below reef crest height.
claims.regime: The tested Virginia intertidal reef designs and wind-wave conditions; storm-scale and long-term transfer remain unresolved.

claims.text: Regular-wave experiments over an idealized steep-faced fringing reef showed that wave transformation is controlled by shoaling and breaking at the reef edge followed by reforming waves over the reef flat, providing a bounded laboratory basis for predicting reef-flat wave heights and setup.
claims.regime: Regular waves over the tested steep-face, sloping reef-top physical models; extrapolation to irregular, directional and strongly three-dimensional reefs is limited.

claims.text: Across the coral-reef studies synthesized by the meta-analysis, reefs reduced wave energy by an average of 97%, with reef crests accounting for 86% dissipation; these global averages should not be treated as site-specific design coefficients.
claims.regime: Global coral-reef evidence synthesized in the indexed abstract; site-specific hydrodynamic regimes are not recoverable from the abstract.

claims.text: Flume measurements showed restored coral-canopy attenuation rose with coral cover; force–velocity energy loss agreed with observed wave-height decay, and well-designed canopies dissipated more than 50% of incoming energy under typical reef-flat conditions.
claims.regime: Wave Attenuation by Restored Coral Reef Canopies: Implications for Coastal Protection

claims.text: An oyster-reef restoration review recommends matching site, substrate, species and genotype to future environmental suitability and explicit ecosystem-service and socioeconomic goals.
claims.regime: Contemporary Oyster Reef Restoration: Responding to a Changing World

equations.name: Wave-energy transformation balance
equations.regime: Regular waves over the tested steep-face, sloping reef-top physical models; extrapolation to irregular, directional and strongly three-dimensional reefs is limited.
equations.variables: {"E": "wave energy density", "C_g": "group velocity", "D_b": "breaking dissipation", "D_f": "bottom-friction or other dissipation"}

nature_based.reefs.breakwalls.label: Living shoreline breakwalls
nature_based.reefs.breakwalls.description: Porous brush, branch, reef, and modular barriers used to attenuate waves while retaining ecological connectivity.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Controls include porosity, relative structure height and submergence, width relative to wavelength, transmitted-to-incident energy, water depth relative to crest, wake steepness, shoreline-change rate normalized by control retreat and maintenance interval relative to material lifetime.
synthesis.disagreements: Greater material density and lower porosity can improve attenuation but increase cost, ecological footprint and failure load; biodegradable components support habitat goals yet require replacement. Short-term wave reduction does not guarantee multi-year shoreline benefit, and shoreline stability does not isolate each component contribution.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Reviewed evidence comprises 290 boat wakes at bundled and unbundled branch breakwalls and 2015-2019 monitoring at three energetic northeast Florida shorelines with brush breakwalls, oyster gabions and paired controls.
synthesis.governing_physics: For the lower-porosity design, transmission rose with tidal depth most clearly for relative structure height hs/h approximately 0.5-1; near emergence, breaking and bottom friction added dissipation absent from the porous-only theory.
synthesis.limitations: Biodegradable branch fill required recurring maintenance and lasted roughly one year, whereas the supporting posts persisted longer; hydraulic performance alone is therefore insufficient for lifecycle design. The observed 0.7-versus-0.9 porosity contrast is not a controlled porosity experiment because branch bundling, field site, and tidal range changed simultaneously.
synthesis.major_equations: Performance is described by wave-energy transmission and reflection ratios, energy-flux balances, porous resistance and shoreline-position or retreat-rate comparisons between treatment and control. Long-term benefit additionally requires a service-life and maintenance balance for biodegradable fill and stable supports.
synthesis.numerical_models: A calibrated porous-transmission formulation represents branch resistance but omits some external breaking and bottom friction near emergence. The shoreline study uses treatment-control field comparison rather than a predictive morphodynamic model.
synthesis.open_questions: Controlled multi-site evidence is needed to separate porosity, material, geometry, tides, breaking, sediment response, ecological performance, durability, storms, and maintenance cost.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent advances combine modular biodegradable fills, oyster gabions and hybrid sills, field spectral monitoring, UAV shoreline and habitat mapping, life-cycle and maintenance accounting, adaptive replacement and coupled hydrodynamic–ecological performance metrics.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Permeable breakwater and brush-fence studies established porous attenuation, while oyster-reef and living-shoreline experiments extended performance to ecological structures and paired shoreline controls, reframing maintenance and biological development as design variables.
synthesis.typical_methods: Studies deploy incident and lee wave sensors across tides and boat wakes, characterize porosity and geometry, pair protected and reference marsh margins, repeat shoreline surveys over years, track oyster or vegetation response and document repair frequency, component loss and functional lifetime.
synthesis.validated_ranges: The bundled n=0.7 design transmitted mostly 9%-70% of incident wake energy and averaged 53% during the GTM deployment. The unbundled n=0.9 design transmitted more than 70% of energy for 84% of wakes and averaged 83% during the North Peninsula deployment.
synthesis.well_established: The reviewed branch-and-post living breakwalls reduced boat-wake energy, but attenuation depended strongly on design and tidal depth rather than following a single transferable transmission rate.

claims.text: For the bundled-branch breakwall with estimated porosity 0.7, observed wave-energy transmission was mostly 9%-70% and averaged 53%.
claims.regime: GTM branch-and-post design, approximately 4.3 by 0.6 by 0.55 m, boat wakes and tides observed in March-April 2018.

claims.text: For the unbundled-branch breakwall with estimated porosity 0.9, energy transmission exceeded 70% in 84% of wake cases and averaged 83%.
claims.regime: NP branch-and-post design, approximately 4.3 by 0.6 by 0.55 m, boat wakes and smaller tidal range observed in April-May 2019.

claims.text: The branch fill required maintenance every four to six months at GTM and had an estimated functional life of 12-18 months, while unbundled NP fill lasted less than one year; fence posts remained stable after three years.
claims.regime: Crepe-myrtle bundled fill at GTM and eastern-cedar unbundled fill at NP under local bioerosion and vessel-wake exposure.

claims.text: From 2015-2019 at three wake-exposed northeast Florida sites, marsh margins protected by brush breakwalls and oyster gabions were stable or advanced about 1 m/y, whereas paired controls retreated at rates approaching 2 m/y.
claims.regime: Vessel-wake-dominated estuarine marshes with 1-1.5 m semidiurnal tide and local oyster recruitment.

claims.text: Replicated oyster-shell breakwater reefs reduced shoreline retreat by more than 40% at one site and enhanced several fish and invertebrate groups, but loss of reef relief compromised protection and erosion remained high.
claims.regime: Oyster Reefs as Natural Breakwaters Mitigate Shoreline Loss and Facilitate Fisheries

claims.text: At Kutubdia Island, oyster breakwaters attenuated 0.1–0.5 m waves, accumulated 29 cm of lee-side sediment, reduced erosion 54% relative to controls and facilitated seaward saltmarsh expansion.
claims.regime: Oyster breakwater reefs promote adjacent mudflat stability and salt marsh growth in a monsoon dominated subtropical coast

claims.text: Across US oyster living shorelines, reefs inundated under 50% of the time attenuated wave height by 68% but were unsuitable oyster habitat, whereas suitable reefs above 50% inundation attenuated only about 5%, exposing an ecological–engineering design trade-off.
claims.regime: Large‐scale variation in wave attenuation of oyster reef living shorelines and the influence of inundation duration

claims.text: Validated FUNWAVE-TVD simulations indicate oyster-reef attenuation depends on waves and depth and can remain sustainable under sea-level rise only with viable growth habitat; modeled maximum capacity required about nine years after construction.
claims.regime: Assessing Wave Attenuation With Rising Sea Levels for Sustainable Oyster Reef-Based Living Shorelines

claims.text: Seven-year Gandy's Beach monitoring found constructed oyster reefs met most habitat objectives but none of the material-stability, wave-attenuation, or sediment-elevation protection objectives fully, demonstrating the need for goal-specific long-term monitoring.
claims.regime: Seven Years of Monitoring the Development of an Oyster Reef Living Shoreline

nature_based.vegetation.label: Vegetation and wave attenuation
nature_based.vegetation.description: Marsh, mangrove, and flexible vegetation effects.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Key controls include Ursell number, Cauchy number, excursion ratio, Keulegan-Carpenter and Reynolds numbers, relative plant/root height and submergence, solid volume fraction, current-to-orbital velocity ratio, effective-length ratio, and layout spacing Sr.
synthesis.disagreements: Apparent conflicts over whether larger or longer waves attenuate more arise because nonlinearity, submergence, flexibility, current, and normalization length vary together. Likewise, local heterogeneity can matter for gaps and extremes even when mean plant properties suffice for bulk engineering attenuation.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Evidence spans four flexible species analogues, a 17.5 m mangrove array, 112 component-resolved tests, 24 simultaneous motion/velocity cases, 177 Tropical Storm Lee wave records, four spatial layouts, five-species validation, and 1205 seasonal plant measurements.
synthesis.governing_physics: Drag depends on relative water-plant velocity and wetted frontal area; flexibility redistributes motion and dissipation vertically; nonlinear orbital kinematics, current-modified group velocity, diffraction through gaps, breaking, and canopy submergence alter spatial decay.
synthesis.limitations: Most evidence uses idealized cylindrical vegetation, short patches, regular or narrow condition sets, fixed beds, and calibrated or assumed force coefficients. Extreme folding, breakage, mortality, currents, directional spectra, morphodynamics, and cross-site ecological variability remain weakly constrained.
synthesis.major_equations: Common formulations balance wave-energy flux against vegetation drag, use transmission or decay coefficients, Ursell and Cauchy scaling, Euler-Bernoulli stem response, a corrected work factor chi, current-aware reciprocal-to-exponential decay, and Weibull statistics for attenuated random heights.
synthesis.numerical_models: Models include Dalrymple/Kobayashi and modified Weibull relations, SWASH, Euler-Bernoulli quasi-flexible damping, NEWFLUME RANS, spacing/diffraction energy balance, and momentum-coupled frequency-distributed MIKE SW.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities include storm-scale field validation across species and seasons, flexible layered architecture under reversing currents, damage and recovery, directional gap effects, uncertainty in extreme tails, and coupling attenuation to sediment, morphology, and ecological persistence.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent work replaces locally tuned damping with measurable mechanics, adds current-induced asymmetry and layout uniformity, and embeds seasonal heterogeneous vegetation into spectral models while preserving field-scale computational efficiency.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Within this screened slice, the 2013 tropical-storm Weibull study provides rare extreme-event field statistics, while the 2014 flexible-vegetation experiments establish multi-trait attenuation ranges beyond rigid-cylinder assumptions.
synthesis.typical_methods: Studies use plant-mimic and live-plant flumes, field pressure arrays during storms, simultaneous stem-motion and velocity measurements, energy-balance theory, RANS or phase-resolving validation, spectral-wave implementation, and stochastic vegetation-property sampling.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Reported ranges include 20-76% reduction over 1 m, transmission 0.21-0.83, Ur about 20-250, quasi-flexible applicability L>1.4 and Ca<700, current ratio -1.5 to 3.0, Sr transition at one, and storm Hs to 0.4 m in 0.8 m depth; each is experiment-specific.
synthesis.well_established: Vegetation attenuates waves through hydrodynamic work on stems, roots, and canopies, but performance is jointly controlled by plant geometry, density, flexibility, vertical submergence, spatial layout, wave nonlinearity, current, patch length, and seasonal state.

claims.text: Across four flexible salt-marsh vegetation analogues, measured wave-height reduction over a 1 m patch ranged from 20% to 76%; damping depended jointly on plant geometry, density, flexibility, submergence, and wave conditions rather than marsh width alone.
claims.regime: The tested flexible mimics, one-metre patch, irregular waves, and submerged-to-emergent conditions.

claims.text: In 200-400 stem/m2 mangrove analogues, increasing Ursell number from about 50 to 250 increased wave-height attenuation by roughly 20 percentage points over one wavelength and 35 over three, while sensitivity weakened above about Ur=250.
claims.regime: Rigid arrays, Ur approximately 20-250, tested broken/non-broken regular and irregular waves.

claims.text: Across 112 stem-root-canopy experiments, vegetation transmission coefficients ranged from 0.21 to 0.83; roots contributed significantly when relative root height exceeded 0.167, and attenuation peaked when still water lay near the canopy centroid.
claims.regime: Fixed-period waves and the tested idealized seven-model, four-density component geometries.

claims.text: For quasi-flexible cylindrical vegetation with excursion ratio L>1.4 and Cauchy number Ca<700, damping was governed by relative water-stem velocity in the upright lower stem, and the model reproduced the order of damping across five species without species-specific drag calibration.
claims.regime: Regular waves, cylindrical vegetation, L>1.4, Ca<700, without extreme folding.

claims.text: During a tropical storm, 177 wave records across 28 m of Spartina marsh showed an upper-tail deficit relative to Rayleigh statistics; a vegetation-modified Weibull distribution fit the local heights for Hs up to 0.4 m in 0.8 m depth.
claims.regime: The measured tropical-storm event, inundated Spartina marsh, and local wave/depth range.

claims.text: For emerged vegetation and current-to-orbital velocity ratios from -1.5 to 3.0, opposing currents attenuated waves more than equal following currents; increasing current shifted decay from reciprocal toward exponential and made strong-current decay insensitive to incident amplitude.
claims.regime: Uniform emergent vegetation, steady following/opposing current, tested velocity-ratio interval.

claims.text: In four flexible-vegetation layouts, the combined spacing parameter separated laterally uniform attenuation at Sr<1 from nonuniform attenuation at Sr>1, and a staggered layout matched full-coverage uniformity with a smaller vegetation footprint.
claims.regime: The tested half, segmented, staggered, and full layouts and the study's Sr definition.

claims.text: A momentum-coupled MIKE SW vegetation model validated against laboratory and Tropical Storm Lee data reproduced significant wave height and spectral period without prescribed Cdis; analysis of 1205 plant measurements found spatial mean vegetation properties sufficient for engineering predictions despite seasonal lognormal variability.
claims.regime: The tested flexible saltmarsh canopies, fixed force coefficients Cm=0.5 and Cd=2.0, and validated laboratory/field conditions.

claims.text: The formal corrigendum states that work factor chi was omitted from printed Eq. 32 of the quasi-flexible vegetation model; implementations must use the corrected expression containing chi.
claims.regime: Any implementation of Eq. 32 in the corrected 2021 quasi-flexible vegetation model.

claims.text: For validated vegetated-wave cases, a depth-varying velocity drag formulation matched fully expanded Boussinesq results, while the linear analytical solution agreed except near-emergent or emergent vegetation and the abstract's stated Ur<5 regime.
claims.regime: Vegetated laboratory cases and Hurricane Isaac peak-wave simulations; linear comparison degraded for stem-height/depth above 0.75 and Ur<5 as stated in the abstract.

claims.text: In a 1:12 model Rhizophora forest, root-zone velocity decreased by up to 50% and turbulence increased fivefold; velocity and individual-tree drag reached fully developed behavior by the fifth row, and properly scaled drag coefficients collapsed as a Reynolds-number function.
claims.regime: Thirty-two 1:12 Rhizophora models with 24 prop roots each in a 2.5 m staggered forest.

claims.text: Living-shoreline marshes aged 12–38 years sequestered 58–283 g C m⁻² yr⁻¹, with lower rates at older sites, showing that shoreline stabilization can add blue-carbon benefits but age affects long-term estimates.
claims.regime: Living Shorelines: Coastal Resilience with a Blue Carbon Benefit

claims.text: At three of four Port Phillip Bay sites kelp beds attenuated less wave energy than urchin-barren controls; only under northerly winds at the fourth site was kelp attenuation about 10% greater, showing substrate and kelp effects must be separated.
claims.regime: Kelp beds as coastal protection: wave attenuation of Ecklonia radiata in a shallow coastal bay

claims.text: Global process-based valuation estimates mangroves avert more than US$65 billion in flood damage annually and protect 15 million people from annual flooding, with many urban coastal stretches exceeding US$250 million in yearly benefit.
claims.regime: The Global Flood Protection Benefits of Mangroves

claims.text: High-resolution flood-loss models estimate northeastern U.S. wetlands avoided US$625 million in direct Hurricane Sandy damage and reduced average annual Barnegat Bay flood losses by 16%.
claims.regime: The Value of Coastal Wetlands for Flood Damage Reduction in the Northeastern USA

claims.text: Ten months of saltmarsh observations found 92% mean wave-height attenuation over 310 m; the first 10 m of vegetation dissipated 2.1% per metre on a ramped edge versus 1.1% at a cliffed edge, with seasonal variation.
claims.regime: Wave dissipation over macro-tidal saltmarshes: Effects of marsh edge typology and vegetation change

claims.text: Field measurements on two salt marshes and a calibrated SWAN model show that vegetation remains effective under severe storm inundation: with bulk drag coefficient about 0.4, vegetation added 25-50% significant-wave-height reduction relative to breaking and bottom friction alone.
claims.regime: Spartina anglica and Scirpus maritimus salt marshes and modeled sloping foreshores under the tested storm loads and vegetation states.

claims.text: Large-flume tests with flexible vegetation mimics show that stiffness and bending-controlled dynamic frontal area, not biomass alone, govern wave drag; an effective-leaf-length model reproduced regular and irregular force time series but missed extra drag from close-neighbor interaction.
claims.regime: Artificial vegetation arrangements of varied stiffness, frontal area and volume under tested regular and irregular wave orbital velocities.

claims.text: Under comparable inundation in a subtropical estuary, saltmarsh and mangrove edges both trap mudflat-derived suspended sediment, but the saltmarsh edge traps more because mangrove-induced flow rotation diverts normal flux; settling and direct capture on plant surfaces jointly build deposits.
claims.regime: Adjacent bare mudflat, mangrove and saltmarsh stands with similar hydroperiod in a subtropical estuary during the observed spring tide.

claims.text: Temperate kelps are ecosystem engineers whose holdfasts, stipes, blades and understory modify physical conditions, support diverse and abundant assemblages and trophic links, and provide coastal-defense and other ecosystem services, but their habitat function varies strongly among species and regions.
claims.regime: Canopy-forming kelps on temperate and subpolar intertidal and shallow-subtidal rocky reefs represented in the reviewed literature.

claims.text: Wakes from adjacent emergent vegetation patches remain locally patch-specific but merge downstream; in staggered layouts the downstream patch shortens and distorts the upstream wake, and density controls interpatch velocity, turbulence and potential sediment/propagule retention.
claims.regime: Two circular emergent rigid vegetation patches under the tested steady flume flow, densities and side-by-side/staggered spacing.

claims.text: A coupled three-dimensional nonhydrostatic model predicts that a surf-zone vegetation patch damps breaking-wave turbulence, reduces sediment pickup, confines suspended material near the bed, and reverses net transport from seaward outside the patch to shoreward within it.
claims.regime: A finite vegetation patch in the surf zone under breaking waves, with canopy drag, turbulence production, suspended sediment, and bed exchange.

nearshore.label: Nearshore hydrodynamics
nearshore.description: Currents and water-level dynamics in the nearshore zone.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Controls include Froude and Reynolds numbers, wave steepness, relative depth, surf similarity, current-to-wave speed ratio, rip spacing relative to surf width, trough area and onshore discharge, directional spread, normalized headland/reef geometry and dispersion scaling.
synthesis.disagreements: Rips may be bathymetrically controlled, transient without fixed channels, forced by directional breaking, or triggered by meteotsunamis. Mean-cell descriptions can understate intermittent exchange, and drifter velocities can differ from Eulerian flow because of Stokes drift and sampling concentration.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Reviewed evidence includes Scripps scanning-sonar rips, longshore-uniform swell-beach drifters, dense laboratory rip trajectories, a Lake Michigan meteotsunami reconstruction, large-scale short-crested-wave validation, WAMFlow imagery, a three-week headland experiment and four North Sea campaigns.
synthesis.governing_physics: Radiation-stress and pressure gradients, wave mass transport, return flow, bottom friction, wave–current interaction, vorticity generation and turbulent mixing govern circulation. Directional waves, tides, headlands, reefs, bars and channels alter forcing and connectivity.
synthesis.limitations: Sparse spatial sampling, rapidly evolving bars, optical visibility, wave breaking complexity, unmeasured vertical structure, uncertain friction, scale effects and short experiments limit transfer. A model matching mean currents may still miss vortices, dispersion or hazard onset.
synthesis.major_equations: Depth-integrated mass and momentum balances include wave forcing, pressure, advection and bottom stress; wave action or phase-resolving equations provide breaking and radiation stress. Sediment continuity closes morphology feedback, while Lagrangian transport diagnoses exchange and dispersion.
synthesis.numerical_models: Representations range from depth-averaged circulation and radiation-stress models to linear morphology stability, mesh-free SPH, O(1 m) event hindcasts and coupled bar models. Phase-averaged models capture mean cells but may need explicit unsteadiness or vorticity closures.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities include transient-rip predictability, compound meteotsunami and wave hazards, vertical exchange, directional spectra, morphology coevolution, headland transport beyond closure, real-time remote sensing, data assimilation and public-warning thresholds.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent advances use kilometre-scale optical velocimetry, dense Lagrangian arrays, high-resolution forensic hindcasts, mesh-free three-dimensional breaking simulations and coupled structure–bar models to resolve circulation modes missed by sparse instruments.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Radiation-stress theory connected breaking waves to setup and mean currents; early surf-zone observations established undertow, longshore and rip cells. Morphodynamic stability theory then formalized feedback with bed patterns, while drifters and imaging exposed strong unsteadiness.
synthesis.typical_methods: Studies combine current meters, pressure sensors, scanning sonar, drifters, dye/turbidity, imagery and bathymetry with field or basin experiments; wave-averaged, stability, SPH and morphodynamic models test forcing and feedback. Eulerian and Lagrangian observations should be reconciled.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Case values include episodic and headland rip speeds near 0.7 m/s, WAMFlow RMSE near 0.1 m/s, submerged-structure longshore RMSE 0.07 m/s and transient rip-neck widths 20–30 m. These are site-specific measurements and validation metrics, not universal thresholds.
synthesis.well_established: Breaking-wave momentum gradients drive setup, undertow, longshore currents, rip cells and vortices. Bathymetry redirects those currents, which in turn transport sediment, tracers and organisms and reshape the bed, producing strongly coupled and often nonstationary nearshore dynamics.

claims.text: Nearshore hydrodynamics requires spatially resolved observation of nonstationary wave-averaged currents because fixed instruments can miss interacting rips, longshore currents and gyres tied to evolving morphology.
claims.regime: Image-visible surf-zone surface circulation at the study sites.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Controls include normalized infragravity energy or runup, surf-similarity and relative slope, wave-group bandwidth, directional spread, relative bar geometry, reflection coefficient, friction parameter, current-to-long-wave celerity ratio, relative water depth and vertical shear normalized by depth-mean velocity.
synthesis.disagreements: Competing generation descriptions emphasize bound-wave release, breakpoint forcing or nonlinear energy transfer, and observed energy may combine gravity and vortical modes. Depth-averaged agreement in surface elevation does not prove velocity or sediment-transport accuracy.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Reviewed evidence spans controlled runup cases over slopes 0.02-0.04, a modeled barred coastal field site, Albufeira Lagoon Inlet observations and modeling for 25-300 s motions, and Duck94 vertical current profiles around 0.005 Hz.
synthesis.governing_physics: Bound long waves generated by group-scale radiation-stress gradients may release as free leaky or trapped edge waves; shoaling, reflection, breaking, bottom friction, directional spreading, bathymetric trapping, currents and rotational shear control their transformation and dissipation.
synthesis.limitations: Sparse low-frequency records, finite deployments, directional ambiguity, sensor noise near boundaries, uncertain friction and bathymetry, mode leakage, nonstationary storms, current interaction and limited vertical arrays constrain attribution and transferability.
synthesis.major_equations: Models use depth-integrated mass and momentum equations forced by radiation-stress gradients or phase-resolving nonlinear shallow-water/Boussinesq equations; modal decompositions distinguish bound, leaky and edge waves, while vertically structured theory augments depth averages with frictional shear and rotation.
synthesis.numerical_models: The set includes phase-resolving barred-beach and inlet simulations, reduced runup analysis and a theoretical vertical-structure extension. Depth-averaged solvers capture many long-wave transformations but omit observed water-column shear and rotation.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities include unified gravity-vorticity separation, three-dimensional structure, current blocking and Doppler effects, reef and headland trapping, sediment suspension, compound surge interactions, climate dependence and operational assimilation of low-frequency observations.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent advances use dense arrays, remote sensing and distributed pressure sensing, three-dimensional and nonhydrostatic solvers, mode-resolving data assimilation, machine-learned surrogates and coupled infragravity–morphodynamic prediction.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Longuet-Higgins and Stewart linked wave groups to bound long waves; breakpoint-forcing and edge-wave theories explained surf-zone generation and trapping, followed by field bispectral studies and nonlinear phase-resolving models.
synthesis.typical_methods: Studies deploy pressure and vertically stacked velocity sensors, separate frequency and directional bands, estimate bispectra and energy fluxes, decompose modes, compare barred and unbarred transects, force phase-resolving models, close energy balances and validate runup, phase and vertical structure independently.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Evidence covers selected plane slopes, one barred coast, one wave-dominated inlet and one Duck94 frequency band. The relative importance of leaky, trapped, current-blocked and vertically sheared motions is conditional on local bathymetry and forcing.
synthesis.well_established: Infragravity motions occupy frequencies below incident wind waves and arise through wave-group forcing, breakpoint variation and nonlinear transfers; they can dominate shoreline runup, harbor or inlet fluctuations and low-frequency surf-zone currents.

claims.text: Over slopes 0.02-0.04, normalized infragravity runup showed no obvious slope dependence and was controlled more strongly by frequency and directional spread.
claims.regime: Limited moderate-slope, mostly dissipative simulations; not evidence of slope independence outside 0.02-0.04.

claims.text: At the modeled barred field site, infragravity energy was generally dominated by leaky waves, but outer-bar trapped edge waves contributed up to 50% of infragravity variance in mild conditions; shoreward losses shifted among nonlinear transfer, bottom friction, and breaking.
claims.regime: Gently sloping barred beach across mild and storm conditions represented by a validated local wavefield.

claims.text: At Albufeira Lagoon Inlet, observed and modeled 25-300 s infragravity motions were blocked during ebb by opposing currents reaching 2.5 m/s, while flood-period fluctuations temporarily reached 100% of the background current magnitude.
claims.regime: Albufeira Lagoon Inlet observations and simulations, including opposing ebb currents to 2.5 m/s.

claims.text: A theory motivated by Duck94 observations extends depth-averaged low-frequency nearshore dynamics to represent vertical structure associated with frictional and rotational effects.
claims.regime: Duck94 barred surf zone near 0.005 Hz

claims.text: Duck94 observations near 0.005 Hz showed significant vertical structure in low-frequency surf-zone current energy, phase and rotation: cross-shore flow decayed toward the bed, while the weaker alongshore component could increase near the bed.
claims.regime: Duck94 barred surf zone near 0.005 Hz

claims.text: Infragravity transport contributed below 20% on a 1:35 beach but reached about 60% during energetic conditions on a 1:80 beach; HIG/HSW indicated suspension mechanism, direction and relative importance.
claims.regime: Cross-shore sand transport by infragravity waves as a function of beach steepness

claims.text: Bispectral laboratory analysis shows shoaling transfers energy from spectral peaks to harmonics and infragravity waves, while nearshore infragravity interactions dominate and cascade energy toward dissipative high frequencies.
claims.regime: Nonlinear Infragravity–Wave Interactions on a Gently Sloping Laboratory Beach

equations.name: Spectral-spread infragravity-runup fit
equations.regime: Idealized matrix with 0.6<(fp/fs)sigma_theta0<30.
equations.variables: {"Rsig": "significant infragravity runup", "fp": "peak frequency", "fs": "frequency spread", "sigma_theta0": "deep-water directional spread"}

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Important controls include breaker angle, relative water depth, wave height and directional spread, current-to-wave velocity scale, cross-shore shear, friction and mixing coefficients, roller scale, eddy scale relative to surf-zone width, and normalized vertical elevation.
synthesis.disagreements: Low-frequency surf-zone currents are not always explained by instability of the mean alongshore current: a 120-day record showed weak correlation with current strength and shear and stronger consistency with breaking-wave-driven inverse energy transfer.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Evidence includes six 1-2 h Huntington Beach dye releases, 120 days of surf-zone currents, Duck two-dimensional arrays and Duck'94 validation, SUPERDUCK conditions, plane/barred-beach profiles, and barred-beach waves from 0.5-2.0 m at 0-15 degrees.
synthesis.governing_physics: Controls include wave angle, height, directional spread and breaking, radiation stress or vortex force, rollers, setup gradients, bathymetry, vertical shear, bottom and turbulent mixing, shear instability, vortex tilting, and upscale energy transfer.
synthesis.limitations: Steady, depth-uniform, fixed-bathymetry assumptions omit rapid morphology, vertical dispersion, rollers, breaking turbulence, inverse cascades, directional spectra, wind and tides. Sparse field arrays and closure calibration limit transfer.
synthesis.major_equations: Frameworks use wave-action and circulation momentum equations with radiation-stress or vortex-force coupling, roller and breaking closures, turbulence models, shear-wave energy and enstrophy balances, Fickian tracer diffusion, and vertical power laws.
synthesis.numerical_models: Depth-uniform, quasi-three-dimensional, and fully three-dimensional models differ in shear-wave energy, confinement, vortex interactions, and vertical profiles. Bathymetric assimilation and spatially variable roller/turbulence parameters improve skill.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities include partitioning shear instability from breaking-generated cascades, resolving three-dimensional saturation and vertical exchange, assimilating storm-time bathymetry, and predicting material pathways under combined wave, wind, and tidal forcing.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent advances combine months-long observations, phase-resolving three-dimensional models, directional-spread-dependent eddy scaling, bathymetric inversion, and explicit inverse-cascade diagnostics to improve transport prediction.
synthesis.seminal_papers: The shear-instability review traces the discovery and theory of shear waves and their finite-amplitude development; later quasi-3D and vortex-force studies extend that lineage to vertical structure and realistic bathymetry.
synthesis.typical_methods: Methods combine current meters and vertical profiles, continuous dye releases, two-dimensional sensor arrays, long-duration low-frequency observations, bathymetric assimilation, theoretical instability analysis, vortex-force circulation models, SWASH, and coupled SWAN-FVCOM.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Reported evidence includes cross-shore diffusivity of 0.5-2.5 m2/s, low-frequency motions at 0.1-4.0 mHz over 120 days, validated 0.5-2.0 m waves at 0-15 degrees, O(10 m) and O(100 m) eddies, and profile exponents from 1/10 to 1/3.
synthesis.well_established: Obliquely breaking waves drive alongshore momentum and currents whose cross-shore and vertical shear can become unstable. The resulting mean flow, shear waves, vortices, and low-frequency eddies advect and disperse sediment, tracers, organisms, heat, and contaminants.

claims.text: Six Huntington Beach dye releases in wave-driven alongshore currents yielded cross-shore diffusivities of 0.5-2.5 m2/s, with plumes often mixed across the surf zone after a few hundred metres and rotational motions contributing to dispersion.
claims.regime: Huntington Beach surf zone; releases of 1-2 h over varied waves and currents

claims.text: At Duck, ensemble assimilation of wave height and alongshore current corrected bathymetry and circulation, showing that hourly storm-driven morphology changes can make daily bathymetric surveys inadequate for current prediction.
claims.regime: Duck natural beach with two-dimensional wave and current sensor array

claims.text: A three-dimensional Un-SWAN-FVCOM vortex-force model agreed with laboratory and Duck'94 measurements across oblique and barred-beach cases, while spatially variable roller and turbulence effects improved vertical current profiles.
claims.regime: planar beach, barred-beach laboratory case, Duck'94 field case, and breakwater case

claims.text: Over 120 field days, 0.1-4.0 mHz surf-zone currents were weakly correlated with alongshore-current shear or strength but were consistent with an inverse energy cascade energized by short-crested breaking waves.
claims.regime: shallow surf zone across a broad wave range; 0.1-4.0 mHz motions

claims.text: Relative to depth-uniform modelling, quasi-three-dimensional SHORECIRC produced weaker, more shoreward-confined shear waves but similar total momentum mixing through combined shear-wave and depth-varying-current transfers.
claims.regime: idealized SUPERDUCK topography and 16 October 1986 waves

claims.text: SWASH reproduced alongshore-current and rip-cell trends for 0.5-2.0 m waves at 0-15 degrees, with directional spread intensifying roughly 10 m eddies and alongshore bathymetric variability enhancing roughly 100 m eddies.
claims.regime: alongshore-variable barred beach; H=0.5-2.0 m and direction=0-15 degrees

claims.text: Shear waves arise from instability of wave-driven alongshore currents, with occurrence and finite-amplitude behavior governed by current structure, mixing, and perturbation dynamics documented across theory, field, and laboratory work.
claims.regime: wave-driven alongshore currents in field, laboratory, and theory

claims.text: Longshore-current profiles were generally represented by a 1/10 power law across laboratory and field data, but barred-beach trough structure required a substantially different 1/3 exponent.
claims.regime: plane beach, bar trough, bar crest, and published profile datasets

claims.text: Tri-cuspate beach measurements resolved repeated rip-fed circulation cells for normal waves and a stable meandering longshore current above 0.5 m/s for oblique waves, with predominantly depth-uniform rip flow above the boundary layer.
claims.regime: Wave-induced nearshore currents at a tri-cuspate beach in the UKCRF

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Transfer depends on normalized wave height and breaking state, wave angle and spectral partition, relative water level and bar/channel geometry, morphology wavelength relative to surf-zone width, and time or separation scaling of dispersion.
synthesis.disagreements: The traditional persistent exit-flow picture is incomplete: field evidence also shows recirculation and nearshore retention. Regular spacings from stationary models contrast with irregular morphology under time-varying forcing and antecedent-bathymetry sensitivity.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Evidence includes eight movable-bed morphologies, five roughly 30 m wide and 1.5 m deep dredged channels, seven Sand City drifter days, 32 macro-tidal cycles, Duck remote sensing, and month-long canyon-coast observations.
synthesis.governing_physics: Breaking-wave setup gradients, pressure gradients, vorticity, advection, vortex force, wave direction and spectrum, water level, bathymetry, and boundary geometry jointly determine rip occurrence, strength, position, and pathway.
synthesis.limitations: Prediction is limited by unknown and evolving bathymetry, transient wave spectra and angles, tide, mixed forcing mechanisms, model dimensionality and closures, sparse three-dimensional observations, and uncertain links from flow to human hazard.
synthesis.major_equations: Reviewed approaches span extended-Boussinesq wave-current equations, depth-averaged momentum and continuity, wave-action and breaking closures, sediment continuity and transport, Lagrangian dispersion measures, and ensemble state estimation.
synthesis.numerical_models: Models reproduce laboratory rip instability, bar-channel self-organization, nonlinear merging and migration, breaking and setup gradients in dredged channels, tidal modulation, canyon-controlled intermittency, and bathymetric data assimilation.
synthesis.open_questions: Key needs are operational flash-rip prediction, three-dimensional vertical structure, morphology-aware ensembles, boundary and offshore-feature interactions, swimmer and rescue response, and standardized hazard validation across rip types.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent advances use dense drifters, remote-sensing assimilation, controlled dredged channels, time-varying morphodynamic forcing, and month-scale spectral simulations to resolve intermittency, retention, and forecast sensitivity.
synthesis.seminal_papers: The branch connects early extended-Boussinesq rip-system validation and instability-based bar models to later Lagrangian field studies and the six-type process classification; detailed historical attribution remains a full-text task.
synthesis.typical_methods: Methods combine process classification, field current meters and drifters, remote sensing, dredged channels, movable-bed laboratories, Boussinesq and wave-averaged circulation models, morphodynamic stability models, COAWST, and ensemble Kalman filtering.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Reported values include morphological wavelengths of 180-250 m linearly and 165-320 m nonlinearly, cross-shore diffusivity initially 5.4-6.1 m2/s, total-to-turbulent dispersion ratios of 3-30, and macro-tidal peaks about 1.5 h around low water.
synthesis.well_established: Rip currents are concentrated seaward flows in and beyond the surf zone. They may form exiting jets or semi-enclosed circulations and arise from hydrodynamic instability, bathymetric focusing, or lateral boundaries.

claims.text: Rip currents can be classified as hydrodynamically controlled shear-instability or flash rips, bathymetrically controlled channel or focused rips, and boundary-controlled deflection or shadow rips, while real beaches commonly mix these mechanisms.
claims.regime: wave-exposed coasts and six rip types

claims.text: A fully nonlinear extended-Boussinesq model with localized breaking dissipation and moving shoreline reproduced measured wave height, mean water level, velocity components, and rip-current instability.
claims.regime: laboratory rip-current system with moving shoreline

claims.text: In the modelled single-barred coast, rip-cell spacing scaled with shore-to-bar crest distance, increased with wave height toward saturation, and responded jointly to wave incidence angle and period.
claims.regime: straight single-barred sandy coast under normal and near-normal waves

claims.text: Modelled feedback between wave-driven currents and sediment-concentration gradients favoured crescentic bars under energetic fine-sediment conditions and transverse bars under milder coarse-sediment conditions.
claims.regime: initially planar sandy slope under normally incident saturated-surf-zone waves

claims.text: A nonlinear morphodynamic model reproduced longshore-bar to rhythmic-bar to transverse-bar-and-rip transitions, with wavelengths of 180-250 m in the linear regime and 165-320 m in the nonlinear regime.
claims.regime: longshore bar evolving through linear and nonlinear regimes

claims.text: Across eight moveable-bed morphologies under identical waves, rip-current intensity increased linearly with beach alongshore nonuniformity, while neck-flow pulsation and directional variability changed systematically with morphology.
claims.regime: eight beach morphologies under identical shore-normal waves and water level

claims.text: At Duck, assimilating remote-sensing products with an ensemble Kalman filter improved nearshore bathymetry estimates and rip-current forecasts without requiring in-situ observations.
claims.regime: September 2010 Duck, North Carolina field experiment

claims.text: Rip-channel spacing and growth are inherently sensitive to the initial cross-shore bathymetry at a level comparable to wave-height sensitivity, so predictors must retain antecedent morphology.
claims.regime: pattern development on barred beaches

claims.text: Time-varying wave incidence produced different mean rip spacing, weaker and more irregular morphology, more merging and splitting, and net longshore migration not reproduced by time-invariant forcing.
claims.regime: rip-channel formation under time-varying versus integrated stationary forcing

claims.text: For five dredged surf-zone channels, maximum offshore flow correlated with breaking-driven setup gradients and alongshore flow, increasing with bar dissipation until limited by the vertical scale of bathymetric variability.
claims.regime: channels about 30 m wide and 1.5 m deep across the surf zone

claims.text: At Sand City, rip flow produced initial cross-shore diffusivity of 5.4-6.1 m2/s before declining to 0.9-2.2 m2/s, and total dispersion exceeded small-scale turbulent diffusion by factors of 3-30.
claims.regime: rip-channeled Sand City beach across waves and tides

claims.text: On a rip-channeled beach, drifters exited in rip pulses and returned over shoals, demonstrating wave-driven surf-zone-inner-shelf exchange that retained surface material nearshore and was not due to Stokes drift alone.
claims.regime: rip-channeled Sand City beach under weak winds

claims.text: Across 32 tidal cycles, macro-tidal rip-neck flow peaked about 1.5 hours before and after low water as breaking and alongshore pressure gradients shifted across bar-rip morphology.
claims.regime: macro-tidal bar-rip beach across wave and tidal conditions

claims.text: During a month-long canyon-coast simulation, incident energy direction and the energy ratio of bimodal spectra controlled rip-current formation, wave period controlled position, and persistent offshore bathymetry dominated the circulation response.
claims.regime: Nearshore Canyon Experiment coast with strong offshore bathymetric gradients

claims.text: Scanning sonar observed episodic rip jets recurring roughly one to four times per hour, lasting minutes and reaching about 0.7 m/s while exporting warm, turbid, bubble-rich surf-zone water offshore.
claims.regime: Observations of nearshore circulation: Rip currents

claims.text: On a longshore-uniform swell beach, transient non-topographic rips formed 20–30 m necks and spreading vortex-rich heads; intermittent heads greatly enhanced dispersion outside the surf zone.
claims.regime: Transient rip currents and nearshore circulation on a swell‐dominated beach

claims.text: Dense laboratory drifters showed highly unsteady rip circulation, significant Stokes-drift contributions, circulation generation balanced by bottom-friction dissipation, and biases from depth-varying transport and drifter concentration.
claims.regime: Drifter measurements in a laboratory rip current

claims.text: A roughly 0.3 m Lake Michigan meteotsunami generated hazardous rip currents on an O(1 m) model grid within minutes of calm conditions and sustained them for hours, identifying a distinct rip-generation mechanism.
claims.regime: Unexpected rip currents induced by a meteotsunami

claims.text: At a headland-and-reef beach, small wave/tide changes shifted three circulation regimes; under 4 m oblique waves a deflection rip reached 0.7 m/s 800 m offshore in 12 m depth and could export sediment beyond closure depth.
claims.regime: High‐Energy Surf Zone Currents and Headland Rips at a Geologically Constrained Mesotidal Beach

claims.text: Four North Sea field datasets indicate transitions between undertow and rip-cell circulation depend jointly on onshore wave mass transport, rip spacing and trough cross-section, separating regimes in a simple parameter space.
claims.regime: Cross-Shore Currents in the Surf Zone: Rips or Undertow?

claims.text: Among 407 UK beach users, 263 showed poor rip-current knowledge, while 314 understood safety flags and 339 complied; prior education improved knowledge and lifeguards were the most effective source.
claims.regime: Public Understanding and Knowledge of Rip Currents and Beach Safety in the UK

claims.text: Video and buoy analysis at Alassio associated rips with Hs 0.5–1.34 m, mean periods 4.7–7.0 s and directions 150–227°, yielding high annual hazard but moderate tourist-season hazard.
claims.regime: Rip current hazard assessment on a sandy beach in Liguria, NW Mediterranean

nearshore.surfzone.label: Surf-zone circulation
nearshore.surfzone.description: Wave-driven circulation within the surf zone.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Important groups include breaker index, Iribarren-type slope and steepness measures, relative depth, reflection coefficient, roller geometry and density, roughness ratio, directional spread, normalized dissipation, and eddy scale relative to surf-zone width.
synthesis.disagreements: Bulk or equilibrium closures can fail locally: roller-area formulae overestimated measured dissipation, log-profile stress inference fails when breaking homogenizes shear, and outgoing swash waves materially change wave ratios and undertow that incident-only analyses omit.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Evidence includes about 70 drifter releases, Duck94, a 4 s and 0.85 m large-scale barred-beach breaker at 12 stations, prototype BARDEXII reflection tests, LiDAR roller observations, and a shore-platform array from 10 m depth to shore.
synthesis.governing_physics: Key controls are breaker type and location, wave height and period, directional spread, crest length, roller geometry, turbulence production and advection, vorticity cascades, undertow, bed roughness, slope, reflection, wind, and water depth.
synthesis.limitations: Laboratory scale, two-dimensionality, fixed morphology, uncertain aeration and roller density, sparse vertical observations, wind and roughness parameterization, reflection separation, and intermittent directional breaking limit transfer.
synthesis.major_equations: Frameworks use wave-energy and roller balances, hydraulic-jump dissipation, RANS or k-epsilon turbulence closures, Boussinesq phase-resolving equations, vortex-force circulation, Lagrangian dispersion statistics, and setup momentum balances.
synthesis.numerical_models: Models span wave-resolving Boussinesq dispersion, vertical k-epsilon circulation, phase-resolving reflection, roller dissipation, coupled three-dimensional vortex-force circulation, and air-water two-phase breaking with wind.
synthesis.open_questions: Needs include unified bubble-roller-turbulence energetics, three-dimensional breaking and cascades, morphology feedback, wind-wave-current coupling, rough natural platforms, reflection under random storms, and operational dispersion uncertainty.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent advances directly measure roller geometry, resolve wave-by-wave reflection, observe scale-dependent drifter dispersion, quantify residual breaker-bar turbulence, and separate roughness effects on dissipation from circulation-driven setup.
synthesis.seminal_papers: The branch connects bore and roller energy concepts, breaking turbulence closures, Boussinesq wave-resolving circulation, and Lagrangian dispersion theory; exact historical formulation lineage remains a full-text task.
synthesis.typical_methods: Methods include dense drifter releases, LDA/ADV velocity profiles, field LiDAR rollers, storm arrays, phase-resolving Boussinesq models, vertical turbulence models, two-phase air-water RANS, Radon wave separation, and 3-D vortex-force circulation.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Reported regimes include Hs=0.5-1.4 m drifter days, 5-50 m observed eddies, 5-10 m enstrophy and 20-100 m inverse-cascade scales, undertow to 0.8 m/s, reflection-driven gamma changes to 40%, and roughness-driven setup contributions to 26%.
synthesis.well_established: The surf zone transforms incident waves through shoaling, breaking, rollers, reflection, bottom friction, and nonlinear interactions. These processes drive setup, undertow, alongshore flow, turbulence, eddies, dispersion, and sediment transport.

claims.text: About 70 surf-zone drifter releases showed anisotropic time-dependent dispersion, 5-50 m eddies, relative dispersion proportional to time^(3/2), and scale-dependent diffusivity proportional to separation^(2/3).
claims.regime: alongshore-uniform beach within 200 m of shore and depths below 5 m; Hs=0.5 and 1.4 m

claims.text: A vertical turbulence model showed that breaking-wave turbulence substantially reduces surf-zone vertical shear, so fitting a logarithmic current profile can misestimate bottom stress even when mean alongshore flow is reproduced.
claims.regime: 4.5 m depth sandy beach and Duck94 cross-shore transect

claims.text: A Boussinesq model reproduced observed drifter dispersion through breaking-generated rotational flow, with an enstrophy cascade at about 5-10 m and inverse-energy cascade at 20-100 m that strengthened with wave directional spread.
claims.regime: uniform natural beach under small normally incident directionally spread waves

claims.text: In a large-scale barred-beach experiment, a 4 s, 0.85 m plunging wave generated undertow to 0.8 m/s, persistent turbulence reaching the bed, and undertow TKE transport about an order of magnitude larger than wave and turbulent fluxes.
claims.regime: T=4 s, H=0.85 m regular wave over fixed barred beach at 12 stations

claims.text: For prototype-scale beaches steeper than 1:9, swash reflection changed individual wave-height-to-depth ratios by up to 25-40%, altered significant-wave ratios by 15%, strengthened undertow, and generated near-bed onshore streaming.
claims.regime: prototype-scale steep beach with tan(beta)>1:9 under regular and irregular waves

claims.text: Direct LiDAR roller measurements showed that common roller-area formulations overestimate inner-surf-zone dissipation, which was close to but below an equal-height hydraulic jump and was better represented using roller-density effects.
claims.regime: broken waves in the inner surf zone

claims.text: On a storm-exposed shore platform, bottom friction caused about 40% of wave dissipation, while roughness both reduced setup through prebreaking attenuation and increased circulation-driven setup by up to 26% on a 1:20 slope.
claims.regime: gently sloping shore platform instrumented from 10 m depth to shore

claims.text: Two-phase modelling over a 1:35 beach showed that wind increases vorticity and water-particle velocity and causes spilling and plunging waves to break earlier and farther seaward.
claims.regime: periodic breakers over a 1:35 beach with wind

claims.text: Linear stability analysis shows radiation-stress-driven circulation can amplify crescentic surf-zone bed patterns, while allowing breaker-line displacement suppresses a giant-cusp mode but leaves crescentic growth largely unchanged.
claims.regime: A mechanism for the generation of wave‐driven rhythmic patterns in the surf zone

claims.text: On a reflective beach with 26–32 m cusps, meiofauna, macrofauna, zooplankton and fish distributions differed between horns, bays, rip-current margins and rip heads, linking circulation and morphology to habitat use.
claims.regime: Faunal response to morphology and water circulation of a sandy beach with cusps

claims.text: Validated SPH simulations show intersecting short-crested waves generate undertow, rip currents, isolated breaking crests, multiple low-frequency circulation cells and three-dimensional vorticity under both discrete and directional wavefields.
claims.regime: Short‐crested waves in the surf zone

claims.text: WAMFlow optical processing resolved kilometre-alongshore surf-zone currents and captured longshore flows, rips and gyres; filtered velocities had about 0.1 m/s RMSE against drifters.
claims.regime: Quantifying Optically Derived Two-Dimensional Wave-Averaged Currents in the Surf Zone

claims.text: A calibrated Sète model found breakwater-edge differential breaking drove 0.4 m/s circulation and suppressed inner-bar rip-channel development and offshore bar transport in the lee; longshore current RMSE was 0.07 m/s.
claims.regime: Modeling the Impact of the Implementation of a Submerged Structure on Surf Zone Sandbar Dynamics

claims.text: A time-averaged surf-zone model using roller-inclusive approximations for energy flux, radiation stress and dissipation reproduces measured wave-height and mean-water-level setup and interprets the post-breaking transition through shoreward roller transport.
claims.regime: Regular breaking waves and the laboratory surf-zone measurements evaluated in the article.

claims.text: A wave-current interaction review finds mean bed shear may increase, decrease or remain unchanged depending on nonlinear interaction, relaminarization or linear superposition; non-collinear waves can rotate currents with depth, while common eddy-viscosity and URANS models remain weakly validated outside near-bed regions.
claims.regime: Turbulent wave-current interaction in nearshore boundary layers, including collinear and oblique forcing.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Resolution and regime depend on Courant, Reynolds, Froude, Keulegan–Carpenter, relative-depth, steepness, Ursell, Shields, grid-to-feature and time-step ratios, plus error, skill, convergence and sensitivity measures.
synthesis.disagreements: Higher-fidelity models expose vortices, aeration and three-dimensional response but cost more and still require closures; simpler phase-averaged or depth-averaged systems support regional prediction yet can omit process-scale dynamics. Agreement in one variable does not guarantee all fluxes are correct.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Evidence includes ultrasonic dune winds and LiDAR terrain, British shelf wave climates, dam-break swash, large-scale barred-beach breaking, rough and smooth reef flumes, pile-scour benchmarks and Iraqi coastal water-level, wind and wave observations.
synthesis.governing_physics: Models conserve mass, momentum and tracers while representing pressure, gravity, turbulence, viscosity, free surfaces, wave dispersion and breaking, bottom stress, porous or structural forces and sediment exchange; coupled systems pass forcing and feedback among components.
synthesis.limitations: Uncertain boundary data and bathymetry, grid and time-step dependence, turbulence and breaking closures, scale effects, sparse validation, parameter compensation, one-way coupling, computational cost and incomplete uncertainty reporting constrain confidence.
synthesis.major_equations: Common frameworks include depth-averaged and three-dimensional Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes equations, LES, volume-of-fluid and particle methods, nonhydrostatic and Boussinesq systems, spectral wave-action balance, sediment advection–diffusion and Exner bed evolution.
synthesis.numerical_models: Reviewed approaches include OpenFOAM LES, COAWST wave–tide coupling, RANS–VOF, SPH, nonhydrostatic phase-resolving reef flow, REEF3D scour and MIKE21 FM coupled waves and hydrodynamics, alongside general model-assurance guidance.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities include coupled atmosphere–wave–ocean–sediment prediction, differentiable and adjoint methods, adaptive meshes, hybrid physics–ML, reproducible benchmarks, probabilistic calibration, extreme-event validation and decision-relevant error propagation.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent advances apply particle and nonhydrostatic methods at near-natural scales, couple wave and tide resources, resolve reef roughness, use LiDAR-derived complex terrain, quantify field-linked model skill and emphasize fit-for-purpose uncertainty documentation.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Finite-difference shallow-water and spectral wave models established regional simulation; RANS, Boussinesq, boundary-element and morphodynamic approaches expanded process coverage, while formal verification and validation established numerical credibility practice.
synthesis.typical_methods: Workflows define purpose and conceptual model, assemble bathymetry and boundaries, generate meshes, choose closures, calibrate limited parameters, verify numerics, validate independent variables, quantify sensitivity and uncertainty, and document applicability and reproducibility.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Examples report swash r² above 0.97 and stress error within 20%, reef geometry from a 1:5 fore-reef to 500 m prototype flat, 49–93% oblique wave occurrence at tidal sites and 46.8% wave-height bias when Iraqi wind forcing is omitted.
synthesis.well_established: Coastal numerical models discretize conservation laws and process closures to represent waves, circulation, sediment, morphology and structures. Credible use requires equations and resolution appropriate to scale plus calibration, validation, sensitivity and uncertainty evidence matched to the decision.

claims.text: A 2018 coastal-modeling workshop identified common benchmarks, grid and validation standards, standardized I/O and reporting, and stronger parameter estimation and uncertainty quantification as central requirements for reducing subjectivity and improving reproducibility.
claims.regime: Findings of a 2018 United States workshop on physical coastal and estuarine modeling.

claims.text: Fit-for-purpose shelf and estuary modeling requires explicit setup, input-data, calibration, validation, error, uncertainty and performance-metric documentation rather than model execution alone.
claims.regime: Guidance on Setup, Calibration, and Validation of Hydrodynamic, Wave, and Sediment Models for Shelf Seas and Estuaries

claims.text: A coastal-hydrodynamics review identifies tidal and wave modeling foundations and emerging SPH fluid–solid interaction, adjoint prediction, renewable-energy and large-scale morphodynamic applications.
claims.regime: Coastal hydrodynamics – present and future

numerical.cfd.label: Computational fluid dynamics
numerical.cfd.description: RANS, LES, DNS, and multiphase methods.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Key controls include Reynolds, Froude, Weber and Keulegan–Carpenter numbers, relative depth and steepness, Courant number, cells per wavelength and wave height, y-plus, interface thickness, reflection coefficient, mass error, grid-convergence index and runtime or cell-count ratios.
synthesis.disagreements: No solver is uniformly superior: viscous multiphase CFD resolves breaking and local loads but is costly; potential, spectral and nonhydrostatic models are efficient away from strongly viscous regions; RANS, LES, VOF, CLSVOF and SPH trade dissipation, interface sharpness, robustness and resolution differently.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Reviewed benchmarks include dike overtopping, regular deep-water propagation, steep focused groups, dam break, solitary runup, submerged obstacles, shallow-foreshore transformation, numerical-flume turbulence tests, irregular-wave generation and multiphase sediment or landslide cases.
synthesis.governing_physics: Coastal CFD resolves incompressible momentum and continuity with gravity, viscosity and turbulence while tracking air–water and sometimes sediment or granular phases; nonlinear waves, breaking, runup, overtopping, entrained air, currents and moving or porous boundaries create strong multiscale coupling.
synthesis.limitations: Persistent limitations include numerical diffusion and reflection, mass imbalance, grid and time-step sensitivity, turbulence overproduction beneath waves, uncertain air entrainment and compressibility, expensive three-dimensional resolution, closure dependence, boundary inconsistency and sparse validation of local extremes.
synthesis.major_equations: Core equations are Navier–Stokes mass and momentum conservation, Reynolds-averaged or filtered turbulence equations, phase-fraction advection for VOF/CLSVOF, constitutive stress or rheology for additional phases, and kinematic/dynamic free-surface and wave-generation boundary conditions.
synthesis.numerical_models: The evidence spans OpenFOAM interFoam, multiPhaseInterFoam and sedInterFoam, ANSYS Fluent, DualSPHysics, SWASH, HOS-NWT, fully nonlinear potential solvers, RANS k-epsilon and k-omega, LES, VOF and CLSVOF, plus one- and two-way domain decomposition.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities include conservative sharp interfaces, robust breaking turbulence, air-pocket compressibility, adaptive meshes, porous and moving media, flexible coupling, sediment feedback, uncertainty quantification, reproducible high-performance implementation and field-scale validation.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent advances use coupled potential–viscous domains, cross-solver benchmark campaigns, multiphase rheology, three-phase air–water–sediment models, improved interface schemes, realistic spectral boundaries and explicit accuracy–cost intercomparison across open-source solvers.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Finite-volume Navier–Stokes solvers, Reynolds averaging, LES, VOF free-surface capture and numerical wave tanks established modern coastal CFD; absorbing boundaries, wave-generation toolboxes and formal verification/validation made engineering applications increasingly reproducible.
synthesis.typical_methods: A defensible workflow verifies still water and conservation, calibrates wave generation and absorption, performs mesh/time-step and domain tests, compares turbulence and interface schemes, validates kinematics and integral outputs against laboratory data, audits reflection and mass balance, then reports cost and uncertainty.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Validation covers selected two- and three-dimensional flume-scale regular, solitary, focused, irregular, overtopping, breaking and multiphase cases; solver performance remains conditional on grid, boundary treatment, turbulence closure, phase model and application geometry.
synthesis.well_established: Credible coastal CFD requires separate verification of conservation, discretization, interface transport and wave boundaries plus validation against measurements for the target processes; agreement in surface elevation alone does not establish turbulence, pressure, load or transport accuracy.

claims.text: The parabolic-basin calculation changed total water volume by approximately 1e-7 relative after ten periods, although accuracy deteriorated after several periods because a Cartesian grid represented the circular geometry.
claims.regime: The paper's frictionless circular parabolic-basin test on a Cartesian grid.

claims.regime: A review of computational methods for studying oscillating water columns – the Navier-Stokes based equation approach

claims.text: A multiPhaseInterFoam solver represents granular landslide tsunamis with Coulomb viscoplastic rheology and a small set of physical parameters, validated against generation and propagation evidence.
claims.regime: Numerical modeling of tsunamis generated by granular landslides in OpenFOAM®: A Coulomb viscoplastic rheology

claims.text: A zonal method weakly couples two-phase OpenFOAM near a structure with fully nonlinear potential flow in the outer wave–current domain to concentrate viscous resolution where needed.
claims.regime: A zonal hybrid approach coupling FNPT with OpenFOAM for modelling wave-structure interactions with action of current

claims.regime: Performance Assessment of Three Turbulence Models Validated through an Experimental Wave Flume under Different Scenarios of Wave Generation

claims.regime: sedInterFoam 1.0: a three-phase numerical model for sediment transport applications with free surfaces

claims.regime: Wave–structure interaction by a two–way coupling between a fully nonlinear potential flow model and a Navier–Stokes solver

claims.regime: Theoretical Recommendations and Validation for the Generation of Realistic Irregular Waves Through the WaveMIMO Methodology

claims.regime: Investigation of three‐dimensional wind flow behaviour over coastal dune morphology under offshore winds using computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and ultrasonic anemometry

claims.regime: Modeling swash‐zone hydrodynamics and shear stresses on planar slopes using Reynolds‐Averaged Navier–Stokes equations
