claims.regime: Large-scale wave breaking over a barred beach: SPH numerical simulation and comparison with experiments

claims.text: Calibrated REEF3D RANS simulations indicate current-dominated pile hydrodynamics for co- and counter-directed waves; extrapolated equilibrium scour is smaller for opposing flow and requires modifying the usual relative-current parameter.
claims.regime: Numerical Study of the Hydrodynamics of Waves and Currents and Their Effects in Pier Scouring

claims.text: A review of numerical wave flumes identifies free-surface Navier–Stokes interface-capturing methods and their roles in innovative coastal-structure design.
claims.regime: Computational wave dynamics for innovative design of coastal structures

claims.text: A finite-volume incompressible Navier-Stokes solver combining fixed Cartesian cut cells with VOF advection and a local height function can conserve mass and robustly resolve violent free-surface impact, provided that free-surface velocity boundary conditions and moving-body coupling are treated carefully.
claims.regime: Violent incompressible free-surface flows involving dam-break impact on an obstacle, wave loading and green water on offshore structures, and prescribed or freely moving water-entry bodies.

claims.text: Field-validated LES with atmospheric-boundary-layer roughness reproduced dune-induced offshore-wind steering and back-beach recirculation better than simulations without terrain roughness; for the two measured directions, reference winds of 12.1 and 7.1 m/s were sufficient to produce the 3.28 m/s back-beach velocity estimated to initiate dry-sand transport.
claims.regime: Offshore and obliquely offshore winds over the complex Magilligan foredune and back beach, represented by LiDAR/DGPS terrain and compared with mast-mounted 50 Hz three-dimensional ultrasonic-anemometer profiles; threshold calculation assumes dry 0.17 mm quartz sand.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Controls include parent-to-child grid ratio, coupling interval relative to process time scale, Courant number, overlap width, relaxation strength, flux or mass imbalance, interpolation error, scale-separation ratio, feedback gain, forecast skill change and parallel efficiency.
synthesis.disagreements: One-way offline nesting is simple and reproducible but omits feedback; two-way online coupling is more physically complete but can amplify interface and component biases. Shared grids ease exchange yet restrict component discretization, while separate grids add remapping and conservation error.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Evidence includes nested Mediterranean and Adriatic circulation, Hurricane Ike waves, California upwelling, Gulf Stream and Agulhas currents, Scituate nor’easter inundation, southern North Sea forecasts, northwest-European shelf operations and Taranto multi-scale observations.
synthesis.governing_physics: Coupled coastal systems exchange momentum, mass, energy and tracers among atmosphere, waves, circulation, rivers, inundation and morphology. Feedback can alter wind stress, wave growth, currents, water levels and dissipation rather than merely pass forcing downstream.
synthesis.limitations: Major limitations are inconsistent grids and vertical coordinates, nonconservative interpolation, boundary reflection, asynchronous clocks, spin-up shocks, feedback double counting, unresolved scale overlap, component bias compensation, high communication cost, fragile restart provenance and sparse coupled observations.
synthesis.major_equations: Coupling links component conservation equations through boundary conditions and source terms: stress and heat flux, radiation stress or vortex force, wave action, water level and velocity, discharge, sediment flux and moving geometry, with interpolation, relaxation and conservative remapping operators.
synthesis.numerical_models: Reviewed systems include OASIS3-MCT/SURFEX infrastructure, COSMO–WAM, wave-coupled shelf models, FVCOM inundation nesting, TELEMAC wave–3D hydrodynamics, WAVEWATCH III domain decomposition and high-resolution coupled atmosphere–ocean models.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities include conservative adaptive remapping, wet/dry nested boundaries, coupled data assimilation, ensemble uncertainty, moving morphology, wave–atmosphere–ocean–river feedback, error attribution, coupling-frequency optimization, standardized metadata and operational fault tolerance.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent advances use community middleware, unstructured nested inundation, multi-way wave–ocean–atmosphere exchange, high-resolution current feedback, domain-decomposed parallel waves and validated open-source multiple-nesting workflows for operational coasts.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Nested ocean models established basin-to-coast downscaling, while wave–current and atmosphere–ocean systems introduced online feedback; community couplers and Earth-system interfaces later standardized field exchange, synchronization and parallel execution.
synthesis.typical_methods: Workflows define components and exchanged fields, choose online/offline and one-/two-way direction, harmonize coordinates and conventions, remap states or fluxes, synchronize clocks and restarts, test idealized interfaces and conservation, compare forced and coupled runs, then validate integrated outputs.
synthesis.validated_ranges: The reviewed systems span submesoscale coastal currents to global-parent/regional-child hierarchies and event to operational scales; demonstrated skill is conditional on component versions, exchanged fields, grid hierarchy, coupling interval, forcing and regional observations.
synthesis.well_established: Coupling is necessary when feedback or scale interaction affects the answer; a coupled system must be evaluated against uncoupled baselines and observations because individually valid components can exchange inconsistent states, fluxes or boundary information.

claims.text: The unified wave-generation interface transferred surface-elevation and depth-averaged-velocity time series from MIKE 21 BW to 2D or 3D piston wavemakers while accounting for dispersion, shallow-water nonlinearity, and evanescent modes.
claims.regime: One-way coupling to DHI-style piston wavemakers; reflected physical waves are not fed back numerically.

claims.text: Across analytical, laboratory, and field benchmarks, the shared-grid SELFE-WWM-II coupling captured wave-current interaction with stable convergence over multiple scales, while the authors identified three-dimensional wave-induced effects as still requiring further research.
claims.regime: Unstructured-grid multiscale wave-current benchmarks and applications described in the indexed abstract.

claims.text: Coupled California-upwelling simulations show that passing ocean surface currents back to atmospheric stress reduces surface eddy kinetic energy by about half and exposes feedback absent from uncoupled forcing.
claims.regime: Modulation of Wind Work by Oceanic Current Interaction with the Atmosphere

claims.text: A three-level Mediterranean–Adriatic–northern-Adriatic hierarchy uses one-way offline nesting to downscale basin circulation to resolved coastal fields and tests reproduction of known regional features.
claims.regime: The Adriatic Sea modelling system: a nested approach

claims.text: WAVEWATCH III domain decomposition and an implicit scheme enable high-resolution unstructured hurricane-wave calculations compatible with community coupling infrastructure and validated for Hurricane Ike.
claims.regime: Large-scale hurricane modeling using domain decomposition parallelization and implicit scheme implemented in WAVEWATCH III wave model

claims.text: A SURFEX–OASIS3-MCT interface provides a shared atmosphere-to-ocean, wave, ice and hydrology coupling structure from process and coastal domains to regional and global systems.
claims.regime: SURFEX v8.0 interface with OASIS3-MCT to couple atmosphere with hydrology, ocean, waves and sea-ice models, from coastal to global scales

claims.text: Coupled Gulf Stream and Agulhas simulations show current feedback produces eddy killing and materially changes boundary-current energy transfers.
claims.regime: Remarkable Control of Western Boundary Currents by Eddy Killing, a Mechanical Air‐Sea Coupling Process

claims.text: High-resolution coupled California simulations show surface-stress feedback damps submesoscale currents, demonstrating that coupling effects persist below mesoscale resolution.
claims.regime: Dampening of Submesoscale Currents by Air-Sea Stress Coupling in the Californian Upwelling System

claims.text: A nested FVCOM inundation system for Scituate represents flooding/drying, coastal structures and wave–current effects and reproduces the compound tide–surge flooding of a 2010 nor’easter.
claims.regime: Coastal flooding in Scituate (MA): A FVCOM study of the 27 December 2010 nor'easter

claims.text: Two-way COSMO–WAM coupling with wave-induced atmospheric drag reduces surface-wind and wave-height forecast errors in the dynamically complex southern North Sea and a nested German Bight grid.
claims.regime: An atmosphere–wave regional coupled model: improving predictions of wave heights and surface winds in the southern North Sea

claims.text: Operational northwest-European shelf experiments demonstrate how wave coupling changes atmosphere–ocean momentum exchange and can improve regional ocean forecasts relative to externally forced mode.
claims.regime: Can wave coupling improve operational regional ocean forecasts for the north-west European Shelf?

claims.text: A validated multiple-nesting workflow downscales large-scale ocean fields into high-resolution coupled TELEMAC wave–3D hydrodynamics for the Gulf of Taranto and Mar Grande.
claims.regime: A coupled wave–3-D hydrodynamics model of the Taranto Sea (Italy): amultiple-nesting approach

claims.text: At 18 British tidal-energy sites, 49–93% of waves were oblique to tidal flow; coupled COAWST experiments reduced theoretical tidal resource by about 10% per metre of wave-height increase, conditional on period and direction.
claims.regime: Realistic wave conditions and their influence on quantifying the tidal stream energy resource

claims.text: A March 2019 MIKE21 FM wave–hydrodynamic simulation agreed acceptably with Iraqi coastal observations; omitting wind lowered significant wave height by 46.8%, while wave-period Nash efficiency reached 0.92.
claims.regime: Numerical Simulation of Hydrodynamic and Spectral Model of Iraqi Coastal Water at the Northern Arabian Gulf

claims.text: An economical surface-wave model retains depth/current refraction and depth-variable coupling and was demonstrated against Hurricane Katrina buoy data and SWAN calculations before full ocean coupling.
claims.regime: A Surface Wave Model for Coupling with Numerical Ocean Circulation Models

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Controls include Froude, Rossby, Reynolds and Richardson numbers, relative depth, aspect ratio, stratification and baroclinic Rossby radius, bottom-drag coefficient, Courant number, grid Peclet number, wetting threshold and normalized mass and energy errors.
synthesis.disagreements: Depth-integrated models offer efficiency and horizontal resolution but omit vertical shear and baroclinicity; three-dimensional models add physics at greater data, closure and computational cost. Numerical robustness obtained through excess drag or diffusion can conflict with physical fidelity.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Reviewed evidence includes analytical shoreline-motion and oscillating-basin cases, mass-conservation tests, the Monai laboratory tsunami benchmark and formal operational verification criteria. Direct circulation, tide and wetland datasets remain in the lawful-full-text queue.
synthesis.governing_physics: Pressure gradients, gravity, Coriolis acceleration, advection, bed and surface stress, turbulence, density gradients, tides, wind, waves and boundary fluxes control circulation; wetting and drying, breaking, bores and hydraulic transitions introduce strong nonlinearities and numerical constraints.
synthesis.limitations: Bathymetric and boundary uncertainty, wet/dry thresholds, turbulence and friction closure, numerical diffusion and dispersion, stability-driven tuning, unresolved breaking, grid anisotropy and incomplete conservation audits can produce plausible levels with incorrect velocities, fluxes or inundation.
synthesis.major_equations: Core equations are free-surface continuity and horizontal momentum, optionally coupled to hydrostatic vertical structure, tracer transport, turbulence closure and wave radiation stresses. Conservative finite-volume or finite-difference forms must balance storage and boundary fluxes and preserve physically meaningful momentum across wet/dry fronts.
synthesis.numerical_models: The reviewed implementation is UBO-TSUFD, a nonlinear shallow-water finite-difference model with inundation capability, evaluated within a broader tsunami verification and validation framework that supplies analytic, laboratory, conservation and operational tests.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities include conservative multiscale nesting, robust positivity without artificial drag, adaptive dimensionality, coupled baroclinic–wave–sediment physics, uncertainty-aware boundary assimilation, differentiable calibration and validation metrics that expose compensating errors.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent advances use unstructured high-order and discontinuous Galerkin methods, GPU acceleration, adaptive meshes, locally three-dimensional or nonhydrostatic patches, conservative subgrid structures, ensemble data assimilation and reproducible benchmark suites.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Saint-Venant shallow-water equations established depth-integrated long-wave modeling; primitive-equation coastal ocean models introduced sigma coordinates and turbulence closures, while finite-volume Riemann methods advanced conservative shocks, bores and wetting/drying.
synthesis.typical_methods: Workflows select dimensionality from the physics, construct datum-consistent bathymetry and boundaries, verify analytic waves and basins, test conservation and grid/time convergence, validate laboratory and field water levels and velocities, audit phase and extrema separately and document stabilization, friction and wet/dry sensitivity.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Support covers selected long-wave analytical and laboratory regimes and Monai behavior through 30 s. It does not validate post-breaking flow, stratified three-dimensional circulation, wave-resolving dynamics or arbitrary wetting/drying configurations.
synthesis.well_established: Coastal hydrodynamic models solve conservation of water mass and momentum under approximations matched to scale: depth-integrated shallow-water equations for long waves and vertically mixed flows, multilayer or three-dimensional hydrostatic models for stratification and shear, and nonhydrostatic or phase-resolving models where vertical acceleration matters.

claims.text: UBO-TSUFD reproduced the selected analytical shoreline-motion, oscillating-basin, mass-conservation, and laboratory tsunami benchmarks with generally satisfactory agreement.
claims.regime: The four paper-specific benchmarks on single structured grids; this does not validate nested grids, landslide generation, dispersive physics, or wave breaking.

claims.text: The nonlinear shallow-water model reproduced the Monai laboratory arrival and inundation behavior through 30 s but was not compared later because breaking waves are outside its physics.
claims.regime: Matsuyama-Tanaka Monai Valley benchmark, 5.446 x 3.406 m region, maximum depth 0.135 m; pre-breaking interval through 30 s.

claims.text: A tsunami-model mass audit should integrate disturbed free-surface elevation and account for open-boundary fluxes; integrating total depth can mask numerical errors offshore.
claims.regime: Depth-integrated water-wave computations with closed, open, or absorbing boundaries.

claims.text: Ad hoc friction factors introduced mainly to stabilize marginally stable inundation computations create reliability that cannot be known a priori outside tested cases.
claims.regime: Numerical inundation models using empirically adjusted friction primarily for stability.

claims.text: Modeling 0.5–1.0 m sea-level rise over 1–2 m reef flats increases waves, setup, shear, resuspension and offshore sediment flux while reducing sediment residence time and light availability.
claims.regime: Numerical modeling of the impact of sea-level rise on fringing coral reef hydrodynamics and sediment transport

claims.text: A finite-element formulation solves layer-averaged circulation for two vertically homogeneous coastal layers, retaining interfacial exchange and density-driven structure absent from a single-layer model.
claims.regime: FINITE ELEMENT MODEL OF TWO LAYER COASTAL CIRCULATION

equations.regime: Nonlinear shallow-water formulation in Cartesian coordinates.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Controls include Shields mobility, relative grain size, fall-velocity and suspension parameters, wave asymmetry and skewness, surf similarity, sediment Courant number, morphological acceleration factor, active-layer thickness ratios and normalized bed or shoreline error.
synthesis.disagreements: Detailed process models represent more feedback but accumulate closure and numerical uncertainty, whereas reduced models can be robust for aggregate volume or shoreline response yet omit inlets, cross-shore exchange and event sequencing. Similar fit can coexist with physically implausible parameters.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Reviewed evidence includes storm-profile erosion, Wilson Inlet waves–currents–bed observations, multiple laboratory benchmarks plus Pescara Harbor evolution, and post-nourishment volume series at Folly Beach and Hunting Island.
synthesis.governing_physics: Bed evolution reflects gradients in bedload and suspended transport driven by waves, currents, runup and gravity, with feedback through water depth, breaking, circulation and inlet exchange; relevant scales range from intra-wave transport to seasonal and engineering evolution.
synthesis.limitations: Limitations include uncertain transport formulae, compensating calibration, sparse subaqueous observations, boundary sediment flux, scale-dependent skill, numerical diffusion, morphological acceleration, bed-layer and wet/dry choices, storm sequencing and weak transfer across grain sizes and coast types.
synthesis.major_equations: The core system combines hydrodynamic mass and momentum equations, sediment advection–diffusion or bulk transport formulae, and the Exner bed-continuity equation, often with separate cross-shore and longshore components, wetting/drying, avalanching and porosity corrections.
synthesis.numerical_models: The evidence spans a cross-shore storm-profile model, coupled cross-/longshore inlet morphodynamics, weak phase-resolving-wave to wave-averaged-sediment coupling, and reduced linear, exponential, one-line and combined nourishment-evolution models.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities include scale-selective validation, probabilistic structural uncertainty, mixed and cohesive sediment, event-to-decadal acceleration, coupled inlet–beach exchange, climate nonstationarity, observation updating and reliable extrapolation beyond calibration conditions.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent work emphasizes weak multiscale coupling, phase-resolving forcing of longer-term transport, probabilistic ensembles, scale-aware skill metrics, data assimilation and efficient reduced emulators while retaining conservation and physically constrained parameters.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Exner bed continuity, energetics and equilibrium-profile concepts, one-line shoreline diffusion and early coupled wave–current–sediment models established the hierarchy from reduced shoreline response to process-based area morphodynamics.
synthesis.typical_methods: Workflows define sediment classes and closures, spin up hydrodynamics, couple transport and Exner updating, test conservation and morphological time step, calibrate a constrained subset, validate against independent profiles or volumes at multiple scales, and audit parameter plausibility and boundary flux.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Current evidence is case-bound to sandy storm profiles, one microtidal wave-dominated seasonal inlet, laboratory tests and one harbor coast, and two South Carolina nourishment sites; it does not establish universal closures or acceleration factors.
synthesis.well_established: Process-based coastal morphodynamic models couple hydrodynamics, sediment transport and bed updating through feedback: flow moves sediment, divergence changes elevation, and the changed bed modifies subsequent waves and currents. Calibration fit alone does not establish predictive skill.

claims.text: Leont'yev's storm-profile model decomposes total cross-shore transport into wave/current and runup components, using only runup transport in swash, only wave/current transport in shoaling water, and both in the surf zone.
claims.regime: The proposed 1996 short-term sandy beach-profile model; coefficients and tested forcing ranges are unavailable from the abstract.

claims.text: A weakly coupled phase-resolving hydrodynamic and wave-averaged sediment model was validated against multiple experiments and reproduced long-term bed evolution opposite Pescara Harbor.
claims.regime: The model's articulated coastal grids, tested sediment closures, and Pescara Harbor case.

claims.text: Tidal-basin morphodynamic modeling shows sea-level rise reorganizes channel-flat morphology and sediment demand through coupled hydrodynamic and bed-evolution feedbacks.
claims.regime: Numerical modeling of the impact of sea level rise on tidal basin morphodynamics

claims.text: In the LIP profile tests, the model reproduced two nearshore bars that migrated about 7 m seaward, with initial crest heights near 0.10 and 0.12 m.
claims.regime: LIP fine-sand regular-wave profile tests 1a and 1b.

claims.text: For the 1997–2000 Pescara hindcast, simulated annual settlement was about 38,500 m³/year versus about 40,000 m³/year inferred from bathymetric surveys.
claims.regime: Pescara Harbor under the dominant 1.5 m wave class and modeled 1997 bathymetry.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: No single universal dimensionless parameter governs spectral-model validity. Relative depth, spectral bandwidth, directional spreading, exposure, and ratios of local wind-sea, sea-swell, and infragravity energy define process regimes and numerical sensitivity.
synthesis.disagreements: The Ningaloo comparison favored phase-averaged SWAN over surfbeat XBeach because local wind growth dominated, but this does not show that infragravity resolution is generally secondary; model ranking reverses when the omitted process changes.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Reviewed evidence includes extreme diffraction benchmarks, a roughly 300 by 300 km Southern California Bight transformation case, and TC Olwyn observations with sustained winds above 130 km/h and forereef significant waves reaching 6 m.
synthesis.governing_physics: The spectral action balance transports energy through physical and spectral space while wind input, whitecapping, bottom friction, breaking, triad and quartet interactions, and Bragg scattering act as source terms; bathymetry controls refraction and diffraction.
synthesis.limitations: Phase averaging excludes coherent standing-wave fields and explicit infragravity phase dynamics; exact quartet interactions are expensive; sheltered predictions are sensitive to numerical bias; and agreement in wave height alone does not validate currents, sediment transport, or morphology.
synthesis.major_equations: Core formulations are the wave-action balance and its additive source terms, the Hasselmann Boltzmann integral for resonant four-wave transfer, and mild-slope-derived directional turning used for phase-decoupled diffraction.
synthesis.numerical_models: Models include SWAN with phase-decoupled diffraction, the WRT exact quartet-interaction solver, Longuet-Higgins spectral refraction, Kirby's parabolic refraction-diffraction method, and XBeach surfbeat as a complementary low-frequency comparator.
synthesis.open_questions: Needs include efficient accurate nonlinear source terms, robust diffraction near singular obstacles, joint wind-sea and infragravity capability, uncertainty propagation from offshore spectra and bathymetry, and validation of coupled wave-current-sediment responses.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent work increasingly diagnoses models by process completeness rather than class alone: the 2019 reef study identifies local wind-wave generation as decisive, while related nonhydrostatic studies expose breaking-turbulence and morphodynamic errors hidden by surface-wave calibration.
synthesis.seminal_papers: The 1993 Southern California Bight comparison is the earliest directly reviewed regional validation in this slice; the 2003 phase-decoupled diffraction paper is a foundational extension of SWAN's coastal-process capability.
synthesis.typical_methods: Typical evaluation uses analytical benchmarks, laboratory diffraction observations, exact source-term solvers, regional model intercomparison, sensitivity to spectra/bathymetry/tides, and event-scale field validation against phase-resolving alternatives.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Validation is case-bound: phase-decoupled diffraction is for random short-crested fields without coherent standing patterns; Bight models perform best at moderately exposed sites; and SWAN's cyclone advantage was demonstrated for a shallow Ningaloo lagoon dominated by local wind growth.
synthesis.well_established: Phase-averaged spectral models efficiently propagate random directional wave energy across large coastal domains while representing generation, dissipation, refraction, shoaling, and nonlinear source terms; their reliability depends on whether omitted phase-coherent or low-frequency processes control the site.

claims.text: A mild-slope-derived phase-decoupled turning-rate formulation allowed SWAN to combine random-wave diffraction with refraction, shoaling, generation, dissipation, and wave-wave interactions, with reasonable agreement in extreme diffraction tests.
claims.regime: Random short-crested waves without coherent standing-wave patterns; diffraction regions require adequate local resolution.

claims.text: The WRT method evaluates the first-principles nonlinear four-wave interaction integral for discrete spectra and serves as an accuracy reference, but its computational cost limits direct operational use.
claims.regime: Weakly nonlinear spectral surface-gravity waves represented on discrete frequency-direction grids.

claims.text: In the roughly 300 km by 300 km Southern California Bight, broader incident frequency-direction spectra reduced model sensitivity and improved agreement, but neither the refraction nor refraction-diffraction model was accurate at highly sheltered sites.
claims.regime: The tested Southern California Bight bathymetry and incident spectra; strongest limitation where diffraction dominates low local energy.

claims.text: During category-3 TC Olwyn at Ningaloo Reef, locally generated lagoon wind waves dominated over infragravity waves, so phase-averaged SWAN was more accurate than surfbeat-resolving XBeach for this specific event because SWAN represented wind-wave growth.
claims.regime: TC Olwyn at the roughly 1 km wide, 1 m deep Ningaloo lagoon; infragravity importance at other reefs is not negated.

claims.text: Semiempirical spectral dissipation activates breaking above an observed nondimensional threshold, represents nonlinear swell and short-wave loss, and validates wave height, period and spectra from global to coastal scales despite residual systematic defects.
claims.regime: Semiempirical Dissipation Source Functions for Ocean Waves. Part I: Definition, Calibration, and Validation

claims.text: SWAN verification across five increasingly complex coastal field cases produced average RMS errors of 0.30 m in significant wave height and 0.7 s in mean period, about 10% of incident values.
claims.regime: A third‐generation wave model for coastal regions: 2. Verification

claims.text: Coastal WAVEWATCH III accuracy improves when currents, reflection and spatially varying bottom sediment are represented on efficient unstructured grids, but sub-100-m surf-zone resolution still requires better numerical schemes and coupled forcing.
claims.regime: French Atlantic, Channel and North Sea coastal wave fields on regional unstructured grids with currents, reflection and mapped bottom type.

claims.text: Third-generation spectral wave modeling has reduced bias in integral parameters, but improving spectral shape—especially high-frequency tails, extreme-condition physics, wave–current interaction and coastal boundary treatment—remains central to better forecasts and coupled applications.
claims.regime: Phase-averaged wind-wave modeling from deep water through shallow/coastal applications within spectral-model assumptions.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Controls include relative depth kh, wave steepness, Ursell and Froude numbers, relative amplitude and submergence, directional spread, Courant number, cells per wavelength, layer count, breaking or dissipation parameters, wetting depth and morphological acceleration factor.
synthesis.disagreements: Boussinesq models efficiently capture weak-to-moderate dispersion but need breaking closures; nonhydrostatic multilayer models broaden dispersion at higher cost; RANS resolves overturning but is expensive. Surface-elevation tuning can leave velocity and sediment errors unresolved.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Reviewed evidence includes Synolakis plane-beach and conical-island runup, controlled frequency/directional-spread runup, vegetation attenuation, FORCE-scheme verification cases, a large-scale barred beach, weakly coupled bed evolution, deterministic physical–numerical combinations and multimodal harbor spectra.
synthesis.governing_physics: Nonlinear free-surface motion, frequency dispersion, shoaling, refraction, diffraction, reflection, breaking, infragravity generation, wetting/drying, currents and structure or vegetation interactions govern resolved waves. Depth-averaged formulations still approximate vertical shear, turbulence and overturning.
synthesis.limitations: Boundary reflection, sponge design, numerical dispersion, grid and time resolution, breaking and turbulence closures, wet/dry thresholds, vertical averaging, bathymetric error and morphology coupling can dominate results. Phase accuracy degrades over long domains without careful dispersion control.
synthesis.major_equations: Boussinesq-type equations extend shallow-water mass and momentum with dispersive terms; depth-averaged nonhydrostatic models solve pressure corrections, while fully nonlinear potential flow, RANS/VOF and multilayer formulations add successively more vertical physics. Bed evolution couples sediment-flux divergence to morphology.
synthesis.numerical_models: The set spans higher-order Boussinesq, FORCE-based depth-averaged nonhydrostatic, XBNH/XBNH+, weakly coupled wave-resolving–wave-averaged morphology and hybrid numerical/physical modeling, with applications from tsunami runup to vegetation and harbors.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities include parameter-robust breaking, adaptive vertical resolution, conservative nested phase coupling, irregular directional seas, air and porous structures, wave-current-vorticity interactions, scalable GPU solvers, uncertainty propagation and multi-variable morphodynamic validation.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent advances use multilayer nonhydrostatic and high-order unstructured solvers, adaptive meshes, immersed and porous boundaries, GPU acceleration, deterministic physical–numerical coupling, differentiable calibration and phase-resolving data assimilation.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Peregrine and later enhanced Boussinesq equations established dispersive coastal-wave simulation; fully nonlinear potential flow, nonhydrostatic pressure correction and VOF/RANS expanded regimes, while FUNWAVE, BOSZ, SWASH and XBeach-NH enabled practical applications.
synthesis.typical_methods: Workflows verify linear dispersion, shoaling, conservation and still-water balance; validate solitary waves, runup, breaking, bars, vegetation and harbor spectra; test convergence and boundaries; separate surface elevation, velocity and morphology skill; and compare against phase-averaged or physical models.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Support is benchmark- and site-specific. synthesis.well_established: Phase-resolving models simulate individual wave crests and troughs, retaining nonlinear interactions, dispersion, reflection and runup that phase-averaged spectral models parameterize; their added detail requires finer space-time resolution, consistent boundaries and process-specific validation.

synthesis.numerical_models: Model chains couple regional wave forecasts to harbor agitation, vessel response and operational thresholds; navigation tools combine water level, squat, heel and waves. synthesis.well_established: Port performance couples wave agitation, currents and water levels with vessel motion, navigation clearance, mooring response and sediment exchange. claims.text: A nested sequence of spectral-energy, extended mild-slope, and Boussinesq wave models transfers a 50-year design wave from regional generation scale to detailed Samchunpo harbor-entrance conditions for renovation design.
claims.regime: Typhoon design waves propagating from offshore through the south Korean coast into the Samchunpo (Sin Hyang) fishery harbor entrance.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Relevant groups include settling-to-advection timescale, Rouse- and Shields-type mobility, tidal excursion relative to entrance scale, spring-neap forcing, aggregate-to-primary-particle size, concentration and density stratification, and channel depth relative to ambient morphology.
synthesis.disagreements: At Zeebrugge, an erodible compact bed and reduced water-bed exchange reproduced available data comparably but predicted sediment export versus strengthened convergence. Existing observations therefore do not uniquely identify the maintaining mechanism.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Evidence includes two Belgian harbor-basin exchange datasets, Zeebrugge field and dredging records, Nowshahr field calibration, tidal James River cores, Gladstone source samples, Lekki post-construction operation, and Dinh An channel surveys.
synthesis.governing_physics: Controls include tidal filling and exchange, entrance gyres and flow separation, waves and wind currents, longshore and fluvial supply, aggregation and settling, salinity and sediment stratification, bed erosion and consolidation, and structure-induced sediment-cell changes.
synthesis.limitations: Sparse near-bed exchange, floc, density, consolidation, and bedload data; uncertain sediment provenance; bathymetric sampling; operational dredging feedback; ship effects; extreme events; and model equifinality constrain forecasts.
synthesis.major_equations: Frameworks combine suspended-sediment advection-diffusion-settling, erosion-deposition and consolidation, hydrodynamic momentum, bed evolution, particle or aggregate transport, source mixing, and geometric decomposition of tidal filling and horizontal/vertical exchange.
synthesis.numerical_models: Models diagnose entrance recirculation, water-bed exchange alternatives, aggregate transport modes, coupled hydrodynamic-bed change, and structural countermeasures. Equifinality remains possible when different near-bed mechanisms fit the same observations.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities are continuous mass budgets, fluid-mud rheology, aggregate-resolved transport, dredging and disposal feedback, climate and storm nonstationarity, source apportionment uncertainty, and whole-cell effects of port interventions.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent advances combine isotope fingerprints, aggregate imaging, multi-timescale fluid-mud monitoring, calibrated competing-mechanism models, nature-based sediment accommodation, and scenario optimization for channel stability.
synthesis.seminal_papers: The branch builds from classical tidal-prism, exchange-flow, settling, erosion, and dredging-maintenance concepts toward geometric flux decomposition, cohesive aggregation, provenance tracing, and operational morphodynamic design.
synthesis.typical_methods: Methods use multilevel turbidity and mud-density observations, bathymetric and dredging records, satellite imagery, calibrated hydrodynamic-sediment models, flux decomposition, core erosion imaging, elemental and isotope provenance, and intervention scenario modelling.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Explicit findings include 50-100 Mt of hypothesized legacy mud, aggregates 50-270 times primary-particle size, spring-tide import 2-4 times neap, and import concentrated from roughly two hours before high water to high water.
synthesis.well_established: Port and channel sedimentation occurs when imported or locally resuspended material converges, settles, consolidates, or migrates into sheltered basins and maintained depths faster than natural export or dredging removes it.

claims.text: At Zeebrugge, two models that fit concentration, satellite, bed-level, mud-content, and dredging data predicted opposite convergence responses, showing that uncertain near-bed exchange obscures whether decades-old port construction and 50-100 Mt of mobilized mud sustain the turbidity maximum.
claims.regime: Belgian-Dutch coast around Zeebrugge port

claims.text: At Nowshahr, field-validated modelling showed that eastward wind-driven current separates around the western breakwater and forms a recirculation zone that imports resuspended shoreline sediment into the port entrance and access channel.
claims.regime: Nowshahr port entrance on the southern Caspian Sea under storms

claims.text: The Lekki Sandbar Breakwater deliberately uses heavy updrift accretion to supplement sand construction and pairs it with a replenishable sand engine, maintaining port operation while managing downdrift sediment balance.
claims.regime: Lekki, Nigeria, on the high-drift Gulf of Guinea coast

claims.text: A geometric decomposition of two Belgian harbor datasets separates tidal filling, horizontal exchange, and vertical exchange, providing a calibration-ready diagnosis of the phasing and spatial correlations governing harbor siltation.
claims.regime: two Belgian tidal harbor basins

claims.text: In the tidal James River, eroded muddy-bed aggregates were 50-270 times larger than disaggregated sediment and were modelled in incipient suspension or bedload, materially changing predictions of navigation-channel infill.
claims.regime: tidal James River navigable waterway

claims.text: At Zeebrugge, suspended-mud import occurred from about two hours before high water to high water and was 2-4 times larger at spring than neap tide, while constant dredging permitted spring accumulation and winter deposits were thicker and less dense.
claims.regime: Port of Zeebrugge harbor basin and docks

claims.text: At the Port of Gladstone, combined particle-size, elemental, and isotope tracers differentiated candidate sources, with beryllium-7 indicating recent channel deposition from mudflats or catchments.
claims.regime: Port of Gladstone navigation channels and catchment, mudflat, and littoral sources

claims.text: For the sediment-choked Dinh An route and Duyen Hai harbor bottlenecks, coupled MIKE 21 simulations compared five structural layouts using water level, velocity, and bed change to identify a preferred channel-stabilization option.
claims.regime: Dinh An estuary and Duyen Hai harbor basin, Vietnam

claims.text: A meta-analysis identifies suspended sediment, contamination, hydraulic entrainment, and underwater noise as distinct dredging stressors affecting fish.
claims.regime: A critical analysis of the direct effects of dredging on fish

claims.text: Field monitoring around offshore dredging and beach nourishment documents spatial changes in turbidity, suspended sediment, and water-quality conditions.
claims.regime: Turbidity and Other Effects Resulting from Trafalgar Sandbank Dredging and Palmar Beach Nourishment

claims.text: Scale experiments and global examples show that sea-level rise and navigation dredging interact to alter estuary morphology and enhance channel-bend migration.
claims.regime: Effects of Sea‐Level Rise on Dredging and Dredged Estuary Morphology

claims.text: Analysis of Mar del Plata Harbor identifies recurrent access-channel and basin sedimentation as a controlling constraint on port development.
claims.regime: Analysis of Sedimentation Problems at the Entrance to Mar del Plata Harbor

claims.text: The Port of Newcastle case documents maintenance-dredging and unconfined sea-disposal practice in a high-throughput river port, linking navigability requirements to sediment-management and environmental monitoring.
claims.regime: PORT OF NEWCASTLE, NSW, AUSTRALIA – MAINTENANCE DREDGING AND UNCONFINED SEA DISPOSAL OF DREDGE MATERIAL

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Key descriptors include pixel or point spacing relative to feature scale, signal-to-noise and contrast, overlap and baseline ratios, incidence angle, depth-to-attenuation scale, tide range-to-beach slope effect, classification accuracy and normalized positional error.
synthesis.disagreements: A shoreline is not unique: wet–dry, vegetation, waterline and datum-based proxies differ systematically. Automated methods improve repeatability but can mask tide, runup, turbidity and geolocation error; higher spatial resolution often trades against coverage and revisit.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Evidence spans forty years at Narrabeen–Collaroy, microtidal Landsat and Sentinel beaches, UAV beach and tombolo surveys, Langue de Barbarie and Bangladesh shoreline archives, Baltic bathymetric LiDAR and coastal topography–bathymetry demonstrations.
synthesis.governing_physics: Optical reflectance depends on illumination, atmosphere, water constituents and bottom signal; radar backscatter responds to roughness, moisture and geometry; LiDAR travel time and refraction yield elevation or depth; photogrammetry reconstructs geometry from parallax and control.
synthesis.limitations: Clouds, haze, sun glint, turbidity, waves, refraction, limited LiDAR penetration, SAR speckle, vegetation, weak texture, ground-control error, sensor changes and sparse validation constrain accuracy and long-term consistency.
synthesis.major_equations: Retrievals use sensor geometry, radiometric correction, refraction and travel-time relations, structure-from-motion bundle adjustment, spectral indices, classifiers and edge detection. Change rates regress proxy positions through time with positional and temporal uncertainty.
synthesis.numerical_models: Processing uses threshold and index methods, supervised or unsupervised classification, machine learning, structure from motion, stereo reconstruction, LiDAR classification, bathymetric inversion, SAR speckle reduction and multitemporal change models.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities include analysis-ready multi-sensor archives, robust uncertainty across proxies, turbid-water bathymetry, global validation, near-real-time hazards, automated quality control, physics-aware ML and equitable access to repeat coastal surveys.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent advances integrate UAV structure from motion, satellite-derived topography–bathymetry, cloud-scale processing, SAR–optical complementarity, machine learning and dense multitemporal archives to observe the coast as a connected continuum.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Aerial photogrammetry and shoreline mapping established repeat coastal surveys; Landsat enabled global multidecadal archives, while airborne LiDAR, SAR and video expanded elevation, all-weather and high-frequency observation.
synthesis.typical_methods: Workflows calibrate and georeference imagery, correct atmosphere and water level, segment land and water, build orthomosaics or point clouds, classify returns, validate against surveys, propagate error and analyze repeated acquisitions or fused sensors.
synthesis.validated_ranges: The reviewed corpus spans centimeter-to-decimeter UAV products, meter-scale airborne or spaceborne elevation and 10–30 m multispectral archives, with instantaneous to four-decade coverage. Valid ranges remain sensor-, water-clarity- and proxy-specific.
synthesis.well_established: Coastal remote sensing derives shoreline, elevation, bathymetry, waves and land-cover change from optical, radar, laser and photogrammetric measurements. Every product represents a defined physical or image proxy whose resolution, datum, acquisition conditions and uncertainty must be explicit.

claims.text: Coastal-current monitoring platforms are complementary: HF radar can map surface currents to roughly 200 km offshore, while satellites and drifters extend coverage but impose revisit, cloud, or tracking limitations.
claims.regime: Surface-current observation and the sensor technologies available through 2012.

claims.text: Shoreline mapping requires an explicit physical shoreline definition and sensor-appropriate proxy because extracted position varies with tide, wave conditions, morphology, image characteristics and interpretation method.
claims.regime: Shoreline Definition and Detection: A Review

claims.text: Coastal remote sensing combines satellite, airborne and in-situ non-contact observations to monitor shoreline, water, habitat and hazards across scales, with sensor fusion and validation central to operational use.
claims.regime: Remote Sensing Applications in Coastal Areas

claims.text: Field hyperspectra can discriminate many salt-marsh vegetation types because pigment absorption and especially canopy-structure effects create distinct spectral signatures; continuum removal improves visible-band separability but reduces near- and shortwave-infrared separability.
claims.regime: Field reflectance spectra from 27 salt-marsh vegetation types on the Dutch Wadden Sea coast, measured from 400 to 2500 nm during the growing season.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Classification accuracy, relative volume difference, and compliance fraction are useful dimensionless performance measures, but their meaning is conditional on class balance, change magnitude, reference uncertainty, and the engineering threshold being tested.
synthesis.disagreements: LiDAR clearly outperformed photogrammetry for local ground and vegetation retrieval in dense marsh and dune settings, while paired Baltic surveys differed by only 0.48% in net volume change. This is a scale-and-metric distinction, not a contradiction: bulk change can agree while local errors persist near water and vegetation.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: The reviewed datasets include a nine-class Spartina marsh, paired UAV marsh sensors, 526 RTK dune checkpoints, federal and local Louisiana levees, Staten Island terrain, and eight paired Baltic campaigns producing 16 DEMs and 895 profiles.
synthesis.governing_physics: Return elevation depends on laser interaction with canopy and ground, whereas coastal engineering interpretation depends on whether mapped terrain represents the hydraulic surface, drainage pathways, and morphologic change rather than vegetation or water artifacts.
synthesis.limitations: Limitations include vegetation interception, sparse ground returns, water-surface artifacts, scan geometry, DEM vertical uncertainty, site-trained classifiers, cross-survey coregistration, and failure of elevation-only inundation to represent culverts, barriers, friction, and timing.
synthesis.major_equations: The reviewed slice relies on point-to-reference residuals, MAE and RMSE, classification accuracy, DEM differencing, cross-section integration for sediment volume, and threshold-plus-connectivity inundation logic; it does not establish a universal coastal LiDAR transfer equation.
synthesis.numerical_models: Models range from cover-conditioned decision trees and genetic-algorithm ground estimators to automated levee-axis extraction, connected-cell inundation screening, DEM differencing, and data-driven attribution of morphologic change.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities are transferable vegetation corrections, standardized uncertainty budgets, repeated validation across tidal states and storm magnitudes, automated representation of culverts and defenses, and decision thresholds that compare expected change with the survey error floor.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent work couples compact UAV LiDAR with field-calibrated learning, direct paired comparison with SfM, and repeat morphodynamic monitoring, shifting LiDAR from episodic mapping toward change detection and method selection by terrain regime.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Within this screened branch, the 2013 salt-marsh study establishes cover-conditioned correction of vegetation-biased LiDAR elevation, and the 2014 levee study demonstrates engineering screening of long, irregular coastal defenses from airborne terrain.
synthesis.typical_methods: Typical workflows acquire airborne or UAV point clouds, classify ground and vegetation returns, build a DEM or DTM, coregister repeat surveys or auxiliary imagery, validate with RTK or field elevations, and propagate the terrain into habitat, morphology, defense, or inundation analyses.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Reported validation spans marsh DEM RMSE improvement from 0.15 to 0.10 m, UAV-LiDAR marsh ground RMSE of 5.9 cm, vegetated-dune RMSE of 9.86 cm, and a 0.48% LiDAR-SfM difference in bulk Baltic volume change; these values are site- and workflow-specific.
synthesis.well_established: Coastal LiDAR provides high-resolution elevation and structure for marsh, dune, defense, and flood applications; quantitative use still requires independent vertical validation and explicit treatment of vegetation, water, and hydraulic connectivity.

claims.text: Hyperspectral cover-class corrections reduced salt-marsh LiDAR DEM RMSE from 0.15 to 0.10 m while a multisensor decision tree achieved 90% habitat-classification accuracy.
claims.regime: The studied southeastern US Spartina marsh and its nine cover classes.

claims.text: At Little Sapelo marsh, UAV LiDAR ground-elevation RMSE was 5.9 cm versus 17.2 cm for photogrammetry, and vegetation-height RMSE was 17.5 versus 38.1 cm.
claims.regime: Dense Spartina marsh, 0.40 m output maps, and the tested UAV acquisition/classification workflow.

claims.text: Across eight paired Baltic UAV surveys and 895 profiles, LiDAR and SfM net beach-plus-dune volume change differed by only 0.48%, although SfM produced more local artifacts over water and vegetated dunes.
claims.regime: The 2022-2023 Mrzezyno survey geometry and bulk-change metric; local small changes may not be equivalent.

claims.text: Bathymetric LiDAR supplies integrated elevation measurements across shallow water and land for coastal-zone assessment, subject to water clarity, depth penetration, classification and ground validation.
claims.regime: Bringing Bathymetry LiDAR to Coastal Zone Assessment: A Case Study in the Southern Baltic

claims.text: Elevated 2D scanning LiDAR resolved wave-by-wave overtopping on an evolving porous cobble revetment; two reconstruction methods agreed within a factor of two for most events and showed rapid landward discharge decay from infiltration.
claims.regime: Laboratory dynamic cobble revetments with time-varying crest geometry under the tested waves and material configurations.

claims.text: Structure-from-motion photogrammetry can efficiently recover elevation-dependent mangrove pneumatophore geometry needed by hydrodynamic drag models, matching manual stem count and number-times-mean-diameter while capturing barnacle-encrusted complexity that calipers miss.
claims.regime: Dense Sonneratia caseolaris pneumatophore canopies, including barnacle-encrusted roots, exposed at low tide on Cù Lao Dung Island in Vietnam's Mekong Delta.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Correlation, normalized scatter, detection rate, and regression slope quantify skill but are dataset-specific statistical measures. No universal dimensionless parameter removes the effects of coast distance, waveform contamination, or sampling geometry.
synthesis.disagreements: Altimetry can agree closely with buoys in favorable coastal collocations yet still miss extremes or become biased near shore. This is a resolution, sampling, and waveform-regime difference rather than conflicting evidence about universal sensor accuracy.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Reviewed datasets include 36 months of Iberian radar-buoy-Sentinel observations, five-mission northeastern US metocean composites, 27 years at 50 Southeast Asian VLM sites, a ten-year Gulf of Lion simulation/altimetry record, and continent-wide Australian tide-model rankings every 10 km.
synthesis.governing_physics: Radar range and returned-waveform shape determine sea surface height and sea-state estimates; land contamination, surface roughness, atmosphere and geophysical corrections, track geometry, tides, and land motion all affect coastal interpretation.
synthesis.limitations: Land-contaminated waveforms, sparse repeat tracks, asynchronous sampling, correction uncertainty, sun-synchronous tidal aliasing, fixed-sensor coverage, and site-trained machine learning constrain transferability and event detection.
synthesis.major_equations: Core calculations combine corrected radar range with satellite orbit height, derive wave and wind metrics from waveforms/backscatter, difference relative tide-gauge and absolute altimeter trends for vertical land motion, and use correlation or error metrics to rank products and tide models.
synthesis.numerical_models: Relevant models include multi-mission objective analysis, geophysical correction and retracking chains, random-forest event classifiers, global ocean tide models, and the eo-tides locally adaptive ensemble.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities include high-resolution coastal retracking, uncertainty-aware multi-mission fusion, event-scale sampling, joint absolute and relative sea-level attribution, transferable current classifiers, and exploitation of SWOT and future missions.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent advances combine sensors and models rather than relying on one product: tide gauges plus altimetry recover VLM, optical NDWI plus altimetry guides tide ensembles, and simulation-altimetry-ADCP fusion enables event classification.
synthesis.seminal_papers: The 2023 altimetry review is the synthesis anchor in this screened slice, documenting the multi-decadal mission lineage and transition from open-ocean measurement toward operational coastal applications.
synthesis.typical_methods: Typical workflows collocate altimeters with buoys or tide gauges, merge multiple missions, retrack coastal waveforms, apply objective mapping, combine optical wetting indices with tide predictions, fuse numerical simulations with machine learning, and validate against independent fixed instruments.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Skill is product and regime bound: Iberian Sentinel-3 SWH validation achieved R above 0.94 and RMSE 0.17-0.42 m; northeastern US composites are climatological and weaken near land; Australian NDWI rankings sample tidal phase more directly than amplitude.
synthesis.well_established: Satellite radar altimetry provides long, repeatable observations of sea surface height, significant wave height, and wind speed that complement sparse in situ coastal networks, but quality generally deteriorates close to land and sampling is not continuous.

claims.text: More than 30 years of multi-mission satellite altimetry provide operational observations of ocean surface topography, sea level, waves, and circulation, with newer systems extending useful measurements closer to coastlines.
claims.regime: Validated radar-altimetry products; coastal performance remains mission-, correction-, and distance-dependent.

claims.text: Five-mission altimetry composites reproduced northeastern US seasonal wind and wave patterns, but bias increased near shore and aggregated observations missed some buoy extrema within 40 km of the coast.

claims.text: Five decades of coastal-wetland remote sensing show a progression from extent mapping to structural and physiological retrieval and then ecosystem-function and biogeochemical assessment, with future gains depending on multi-sensor fusion, ecological-process coupling, and artificial intelligence.

claims.text: A calibration-free Sentinel-2/GEE workflow classified intermittent river-mouth connectivity across about 1,500 km of Western Mediterranean coast, with fixed-threshold NDWI achieving roughly 80% agreement and showing discharge promotes breaching while waves promote bar formation and closure.
claims.regime: Intermittently open/closed river mouths on the microtidal, wave-dominated Western Mediterranean coast over the Sentinel-2 record.

claims.text: No single multispectral-image method can extract shoreline indicators across all coast types: current work is dominated by instantaneous waterlines, so global monitoring requires indicator- and setting-specific combinations of spectral, segmentation and machine-learning methods.
claims.regime: Landsat, Sentinel-2 and related multispectral imagery used to identify waterlines, cliffs, dunes, vegetation and other shoreline indicators from local to global scales.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Important nondimensional quantities include spectral indices, normalized reflectance and band ratios, spectral angle, classification agreement such as kappa, relative vertical error, overlap and geometry quality measures, and habitat or vegetation fractions; dimensional pixel size alone is not an accuracy guarantee.
synthesis.disagreements: LiDAR's superior local marsh elevation accuracy and SfM's close agreement in integrated dune-volume change are not contradictory: point elevation, profile artifacts, and spatially integrated volume are different metrics over different surfaces. Likewise, UAV's finer pixels did not universally outperform airplane or satellite habitat mapping because target separability and water effects controlled skill.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: The branch includes seasonal biomass and multispectral imagery at Carpinteria, paired LiDAR-photogrammetry marsh observations at Little Sapelo, eight paired dune surveys and 895 profiles in the Baltic, nine morphology surveys of a New Jersey groin field, multiline LiDAR in dense marsh, and paired aerial-surface hyperspectral habitat maps.
synthesis.governing_physics: Passive SfM requires stable visible texture and is degraded by moving or reflective water and canopy occlusion; LiDAR samples range and may penetrate canopy but still needs ground classification; multispectral and hyperspectral products depend on illumination, spectral contrast, water-column attenuation, turbidity, depth, and mixed pixels.
synthesis.limitations: Small footprints, battery and weather limits, flight regulation, tide and sun-glint timing, ground-control distribution, moving water, dense or flexible vegetation, turbidity, processing choices, scarce reference data, and site-specific calibration limit repeatability and transfer. Newer 2026 evidence also remains lightly replicated.
synthesis.major_equations: Representative formulations include SfM bundle adjustment and surface differencing, NDVI and its calibrated biomass regression AGB=2428.2 NDVI+120.1, spectral-angle similarity, Random-Forest or ANN classification, allometric biomass regressions, and error metrics such as RMSE and Cohen kappa.
synthesis.numerical_models: Models range from photogrammetric reconstruction and DEM differencing to NDVI regression, vegetation allometry, spectral-angle mapping, Random Forest habitat classification, and ANN LiDAR filtering. Each model requires calibration and validation matched to the target variable and environment.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities are standardized uncertainty budgets, synchronized multi-sensor benchmarks, cross-site classifier and allometry transfer, water-column correction, canopy and ground separation, automated quality flags, defensible change-detection thresholds, and scalable fusion with satellite and in-situ observations.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent advances move beyond RGB surface reconstruction toward spatial-spectral ANN ground filtering, multi-temporal sensor intercomparison, UAV-derived vegetation allometry, multiscale hyperspectral habitat mapping, and target-specific comparisons spanning drone, airplane, surface vehicle, and satellite observations.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Within this screened branch, the 2015 overview framed the platform and sensor opportunity, while the 2021 Little Sapelo comparison established quantitative LiDAR-versus-photogrammetry accuracy for vegetated coastal terrain.
synthesis.typical_methods: Workflows combine flight and tide planning, RTK/PPK or ground control, camera or LiDAR calibration, overlapping imagery and SfM, point-cloud filtering, orthomosaic or DEM creation, repeat differencing, spectral indices or supervised classification, and independent checkpoints, field plots, profiles, or underwater video.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Reported tests span 1-10 cm imagery in the foundational review; 5.9 versus 17.2 cm marsh-ground RMSE for LiDAR and photogrammetry; 0.48% difference in integrated Baltic volume change across eight surveys and 895 profiles; 1-10 cm hyperspectral pixels over 230-20,200 m2; and 0.04 m UAV through 10-20 m satellite imagery with mean kappa 0.71-0.77.
synthesis.well_established: Coastal UAS provide operator-timed centimetre-scale observations between ground surveys and crewed or satellite platforms, but accuracy depends on sensor physics, control and georeferencing, surface texture, vegetation, water, tide, weather, processing, validation, and the spatial scale of the reported metric.

claims.text: Coastal UAVs offer operator-controlled revisit timing and sub-10-cm imagery with diverse sensors, but payload, endurance, weather, regulation, and ground control constrain performance.
claims.regime: beaches; wetlands; nearshore waters

claims.text: At Carpinteria Salt Marsh, seasonal NDVI biomass calibration outperformed pooled calibration, with spring r2=0.67 and RMSE=344 g m-2 versus pooled r2=0.36 and RMSE=496 g m-2.
claims.regime: California salt marsh

claims.text: Spatial-spectral ANN filtering of drone LiDAR improved salt-marsh ground-point discrimination needed for terrain reconstruction under dense vegetation.
claims.regime: vegetated coastal salt marsh

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Normalized RMSE, IoU, F1, and automatic-success fraction quantify retrieval performance but are dataset-specific. Viewing-angle geometry and relative feature density are central conditioning factors rather than universal similarity parameters.
synthesis.disagreements: High pixel-level segmentation scores do not guarantee accurate real-world shoreline coordinates: calibration drift can create tens to hundreds of metres of positional error. These evaluate different pipeline stages and must be validated jointly.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Reviewed evidence includes about 900 breaker-height records across five sites, five years of three-camera Anglet imagery, a three-camera UCalib conditioning study, and a labeled fixed-camera Timex segmentation dataset.
synthesis.governing_physics: Timex imagery converts persistent optical signatures into measurable spatial patterns: breaking foam marks the breaker zone and time-averaged land-water contrast marks the shoreline; perspective projection maps those pixels into coastal coordinates.
synthesis.limitations: Performance degrades with missing static features, poor visibility or illumination, foam ambiguity, occlusion, long camera range, thermal motion, unrepresented sites, and error propagation from calibration through rectification and extraction.
synthesis.major_equations: Core operations include projective camera geometry, image registration transforms, cross-correlation displacement, foam-length empirical breaker-height relations, and segmentation metrics such as intersection over union and boundary F1.
synthesis.numerical_models: Models include Hsb,v/Hsb,v24 empirical breaker estimators, edge-keypoint geometric stabilization, UCalib feature-transfer calibration, and U-Net/DeepLabv3+ semantic segmentation with several CNN backbones.
synthesis.open_questions: Needs include standardized multi-site benchmarks, calibrated uncertainty from pixels to ground coordinates, robust feature-free calibration, domain adaptation across lighting and morphology, and fusion with satellite, UAV, buoy, and model observations.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent advances shift from hand-designed thresholds toward autocalibration and deep segmentation, while adjacent satellite studies supply longer spatial context for waterline and shoreline interpretation.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Within this screened slice, the Anglet stabilization study establishes the scale of long-term geometry error, while the Timex breaker-height paper demonstrates a directly engineering-relevant hydrodynamic retrieval.
synthesis.typical_methods: Typical workflows create snapshot and Timex images, detect static edges or features, stabilize and calibrate each frame, rectify pixels to ground coordinates, then apply empirical foam geometry, thresholding, or semantic segmentation and validate against independent waves or shorelines.
synthesis.validated_ranges: The bathymetry-free breaker method spans 0.1-3.8 m with 18% mean normalized RMSE; Anglet stabilization automated at least 90% of frames; UCalib ranged from above 90% to about 40% success by feature availability; segmentation mIoU was 0.95-0.97 in-domain.
synthesis.well_established: Fixed coastal cameras provide frequent, low-cost observations of shoreline and breaker-zone behavior, but quantitative products require stable geometry, accurate calibration, visible scene features, and algorithms validated for the site and image conditions.

claims.text: A bathymetry-free Timex foam-signature method estimated breaking wave heights of 0.1-3.8 m across five sites with mean normalized RMSE of 18% over about 900 records.

risk.label: Coastal hazards and risk
risk.description: Hazard, exposure, vulnerability, consequences, and decisions.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Controls include annual exceedance probability, return-period-to-lifetime ratio, conditional failure probability, damage ratio, vulnerability index, protection reliability, hazard and loss correlation, benefit-cost ratio, expected annual loss relative to GDP or budget and recovery-time ratios.
synthesis.disagreements: Composite indices improve comparability but can obscure causal mechanisms and weighting; detailed fragility models are mechanistic but data intensive. Expected annual loss supports portfolios yet can hide tail, distributional and nonmarket consequences. Static rankings may reverse under future development or adaptation.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Reviewed evidence includes global roads/railways, WorldRiskIndex and INFORM outcomes, Po flood and levee scenarios, British bridge failures, 726 Tohoku source realizations, Catalan beach sectors, masonry flood cases and Bangladesh cyclonic-flood literature and census indicators.
synthesis.governing_physics: Storms, waves, surge, rainfall, rivers, erosion, tsunami and defense failure generate loads and inundation; receptor geometry, materials, social capacity and networks govern damage and recovery. Climate, development and adaptation make hazard, exposure and vulnerability nonstationary.
synthesis.limitations: Sparse loss and failure data, reporting bias, uncertain extremes, dependence, defense behavior, indirect and cascading effects, informal assets, social inequity, model resolution and future scenarios limit confidence. Validation of hazard alone does not validate risk.
synthesis.major_equations: Expected risk integrates consequence over hazard intensity and probability, often as expected annual damage. Fragility gives conditional failure probability; vulnerability maps intensity to damage ratio or sensitivity; reliability compares stochastic load and resistance, and multihazard models represent joint, conditional or cascading events.
synthesis.numerical_models: Models include extreme-value and stochastic-event sets, copulas and joint probabilities, hydraulic and tsunami simulations, Monte Carlo reliability, fragility and damage functions, GIS exposure/vulnerability overlays, network disruption and scenario-based future risk.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities include compound and cascading dependence, dynamic vulnerability and recovery, indirect network losses, ecosystem and cultural consequences, equity, behavioral adaptation, deep uncertainty, transferable fragility and transparent validation of composite indices.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent work uses stochastic source ensembles, spatial multihazard interaction, dynamic exposure and vulnerability scenarios, global infrastructure networks, uncertainty visualization and impact chains that connect climate drivers to physical and socioeconomic consequences.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Risk theory formalized probability–consequence integration; engineering reliability introduced load–resistance and fragility functions; hazard mapping and vulnerability research then combined spatial exposure with physical and social susceptibility. Disaster-risk frameworks broadened analysis to resilience and governance.
synthesis.typical_methods: Workflows define system and receptors, construct probabilistic hazards, map exposure, estimate fragility/vulnerability and losses, model dependence and cascades, validate each component, aggregate uncertainty and compare mitigation. Participatory and distributional analysis complements physical-economic metrics.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Reported values are context-specific: global transport EAD spans $3.1–22 billion, high-vulnerability countries show 15-fold event mortality, and 726 tsunami sources represent one Tohoku case. Such values cannot be transferred without harmonized exposure, vulnerability and uncertainty.
synthesis.well_established: Coastal risk arises from the joint occurrence of hazard, exposed people/assets/ecosystems, vulnerability or fragility, and consequences. Changes in any component can dominate risk, and correlated or sequential hazards can amplify impacts beyond independent single-hazard estimates.

claims.text: Coastal risk assessment should integrate probabilistic hazard, exposure, vulnerability and consequences across present and future conditions while borrowing validated methods across hazard communities only with explicit transfer assumptions.
claims.regime: Global and regional natural-hazard risk assessment including floods and tsunamis.

claims.text: Comparative evidence from Hong Kong and Singapore indicates that resilient coastal-city flood management requires integrating flood-risk and climate-adaptation policy into spatial planning, resolving agency responsibilities, and coupling engineered controls with long-term inter-agency governance.
claims.regime: Dense Asian coastal cities exposed to pluvial, fluvial, tidal, storm-surge, and sea-level risks under continued urbanization and climate change.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Hazard and exposure indices, conditional damage ratios, exceedance probability, return period, normalized connectivity loss and intervention-effect ratios organize comparisons; their definitions and normalization are study-specific and are not interchangeable by default.
synthesis.disagreements: The studies do not establish one universal consequence measure. Exposure-only maps omit fragility and welfare loss, asset-value loss can dominate modeled totals while obscuring social vulnerability, and hazard inventories such as ice zonation identify potential harm without estimating realized loss.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Case evidence covers ten European RISC-KIT sites, Ria Formosa barrier scenarios, Galveston roads and emergency facilities, Québec municipal asset inventories, Mississippi oyster landings and revenue, eastern North Carolina property and labor data, and mapped Alaskan nearshore-ice zones.
synthesis.governing_physics: Storm waves, water levels, erosion, overwash, inundation, hurricane wind, debris transport and seasonal ice govern the retained cases. Consequences emerge only after these processes interact with asset location, fragility, network topology, ecosystem production or operational exposure.
synthesis.limitations: Transfer is constrained by local inventories, vulnerability functions, economic valuation, network topology, scenario discretization and model-form uncertainty. Indirect, intangible, distributional and recovery consequences remain inconsistently represented, and abstract-limited sources support fewer implementation details.
synthesis.major_equations: Common forms include risk as event probability times conditional consequence, indicator combinations such as CI=sqrt(i_hazard i_exposure), depth- or intensity-damage functions, Bayesian conditional probabilities, network-connectivity loss and discounted or cumulative economic-loss accounting.
synthesis.numerical_models: XBeach and LISFLOOD-FP support detailed hotspot analysis; Bayesian networks emulate morphodynamic scenario chains; debris, fragility and graph models estimate road service loss; GIS and probabilistic hurricane models join hazard fields to spatial assets and economic quantities.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities include transferable multi-sector consequence functions, uncertainty propagation from hazard through recovery, treatment of cascading infrastructure failures, ecosystem-service and intangible loss, distributional welfare, behavioral adaptation, and validation against observed longitudinal recovery.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent work adds debris-mediated network disruption and jointly maps property and labor consequences, while building-level adaptive pathways update decisions as sea-level projections change. The advance is increasingly explicit coupling among physical hazards, exposed systems and decisions rather than hazard mapping alone.
synthesis.seminal_papers: The 1981 Alaskan ice-zonation study is an early engineering-hazard inventory. The 2017–2018 CRAF and Ria Formosa studies are central to multiscale and probabilistic coastal impact assessment because they connect regional screening, process models and risk-reduction choices.
synthesis.typical_methods: The evidence spans regional indicator screening followed by process modelling, Bayesian-network surrogates, probabilistic debris and transport-network analysis, GIS exposure overlays, economic accounting, and coupled property/labor loss simulation.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Evidence is bounded to the reported cases: European screening sectors near 1 km and hotspots of 1–10 km; a Ria Formosa 50-year storm plus spring tide; a representative Galveston 500-year hurricane; Mississippi fishery impacts from 2005–2016; and each study's mapped asset inventory.
synthesis.well_established: Coastal consequence assessment must explicitly connect hazard intensity to exposed receptors and an impact metric. Direct physical damage, network-service loss, livelihood loss, indirect economic disruption and systemic effects are distinct endpoints and should not be collapsed without a stated aggregation rule.
