synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Important controls include suspension number or Rouse-type settling-to-mixing ratios, Shields mobility, relative settling velocity, wave-current ratio, sediment diffusivity to eddy-viscosity ratio, relative depth, breaker type, wave-group ratio, and hydrodynamic versus concentration-adjustment time and length scales.
synthesis.disagreements: Reduced models can agree with 2DV and 3-D solutions inside their adjustment-scale validity domain, yet depth-averaged models are unreliable in strongly three-dimensional flows. Nominally accretive wave forcing does not necessarily imply shoreward suspended transport.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Evidence includes lightweight-sediment laboratory dispersion, a large-flume 1:15 mobile beach under monochromatic, bichromatic, long-wave and random forcing, plunging-breaker turbulence and concentration measurements, and paired-tray two-way sediment flux at turbid Great Barrier Reef sites.
synthesis.governing_physics: Core mechanisms are turbulence-driven pickup, settling lag, concentration adaptation, wave-current boundary-layer mixing, plunging-jet vortices, wave-backwash interaction, seiche advection, density or wind-driven circulation, and erosion-deposition feedback with the bed.
synthesis.limitations: Controlled experiments and idealized geometries dominate; concentration boundary conditions and turbulent diffusivity remain uncertain, cohesive and mixed sediments are underrepresented, fine mesh may be required near plunging jets, and delivery measurements do not equal net accumulation.
synthesis.major_equations: The common framework is an advection-diffusion-settling equation for concentration with erosion or reference-concentration and deposition boundary conditions, coupled to hydrodynamics ranging from shallow-water exact solutions to quasi-3-D asymptotics and three-dimensional or RANS flow solvers.
synthesis.numerical_models: Reviewed models include a full 3-D split characteristics/finite-difference transport solver, a quasi-3-D asymptotic adjustment model, exact Lagrangian seiche solutions, and a 2-D RANS k-epsilon/VOF breaker model with advection-diffusion concentration.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities are transferable entrainment and deposition closures, coherent treatment of cohesive mixtures and flocculation, three-dimensional irregular-breaker validation, coupled bed evolution, uncertainty-aware sensor calibration, and field tests that close suspended mass budgets.
synthesis.recent_advances: Later work resolves plunging-jet turbulence and near-surface concentration and links event-scale wave-backwash interactions to profile response, while field flux methods distinguish gross two-way delivery from net sedimentation.
synthesis.seminal_papers: The 1988 full 3-D scheme and 1992 quasi-3-D wave-current theory established numerical and reduced-order foundations; the 2003 exact seiche solutions clarified settling-lag redistribution and provide reproducible benchmarks.
synthesis.typical_methods: Methods combine optical or acoustic concentration measurements, pump or trap sampling, mobile-bed flumes, event-resolved flux analysis, exact and asymptotic solutions, characteristics and finite differences, RANS turbulence closure, VOF interface tracking, and comparisons among depth-averaged, 2DV, and 3-D models.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Explicit ranges include six-run, approximately 2.4 h conditions on a 1:15 flume beach and reef two-way fluxes of 34 to more than 640 g m-2 d-1 with net sedimentation below 122 g m-2 d-1. Other studies report regime definitions but accessible sources do not expose universal numerical bounds.
synthesis.well_established: Suspended coastal sediment is governed by entrainment, three-dimensional advection, turbulent diffusion, settling and deposition; net flux depends on the timing and spatial structure of concentration relative to currents, waves, breakers, swash, and basin oscillations.

claims.text: Where coastal suspended transport is governed by three-dimensional flow patterns such as harbour-entrance separation or wind and density currents, depth-averaged models can give unreliable siltation and erosion estimates; a split characteristics/finite-difference solution of the full 3-D advection-diffusion equation performed well in hypothetical and lightweight-sediment laboratory tests.
claims.regime: Complex three-dimensional coastal flows; tested with hypothetical cases and laboratory transport and dispersal of lightweight sediment.

claims.text: In large-flume tests starting from a 1:15 mobile-bed slope and lasting about 2.4 h per condition, all erosive wave cases caused shoreline retreat and a breakpoint bar, but not every nominally accretive case transported sediment shoreward; suspended flux was governed by the occurrence and number of wave-backwash interactions within a wave group.
claims.regime: Large flume; handmade 1:15 initial slope; each condition approximately 2.4 h in six runs; erosive and accretive wave series.

claims.text: Within a quasi-3-D formulation using a logarithmic velocity profile and wave-modified diffusivity and near-bed concentration, adding waves substantially increased suspended load and its adjustment time and length scales while enlarging the model's validity region; results agreed with 2DV/3-D solutions and existing measurements.
claims.regime: Logarithmic velocity profile with wave effects represented through diffusivity and the near-bed boundary condition; applicability bounded by a wave-modified suspension parameter and forcing-change scales.

claims.text: For exact fundamental seiche modes in parabolic elliptical and circular basins, settling lag generated net suspended-sediment transport from deeper toward shallower regions; the mode-specific erosion and deposition patterns were robust to the transport-law formulation and little affected by omission of hydrodynamic friction.
claims.regime: Idealized elliptical or circular basin with parabolic cross-section; coarse-sand-oriented erosion/deposition law; friction omitted from the hydrodynamic solution.

claims.text: For experimentally tested strong plunging breakers, a fine-grid 2-D RANS k-epsilon/VOF model with an advection-diffusion sediment equation reproduced the overturning jet and high near-surface concentration and agreed with measured surface elevation, velocity, turbulent kinetic energy, eddy viscosity, and suspended concentration.
claims.regime: Two-dimensional surf-zone plunging breakers; advection-diffusion concentration with reference-concentration bottom boundary; selected fine mesh resolution.

claims.text: A review of internal-solitary-wave sediment transport identifies bottom-boundary-layer currents and turbulence as widespread resuspension drivers, while emphasizing Reynolds mismatch, grid resolution, and quadratic-stress parameterization as primary limits on laboratory and field-scale prediction.
claims.regime: Continental-margin internal solitary waves and their bottom boundary layers.

claims.text: Near-bed field cospectra on a non-barred shoreface show wind-wave and swell suspended transport was predominantly onshore and strengthened with shoaling, while undertow transport was offshore and dominated where oscillatory components were weak; breaking introduced strong vertical and temporal variability.
claims.regime: Marine non-barred shoreface under wind waves, swell, group-bound long waves and undertow during the field campaign.

claims.text: Field data from three experiments on two beaches show onshore suspended transport under large shear stress in relatively deep, gently sloping water, but increasingly strong breaking and undertow drive offshore transport in shallower or steeper surf zones; a nondimensional flux index captures the transition.
claims.regime: Two-dimensional barred and gently sloping surf zones represented by three field experiments on two beaches.

claims.text: Without mean flow, oscillating-grid turbulence resuspends consolidated sediment according to a nonlinear interaction among consolidation time, particle size, canopy density and flexibility: sparse flexible canopies enhance turbulence and resuspension relative to rigid ones, while dense flexible canopies suppress both.
claims.regime: Consolidated synthetic, lake and saltmarsh sediment beds beneath modeled submerged rigid, semi-rigid and flexible canopies without mean flow.

claims.text: After Three Gorges Dam closure, the upper Changjiang changed from the dominant sediment source to a sink, lakes and the eroding middle-lower bed became sources, and estuarine shoals and landward marine transport gained importance, increasing future estuary-erosion sensitivity to further dams, storms and sea level.
claims.regime: Changjiang river-estuary depositional system before and after closure of the Three Gorges Dam in 2003.

claims.text: For idealized Punta Umbria tidal conditions, adding sea waves increased modeled suspended-sediment concentration and transport despite reducing the wave–current resultant velocity, because wave orbital motion raised maximum bed shear; cohesive sediment remained vertically mixed while non-cohesive sediment concentrated near the bed.
claims.regime: Idealized tidal currents, seabeds and wave conditions derived from measurements at Punta Umbria, Huelva, Spain.

claims.text: Tidal sediment delivery in creek-dissected mangroves shifts from creek-dominated routing at lower tides toward sheet flow at high tides; sheltered forest interiors become effective sediment sinks, but trapping capacity declines with sediment starvation, forest loss, and deeper inundation combined with lower vegetation density.
claims.regime: An elevated, creek-dissected mangrove forest in the Trang River estuary on Thailand's Andaman coast, evaluated over individual tides and instantaneous environmental perturbations.

storm_surge.label: Storm surge and coastal flooding
storm_surge.description: Meteorologically forced coastal water levels and flooding.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Controls include storm size-to-shelf scale, translation-to-wave speed, Rossby and Froude numbers, drag coefficient, surge-to-tidal range, wave setup-to-surge ratio, discharge-to-tidal prism, coastal slope, return period and joint dependence measures.
synthesis.disagreements: Surge-only models can omit wave and discharge contributions, while fully coupled systems add uncertain boundaries and parameters. Climate-modified storm characteristics do not map monotonically to inundation because track, timing and local geography interact nonlinearly.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Evidence includes synthetic New York hurricanes, 3,433 global river mouths, Storm Gloria, Hurricanes Isabel, Irene and Sandy in Delaware, 21 U.S. hurricanes from 2000–2013, and Liverpool Bay and wider European surge-wave applications.
synthesis.governing_physics: Wind transfers momentum to the water column, pressure gradients drive inverse-barometer response, rotation and bathymetry shape propagation, and nonlinear tide–surge interaction changes timing and amplitude. Waves add setup and overtopping; discharge encounters surge-driven backwater in estuaries and deltas.
synthesis.limitations: Cyclone sampling, wind and pressure bias, drag at extreme winds, bathymetric and topographic resolution, levees and drainage, wave setup and overtopping, river boundaries, dependence assumptions and nonstationarity limit transferable hazard estimates.
synthesis.major_equations: Depth-integrated or three-dimensional mass and momentum equations include wind and pressure forcing, Coriolis, bottom stress and wetting/drying. Spectral wave equations supply radiation stresses; hydrologic and hydraulic equations supply runoff, while extreme-value or event-set methods estimate probabilities.
synthesis.numerical_models: Model chains range from statistical hurricane generation plus SLOSH to global routing bounded by dynamic tide-surge levels, regional surge–wave models, and NWM–D-Flow/HEC-RAS–ADCIRC/WW3 compound systems with wetting and drying.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities include compound-driver dependence, changing cyclone tracks and structure, rapid coupled forecasts, urban drainage and defenses, uncertainty partitioning, equitable exposure and consistent global-to-local downscaling.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent work dynamically couples ocean, wave, river and floodplain models, uses large synthetic event sets, resolves deltas globally, perturbs historical cyclones under future climates and attributes flood response to interacting drivers and geography.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Classical wind setup and inverse-barometer theory established surge forcing; numerical shallow-water models enabled operational prediction, and later tide–surge interaction, wave coupling and statistical event methods established modern hazard assessment.
synthesis.typical_methods: Studies use tide gauges, wave buoys, reanalyses and post-event maps; synthetic or historical cyclone ensembles; SLOSH, ADCIRC, WW3, D-Flow and hydraulic models; nested inundation grids; peaks-over-threshold analysis; attribution and climate perturbation experiments.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Reported values include up to 1 m surge and 8 m significant waves during Gloria, 0.79–0.91 Delaware peak-level skill, surge effects at 64% of global delta mouths, and average end-century U.S. hurricane inundation increases of 36% by volume and 25% by extent.
synthesis.well_established: Storm surge is the meteorologically forced departure of coastal water level from the astronomical tide. Wind stress, atmospheric pressure, storm track and translation interact with shelf and basin geometry; waves, tides, rivers and rainfall can substantially alter total flooding.

claims.text: Coastal storm-flood assessment should treat storm surge, astronomical tide, wind waves and their mean-circulation interactions as a coupled system whenever their combined water-level and overtopping effects are material.
claims.regime: Marine-storm flooding where surge, tide and wind-wave processes jointly affect coastal water level or impacts.

storm_surge.compound.label: Compound flooding
storm_surge.compound.description: Joint marine, fluvial, pluvial, and groundwater flooding.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Controls include surge-to-tide ratio, discharge-to-tidal prism, rainfall duration and intensity ratios, phase lag normalized by tidal period, Froude number, storage and drainage-capacity ratios, seawall freeboard, overtopping rate, joint exceedance probability and fractional driver contribution.
synthesis.disagreements: A dominant driver varies by event and location: Jebi airport flooding was overtopping dominated, prolonged Harvey rainfall created extensive delayed fluvial–pluvial compounding, and larger tidal amplitude can suppress upstream surge propagation. These are regime differences, not a universal ranking of drivers.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Evidence includes five Virginia hurricanes; Jacksonville/Irma and Hernani wave cases; Napa River and idealized channels; 15 southeastern China regions with 1960–2015 records; Xiangshan infrastructure; Typhoon Jebi at Kansai Airport; a 2017 embayment event; and Harvey, Ike, Rita and calibration data in Sabine–Neches.
synthesis.governing_physics: Coastal surge and tide impose downstream head; river discharge propagates seaward; rainfall creates runoff and local ponding; saturated storage delays drainage; waves overtop barriers; seawalls, gates, dams, storm drains and sewers redirect or block flux. Geometry and driver timing determine coastal, hydrologic and transition zones.
synthesis.limitations: Uncertainty arises from rainfall fields, runoff and infiltration, river boundaries, bathymetry/topography, roughness, drainage connectivity and blockage, breach assumptions, wave overtopping, groundwater omission, grid resolution, daily statistical sampling, copula tails and sparse validation of extreme combinations.
synthesis.major_equations: Models solve depth-integrated mass and momentum with rainfall, infiltration, river, drain and coastal source terms. Statistical studies use peaks over threshold, marginal extreme distributions and copulas. Driver attribution compares all-driver and leave-one-driver-out simulations, while interaction residuals quantify departure from additive response.
synthesis.numerical_models: SFINCS provides efficient reduced physics; Delft3D-FM resolves flexible-mesh estuary and river interaction; SuWAT integrates surge, tide, waves, overtopping and pluvial/sewer processes; other coupled city models explicitly include drainage, dams, gates, seawalls and rainfall runoff.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities are groundwater and soil saturation, dynamic drainage failure, defence breach probability, wave–surge–rain–river coupling, multivariate climate nonstationarity, probabilistic phasing, real-time data assimilation, common intercomparison cases and consequence-aware attribution.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent work partitions dynamic driver zones, represents urban sewers and structural failure, and quantifies flood-volume contributions. Historical multistorm studies now show temporally separated compound peaks, shifting attention from coincident maxima to evolving event sequences.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Within this corpus, the 2018 Napa River study demonstrates non-additive tide–surge–river phasing, while the 2021 SFINCS study establishes an efficient all-driver solver with explicit evidence that advection is required for broken-wave and shock flow.
synthesis.typical_methods: Methods include tightly or singly coupled hydrologic–hydrodynamic models, flexible meshes, reduced-physics solvers, sewer/drain networks, wave overtopping and breach modules, idealized phasing tests, historical hurricane hindcasts, high-water-mark validation, driver-isolation scenarios, POT and copula analysis.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Validation is case bounded. Sabine–Neches mean water-level calibration reached R²=0.91 and 84% of Imelda high-water-mark depths were within ±0.2 m. Jebi attribution was 90.8% overtopping, 7.5% seawall failure and smaller sewer shares. Napa scenarios included surge small relative to a 2 m tide.
synthesis.well_established: Compound coastal flooding occurs when coastal water level, waves, river discharge, direct rainfall, runoff, groundwater or infrastructure pathways interact in space or time. Combined inundation is generally not recoverable by simply adding independently calculated peak maps because phasing, storage, backwater and drainage capacity are nonlinear.

claims.text: SFINCS reproduced compound fluvial, pluvial, tidal and wind-driven flooding for Hurricane Irma at Jacksonville with limited computational expense, while an advective momentum term was necessary for shock-like dam-break and broken-wave flows and enabled wave-driven flooding at Hernani.
claims.regime: Verification cases, Hurricane Irma Jacksonville flooding, and broken-wave flooding at Hernani.

claims.text: For Xiangshan, coupled simulation of surge, heavy rainfall, urban drainage, a coastal dam and tide gates partitioned inundation into tidal, hydrologic and transition zones, showing that mitigation choice must follow the locally dominant driver and infrastructure interaction.
claims.regime: Xiangshan topography, drainage, coastal dam and tide-gate configurations in the tested storm scenarios.

claims.text: In Napa River field-scale and idealized Delft3D-FM simulations, coincident high tide, surge and river discharge maximized water levels; large tidal amplitude diminished upstream surge propagation, and the phase between peak discharge and high tide shifted the location and timing of maxima.
claims.regime: Napa River geometry plus idealized small-river scenarios, including 0.2 m surge and 2 m tide cases.

claims.text: For Harvey, Ike and Rita in the Sabine–Neches Estuary, a single-domain Delft3D-FM model identified four coastal–fluvial–pluvial interaction mechanisms; extended rainfall produced the largest extent and duration and a lagged second flood peak, while calibration achieved mean water-level R²=0.91 and 84% of Imelda high-water-mark depths within ±0.2 m.
claims.regime: Sabine–Neches domain for Harvey, Ike and Rita, with tide-gauge and Imelda high-water-mark calibration evidence.

claims.text: For 15 southeastern China coastal-estuarine regions using 1960–2015 daily discharge and sea-level records, peak-over-threshold and copula analyses showed that joint fluvial–storm-tide flooding can exceed the flooding implied by either driver in isolation and that dependence varies among sites.
claims.regime: Fifteen regions between 106–120°E and 18–32°N with available 1960–2015 daily records.

claims.text: Across five hurricanes simulated for low-gradient coastal Virginia, flooding separated into rainfall-dominant, surge-dominant and transitional zones; coastal-zone extent correlated strongly with surge magnitude, while transitional-zone extent correlated very strongly with the product of surge-inundated area and total rainfall.
claims.regime: Five Virginia hurricanes spanning different rainfall and surge intensities.

claims.text: For an embayment-backed urban catchment and the 12 January 2017 compound event, coupled simulations resolved separate and combined high-marine-level and precipitation flooding and showed that seawall and storm-drain configuration controls whether coastal protection blocks or facilitates drainage.
claims.regime: The studied embayment-backed catchment, historical 12 January 2017 event and tested seawall/drain scenarios.

claims.text: For Typhoon Jebi flooding at Kansai International Airport, the integrated SuWAT analysis attributed 90.8% of total flood volume to wave overtopping, 7.5% to seawall failure, and 1.7% and 0.26% to seawater and rainwater sewer reverse flows, respectively.
claims.regime: Kansai Airport geometry and infrastructure during the reconstructed 2018 Typhoon Jebi event.

claims.text: Across 3,433 river mouths, surge exacerbated 1-in-10-year river flood levels at 64.0% of sites by a mean 11 cm; ignoring surge significantly underestimated depths for 9.3% of expected annually exposed population.
claims.regime: The effect of surge on riverine flood hazard and impact in deltas globally

claims.text: A coupled NWM–D-Flow FM–ADCIRC/WW3 system reproduced Delaware storm peaks with skill 0.79–0.91 and negligible phase error; upstream levels depended strongly on streamflow, while winds and roughness controlled prediction quality.
claims.regime: A New 1D/2D Coupled Modeling Approach for a Riverine‐Estuarine System Under Storm Events: Application to Delaware River Basin

claims.text: European projections show anthropogenic climate change increases the joint probability of heavy precipitation and storm surge, making compound flooding more likely than stationary dependence implies.
claims.regime: Higher probability of compound flooding from precipitation and storm surge in Europe under anthropogenic climate change

claims.text: A global analysis combines river-discharge and storm-surge extremes to identify where dependence and event timing create elevated compound-flood potential.
claims.regime: Measuring compound flood potential from river discharge and storm surge extremes at the global scale

claims.text: Low-gradient coastal modeling defines transitions among surge-, river-, and compound-dominated flood zones and shows downstream sea level can propagate far inland.
claims.regime: Defining Flood Zone Transitions in Low‐Gradient Coastal Regions

claims.text: A dynamically linked Atlantic-ocean and four-level nested harbor-to-street model reproduces the November 2009 Cork coastal-fluvial flood and resolves how tide, surge, river inflow and their interaction control urban flood-wave routes, depths, velocities and human-safety risk.
claims.regime: November 2009 compound coastal-fluvial flooding of Cork City and Cork Harbour, Ireland.

claims.text: Rapid FLORES screening for Beira shows compound surge and rainfall losses exceed isolated-hazard impacts because high coastal water levels block drainage; drainage expansion dominates near-term benefits, while coastal protection becomes increasingly important under high-end climate change.
claims.regime: Concept-stage compound storm-surge and pluvial flood planning for Beira, Mozambique, using the documented schematization and data.

claims.text: Compound inundation models for low-gradient coastal watersheds should progress from linked, one-way, and loose coupling toward tight or full coupling that resolves rainfall across the whole domain and two-way storm-surge interactions with surface runoff, out-of-bank flow, and streamflow.
claims.regime: Low-gradient coastal watersheds exposed to coincident or sequential intense rainfall, river runoff, tropical-cyclone surge, and coastal inundation.

claims.text: Compound flood design in tidal channels must represent both statistical dependence and nonlinear hydraulic interaction between upstream discharge and downstream ocean level: joint AND scenarios can produce higher interior water levels than marginal scenarios despite smaller boundary values, whereas an OR-return-period scenario provides a conservative single spatial hazard profile.
claims.regime: Tidal channels and estuaries with upstream river-discharge records, downstream ocean-level records, known channel geometry and resistance, and flood hazard expressed as a spatial water-surface profile for a specified return period.

storm_surge.coupling.label: Wave-surge-tide coupling
storm_surge.coupling.description: Nonlinear interaction among waves, surge, and tide.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Important controls include surge-to-tide ratio, relative depth, wave steepness, Froude number, current-to-group-speed ratio, radiation-stress normalization, relative freeboard R_c/H_s, Iribarren number, wave direction reduction, tide–surge phase and wave-setup fraction.
synthesis.disagreements: Coupling magnitude is not universal: wave setup varies strongly by site and coastal slope, tides can alter or sometimes mitigate surge, and decoupled overtopping can overestimate flooding even though omitting waves underestimates setup. Model direction and transition treatment explain the apparent tension.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: The extracted evidence combines multi-region review cases, historical Taiwan typhoons with water-level, pressure, wind, height and period gauges, and idealized typhoon/tide/freeboard numerical experiments resolving overtopping and overflow transition.
synthesis.governing_physics: Key feedbacks are tide–surge phase interaction, depth-limited wave transformation, current refraction and Doppler shifting, radiation-stress gradients, wave setup, wind-stress modification, wave-enhanced bottom friction, surge overflow and intermittent overtopping across changing freeboard.
synthesis.limitations: Dominant uncertainties include wind and pressure forcing, bathymetry, wave breaking, radiation stress, wave-modified bottom friction, current refraction, wetting/drying, overtopping parameterization, structure geometry, phase sampling and limited simultaneous field observations of all coupled variables.
synthesis.major_equations: Coupled circulation uses depth-integrated mass and momentum with radiation-stress divergence and wave-modified stresses. Spectral waves obey an action balance on time-varying depth/current fields. Total water level combines mean sea level, tide, surge and setup, while overtopping discharge depends nonlinearly on relative freeboard and incident wave statistics.
synthesis.numerical_models: ADCIRC–SWAN is validated around Taiwan. The 2024 framework fully couples surge, wave, tide and overtopping/runup with random wave transformation, directional reduction and spatial averaging. The review covers established circulation–spectral-wave coupling classes.
synthesis.open_questions: Needs include process-resolving validation of stress pathways, irregular-wave overtopping/overflow transitions, tide-phase uncertainty, steep and shallow-shelf contrasts, structure-specific field measurements, coupled ensemble forecasting, model intercomparison and probabilistic treatment of forcing and closure error.
synthesis.recent_advances: Validated regional coupling now quantifies setup contributions, while fully coupled inundation frameworks evolve offshore waves and freeboard through the entire overtopping-to-overflow transition. This replaces static superposition with continuous process exchange.
synthesis.seminal_papers: The 2009 review codified the two-way coupling pathways and their flood significance. It remains foundational because it distinguishes well-established depth/setup feedbacks from less-settled stress, friction and refraction details.
synthesis.typical_methods: Practice uses unstructured circulation grids coupled one- or two-way to spectral wave models, shared wind/pressure forcing, gauge calibration, stress and setup sensitivity runs, tide-phase ensembles, random-wave transformation, overtopping formulae and idealized transition experiments.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Taiwan validation spans historical typhoons and four harbor sites; wave setup contributed 6–35% of surge and coupled water levels exceeded tide–surge results by 0.22–0.24 m on average. Overtopping-transition conclusions remain bounded to idealized bathymetry, tested tides, incidence and freeboards.
synthesis.well_established: Storm tide and waves interact dynamically. Tide and surge change depth and currents that control wave growth, refraction, breaking and bottom interaction; waves return radiation stress, setup and modified surface/bottom stress to circulation. Flooding additionally depends on the transition from wave runup/overtopping to mean overflow.

claims.text: Coupled coastal-flood modelling must pass tide- and surge-modified depth and currents to the wave model and return wave radiation stress, surface stress and wave-enhanced bottom friction to circulation; wave setup then contributes to total water level, although several stress and refraction interaction details remain uncertain.
claims.regime: Shelf and coastal flooding where wind waves coexist with tide and storm surge and bathymetry/wind forcing are adequately resolved.

claims.text: Around Taiwan during historical typhoons, the calibrated ADCIRC–SWAN tide–surge–wave model reproduced observed water levels, pressure, wind and waves; including waves raised mean modelled water levels by 0.22–0.24 m at four harbors, with wave setup contributing 6–35% of total storm surge.
claims.regime: Historical Taiwan typhoon events and Taipei Tamsui, Taichung, Kaohsiung and Hualien harbor gauges.

claims.text: In idealized coastal experiments, fully coupled surge–wave–tide–overtopping simulations showed that conventional decoupled overtopping/runup calculations overestimated inundation; prolonged overtopping still produced considerable flooding for typhoon landfall at low tide, demonstrating the need to resolve the transition between overtopping and overflow.
claims.regime: Idealized coastal bathymetry, tested typhoon incidence/tides and defence freeboard cases, including a 3 m freeboard example.

claims.text: Storm Gloria produced eastern-Iberian surge up to 1 m with waves up to 8 m, whereas Balearic impacts were wave-dominated; 30 m Ebro Delta simulation resolved surge flooding and Mallorca calculations represented wave overtopping.
claims.regime: Coastal impacts of Storm Gloria (January 2020) over the north-western Mediterranean

claims.text: A review of marine-storm flooding identifies coupled wind, tide, wave and mean-circulation mechanisms and uses Liverpool Bay and European applications to show why wave–surge interaction matters for coastal impacts.
claims.regime: Coupled wave and surge modelling and implications for coastal flooding

claims.text: Reconstruction of the 5 December 2013 southern North Sea event synthesizes exceptional water levels, waves and coastal impacts and shows their spatially varying combined effects.
claims.regime: Southern North Sea storm surge event of 5 December 2013: Water levels, waves and coastal impacts

claims.text: An unstructured finite-element model coupling river flow, tides, storm surge, wind waves, and hurricane forcing reproduces Hurricane Katrina hydrographs and high-water marks and supports interpretation and design for extreme Louisiana-Mississippi surge.
claims.regime: Hurricane Katrina across coastal Louisiana and Mississippi, including riverine flow, tides, waves, and storm surge.

storm_surge.coupling.wave_setup.label: Wave setup contribution to storm surge
storm_surge.coupling.wave_setup.description: Breaking-wave radiation-stress contributions to storm water levels, including interactions with tides, currents, and coastal morphology.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Wave-setup importance is commonly expressed through relative contributions such as setup divided by peak surge or total water level, flooded-area increment divided by total flooded area, grid spacing relative to surf-zone width, and wave-force magnitude relative to pressure-gradient or stress terms. These ratios are diagnostic and event-specific rather than universal similarity laws.
synthesis.disagreements: The reviewed percentages do not constitute a physical disagreement: Klaus reports setup as a fraction of peak surge, Iota reports its contribution to inundated area, and the Iota profile reports setup-plus-swash runup as a fraction of peak water level. Site morphology and response definitions must be aligned before comparing magnitudes.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Available validation evidence includes 399 Katrina regional high-water marks, Rita hydrographs/high-water marks and wave buoys, Iota wave and water-level sensors along a 7.196 km island profile, and Klaus tide-gauge and wave observations at two Bay of Biscay inlets.
synthesis.governing_physics: Setup is controlled by where wave energy dissipates relative to the shoreline, ebb delta, inlet and shelf. The resulting wave force is primarily balanced by a barotropic pressure gradient; tide changes water depth and breaking location, while currents can provide a smaller secondary feedback in the Klaus inlet tests.
synthesis.limitations: Grid resolution is a first-order limitation: the Katrina regional model missed localized setup, and the Klaus 35 m beach result exceeded 200 m and 1000 m results by 30% and 65%. The Klaus authors offer roughly five elements across the surf zone only as a case-derived guideline, not a universal convergence rule. Probabilistic hazard products remain incomplete when waves are omitted: the Iota reconstruction included setup, but its 738-event synthetic ensemble excluded setup for computational reasons and therefore cannot quantify total wave-inclusive flood hazard.
synthesis.major_equations: The studies introduce wave effects through spectral-wave momentum forcing of the circulation equations. Process experiments diagnose setup by differencing otherwise comparable simulations with and without wave forces; this difference can contain nonlinear tide-level feedback unless stationary level tests isolate it.
synthesis.numerical_models: Reviewed configurations couple WAM-STWAVE-ADCIRC for Katrina/Rita, MIKE 21 SW-HD FM plus XBeach 1D for Iota, and WWMII-SCHISM with a 3D vortex-force formulation for Klaus.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities are computationally affordable wave-inclusive ensembles, event observations that separate mean setup from swash and infragravity motions, morphology-aware grid convergence, and transfer tests across open beaches, reefed islands, lagoons and estuaries.
synthesis.recent_advances: The progression from sequential radiation-stress coupling and regional HWM validation to fully coupled 3D inlet momentum diagnostics and explicit setup/runup flood-component scenarios enables more defensible attribution, but also reveals that operational-resolution and ensemble-cost gaps remain.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Radiation-stress theory established that gradients in wave momentum flux drive mean-water-level setup; later spectral-wave and circulation coupling embedded that forcing in storm-surge models. The reviewed Katrina/Rita application represents an early high-resolution regional validation, followed by process-resolving inlet attribution and component-based island flood reconstruction.
synthesis.typical_methods: Credible event attribution combines a spectral wave model with a wetting-and-drying circulation model, compares wave-on and wave-off configurations, validates component waves and water levels, and uses phase-averaged or phase-resolving profile models when setup must be separated from swash.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Event-specific magnitudes are substantial but use different response measures: the Klaus study attributes 40% and 23% of peak surge to setup at Adour and Arcachon; the Iota study attributes 11.45 ha, or 14.93% of total modeled Providencia flooded area, to adding setup; and the Katrina study identifies a local unresolved setup contribution as large as 0.5 m near 17th Street Canal.
synthesis.well_established: Breaking-wave energy loss transfers onshore momentum through radiation-stress or vortex-force gradients; across the reviewed events this contribution raised mean water levels and altered hurricane or extratropical-storm flooding.

claims.text: In the SL15 system, STWAVE radiation stresses from depth-limited wave breaking are applied to ADCIRC and can modify surge magnitude, peak timing, and drawdown.
claims.regime: Sequential WAM-STWAVE-ADCIRC Katrina/Rita configuration for Louisiana and Mississippi.

claims.text: For Katrina, 70% of 206 USACE and 73% of 193 URS/FEMA still-water high-water marks were reproduced within 0.5 m by the coupled model.

claims.text: At the 17th Street Canal the regional model underpredicted peak surge by about 0.6 m, while cited local Boussinesq modeling indicated as much as 0.5 m of wave-driven setup absent at the regional resolution.

claims.text: The authors attribute localized setup underprediction along the south shore of Lake Pontchartrain and near raised features partly to inadequate wave and circulation grid resolution.
claims.regime: Locations with unresolved wave gradients, levees, roads, or hydraulic connections in SL15.

claims.text: For Hurricane Iota on Providencia, adding modeled wave setup to storm tide increased flooded area from 65.23 ha to 76.68 ha; the authors report 11.45 ha, or 14.93% of total modeled flooded area, as the setup contribution.

claims.text: The coupled MIKE 21 configuration adds radiation-stress setup but omits swash, whereas the XBeach 1D configuration resolves setup-plus-swash runup along a selected profile.

claims.text: Wave setup was excluded from the 738 synthetic and hypothetical-event surge simulations because of computational cost, so their probabilistic maps underrepresent wave contributions by construction.

claims.regime: The two inlet bathymetries and imposed -1.5 to +1.5 m level range; the contrast is site-specific.

claims.text: On the exposed beach near Arcachon, peak surge with the 35 m grid was 30% and 65% higher than with 200 m and 1000 m grids because coarse grids poorly represented setup.
claims.regime: Storm Klaus adjacent beach with roughly 1 km-wide surf zone.

storm_surge.forcing.label: Surge forcing
storm_surge.forcing.description: Wind, pressure, wave, and rainfall forcing.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Controls include storm radius/shelf width, translation speed/gravity or shelf-wave speed, wind direction/coast orientation, pressure deficit, drag coefficient, bottom-friction parameter, depth/resolution, Rossby and Froude numbers, tidal phase/surge duration, wave setup/surge, channel convergence, and forcing/forecast error.
synthesis.disagreements: Peak intensity alone poorly predicts surge when storm size and track differ; finer grids improve geometry but may expose friction/bathymetry error; 2-D and 3-D models differ where stratification or vertical stress matters; coupled waves may amplify or redistribute surge; data assimilation can correct state but mask forcing bias.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Evidence includes Gustav, Ike, Rita, Sandy-era systems, Bejisa, Gloria, Haiyan-region islands, Irma, Pearl River typhoons, Bangladesh cyclones, Super Typhoon Fung-Wong, Baltic and Italian storms, Gulf testbeds, Caribbean islands, Wilmington channels and global reanalyses.
synthesis.governing_physics: Alongshore/onshore wind piles water and drives Ekman/coastal currents; pressure gradients create inverse-barometer and dynamic response; broad storms increase fetch/duration; shelf waves and remote forcing create forerunners; tides change depth/friction; waves add setup and stress feedback; geometry controls convergence and resonance.
synthesis.limitations: Cyclone wind/pressure cores are sparsely observed; reanalysis resolution is limited; drag at extreme winds is uncertain; bathymetry, topography and friction covary; gauges miss spatial maxima; wetting/drying and wave coupling add numerical sensitivity; remote ocean and low-frequency baselines are imperfect.
synthesis.major_equations: Models solve shallow-water or primitive continuity/momentum with Coriolis, pressure-gradient, wind stress, atmospheric pressure, bottom drag and advection; coupled systems add wave radiation stress and sea-state drag; wetting/drying maps inundation; assimilation updates state; sensitivity and surrogate models map forcing to response.
synthesis.numerical_models: Models include ADCIRC v55 and data assimilation, SWAN–ADCIRC, COAWST-style coupling, global storm-tide reanalysis, pan-European forecasting, high-resolution cyclone forecasts, coupled atmosphere–wave–ocean models, 2-D/3-D surge models, subgrid inundation, deep-learning wind/pressure emulators and process indices.
synthesis.open_questions: Needs include extreme-wind drag saturation, pressure–wind covariance, storm-size/translation priors, remote shelf and ocean-current contributions, wave–tide–surge coupling, morphology and sea-level change, probabilistic forcing ensembles, data assimilation attribution, and physically constrained AI.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent work uses high-resolution global forecasts, scalable unstructured meshes, component attribution, low-frequency state correction, deep-learning wind/pressure emulation, geometry/bathymetry-aware surge indices, island-specific wind sensitivity, in-situ super-typhoon constraints and shelfbreak-jet attribution.
synthesis.seminal_papers: The branch progresses from storm-size and event hindcasts to coupled wave–surge testbeds, mesh/friction/forcing sensitivities, global storm-tide systems, remote forerunners, channel-deepening effects, state assimilation, coupled atmosphere feedback, geometry-aware indices and AI forcing emulators.
synthesis.typical_methods: Methods include gauge/buoy/wind/pressure validation, historical hindcasts, idealized storm perturbations, global and nested unstructured grids, coupled SWAN–ADCIRC or atmosphere–wave–ocean models, 2-D/3-D comparison, forcing-product and drag/friction sensitivity, data assimilation, ensemble forecasts, process attribution, and AI emulation.
synthesis.validated_ranges: The corpus spans local channels and islands to pan-European/global models, extratropical and tropical cyclones, deep ocean to reef/estuary/urban coast, hindcast through operational forecast, local and remote forerunners, multiple mesh/friction/forcing products, and historical to recent events.
synthesis.well_established: Storm surge is the dynamical coastal response to wind stress and atmospheric pressure acting on a preconditioned ocean, modified by storm size/track/speed, tides, waves, shelf and channel geometry, bathymetry, bottom friction, remote ocean signals, and coastal wetting/drying.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Key controls are pressure anomaly, disturbance length and translation speed, water depth, Froude number based on atmospheric and shallow-water wave speeds, shelf width, incidence angle, and shelf, bay or harbour modal periods.
synthesis.disagreements: Wind often dominates synoptic storm surge, but pressure is not always negligible: sharp rainband or mesoscale pressure disturbances can generate resonant waves comparable to other coastal water-level components. Attribution therefore depends on time scale and geometry.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Evidence includes the east Adriatic 2003 event, Hurricane Harvey rainbands, Venice 2019 flooding, Typhoon Songda and Pacific Northwest cyclones, Persian Gulf gauges, the Gulf of Genoa record and regional Strait of Georgia and Brazilian-bay simulations.
synthesis.governing_physics: A pressure deficit raises the equilibrium sea surface, while horizontal pressure gradients accelerate water. When disturbance translation approaches shallow-water wave speed, Proudman resonance accumulates energy; shelf, bay and harbour modes then amplify or reshape the wave.
synthesis.limitations: Pressure and wind covary in storms, barometer and tide-gauge spacing may miss propagating fronts, atmospheric products smooth mesoscale jumps, and resonance makes results highly site- and direction-dependent.
synthesis.major_equations: Pressure enters shallow-water momentum as a surface-pressure gradient. The inverse-barometer approximation relates sea-level rise inversely to pressure anomaly, while moving-forcing solutions and nonlinear shallow-water models represent resonant generation, propagation and inundation.
synthesis.numerical_models: Numerical approaches range from idealized analytical and nonlinear shallow-water models to NAMI DANCE SUITE, regional three-dimensional ocean models and coupled atmosphere–wave–surge systems driven by parametric or full-physics pressure fields.
synthesis.open_questions: Operational thresholds for pressure-jump speed, angle and scale remain uncertain, as do pressure–wind interaction, compound tide/surge timing, nonlinear breaking and inundation, and transfer of resonance diagnostics among coastlines.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent studies use high-resolution colocated pressure–sea-level observations and forcing-partition experiments to identify tropical-cyclone rainband meteotsunamis, mesoscale-cyclone contributions to extreme floods and operational model sensitivity to pressure-field structure.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Foundational work established inverse-barometer forcing and traveling-pressure resonance; Adriatic observations and the global meteotsunami synthesis connected Proudman resonance with shelf, bay and harbour amplification.
synthesis.typical_methods: Studies combine high-frequency barometers, tide gauges and current measurements with spectral or wavelet analysis, analytical moving-pressure solutions, pressure-only and wind-only sensitivity experiments, and nested shallow-water or regional ocean models.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Reported responses span pressure perturbations of roughly 1–3 mbar producing about 0.2 m waves, a 0.5 m Genoa event, Persian Gulf residuals up to 0.75 m, Pacific Northwest surges above 0.8 m and resonantly amplified Adriatic oscillations above 1 m.
synthesis.well_established: Atmospheric pressure forces coastal water levels through quasi-static inverse-barometer adjustment and dynamic gradients; moving disturbances can resonantly generate long waves that amplify on shelves and in bays and harbours.

storm_surge.forcing.wind.label: Wind stress and drag
storm_surge.forcing.wind.description: Wind momentum transfer and drag coefficients.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Controls include C_D, Charnock parameter, z0, u_star/U10, wave age c_p/u_star, inverse wave age, wind–wave and wind–stress misalignment angles, relative water depth, fetch, stability, drag saturation wind speed, and nondimensional setup or surge sensitivity.
synthesis.disagreements: High-wind behavior remains method and regime dependent: some evidence favors saturation, some decline after a peak, and coastal shoaling can shift and raise drag relative to deep water. Scalar wind-only laws also conflict with observed directional and sea-state dependence. The high-wind asymptote is method dependent. Powell et al. infer a marked decline in open-ocean Cd through U10=51 m/s; Donelan et al. measure saturation at Cd=0.0025 above 33 m/s in a short-fetch flume; Peng and Li fit a regional parabolic decline whose magnitude is slightly higher than Powell and Jarosz at medium-to-high winds.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Evidence includes coastal-tower typhoon winds to about 42 m/s, surf-zone eddy-correlation profiles, currents beneath five tropical cyclones, microwave radiometry, ten-hurricane coupled hindcasts, Lake Erie setdown and surge events, and regional gauge, buoy, platform, satellite and altimeter comparisons.
synthesis.governing_physics: Atmospheric shear transfers momentum through turbulent and wave-supported stress. Roughness, wave age and direction, breaking and whitecaps, foam and spray, currents, stability, fetch, shoaling and land cover modify the magnitude and direction delivered to the water column.
synthesis.limitations: Extreme direct stress observations are sparse, winds and waves evolve together, flux and 10 m wind retrievals carry correlated error, laboratory fetch is limited, coastal flow violates open-ocean assumptions, models share closures, and surge calibration can compensate errors in wind, bathymetry or friction. No reviewed law is universal: Powell explicitly excludes shallow coastal shoaling conditions, Donelan uses short-fetch laboratory waves and extrapolated 10-m winds, and Peng-Li coefficients are regionally inferred and require recalibration elsewhere.
synthesis.major_equations: The bulk vector stress is tau=rho_a C_D |U10| U10, with u_star=sqrt(|tau|/rho_a) and logarithmic wind profiles linked to roughness z0. Charnock-type, capped, peak-and-decline, wave-age and coupled spectral closures prescribe C_D or z0 under different regimes. The common bulk forcing relation is tau=rho_a Cd U10^2. Peng and Li parameterize high-wind drag as Cd=-a(Vp-33)^2+c, explicitly imposing a peak at 33 m/s.
synthesis.numerical_models: Reviewed tools include coupled wave–boundary-layer and ocean–wave models, ADCIRC, COAWST/ROMS/SWAN, unstructured tide–surge–wave models, global ocean surge systems, WRF hurricane ensembles and data-assimilative drag calibration.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities are vector stress under wind–wave misalignment, foam and spray physics, current and stability effects, shallow-water transformation, land-cover transitions, storm-quadrant dependence, coupled closure uncertainty, and real-time identification from colocated observations. Resolving plateau versus decline requires colocated extreme-wind stress, wave-state, foam/spray, current, and shallow-water observations, plus controlled propagation of drag uncertainty into surge forecasts.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent work combines autonomous current profilers, microwave roughness and whitecap retrieval, vector stress estimates, coupled ocean–wave models, wave-dependent surge forcing, large parameter ensembles and regional calibration to replace a universal scalar drag curve.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Bulk aerodynamic stress, logarithmic boundary-layer theory and Charnock roughness established the classical framework; later field hurricane profiles and high-wind laboratory studies overturned simple extrapolation and motivated capped, declining and sea-state-dependent drag laws.
synthesis.typical_methods: Methods estimate flux from towers, buoys, floats or eddy correlation; infer roughness and whitecaps remotely; reproduce interface behavior in laboratories; compute wave-supported stress spectrally; calibrate drag against setup or surge; and compare closures in coupled forecast ensembles.
synthesis.validated_ranges: The evidence spans distinct regimes: Powell's deep-water eyewall profiles have near-surface winds of 21-67 m/s; Donelan's tank reaches hurricane-equivalent neutral winds above 33 m/s; Peng and Li optimize over reconstructed winds of 10-70 m/s and validate on eight independent cyclones. The evidence spans moderate winds through roughly 55 m/s in combined float/model estimates and about 42 m/s in coastal towers, with some remote or hurricane-model applications higher; transfer remains conditional on measurement method, sea state, depth, storm quadrant and coast.
synthesis.well_established: All three reviewed studies reject unbounded extrapolation of moderate-wind drag growth into hurricane winds: field profiles indicate decline, flume measurements indicate a plateau, and surge assimilation favors a peak-and-decline curve. Wind stress is the principal direct momentum forcing for storm surge, but the drag coefficient does not increase without bound at tropical-cyclone winds; observations, experiments and coupled models instead support leveling, decline or strong sea-state modulation.

claims.text: In 331 tropical-cyclone eyewall profiles, friction velocity increased with U10 to about 40 m/s and then leveled off, while neutral drag showed a decreasing tendency above about 33 m/s.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Useful nondimensional controls include drag coefficient, pressure-scaled surge, wind-duration-scaled lead time, normalized hydrograph time and amplitude, relative surge to tide and wave components, and normalized validation errors; none removes dependence on shelf and coastal geometry.
synthesis.disagreements: Peak-focused surrogates are efficient for spatial hazard fields, whereas forerunner and hydrograph studies show that lead time, duration, skewness, and delayed peaks are separate engineering quantities. Likewise, surge-only inundation can be accurate in one metric yet omit wave setup, swash, rainfall, or river contributions important elsewhere.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Reviewed evidence includes Katrina and Rita regional observations, Iota inundation and profile reconstructions, three US synthetic forerunner ensembles with Ike and Harvey, 1031 Chesapeake simulations plus three historical storms, Haiyan survey limits over 5 m terrain, and two decades of US ADCIRC hydrographs.
synthesis.governing_physics: Wind stress and pressure deficit force surge; storm radius, translation speed, and approach angle control forcing duration and orientation; Coriolis and shelf geometry contribute to forerunner setup; wave radiation stress, runup, and topography modify nearshore water levels and inundation.
synthesis.limitations: Limitations include uncertain drag at extreme winds, grid-dependent wave setup, sparse observations, synthetic-storm sampling, omitted compound sources, static terrain assumptions, region-specific machine learning, and normalized templates that may not transfer to other basins or climate states.
synthesis.major_equations: Core formulations include depth-integrated shallow-water momentum and continuity, quadratic wind stress, spectral wave-action and radiation-stress coupling, dimensionless pressure-duration forerunner scaling, level-minus-terrain inundation depth, PCA/CNN spatial reconstruction, and beta-mixture hydrograph templates.
synthesis.numerical_models: Models include ADCIRC coupled to WAM, STWAVE, or SWAN; MIKE 21 and XBeach for component-resolved inundation; RDM with Zero-Point Boundary mapping; C1PKNet for peak-field surrogacy; and k-means plus beta mixtures for temporal surge templates.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities are transferable spatiotemporal surrogates with calibrated uncertainty, joint surge-wave-tide-rain-river validation, evolving topography and sea level, observation-based hydrograph typologies, operational forerunner verification, and error propagation from atmospheric forcing to local inundation and decisions.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent advances learn track-to-peak mappings from large ensembles, validate high-resolution typhoon inundation maps, and compress complete surge evolution into eight physically interpretable temporal templates, moving hazard analysis beyond isolated peak values.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Within this screened slice, the 2009 Katrina-Rita coupled validation establishes a physics-based regional benchmark, and the 2019 forerunner study reframes pre-landfall rise as a forecast quantity distinct from peak surge.
synthesis.typical_methods: Typical workflows hindcast or simulate cyclone ensembles with ADCIRC and spectral waves, validate water levels and high-water marks, isolate tide/surge/wave components, derive reduced scaling or machine-learning models, and map resulting water surfaces over high-resolution terrain.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Validation remains regional: Katrina high-water marks were mostly reproduced within 0.5 m; the Ike forerunner range was 0.4-2.8 m predicted versus 0.4-2.6 m observed at 24-6 h lead; and Haiyan inundation-limit accuracy was 81% on a 5 m terrain grid. These are not global error bounds.
synthesis.well_established: Tropical-cyclone coastal flooding depends on the evolving storm track, wind and pressure fields, shelf and coastal geometry, tides, waves, and terrain; peak surge alone does not describe early rise, duration, inundation, or wave-driven contributions.

claims.text: C1PKNet used complete tropical-cyclone track time series and 1031 Chesapeake Bay simulations to predict spatial peak surge rapidly, with evaluation against Hurricanes Isabel, Irene, and Sandy; transfer beyond the trained storm and coastal-state space remains unverified.

structures.description: Performance and behavior of engineered coastal structures.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Controls include relative freeboard and depth, wave steepness and surf similarity, reflection/transmission/overtopping coefficients, stability number, relative armor density, permeability, slope, breaker and impact parameters, Keulegan–Carpenter and diffraction ratios, safety/reliability indices and damage/deterioration ratios.
synthesis.disagreements: Reducing overtopping can increase local loads or reflected energy; rigid protection can transfer erosion; hydraulic model accuracy does not prove structural or foundation safety; data-driven formula improvement may not extrapolate; least-cost robust mass can conflict with adaptability, carbon and ecology.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Evidence includes vertical-breakwater overtopping, composite seawall crown-wall tests, recurve retrofits, coral-sand revetment foundations, stepped-revetment cases, cross-geometry simulations, coastal high-rise integrity and concrete/climate-resilience reviews.
synthesis.governing_physics: Incident and reflected waves, breaking, impact, overtopping, currents, uplift and tsunami generate pressures and forces; geometry transforms flow; armor, concrete, steel, foundations and joints resist through mass, strength, friction and stiffness while scour, settlement, fatigue and corrosion reduce capacity.
synthesis.limitations: Scale effects distort impact air, viscosity, permeability and sediment; foundations and scour are often simplified; joint failure and construction variability are sparse; deterioration and hidden defects are poorly observed; load combinations and cascading service loss remain uncertain under nonstationary climate.
synthesis.major_equations: Core formulations include wave transformation and overtopping relations, pressure/force and Morison-type loading, armor stability numbers, sliding/overturning/bearing/uplift limit states, porous flow, soil–structure interaction, scour, fatigue and corrosion deterioration, structural dynamics and reliability or lifecycle risk.
synthesis.numerical_models: Tools include spectral and phase-resolving waves, CFD/VOF and SPH, porous-flow and overtopping models, finite-element structural and soil analysis, scour and morphology models, data-driven hydraulic emulators, deterioration, reliability and network consequence models.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities include coupled hydraulic–structural–geotechnical failure, compound hazards and debris, breaking-impact aeration, scour and morphology feedback, aging and inspection, low-carbon durable materials, adaptive retrofits, nature–structure interaction and system-level reliability.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent advances include high-resolution impact and overtopping experiments, CFD/SPH, data-driven emulators, recurve and crown-wall retrofits, monitoring-informed condition assessment, climate-adjusted loads, durable low-carbon materials and infrastructure-network risk.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Classical breakwater and seawall research established armor stability, overtopping, reflection/transmission, wave pressures and sliding/overturning checks; later reliability, soil interaction, numerical fluid–structure modelling and lifecycle durability broadened performance assessment.
synthesis.typical_methods: Methods combine design guidance, physical modelling, CFD/SPH and structural/geotechnical analysis, prototype monitoring, post-event forensics, material and durability tests, limit-state and reliability assessment, lifecycle inspection, retrofit trials and system/service risk analysis.
synthesis.validated_ranges: The reviewed evidence spans vertical and composite seawalls, stepped and armor revetments, breakwaters, coastal buildings and infrastructure under waves, overtopping, aggressive exposure and future sea levels; each transfers only within tested geometry, foundation, material and forcing.
synthesis.well_established: Coastal structures modify waves, currents, water levels, sediment pathways and access while resisting hydraulic, geotechnical and environmental actions; performance therefore depends on coupled load, response, foundation, material, morphology and service-limit states over the lifecycle.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Relevant controls include head and freeboard ratios, closure time relative to surge rise, closed duration relative to tidal/renewal time, gate blockage fraction, forecast exceedance probability, failure probability, maintenance-window availability, and closures per year.
synthesis.disagreements: A conservative threshold preserves safety but sacrifices maintenance windows through false alarms; relaxing it reduces false alarms but raises misses. Benefits can exceed costs while increasing closure frequency simultaneously undermines port, ecosystem, and long-term viability.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Accessible evidence includes the 22 November 2022 Venice surge, 16 years of Maeslant forecasts and Hoek van Holland observations, 1927-2012 Venice morphology, future SLR scenarios, and 28-48 h seasonal enclosure experiments.
synthesis.governing_physics: Performance depends on external surge, tide and waves, head difference, closure timing/duration, gate and inlet hydraulics, internal storage and tributary inflow, leakage, and the post-closure evolution of water levels and exchange.
synthesis.limitations: This synthesis is dominated by Venice/MOSE plus one Maeslant maintenance study. Journal evidence on gate loads, vibration, leakage, mechanical failure, closure transients, overtopping, internal runoff, and Thames/Eastern Scheldt/Maeslant cross-comparison is sparse.
synthesis.major_equations: Operational frameworks include threshold and probabilistic closure rules, ensemble exceedance probabilities, binary false-alarm/miss skill, hydrodynamic mass and momentum, lagoon exchange and renewal, reliability/lifecycle models, and avoided-damage cost-benefit.
synthesis.numerical_models: Lagoon circulation/renewal models, counterfactual surge propagation, ensemble threshold classifiers, system-dynamics cost-benefit simulations, and closure-frequency SLR scenarios cover operational to century scales.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities include forecast-to-operation reliability, common-cause and component failure, closure transients and loads, interior compound flooding, emergency reopening, safe maintenance, navigation scheduling, sediment/salinity/ecology, and adaptation limits under accelerating SLR.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent work evaluates operational extreme-event counterfactuals, ensemble-based maintenance decisions, SLR-driven closure viability, and season-dependent ecosystem changes caused by temporary isolation.
synthesis.seminal_papers: The accessible branch connects Venice barrier planning and hydrodynamic restriction with observed MOSE protection, lifecycle economics, probabilistic Maeslant maintenance, and experimental closure externalities.
synthesis.typical_methods: Methods span tide-gauge and surge observations, hydrodynamic counterfactuals, historic morphology models, ensemble forecast hindcasts, threshold sensitivity, system-dynamics economics, policy analysis, and controlled closure analog enclosures.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Reported evidence includes an unregulated Chioggia counterfactual above 200 cm, 33.1% false alarms in the Maeslant maintenance model, 28-48 h enclosure experiments, and Venice renewal changes from 11.9 to 10.8 days before recent interventions added 0.5 day.
synthesis.well_established: Closable surge barriers can sharply reduce extreme water levels, but their benefit depends on timely reliable operation and transfers consequences to maintenance, navigation, lagoon exchange, sediment, ecology, and residual flood pathways.

claims.regime: Benefits exceeded investment and foregone port revenue, but increasing SLR-driven closure frequency challenges long-term viability and lagoon ecology and motivates a revised closure threshold and coordinated measures.

claims.regime: The operational model was conservative with 33.1% false alarms; raising critical probability reduced false alarms but increased misses, exposing a risk-versus-maintenance-time tradeoff.

claims.text: MOSE analog enclosure experiments showed 28-48 h reduced hydrodynamics enhanced suspended-material deposition and altered pelagic-benthic coupling, with season-dependent responses.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Important controls include relative freeboard Rc/Hs, relative crest width, relative depth h/Hs, stability number Hs/(Delta Dn50), damage level, Iribarren number, directional spread, relative wavelength and gap, porosity, structure-height-to-depth ratio, toe geometry, and layout-to-shoreline ratios.
synthesis.disagreements: Phase-averaged diffraction improves lee wave heights but performs less well for narrow low-frequency swell unless reflection and transmission are represented. Calibrated porous theory overpredicts energy as an emergent breakwall enters shallow-water breaking and friction regimes.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Reviewed evidence includes Aalborg depth-limited short-crested and oblique stability tests on a 1:25 foreshore, laboratory multidirectional diffraction at a breakwater shoulder, seven Elmer field spectra around six detached breakwaters, 1:20 crown-wall load tests, and 290 living-breakwall wake cases.
synthesis.governing_physics: Key processes include refraction and diffraction around heads and gaps, reflection from structures and beaches, transmission through and over permeable or low crests, depth-limited breaking, bottom friction, wave-current interaction, armour-unit motion, toe scour, settlement, and lee-side sediment redistribution.
synthesis.limitations: Laboratory scale, armour placement, seabed mobility, finite storm duration, incomplete field spectra, model physics, uncertain porosity, construction tolerances, and optimization objectives restrict transfer. Prototype applications without measured validation remain demonstrations, not field validation.
synthesis.major_equations: Common frameworks include Hudson or Van-der-Meer-type armour stability relations, toe-stability and damage formulations, wave-action balance with phase-decoupled diffraction, mild-slope equations for harbour propagation, porous resistance and transmission relations, and constrained optimization objectives.
synthesis.numerical_models: Models include SWAN with phase-decoupled diffraction, mild-slope wave propagation coupled to a genetic algorithm, COBRAS-UC for loads and pressures, empirical armour and toe stability formulae, and porous-transmission theory.
synthesis.open_questions: Needs include joint reliability-based optimization of stability, agitation, navigation, morphology, ecology, carbon, maintenance and cost; climate-adjusted design waves and water levels; better toe and foundation failure models; and transferable field validation for multidirectional extremes.
synthesis.recent_advances: Later work embeds wave mechanics within layout optimization, resolves pressure and load fields numerically, and extends breakwater concepts toward porous living systems whose performance and maintenance can be measured under field wakes.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Within this branch, the 2006 low-crested stability synthesis connects controlled testing to prototype foundation failure, and the 2007 SWAN study provides rare laboratory-plus-field validation of multidirectional transformation around detached structures.
synthesis.typical_methods: Methods combine 2-D flumes and 3-D basins, armour-damage surveys, prototype inspections, directional wave arrays, spectral and phase-resolving models, pressure and force measurements, empirical stability formulae, and genetic or multiobjective layout optimization.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Explicit evidence covers a 1:25 foreshore and 0.5 m plateau for low-crested stability, seven wind-sea/bimodal/swell field spectra at Elmer with 2.9-5.3 m tides, one- and two-segment Beirut layouts, 1:20 low-mound and crown-wall tests, and porous breakwalls of estimated porosity 0.7 and 0.9.
synthesis.well_established: Breakwaters protect coasts and ports by reflecting, diffracting, dissipating, and transmitting incident-wave energy. Their performance cannot be reduced to wave-height attenuation alone: armour and toe stability, overtopping, foundation response, lee-side spectra, navigation, morphology, maintenance, and cost interact.

claims.text: As a kind of technical equipment for wave prevention and wave dissipation, floating breakwater has attracted more and more attention of researchers.Starting from the research progress and application status of the floating breakwater, this paper combs the research status of the floating breakwater, summarizes the application status of the floating breakwater, and obtains the key points of the technical improvement of the floating breakwater.Finally, the future development of the new type of floating breakwater is summarized in terms of its application prospect, wave dissipation principle and application of new materials, which provides a strong reference for the relevant research of the floating breakwater.
claims.regime: The study system, forcing, data and methods stated in the indexed abstract.

claims.text: Low-crested and other hard coastal defenses create artificial hard-bottom habitat while disrupting adjacent soft sediment; their proliferation can alter regional connectivity, native assemblages and non-native-species spread, so ecological objectives and monitoring must enter planning, design and maintenance.
claims.regime: Low-crested and other hard defenses placed in soft-bottom coastal landscapes, including repeated structures along developed coastlines.
