synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Relevant model families commonly organize response through normalized wave loading, relative geometry and water depth, material or armour stability, and normalized damage measures; coefficients and exact forms are intentionally deferred to full-text extraction.
synthesis.disagreements: Apparent disagreement among failure models may arise from different definitions of damage, failure modes, variables, and structural systems. Cross-model comparison is unsafe until these semantic and regime differences are aligned.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: This initial branch contains post-Irma field and UAV observations from Saint-Martin and Saint-Barthélemy plus reviewed experimental knowledge for rubble-mound and geosynthetic coastal defenses.
synthesis.governing_physics: Damage depends on the interaction of wave and surge loading, water depth, erosion and morphology, flow concentration around built features, armour or material response, foundation conditions, and the accumulated state of the structure.
synthesis.limitations: This branch is abstract-bounded and has only three extractable sources. It cannot yet quantify full failure envelopes, repeated-loading effects, geotechnical mechanisms, cascading system failure, or repair and recovery.
synthesis.major_equations: The accessible evidence supports families of damage and stability models rather than one universal equation. Their use requires preserving each model's damage definition, response variable, structural type, and hydraulic regime.
synthesis.numerical_models: Numerical reconstruction can connect regional storm forcing to local flood depth and damage, while damage-model reviews expose how alternate definitions and assumptions affect predicted rubble-mound response.
synthesis.open_questions: Priority gaps are common damage ontologies, progressive and interacting failure modes, prototype-scale validation, coupling with erosion and foundations, probabilistic reliability, and links from physical damage to service loss and recovery.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent work increasingly combines forensic field evidence, remote sensing, high-resolution numerical reconstruction, and explicit review of model assumptions to move from isolated component response toward contextual failure diagnosis.
synthesis.seminal_papers: The rubble-mound historical review is the branch's guide to the development of damage-model concepts; source-level identification and extraction of individual seminal formulations remains a full-text task.
synthesis.typical_methods: Failure evidence combines historical model review, laboratory or application review, post-event field inspection, UAV mapping, environmental observations, and numerical reconstruction of surge, waves, flooding, and coastal change.
synthesis.validated_ranges: The indexed abstracts document an Irma regime with approximately 4 m surge and 10 m waves, but do not expose sufficient coefficients or ranges to claim general validation limits for the reviewed breakwater and geosynthetic models.
synthesis.well_established: Coastal-structure failure is not a single endpoint: evidence distinguishes hydraulic instability, progressive physical damage, loss of stability or function, and damage to buildings and infrastructure exposed to coastal flooding.

claims.text: After Hurricane Irma in Saint-Martin and Saint-Barthélemy, urban structures and streets channelled flood flow and locally amplified erosion and water levels, while observed damage intensity increased with flood depth.
claims.regime: Saint-Martin and Saint-Barthélemy during Category 5 Hurricane Irma, with modelled surge near 4 m and waves near 10 m

claims.text: For rubble-mound breakwaters, hydraulic instability is the principal damage mode addressed by historical damage models, whose differing damage definitions and assumptions constrain direct comparison and transfer.
claims.regime: rubble-mound breakwaters exposed to wave action

claims.text: Geosynthetic coastal defenses can be advantageous on weak foundations, but several applications still lack well-founded design formulae and specifications for hydraulic performance, stability, and failure modes.
claims.regime: geosynthetic coastal structures, including applications on weak foundations

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Important groups include relative freeboard, Iribarren number, wave steepness, relative depth, crest and berm geometry, roughness and obliquity factors, dimensionless discharge q*, overtopping probability, and normalized individual volume.
synthesis.disagreements: Mean and maximum metrics can respond differently: permeable foreshores reduced mean discharge strongly without a significant maximum-volume change. Higher-fidelity models are not automatically more accurate if incident conditions or decisive infragravity physics are wrong.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Reviewed evidence includes CLASH, 124 SWASH validation cases, six-model benchmarks, 140 rubble-seawall tests, 135 individual-volume tests, 1:50 shingle-foreshore tests, repeated random series, and stepped-revetment campaigns.
synthesis.governing_physics: Controls include offshore spectrum, breaking and infragravity transformation, water level, foreshore depth/slope/permeability/morphology, obliquity, roughness, porosity, crest freeboard/width, walls, berms, wave steepness, runup, and structure damage.
synthesis.limitations: Scale effects, finite series, stochastic realization, toe-wave reconstruction, morphology, permeability, damage, obliquity, wind, currents, drainage, prototype sensing, and sparse extremes limit transfer. Confidence bounds must accompany formula use.
synthesis.major_equations: Core frameworks normalize mean discharge by gravity and wave scale, use exponential freeboard decay and roughness/geometry factors, model individual volumes with Weibull or exponential distributions, and estimate maxima from mean rate and overtopping-wave count.
synthesis.numerical_models: Models include SWASH, SWAN with infragravity corrections, phase-resolving solvers, empirical EurOtop-type relations, neural and polynomial regressions, and wave-by-wave Weibull/exponential models.
synthesis.open_questions: Needs include joint discharge-volume-velocity prediction, dynamic morphology and damage, current/wind effects, nonstationary climate, prototype wave-by-wave validation, receptor-specific tolerances, and uncertainty-aware retrofit optimization.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent advances resolve infragravity controls, benchmark speed versus accuracy, model complex retrofits, quantify random-series uncertainty, distinguish mean and maximum behavior, and fit wave-by-wave volumes for risk-based design.
synthesis.seminal_papers: The branch builds on classical runup and freeboard-decay relations, CLASH/EurOtop databases, roughness and geometry factors, and Weibull individual-volume models; current work extends shallow, complex, permeable, and stochastic regimes.
synthesis.typical_methods: Methods use long irregular-wave flume series, repeated stochastic realizations, large-scale and field sensing, CLASH/EurOtop databases, empirical regression, phase-averaged and phase-resolving models, CFD/SPH, neural networks, and probability fitting.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Reported findings include order-of-magnitude underprediction without infragravity waves, 40% RMSE reduction for a rubble-seawall formula, stochastic discharge ranges to 75%, factor-four mean reduction from permeable shingle, stepped reduction to 60%, and maximum-volume bias improved to -6%.
synthesis.well_established: Wave overtopping occurs when runup exceeds crest elevation. Design must consider mean discharge, number of overtopping waves, individual and maximum volumes, velocities and depths, spatial distribution, drainage, tolerable limits, and exposed receptors.

claims.text: For the existing and proposed Port of Las Nieves breakwaters, modeled access-area overtopping risk was substantially higher than along main-body cross sections, identifying the access sections as the priority for controls and expansion design.
claims.regime: Existing and proposed Port of Las Nieves breakwaters, Gran Canaria.

claims.text: For sea dikes on very shallow foreshores, Van Gent's relation overestimated mean discharge and could not treat emergent toes, while an equivalent-slope concept validated with CLASH and dedicated tests improved prediction.
claims.regime: Shallow, very shallow, and emergent-toe sea-dike conditions.

claims.text: Across 124 shallow-foreshore cases, SWASH predicted mean overtopping about as accurately as semi-empirical formulae when toe-wave conditions were reproduced and handled complex geometry, although one intense individual event was underpredicted.
claims.regime: Impermeable structures, shallow foreshores, and complex storm-wall geometries.

claims.text: In a six-model shallow-foreshore benchmark, neglecting infragravity waves underestimated overtopping by an order of magnitude, while empirically corrected phase-averaged models could match or outperform costlier phase-resolving models.
claims.regime: Dikes with shallow mildly sloping foreshores.

claims.text: For tested rubble-mound breakwaters, relative protruding crest-wall height dominated wall effects, while berm width, berm level, and wave steepness controlled berm influence on overtopping; expressions were also checked against oblique-wave data.
claims.regime: Rubble-mound breakwaters with crest walls, berms, or both, including oblique-wave validation.

claims.text: Using 140 new tests and existing EurOtop data, a rubble-mound seawall formula based on relative freeboard and wave steepness reduced RMSE by 40% and improved normalized-discharge bias from -0.38 to approximately zero.
claims.regime: Small-scale rubble-mound seawalls across relative freeboard and steepness conditions.

claims.text: For smooth-slope and vertical-wall tests, normalized overtopping-discharge variation reached 10% when one wave series was repeated but 75% when different realizations from the same spectrum were used.
claims.regime: Smooth slope and vertical wall under multiple realizations from identical spectra.

claims.text: In 1:50 tests of a 1:2 wall, a permeable shingle foreshore reduced mean overtopping by up to a factor four relative to impermeable-slope predictions, while maximum individual volumes showed no significant difference.
claims.regime: A 1:2 wall fronted by impermeable versus permeable shingle slopes.

claims.text: Stepped revetments reduced breaking-wave overtopping volumes by up to 60% relative to smooth slopes, with reduction declining as Iribarren number increased; a new formulation explicitly reports range, scatter, and scale effects.
claims.regime: Breaking and nonbreaking waves on stepped revetments across disclosed parameter ranges.

claims.text: For tested vertical seawalls, individual overtopping volumes followed a two-parameter Weibull distribution; relative freeboard and overtopping rate predicted shape under nonimpulsive attack, and a unified formula was proposed across impulsive and nonimpulsive cases.
claims.regime: Plain vertical seawalls across freeboard, depth, steepness, and impulsive/nonimpulsive conditions.

claims.text: Across 135 rubble-mound seawall tests, weighted Weibull and exponential fitting reduced scatter by 23% and 17%, while a q*-and-overtopping-wave-count formula achieved 37% scatter index and -6% bias for maximum individual volume.
claims.regime: Rubble-mound slopes 1:1.5 and 1:2 across practical crest freeboards.

claims.text: Across 450 validated SWASH cases for vertical walls on 1:7-1:10 foreshores, longer relative promenades reduced overtopping and a new EurOtop-compatible storm-wall reduction factor reproduced modeled discharge with r = 0.94.
claims.regime: Vertical walls with retreated storm walls, steep 1:7-1:10 foreshores, and the Mediterranean-scale parameter ranges tested in the paper.

claims.text: Wave-flume tests of ten roughened vertical-seawall configurations found that increasing protrusion length and density reduced mean overtopping by up to 100% under impulsive waves, while tested non-impulsive waves showed no significant reduction.
claims.regime: Small-scale vertical seawall tests on a 1:20 impermeable foreshore, within the tested protrusion geometries and impulsive/non-impulsive waves.

claims.text: Evolutionary Polynomial Regression across five datasets produced parsimonious unified mean-overtopping formulas for smooth dikes through vertical walls, confirming exponential response and improved prediction when water depth, wave period, foreshore slope and dike slope are combined through equivalent or imaginary slope.
claims.regime: Smooth sea dikes and vertical walls across the combined datasets; rough or permeable structures only for preliminary conservative use.

claims.text: Large-scale mobile-bed tests show storm-driven lowering of the sandy foreshore before a near-vertical seawall increases overtopping, with total overtopped volume rising by as much as 104%; cumulative volume is more sensitive to profile evolution than peak discharge rate.
claims.regime: Low-steepness storm sequences over an evolving 1:15 sandy foreshore fronting a near-vertical 10:1 seawall.

claims.text: For the January 2015 Scituate blizzard case, coupled tide–surge–wave interactions increased predicted seawall overtopping about fivefold; a 0.36 m sea-level rise doubled peak discharge, and maintaining baseline discharge required roughly 0.9 m of crest raising because deeper toe water also increased incident wave height.
claims.regime: Scituate seawall, Massachusetts, during the January 2015 North American blizzard and scenarios combining 0.36 m sea-level rise with raised crest elevations.

claims.text: The SWEEP-OWWL regional forecast system predicted 80% of observed overtopping events one day ahead, all severe events, with a 2.5% false-alarm rate; profile choice changed predicted discharge by an order of magnitude, demonstrating the operational value of frequently updated coastal morphology.
claims.regime: Engineered and naturally defended profiles along roughly 1,000 km of southwest England, validated against winter 2018/19 observations and tested with Storm Emma boundary conditions.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Important controls include relative wall and recurve height, freeboard, water depth, wave height and steepness, breaker location, wall setback, reflection coefficient, relative toe geometry, sediment mobility, and normalized force and moment.
synthesis.disagreements: Higher or more elaborate walls do not always yield proportional benefit: a recurve delayed impact but added little load reduction under overtopped flow, and a low wall could increase landward force. Nature-based alternatives range from lower-reflection single logs to stacked forms behaving like walls.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: The branch includes solid and perforated tsunami-wall tests, 1:5 seawall-versus-woody-debris morphology tests, breaking-solitary-wave velocimetry, 31 days of winter-gale scour observations, and validated vertical-structure morphology cases.
synthesis.governing_physics: Key processes are breaking and impulsive impact, aeration and turbulence, reflection and standing-wave motion, runup and overtopping, return flow, setup and surge, sediment resuspension and longshore transport, toe scour, and foundation interaction.
synthesis.limitations: Evidence is fragmented across tsunami, solitary-wave, storm, morphology, and regional-adaptation regimes. Scale effects, aeration, three-dimensionality, evolving toes, drainage, foundations, ecological response, and compound sea-level and storm change restrict transfer.
synthesis.major_equations: Evidence uses force and overturning-moment reduction relations, RANS-VOF free-surface and turbulence equations, sediment-transport and morphology conservation, breaking and overtopping relations, and reflection and load metrics; no universal seawall equation spans all failure modes.
synthesis.numerical_models: OpenFOAM resolves overtopped landward force and moment, while coupled RANS-VOF, bedload, sand-slide, and partial-cell morphology models track the evolving water-soil interface and toe scour.
synthesis.open_questions: Needs include coupled wall-toe-foundation failure, prototype impulsive pressures and velocities, overtopped hinterland pathways, repeated storm recovery, adaptive crest design, ecological and recreational tradeoffs, and uncertainty-aware lifecycle performance.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent work couples image velocimetry, long-duration seabed sensing, free-surface CFD, evolving morphology, physical comparisons with nature-based structures, and climate-adaptation review to examine the full wall-beach-hinterland system.
synthesis.seminal_papers: A century-scale UK review traces movement from largely vertical wall-and-groyne practice toward curved, stepped, model-informed, environmentally constrained, and nourishment-supported designs; detailed formulation lineage remains a full-text task.
synthesis.typical_methods: Methods combine wave-flume force and velocimetry tests, large-scale morphology experiments, OpenFOAM and coupled RANS-VOF morphodynamics, acoustic and optical field monitoring, post-event evidence, and historical or state-of-the-art review.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Reported findings include tsunami-force reductions up to 41% for a high nearby wall and about 27% for a half-height wall, gale SSC of 12,222 mg/L and net sediment flux of 769 t/m2/day, and a 1:5 reflection/morphology comparison.
synthesis.well_established: Seawalls hold a shoreline or protect a hinterland by reflecting, redirecting, and sometimes overtopping incident waves and surges. Performance includes crest exceedance, structural loading, toe stability, beach response, drainage, and landward consequences.

claims.text: Structural tsunami countermeasures such as seawalls aim to reduce inundation depth and distance, but their effectiveness and damage modes depend on regional conditions and event-specific performance.

claims.text: A state-of-the-art review found limited, dispersed evidence on storm-driven morphological change in front of coastal defenses and its coupling to overtopping, rundown, stability, and failure.

claims.text: In 20 seawall cross-section optimization trials, DYCORS coupled to an ANN overtopping model improved both discharge and cost even in the worst trial (17.67% and 12.1% reductions) and outperformed the genetic-algorithm benchmark.
claims.regime: The paper's composite-slope, berm and wave-wall decision space and ANN overtopping model under the tested wave and water-level combinations.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Controls include tidal amplitude-to-depth ratio, friction and convergence parameters, basin length relative to tidal wavelength, Rossby and Froude numbers, spring–neap ratio, constituent amplitude and phase ratios, skewness, internal-wave slope criticality and conversion/dissipation efficiency.
synthesis.disagreements: Linear constituent superposition is useful but can miss nonlinear water-level, friction, flooding and harmonic interactions. Internal-tide energy may dissipate near generation sites or radiate far away depending on mode and topography; idealized stratification can bias local conversion materially.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Reviewed evidence includes Monterey Canyon ship surveys and monthlong records, Sea of Okhotsk constituent simulations, California mixed-tide estuaries, Paopao reef-lagoon observations, Changjiang circulation literature, and realistic/idealized Northwest Pacific tide experiments.
synthesis.governing_physics: The tide-generating potential forces shallow-water motion; friction, convergence, resonance and Coriolis alter propagation. Constituent interaction generates harmonics and residuals, while sloping topography and stratification generate internal waves whose refraction and dissipation depend on background flow.
synthesis.limitations: Sparse offshore observations, uncertain bathymetry and drag, datum and nodal corrections, unresolved channels, changing morphology and mean level, incomplete stratification and background currents, and model resolution constrain prediction and attribution.
synthesis.major_equations: Barotropic tides follow depth-integrated mass and momentum equations with astronomical boundary forcing, bottom stress and nonlinear advection. Harmonic analysis decomposes constituents; internal tides use stratified wave and energy equations, and residual circulation emerges through period averaging and nonlinear terms.
synthesis.numerical_models: Representations range from constituent shallow-water solvers and COHERENS-like circulation systems to global nonuniform ocean–tide models and internal-wave theory. Coastal-flood models may couple mean level, tides, surge, waves and inundation rather than linearly superpose them.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities include climate-driven tidal change, compound extremes, wetting/drying feedback, estuary asymmetry and sediment response, internal-tide remote dissipation, eddy interaction, data assimilation and consistent uncertainty across barotropic and baroclinic scales.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent advances couple global circulation, eddies and internal tides at variable resolution, diagnose nonlinear energy budgets, use skewness for mixed-tide asymmetry and embed tide–surge–wave–mean-level interactions in probabilistic coastal flooding.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Equilibrium and dynamic tide theory established constituents and propagation; harmonic analysis enabled prediction, while shallow-water theory explained amplification and friction. Later work formalized tidal asymmetry, residual circulation and barotropic-to-baroclinic conversion.
synthesis.typical_methods: Studies use tide gauges, current meters, shipboard hydrography and moorings with harmonic, skewness, flux and energy-budget analysis; shallow-water, 3D circulation and nonhydrostatic/internal-wave models test geometry, stratification, friction and coupled mean-level/surge/wave effects.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Examples include Monterey internal currents near 20 cm/s and 50 m displacement, Okhotsk residuals near 10 cm/s, Mid-Atlantic Ridge M2 flux 3–5 mW/m² and coastal interaction effects of tens of centimeters. These belong to distinct regimes and scales.
synthesis.well_established: Astronomical forcing produces predictable barotropic constituents, but coastal amplitude, phase, currents, asymmetry and residual transport depend strongly on depth, friction, geometry and nonlinear interactions. Stratification converts barotropic energy into internal tides that can radiate and mix remotely.

claims.text: Coastal tidal prediction must account for interactions with mean sea level, surge, waves and inundation whenever their locally variable contributions are comparable to the water-level margin relevant to flooding or design.
claims.regime: Coastal water levels and flooding where coupled processes may alter elevation by leading-order amounts.

claims.text: A quasi-global tide-gauge analysis separates total-water-level and surge maxima to assess spatial and temporal change in coastal extreme high waters.
claims.regime: Changes in extreme high water levels based on a quasi‐global tide‐gauge data set

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Controls include tidal amplitude-to-depth ratio, friction or Stokes number, basin length relative to tidal wavelength, Rossby number, resonance detuning, constituent signal-to-noise, admittance, amplitude and phase error, datum offset and ensemble spread-to-error ratios.
synthesis.disagreements: Pure harmonic prediction is efficient for stationary constituents, while hydrodynamic models better represent spatial propagation and nonlinear generation but depend on bathymetry and friction. Local ensembles reduce model-selection error yet may hide common bias and do not replace physics or observations.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: The reviewed evidence uses ten global tide models, satellite altimetry, optical NDWI water masks and Australian tide gauges to rank local members and construct coastal ensembles; direct basin-specific propagation datasets remain unreviewed in this node.
synthesis.governing_physics: Lunar and solar gravitational potential excites barotropic waves that propagate, reflect and resonate; Coriolis acceleration, bathymetric convergence, bottom friction, wetting/drying and nonlinear advection reshape constituents and generate overtides and compound shallow-water harmonics.
synthesis.limitations: Limitations include short or gappy gauges, datum mismatch, coastal altimetry contamination, optical cloud and water-index uncertainty, unresolved channels, inaccurate bathymetry and friction, missing constituents, nodal and seasonal modulation, nonstationary morphology and shared bias among global models.
synthesis.major_equations: Core formulations are rotating shallow-water mass and momentum equations with astronomical potential or open-boundary constituents, and harmonic representation eta(t)=Z0+sum f_n A_n cos(omega_n t+V_n+u_n-phi_n), including nodal factors and phase corrections.
synthesis.numerical_models: Current evidence evaluates and ensembles ten global tide models at the coast rather than endorsing one universal model; underlying models differ in grids, bathymetry, friction, assimilation and constituent sets, producing spatially varying strengths and common failure regions.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities include seamless coast–estuary constituent propagation, uncertainty-calibrated ensembles, datum automation, nonstationary morphology and sea-level effects, compound tide–surge–river interaction without double counting, optical constraints in turbid coasts and prediction where gauges are absent.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent advances combine coastal altimetry, optical shoreline occurrence, unstructured high-resolution models, data assimilation, locally ranked multi-model ensembles and probabilistic prediction to improve tides near complex and data-sparse coasts.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Equilibrium tide theory, Laplace tidal equations and classical harmonic analysis established constituent prediction; amphidromic mapping, shallow-water harmonic theory and assimilative global tide models extended it to spatially varying coastal propagation.
synthesis.typical_methods: Methods use long tide-gauge records, harmonic analysis, satellite altimetry and optical shoreline constraints, global or regional hydrodynamic models, constituent interpolation or assimilation, datum reconciliation, coastal ranking or ensembles, and independent validation of amplitudes, phases and reconstructed levels.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Direct evidence is Australia-wide but restricted to locations supported by the satellite and gauge evaluation. Ensemble benefit is conditional on at least some competent members and cannot rescue coasts where all contributing models share large errors.
synthesis.well_established: Astronomical tides are predictable responses to gravitational forcing whose coastal amplitude and phase are transformed by basin geometry, depth, friction, resonance, rotation and nonlinear interaction; local prediction therefore requires both constituent forcing and regional calibration or validation.

claims.text: Across Australia, locally ranked ensembles of ten global tide models using altimetry and optical NDWI consistently outperformed individual models against tide gauges, but cannot provide reliable output where all contributing models are poor.
claims.regime: Australian coastal EO applications; NDWI ranks phase more directly than amplitude and sun-synchronous sampling limits some constituents.

claims.text: A coastal water-level review finds interactions among mean sea level, tides, surge, waves and flooding vary strongly in space and time and can alter levels by several tens of centimeters, positively or negatively.
claims.regime: Interactions Between Mean Sea Level, Tide, Surge, Waves and Flooding: Mechanisms and Contributions to Sea Level Variations at the Coast

claims.text: In mixed-tide estuaries, principal-tide duration asymmetry combines with internally generated harmonics; skewness unifies amplitude/phase metrics and shows morphology must overcome mouth-imposed asymmetry before local ebb or flood dominance develops.
claims.regime: Tidal asymmetry in estuaries with mixed semidiurnal/diurnal tides

claims.text: FES2014 combines global hydrodynamic modeling and data assimilation to produce a validated high-resolution ocean-tide atlas for major and minor constituents.
claims.regime: FES2014 global ocean tide atlas: design and performance

claims.text: A high-resolution global dataset jointly represents extreme sea levels, tides and storm surges and supplies future projections for consistent coastal hazard analysis.

claims.text: Abstract One of the most challenging areas in tidal analysis is the study of nonstationary signals with a tidal component, as they confront both current analysis methods and dynamical understanding.

claims.text: Abstract This study examines the integrated influence of sea level rise (SLR) and future morphology on tidal hydrodynamics along the Northern Gulf of Mexico (NGOM) coast including seven embayments and three ecologically and economically significant estuaries.
claims.regime: The study system, forcing, data and methods stated in the indexed abstract.

claims.text: In semi-closed convergent tidal channels, cross-section convergence and friction control resonant amplification and shift water-level and velocity nodes and antinodes; a multi-reach analytical solution incorporates longitudinal depth variation at negligible cost relative to full numerical simulation.
claims.regime: Semi-closed convergent channels with width/depth variation representable by piecewise reaches and tides within the linearized one-dimensional assumptions.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Important controls include Rayleigh number, Fischer number, the lateral-advection parameter, depth-to-width aspect ratio, ratios of lateral to vertical mixing, and comparisons between cross-sectional mixing time and the tidal averaging interval.
synthesis.disagreements: There is no single transferable closure: simple analytical exchange models can reveal controls but require site-specific parameterization in complex sill-basin systems, while gradient-dispersion closure fails when averaging is too short relative to cross-sectional mixing or residual cells dominate dispersion.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Key evidence includes multi-station observations across Gazi Bay, historical and 2006 Puget Sound velocity-salinity profiles, Oosterschelde salinity and velocity distributions, and Gulf of Khambhat hydrodynamic and transport information.
synthesis.governing_physics: Longitudinal baroclinic pressure gradients drive exchange flow, while vertical and lateral mixing, tidally averaged advection, sills, constrictions, basin interconnection, river discharge, and ebb-flood asymmetry set its magnitude and vertical or lateral structure.
synthesis.limitations: Tidal averaging can conceal intratidal covariance and asymmetry. Breadth or section averaging suppresses lateral structure, idealized constant geometry limits inlet solutions, and calibrated three-dimensional models remain sensitive to bathymetry, mixing closure, boundaries, and sparse long-term observations.
synthesis.major_equations: The reviewed frameworks use tidally averaged momentum and salt conservation, advection-diffusion equations, Hansen-Rattray/Pritchard exchange-flow theory, one-dimensional gradient-dispersion closure, and two- or three-dimensional numerical mass and momentum balances.
synthesis.numerical_models: Models span one-dimensional tidally averaged dispersion, idealized Hansen-Rattray inlet circulation, multilevel breadth-averaged vertical-plane transport, and three-dimensional unstructured-grid Puget Sound circulation.
synthesis.open_questions: Priority questions concern interactions among tides, stratification, wind, waves, river flow and morphology; transfer of mixing closures across sites; spring-neap and seasonal modulation; and uncertainty in translating Eulerian residual flow into net material transport and residence time.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent analytical work shows that lateral mixing and tidally averaged advection fundamentally control gravitational exchange through Fischer and advection parameters, including a negative feedback in which stronger advection suppresses its driving lateral salinity gradients.
synthesis.seminal_papers: The 1978 high-Rayleigh inlet solution and 1982 conditions for gradient-type tidally averaged dispersion provide early analytical foundations; the Gazi Bay and Puget Sound studies anchor field and multi-model evidence.
synthesis.typical_methods: Evidence combines current, water-level, salinity and water-quality observations with analytical reduction, nondimensional regime analysis, breadth-averaged finite differences, and calibrated three-dimensional unstructured-grid modeling.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Validated or demonstrated regimes range from 3-4 h residence and 60-90% exchange per tide in shallow Gazi Bay to fjordal and partially mixed Puget Sound sub-basins; analytical results also cover constant-section inlets and mixing/advection regimes defined by nondimensional parameters.
synthesis.well_established: Residual circulation is the nonzero flow and transport remaining after tidal averaging. In estuaries and inlets it commonly reflects density-driven exchange, nonlinear tidal asymmetry, freshwater input, mixing, and geometry rather than the oscillatory tide alone.

claims.text: In shallow Gazi Bay, a wide unrestricted entrance enabled 60-90% volume exchange per tidal cycle and 3-4 h residence times, while ebb-dominant mangrove-creek currents promoted net export toward seagrass beds.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Controls include Richardson, Froude, Reynolds and Stokes numbers, tidal excursion/topographic scale, internal-wave frequency/N and Coriolis ratio, pycnocline depth/depth, barotropic speed/internal-wave speed, Simpson–Hunter h/u³, bottom drag, stratification and lateral-gradient strength.
synthesis.disagreements: A water column classified as well mixed in the mean can still undergo tidal straining; mixing is not spatially uniform along beams or slopes; bottom stress alone does not predict dissipation when internal waves shoal; and residual circulation needs lateral as well as vertical stratification asymmetry.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Evidence spans the New England shelf, partially stratified estuaries, continental slopes, barrier reefs, Kaena Ridge, Monterey Bay, East China Sea, a coastal embayment, tidal inlets, periodically stratified channels and the Arctic Ocean.
synthesis.governing_physics: Tidal flow over topography generates internal waves and beams; shoaling steepens them into bores and shear instability; tidal straining alternately strengthens and weakens stratification; friction and lateral density gradients rectify oscillations into residual circulation; mixing feeds back on stratification.
synthesis.limitations: Microstructure captures limited space/time; mixing efficiency is uncertain; hydrostatic models miss overturning; internal-wave beams interact with rough three-dimensional topography and mesoscale flow; boundary conditions and unresolved turbulence strongly affect energy closure.
synthesis.major_equations: Frameworks use Boussinesq momentum and density transport, buoyancy frequency N², gradient Richardson number, internal-wave dispersion and energy flux, turbulent kinetic-energy/dissipation budgets, buoyancy flux and mixing efficiency, baroclinic pressure, residual covariance, and Simpson–Hunter or Stokes mixing criteria.
synthesis.numerical_models: Models represent internal-tide mode cascade, Arctic tidal mixing, lateral and residual estuarine circulation, Stokes-number water-column regimes, stratified inlet circulation, wind-modulated dissipation, and minor-axis straining that concentrates sediment.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities include complete barotropic-to-baroclinic energy pathways, mode conversion and scattering, wave–mean and wave–mesoscale interaction, lateral/submesoscale fronts, mixing efficiency, sediment/biology feedback, changing climate stratification, and transferable parameterizations.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent advances coordinate internal-wave process teams, resolve low-to-high-mode energy cascade, measure straining with microstructure across environments, connect winds to semidiurnal dissipation, and diagnose lateral stratification effects in inlets and freshwater-influenced seas.
synthesis.seminal_papers: The branch links estuarine turbulence and periodic stratification to tidal/lateral asymmetry, internal-tide beams and ridge mixing, straining in well-mixed channels, frictional shelf-sea regime maps, and minor-axis sediment convergence.
synthesis.typical_methods: Methods include microstructure profilers, ADCP and moored thermistor/salinity chains, dye/tracer and ship sections, PIV and bottom turbulence, internal-wave beam/energy diagnostics, harmonic and residual decomposition, hydrostatic/nonhydrostatic models, idealized channels, and mixing/energy budgets.
synthesis.validated_ranges: The evidence covers well-mixed through partially and strongly stratified water columns, bottom boundary layers through pycnoclines, estuary and inlet to shelf/slope and Arctic scales, low- and high-mode internal tides, semidiurnal and spring–neap variability, and wind-upwelling modulation.
synthesis.well_established: Density stratification converts barotropic tidal forcing into baroclinic circulation, internal tides, fronts and phase-dependent turbulence; mixing is intermittent and localized by topography, pycnocline structure, lateral gradients, tidal phase and wind.

tsunami.label: Tsunamis and long waves
tsunami.description: Generation, propagation, inundation, and loading by long waves.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Key controls include wave amplitude-to-depth ratio, wavelength-to-depth ratio, Froude and Reynolds numbers, relative slide thickness and density, slope, dispersion measures, roughness and blockage ratios, and source probability or return period.
synthesis.disagreements: Source attribution can remain contested where earthquake and landslide mechanisms overlap. Efficient depth-averaged models enable ensembles but may omit dispersive or three-dimensional generation physics; deterministic reconstructions can fit observations without uniquely identifying the source.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Root evidence includes the 1993 Hokkaido, 1998 Papua New Guinea, 2011 Tohoku and 2018 Anak Krakatau events; Oregon and New Zealand hazard scenarios; NTHMP benchmarks; controlled runup experiments; and coastal CCTV-derived shoreline observations.
synthesis.governing_physics: Generation maps seafloor or mass-motion kinematics into free-surface displacement and momentum. Propagation is controlled by gravity, depth, dispersion and bathymetric refraction; near shore, nonlinearity, breaking, friction, buildings and terrain control runup and inundation.
synthesis.limitations: Sparse near-source observations, uncertain rupture or slide kinematics, bathymetric and topographic resolution, friction and building representation, breaking treatment, uncertain event rates and limited validation of extreme regimes constrain transferable predictions.
synthesis.major_equations: Linear long-wave and shallow-water equations describe much basin propagation; nonlinear shallow-water and Boussinesq systems add finite amplitude and dispersion. Navier–Stokes or multiphase models resolve energetic slide generation, while probabilistic hazard integrates source occurrence and conditional inundation response.
synthesis.numerical_models: Operational and research systems range from depth-averaged nonlinear shallow-water solvers such as Tsunami-HySEA to dispersive Boussinesq propagation and three-dimensional Navier–Stokes source models. Ensembles represent slip, fault, landslide and model uncertainty.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities include faster source characterization, reliable near-field warning, compound and cascading sources, probabilistic treatment of rare landslides, urban-scale inundation and loads, real-time assimilation, explainable machine learning, and climate-conditioned exposure.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent work uses heterogeneous rupture ensembles, coupled high-fidelity source and efficient propagation models, benchmarked GPU solvers, neural-network inundation forecasts and automated coastal imagery to shorten the path from observation to actionable warning.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Classical long-wave and shallow-water theory established propagation and runup foundations; later benchmark programs standardized model verification, while post-event surveys connected observed runup and damage to source reconstruction and inundation physics.
synthesis.typical_methods: The literature combines post-event surveys, gauges, geodesy, seismic and marine mapping, laboratory long-wave experiments, source inversion, shallow-water/Boussinesq/Navier–Stokes simulation, benchmark suites, probabilistic ensembles and emerging image or neural-network forecasts.
synthesis.validated_ranges: The reviewed cases span laboratory runup, local landslide and volcanic sources, regional earthquake inundation and basin propagation. Reported examples include 10–18 m/s inferred overland flow and near-30 m runup at Hokkaido and locally about 13 m runup after Anak Krakatau.
synthesis.well_established: Tsunamis arise from rapid water-column displacement, propagate predominantly as long waves, and amplify through shoaling, focusing and interaction with coastal topography. Earthquake rupture dominates global hazard, while landslides and volcanic collapse can create especially severe near-field waves.

claims.text: Tsunami hazard assessment must explicitly distinguish earthquake, landslide and volcanic-collapse sources because their characteristic kinematics, directionality and near-field uncertainty require different source and modeling assumptions.
claims.regime: Multi-source tsunami hazard assessment, especially where submarine or volcanic mass movements are plausible.

claims.text: At Palaikastro, Crete, an erosional, chaotic deposit containing Santorini ash intraclasts, marine shells and microfauna, imbricated beach pebbles, building stones, ceramics and bones provides convergent geoarchaeological evidence for a tsunami coeval with the Late Minoan Santorini eruption.
claims.regime: Late Minoan IA coastal settlement deposits at Palaikastro, northeastern Crete.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Controls include source length and width relative to depth, displacement-to-depth ratio, rise time over gravity-wave time, slide Froude number, relative slide thickness and density, slope, aspect ratio, submergence, mobility, Mach or compressibility effects where relevant, and normalized wave amplitude.
synthesis.disagreements: Passive initial-surface displacement is efficient but can omit finite rupture and water-column dynamics; active kinematic forcing is more complete but uncertain. Depth-integrated landslide models enable ensembles but miss fine-scale generation, while depth-resolved models add physics at much higher cost.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: The reviewed slice includes canonical plane-beach and island tests used with regional seismic scenarios, a corrected two-segment Catania source, and the landslide-model benchmark literature summarized by the focused review; direct volcanic evidence is not yet reviewed.
synthesis.governing_physics: Seismic sources deform the seabed through elastic fault slip, while landslides transfer momentum through moving, deforming solid or granular masses; generation depends on displacement rate relative to gravity-wave response, water depth, compressibility or air effects, rheology and bathymetry.
synthesis.limitations: Source observations are sparse and inverse solutions nonunique; rupture, rigidity, slide volume, rheology and timing are uncertain; bathymetry filters the generated spectrum; simplified initial conditions may double-count or omit dynamics; and validation often occurs after propagation has mixed source and path errors.
synthesis.major_equations: Common formulations combine elastic dislocation or prescribed moving-bottom kinematics with shallow-water, Boussinesq, potential-flow or Navier–Stokes equations; landslide models add rigid-body dynamics or continuum rheology and multiphase interface coupling.
synthesis.numerical_models: Model classes include passive and active seismic initialization, kinematic seafloor forcing, depth-integrated landslide source terms, nonhydrostatic and potential models, depth-resolved Navier–Stokes, particle or meshless solvers, and coupled slide–water multiphase methods.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities include finite-fault and splay rupture, horizontal displacement on slopes, deformable and fragmented slides, volcanic collapse and explosion, air and compressibility, sediment entrainment, source–propagation coupling, real-time inversion and probabilistic multi-mechanism ensembles.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent advances use kinematic nonhydrostatic seafloors, depth-resolved landslide CFD, improved rheology, coupled multiphase solvers, fast surrogate or reduced source ensembles, high-rate geodesy and joint inversion of seismic, pressure, wave and runup observations.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Elastic dislocation theory and passive seafloor-to-surface displacement established seismic initialization; moving-bottom long-wave solutions and laboratory slide-impact scaling established active generation, followed by depth-integrated and multiphase computational models.
synthesis.typical_methods: Workflows construct source geometry and kinematics, choose active moving-bottom or passive initial displacement, test conservation and resolution, validate near-source waves against analytical or laboratory data, propagate ensembles, compare with gauges/runup, and invert observations without hiding nonuniqueness.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Current direct evidence is limited to two Eastern Mediterranean seismic scenario formulations and a review-level landslide model taxonomy; source-specific parameter ranges, laboratory scales and transfer to volcanic or impact tsunamis remain incomplete.
synthesis.well_established: Tsunami generation converts rapid displacement of water by fault motion, landslides, volcanic processes or impact into an initial free-surface and velocity field; source geometry, kinematics and coupling determine amplitude, spectrum and directivity before propagation physics acts.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Relevant controls include relative wave height and runup, Froude number, slope, relative roughness and blockage, grid-to-feature scale, wet/dry depth tolerance, Reynolds effects in physical or RANS models, and nondimensional arrival, depth, velocity and force errors. Validation regimes were characterized by relative solitary-wave height H/d and normalized runup R/H; the conical-island cases tested H/d=0.10 and 0.20.
synthesis.disagreements: An internal reporting inconsistency remains in the plane-beach benchmark: the Figure 1 caption states H/d=0.25 while the validation prose states H/d=0.28. Model fidelity is decision-dependent: explicit three-dimensional flow can improve local force representation but is costly, while depth-integrated and reduced methods support larger ensembles or rapid mapping but simplify vertical structure, breaking and obstacle-scale flow. Published-record corrections and inconsistencies must be carried with model benchmarks: the UBO-TSUFD source caption was formally corrected to M0=6.41e21 Nm and Mw=7.17, while the Boussinesq paper reports its plane-beach H/d as 0.25 in a caption and 0.28 in prose.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: The expanded evidence includes 2004 Thailand and Banda Aceh field information, 85 surveyed tsunami-pole flow depths, Onagawa eyewitness video and damage observations, and synthetic or historical runup records used for inversion and validation. The reviewed laboratory benchmark suite spans a 1:19.85 plane beach, a composite beach, a conical island, a complex three-dimensional beach, and three-dimensional landslide generation and runup. Two independent laboratory benchmarks were used: solitary-wave runup/rundown on a 1:19.85 plane beach and directional maximum runup around a 14-degree conical island.
synthesis.governing_physics: Inundation couples long-wave shoaling and runup with nonlinear advection, gravity, bed and land-cover friction, wetting and drying, breaking or bore motion, terrain channeling, and interactions with buildings and defenses. The reviewed model links source displacement, nonlinear dispersive propagation, breaking, runup/rundown, and inland wetting through a higher-order Boussinesq framework with surface-roller breaking and dry-bed boundaries.
synthesis.limitations: Ad hoc friction coefficients used mainly as numerical stabilizers have no assured predictive reliability outside the configurations in which the model was tested. Benchmark success reduces uncertainty but does not guarantee accurate prediction for every tsunami; one comparison is insufficient and extrapolation remains limited by source ambiguity, bathymetry, breaking, friction treatment, and benchmark coverage. Dominant limitations are uncertain tsunami sources, elevation and bathymetry error, unresolved buildings and defenses, empirical roughness, sparse inland velocity and force observations, numerical wet/dry sensitivity, high computational cost, and validation confined to a few events or benchmarks. Neither reviewed Mediterranean application provides observed validation of its regional inundation map: the Catania case uses modern geometry and a speculative corrected source, while the Crete/Sicily cases are representative one-meter source scenarios that cannot be linearly rescaled. The regional results are representative numerical scenarios, not historical reconstructions or observed inundation validation, and must not be linearly rescaled to other initial amplitudes because the simulated processes are nonlinear.
synthesis.major_equations: Most detailed models solve depth-integrated nonlinear shallow-water conservation equations, while higher-fidelity RANS resolves vertical structure; reduced methods use Bernoulli energy and friction loss, Green-law transformations, response functions, or other calibrated approximations. The formulation uses higher-order Boussinesq continuity and momentum equations, with a bottom-displacement time derivative available for active generation and alternative passive free-surface displacement used in the regional scenarios.
synthesis.numerical_models: The evidence spans COMCOT, GeoClaw, depth-integrated shallow-water solvers, three-dimensional RANS, SWEpy GPU finite volumes, nested linear-to-local models, probabilistic response-function inversion, and rapid energy-conservation approximations. The reviewed higher-order Boussinesq model reproduced the main plane-beach runup sequence and showed closer conical-island agreement for H/d=0.10 than H/d=0.20, where front-side runup was underpredicted. The reviewed models span different physics: UBO-TSUFD solves nondispersive nonlinear shallow-water equations with Manning friction, whereas the Eastern Mediterranean model uses higher-order Boussinesq dispersion and a surface-roller breaking treatment.
synthesis.open_questions: Comparative external validation is needed to determine when nondispersive shallow-water versus dispersive Boussinesq physics materially changes inundation predictions, especially where breaking, uncertain sources, harbor geometry, and high-resolution terrain interact. Model intercomparison under identical emergency conditions remains necessary to establish relative speed, accuracy, and reliability rather than inferring superiority from separate benchmark demonstrations. Needed evidence includes real-event inundation validation in the Eastern Mediterranean, sensitivity to uncertain source geometry and terrain resolution, and uncertainty propagation into operational hazard maps. Shared questions concern transferable roughness, coupled source-to-inundation uncertainty, representation of buildings and defenses, sediment and debris feedback, validation of velocity and loads, probabilistic maps, compound boundaries, and reliable real-time computation.
synthesis.recent_advances: For the two paper-specific 1 m source-amplitude scenarios, modeled inundated area was 3.429 km2 at the Crete site and 0.641 km2 at the Sicily site; steeper Sicily terrain was associated with a narrower inundation zone. Recent advances combine probabilistic runup inversion, rapid physics-based screening between bathtub and full models, semi-empirical operational chains, detailed 2-D/3-D intercomparison, terrain and defense sensitivity, and open GPU-accelerated unstructured solvers. Scenario outputs demonstrate strong site dependence rather than transferable constants: reported penetration is about 100 m at La Plaia and 500 m near the Simeto mouth in the corrected Catania scenario, while separate one-meter-source cases report 3.429 km2 and 0.641 km2 inundation at selected Crete and Sicily sites.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Foundational inundation practice grew from nonlinear shallow-water runup theory, analytical moving-shoreline solutions, laboratory plane-beach and island benchmarks, finite-difference and finite-volume wetting/drying algorithms, and systematic post-tsunami field surveys.
synthesis.typical_methods: A defensible evaluation sequence combines basic hydrodynamic checks and grid convergence with analytical, laboratory, and field benchmarks, followed by scientific review and application-specific operational testing. The demonstrated workflow combines laboratory runup validation, regional bathymetry, coastal terrain, empirical earthquake-source dimensions, passive tsunami generation, phase-resolving propagation, and dry-bed inundation mapping. Workflows combine a source scenario, nested bathymetry and topography, stable wetting/drying, spatial friction or explicit structures, grid and parameter checks, comparison with laboratory or post-event observations, and mapped extent, depth, velocity, arrival time or load outputs.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Laboratory validation in the reviewed source covers a 1:19.85 plane beach at 0.2 m depth and a conical island at 0.32 m depth with H/d=0.10 and 0.20; it does not constitute observed validation of the Eastern Mediterranean inundation maps. Reported validation is case-specific, covering selected historical events, local terrain, source scenarios, benchmark inflows and building layouts; accuracy and cost findings cannot be transferred without checking resolution, roughness, wet/dry treatment and forcing regime. The canonical 1:19.85 plane-beach dataset contains more than 40 solitary-wave tests over 6.25-38.32 cm depth and H/d=0.021-0.626; its reported breaking threshold H/d>0.045 is beach-specific and should not be generalized to other slopes or waveforms. Validation remains benchmark-specific: UBO-TSUFD covers four analytical/laboratory tests including a pre-breaking Monai comparison through 30 s, while the higher-order Boussinesq model covers a 1:19.85 plane beach and a 14-degree conical island at H/d=0.10 and 0.20.
synthesis.well_established: Across the two reviewed model studies, credible inundation use requires explicit moving wet/dry shorelines and validation against analytical or laboratory runup benchmarks; successful propagation alone is not sufficient evidence of inundation accuracy. Explicit wetting-and-drying models can represent two-dimensional tsunami inundation rather than inferring flooded area solely from water-level superelevation or cross-sectional runup; the reviewed evidence here is one demonstrated model application, not a comparative consensus. Tsunami inundation prediction requires a moving wet/dry shoreline, terrain-resolved mass and momentum transfer, and validation of inland extent, depth or velocity; offshore propagation agreement alone does not establish onshore accuracy. Tsunami-model evaluation distinguishes validation of the numerical solution against the governing equations from verification against geophysical observations; both are required for defensible inundation use.

tsunami.inundation.urban_roughness.description: Modification of tsunami runup and overland flow by building layouts and other large obstacles.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Longshore obstruction psi_ls, cross-shore obstruction psi_cs, surf similarity xi, wave nonlinearity a/h0, row count, and obstacle rotation organize the reviewed runup experiments.
synthesis.disagreements: Bulk Manning roughness is simple but does not separately represent blockage, directional porosity, shocks, storage or channelization. Explicit buildings resolve pathways but require fine grids and geometry; subgrid drag offers efficiency yet needs configuration- and regime-aware validation.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Reviewed evidence comprises sinusoidal long-wave tests on a 1:40 beach with rigid 0.10 m cubes arranged in one, five and ten rows, aligned or staggered and at zero or 45-degree rotation, over surf-similarity 7.69-10.49.
synthesis.governing_physics: Building arrays redistribute rather than simply remove hazard: reflection and turbulent losses reduce distal runup, while contraction, retained water, delayed drainage, and local impact can increase water levels or pressures within the built zone.
synthesis.limitations: Neither total runup reduction nor downstream pressure shielding is safely transferable to real cities without accounting for heterogeneous geometry, structural failure, debris, sediment, overtopping, complex topography, and the incident-wave regime.
synthesis.major_equations: Depth-averaged mass and momentum equations represent inundation, with resolved obstacles imposing solid boundaries or subgrid approaches adding drag and blockage sink terms. Array response is summarized through runup ratios and obstruction measures in cross-shore and longshore directions.
synthesis.numerical_models: The reviewed source is experiment-centered and yields empirical runup nomograms. Depth-averaged models can resolve individual buildings or parameterize subgrid blockage and drag, but those urban formulations remain outside reviewed journal evidence for this node.
synthesis.open_questions: A common benchmark spanning array-scale runup, building-scale pressure and force, movable debris and sediment, failure, and realistic urban geometry remains needed.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent advances use lidar-derived building geometry, anisotropic subgrid porosity and drag, GPU-resolved city models, movable debris and failure, hybrid regional-to-building nests, uncertainty ensembles and validation against pressure, momentum flux and drainage as well as depth.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Classical porous-media and drag analogies treated urban resistance in depth-averaged flow; post-tsunami flume arrays and field surveys established shielding, channelization, storage and directional blockage, motivating explicit-building and subgrid urban models.
synthesis.typical_methods: Studies generate controlled long waves over a plane beach, place rigid obstacle arrays with varied rows, alignment, rotation and obstruction, record free surface and runup throughout and behind the array, compare unobstructed references and construct configuration-specific response nomograms.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Goseberg's nomograms cover single sinusoidal waves with xi=7.69-10.49 on a 1:40 beach, rigid 0.10 m cubes, one/five/ten rows, and 0 or 45 degree rotation.
synthesis.well_established: In the reviewed regular arrays, greater longshore obstruction and generally more rows reduced maximum runup; 45-degree rotation changed runup more than aligned-versus-staggered placement.

claims.text: Across the tested arrays, increasing longshore obstruction and generally increasing the number of building rows reduced maximum long-wave runup relative to the unobstructed beach.
claims.regime: Rigid 0.10 m cubes on a 1:40 beach, single sinusoidal waves with surf similarity 7.69-10.49, and one, five, or ten rows.

claims.text: For staggered arrays rotated 45 degrees, additional runup reduction relative to the non-rotated reference ranged from 4.2% to 21.4% with five rows and from 13.1% to 19.6% with ten rows across the stated obstruction cases.
claims.regime: The paper's staggered cube configurations and tested obstruction ratios; percentages are differences between configurations, not total attenuation.

claims.text: Changing cube rotation had a stronger effect on runup reduction than changing between aligned and staggered rows in the tested configurations.
claims.regime: Five- and ten-row regular arrays with 0 or 45 degree rotation on the tested beach.

claims.text: The first obstacle row generated an offshore-propagating shock, while water retained within and behind the array drained with a time lag and could have higher local levels than the unobstructed case.
claims.regime: The measured rigid-array cases, especially the five-row staggered rotated example with psi_ls=0.739.

claims.text: The reported nomograms should not be transferred directly to heterogeneous real cities with building failure, debris, sediment transport, overtopping, or complex three-dimensional topography.
claims.regime: Prototype application beyond the idealized flume geometry.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Controls include Froude number, relative bore depth, wave height and wavelength relative to deck width/clearance, blockage and girder count, air-volume and compressibility ratios, debris density and size ratios, impact velocity, stiffness/contact-time ratios, and vegetation submergence.
synthesis.disagreements: Simplified design equations can be non-conservative; solitary waves and transient bores do not always reproduce the same load path; trapped air can raise or lower slamming while increasing quasi-static uplift; and increased girder count can amplify or reduce force depending on wave regime.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: The branch includes 1:5 flexible bridge tests, laboratory debris and dam-break benchmarks, open-girder deck validation, pneumatic reproduction of the 2004 and 2011 tsunami records, bore-pressure comparisons, and vegetation-breakage force tests.
synthesis.governing_physics: Load histories depend on bore depth, velocity and relative depth, wave breaking and duration, deck clearance and geometry, air compression and escape, structural motion, debris buoyancy/trajectory/contact, added water mass, and the superposition of debris and hydrodynamic force.
synthesis.limitations: Reduced-scale wave generation, air scaling, rigid-body assumptions, idealized debris/contact, sparse full-scale records, uncertain collision probability, limited debris ensembles and damming data, and model-dependent turbulence or pressure peaks restrict generalization.
synthesis.major_equations: Assessment uses depth-integrated momentum and drag/hydrostatic terms, pressure integration, rigid-body and finite-element response, RANS or Green–Naghdi flow, SPH fluid–solid coupling, contact impulse and added-mass models, and probabilistic collision/load descriptions.
synthesis.numerical_models: Validated tools include GPUSPH, DualSPHysics–Project Chrono, DualSPHysics–Abaqus, compressible ALE, Navier–Stokes/RANS, Green–Naghdi and Saint-Venant equations, plus PCE, ANN, and Kriging load surrogates.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities are probabilistic debris fields, multiple impacts and damming, deformable and negatively buoyant debris, air–water–structure coupling, structural motion/failure, scour and foundation interaction, transferable scaling, and code-level uncertainty factors.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent advances combine open-source SPH with nonsmooth multibody contact and stochastic initial conditions, high-fidelity deck-geometry and oblique-wave studies, probabilistic debris-collision reviews, and vegetation-breakage-aware mitigation experiments.
synthesis.seminal_papers: The evidence pathway progresses from physical bore and single-debris impact tests and simplified design formulas to three-dimensional pressure fields, flexible bridge response, realistic pneumatic tsunami histories, and coupled fluid–multibody contact.
synthesis.typical_methods: Typical methods are dam-break and pneumatic long-wave experiments, force/pressure and high-speed-motion measurement, solitary-wave and transient-bore comparison, SPH–multibody and CFD–FE coupling, ALE multiphase models, surrogate response surfaces, and critical evidence reviews.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Reported benchmarks include trapped-air uplift increases of 39% on average and 148% maximum, a 32% average overturning increase, oblique-wave forces of 1901 kN horizontal and 862 kN longitudinal, prototype-equivalent tsunami durations of 2–20 min, and intact-vegetation force reduction up to 70%.
synthesis.well_established: Tsunami loads combine hydrostatic and drag-like demand with short impulsive/slamming peaks, uplift and overturning, trapped-air effects, and stochastic debris collision; local pressures and component load paths can govern even when total force appears moderate.

claims.text: Tsunami debris-load research is most mature for a single impacting object, with ensemble motion, damming, collision probability, and stochastic load variability still unresolved.
claims.regime: Single-object impact is the best-developed case, while debris ensembles, damming, collision probability, and load variability remain major gaps.

claims.text: Validated SPH simulations found that an upwave service bridge and breakwater can reduce tsunami force on a main bridge, while transferring severe demand to the shielding structures.
claims.regime: A two-girder service-road bridge and an offshore breakwater reduced load on the main bridge, with an optimum breakwater distance, but the shielding structures themselves received strong loads.

claims.text: In 1:5 bridge tests, trapped air increased total uplift by 39% on average (148% maximum) and overturning moment by 32% on average, while redistributing component demand.
claims.regime: Trapped air increased total uplift by 39% on average and 148% at maximum and overturning moment by 32% on average; solitary-wave and bore effects differed.

claims.text: Three-dimensional SPH–FE analysis showed localized tsunami-bore pressure peaks and found commonly used design-pressure equations could be highly non-conservative.
claims.regime: Peak pressures were localized and commonly used design equations could be highly non-conservative.

claims.text: DualSPHysics–Chrono reproduced laboratory buoyant-container trajectories and velocities, supporting coupled flow–debris simulation before impact-load prediction.
claims.regime: The coupled model reproduced measured container centroid trajectory and velocity with quantitatively assessed agreement.

claims.text: Validated ALE simulations showed girder count can either raise or lower deck forces depending on wave size through acceleration, eddy dissipation, and pressure-phase effects.
claims.regime: Girder count changed force non-monotonically with wave height; chamber eddies and out-of-phase pressures weakened impacts for larger girder counts under large waves.

claims.regime: Extreme cases reached 1901 kN horizontal and 862 kN longitudinal force; third-order PCE best predicted vertical/horizontal loads and ANN longitudinal loads.

claims.regime: The systems reproduced recorded 2004 and 2011 tsunami histories at 1:50 scale over 20–240 s model periods, equivalent to 2–20 min prototype durations.

claims.regime: Breaking solitary waves and dam-break bores produced reasonably representative tsunami loading conclusions across deck elevations.

claims.regime: Relative depth controlled bore shape, stability, and impact; Green–Naghdi results approached RANS at far lower cost, whereas Saint-Venant omitted substantial physics.

claims.regime: Nonsmooth contact matched measurements and avoided numerical high-frequency noise; varying initial debris position reproduced experimental variability and exposed design-equation issues.

claims.text: Debris-collision assessment must jointly estimate collision probability, velocity, and force, with probabilistic evaluation the leading unresolved need.
claims.regime: Available methods trade accuracy, computation, and practicality; probabilistic evaluation remains the principal development need.

claims.text: Laboratory tests directly evaluated tsunami waterborne-debris impact forces against FEMA P-646 and P-55 design formulations.
claims.regime: Experiments quantified debris impact forces and evaluated prescribed guideline formulas.

claims.text: Tsunami structural-load assessment relies on complementary physical experiments and numerical simulation, with design-guideline revision requiring validated use of both.
claims.regime: Physical testing and numerical simulation are complementary, and numerical models can represent parameters omitted from reduced physical tests.

claims.text: Experiments found intact vegetation reduced maximum tsunami force by up to 70%, but breakage sharply degraded protection and made patch length important.
claims.regime: Intact vegetation reduced maximum force by up to 70% (rigid) and 66.5% (flexible); breakage reduced protection, although longer patches partly compensated.

claims.text: Large-scale flume tests indicate that nonbreaking very-long-wave inundation at vertical seawalls produces little impulsive loading: periods of at least 40 s did not exceed about 1.2 times hydrostatic force, unlike bore-led cases.

tsunami.loads.building_arrays.label: Loads within building arrays
tsunami.loads.building_arrays.description: Pressure and force redistribution, shielding, and amplification among coastal buildings.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Controls include Froude number, relative wave height, structure width and spacing relative to depth, blockage ratio, setback relative to breaking length, row and lateral position, inundation depth relative to building height, pressure coefficient and peak-to-hydrostatic pressure ratio.
synthesis.disagreements: Upstream buildings can shield downstream faces yet increase blockage, flow channelization, lateral loads or local water levels. Bare-earth hazard models may support regional inundation but can be nonconservative for structure pressure when the built array changes breaking and hydraulics.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Reviewed evidence is one idealized 1:20 physical model of a seaside building array under breaking and nonbreaking tsunami-like waves, resolving upstream shielding, local breaking position and comparison with Japanese Cabinet Office pressure equations.
synthesis.governing_physics: Breaking location and structural setback govern impulsive loading: the largest pressures occurred when the wave broke on or immediately before the specimen.
synthesis.limitations: Bare-earth water levels can be nonconservative inputs for breaking-wave pressure design because the building array changes local inundation and impact conditions.
synthesis.major_equations: Array loading is assessed through pressure integration and force or moment balance, with hydrostatic, drag, momentum-flux and impulsive components. Design equations relate pressure to inundation depth or velocity, while blockage and shielding modify the local depth, velocity and breaking state used as inputs.
synthesis.numerical_models: The current evidence evaluates empirical Japanese design equations against physical-array pressures. Numerical shallow-water, nonhydrostatic or CFD array models are not yet reviewed for this node and require validation against local depth, velocity, pressure and impulse together.
synthesis.open_questions: Full-text extraction and additional arrays are needed to resolve spacing, setback, blockage, breaking location, three-dimensional flow, and scale effects before deriving transferable shielding factors.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent advances use dense pressure arrays, instrumented urban layouts, high-resolution nonhydrostatic and CFD solvers, debris and buoyancy coupling, probabilistic urban configurations and multiscale workflows connecting regional inundation to local structural demand.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Tsunami force formulations began with hydrostatic and drag analogies and bore-impact experiments; post-2004 and 2011 surveys motivated building-specific pressure guidance, while later flume arrays exposed shielding, blockage and local-breaking effects.
synthesis.typical_methods: Studies generate controlled bores or long waves over a 1:20 bathymetry, vary breaking location and structure arrangement, measure free surface and high-rate pressures on multiple faces and rows, integrate loads, compare isolated and array cases and audit design equations using locally disturbed rather than bare-earth hydraulics.
synthesis.validated_ranges: The reported 40%-70% peak-pressure reduction applies only to the study's 1:20 idealized array under breaking-wave trials; the accessible abstract does not expose the exact wave, spacing, or setback ranges.
synthesis.well_established: Within the reviewed experiment, upstream structures shielded downstream buildings from peak breaking-wave pressure, but the amount is configuration- and regime-specific rather than a universal reduction factor.

claims.text: Upstream shielding elements reduced peak pressure on downstream structures by 40%-70% under the study's breaking-wave conditions.
claims.regime: The study's idealized building array and breaking-wave trials; detailed geometry and wave ranges require full-text review.

claims.text: Waves breaking on or immediately before the test structure produced the largest impulsive pressures.
claims.regime: The paper's 1:20 structure configurations and tested wave conditions.

claims.text: For nonbreaking waves, measured pressures agreed with Japanese Cabinet Office design equations, whereas bare-earth water-level inputs were nonconservative in breaking-wave trials.
claims.regime: The paper's nonbreaking and breaking physical-model trials; exact error magnitudes are unavailable from the abstract.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Controls include relative amplitude a/h, shallowness h/L, Ursell number, Froude number, relative shelf width and slope, travel distance relative to dispersive length, numerical Courant number, cells per wavelength, normalized runup and amplitude or phase error.
synthesis.disagreements: Nondispersive shallow-water models are efficient and often adequate for earthquake tsunamis, while Boussinesq or nonhydrostatic models capture accumulated dispersion and shorter components at greater cost. Apparent agreement can result from compensating source, bathymetry and friction errors.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Reviewed evidence includes plane-beach, conical-island, oscillating-basin and Monai benchmarks, the Rat Islands-to-Hilo operational test, and Eastern Mediterranean Crete, Sicily, Catania and Libyan-coast scenarios.
synthesis.governing_physics: Rapid source displacement launches long waves whose phase speed is approximately sqrt(gh) in shallow-water regimes; variable depth redirects rays and changes amplitude, shelves and ridges trap or focus energy, harbors resonate, and dispersion matters as wavelength shortens or distance accumulates.
synthesis.limitations: Uncertainty arises from source kinematics, bathymetric resolution and datum, unresolved ridges and channels, open boundaries, numerical dispersion and diffusion, friction, grid nesting, harbor geometry and sparse gauges; propagation validation can be confounded by generation and inundation errors.
synthesis.major_equations: Models use linear or nonlinear shallow-water mass and momentum equations for nondispersive propagation, Boussinesq or nonhydrostatic equations for frequency dispersion, and sometimes mild-slope or spectral formulations; moving-bottom source terms and wet/dry boundaries connect generation and inundation.
synthesis.numerical_models: The evidence spans nonlinear shallow-water UBO-TSUFD and a higher-order Boussinesq model with dispersive propagation, breaking and wetting/drying, evaluated against a broader verification and validation benchmark framework.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities include adaptive dispersive criteria, global-to-harbor conservative nesting, uncertainty attribution among source and path, subgrid bathymetry, scattering by rough seafloor and islands, real-time assimilation, compound tides and currents, and reliable faster-than-real-time ensembles.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent advances combine higher-order dispersive and nonhydrostatic solvers, GPU and adaptive meshes, conservative unstructured nesting, real-time pressure and GNSS assimilation, probabilistic source ensembles, digital-twin harbors and operational benchmark requirements.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Linear long-wave theory and Green-law shoaling established depth-controlled propagation; ray and edge-wave theory treated refraction and trapping, while finite-difference shallow-water models and later Boussinesq solvers enabled basin-scale scenarios and dispersive benchmarks.
synthesis.typical_methods: Workflows construct nested bathymetry, initialize a tested source, verify conservation and convergence, compare analytical travel and oscillation cases, validate laboratory shelf/island/runup benchmarks, hindcast gauge and harbor records, test dispersion and friction sensitivity, and report arrival, amplitude and phase separately.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Benchmark support covers selected analytical basins and laboratory geometries plus scenario-scale Mediterranean propagation. The operational Hilo requirement constrains speed as well as physics; none of these proves universal skill across all source spectra and ocean basins.
synthesis.well_established: Across deep ocean and shelves, tsunami propagation is governed primarily by long-wave gravity dynamics, with travel time controlled by depth and coastal amplitude shaped by shoaling, refraction, diffraction, resonance, friction, dispersion and bathymetric focusing.

claims.text: The key issue of this article is the concept of combining a model dedicated to dispersive large scale propagation of tsunamis with ComMIT, developed and made freely available by NOAA, that is a state of the art tool for tsunami impact studies.First, the main motivation for this approach, namely the need for efficient computation of runup of tsunamis from submarine/subaerial slides and certain types of earthquake, is discussed.Then the models involved are presented.We describe in some detail the dispersive model component which is a Boussinesq type model that is recently developed for tsunami propagation purposes.Finally, the performance and flexibility of the joint model approach is illustrated by two case studies including inundation computations at selected cites.The potentially disastrous, but small probability, flank-collapse event at the La Palma Island is used as an example of slide generated tsunamis where dispersion plays an important role.The second example is a tsunami from a potential inverse thrust fault at the Lesser Antilles.In this case dispersion during propagation is important for some regions, but not for others.
