synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Controls include relative depth kh, obstacle or gap width over wavelength, mound length over wavelength, directional spread, propagation angle, reflection coefficient, relative wave height H/h, Ursell number and grid points per wavelength. The improved parabolic model was tested to 70 degrees.
synthesis.disagreements: Differences largely reflect model scope rather than incompatible physics: phase-decoupled spectral diffraction is intended for random short-crested waves without coherent standing patterns, parabolic models assume predominantly forward propagation, and phase-resolving solvers retain interference but require finer grids and boundary treatment.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Key evidence includes two natural-harbor physical models with irregular wave grouping, Vincent-Briggs and Berkhoff elliptical-mound benchmarks, and controlled laterally heterogeneous vegetation layouts. These probe shadowing, focusing, reflection-diffraction and lateral nonuniformity.
synthesis.governing_physics: The process follows spatial phase and amplitude gradients governed by dispersion, energy flux and boundary conditions. Important controls are wavelength relative to obstacle/gap scale, water depth, incidence angle, directional spreading, reflection, bathymetric gradients and coherence; focusing can amplify waves locally while shadow zones attenuate them.
synthesis.limitations: One-way marching misses strong backscatter; spectral closures cannot reproduce coherent phase interference; physical models may have scale and reflection artifacts; Cartesian grids distort curved boundaries; breaking, vegetation wakes and complex natural-reef roughness add dissipation that can be confused with diffraction.
synthesis.major_equations: Foundational formulations are the elliptic mild-slope equation and its parabolic forward-marching approximations. Spectral models augment the action balance with a diffraction turning/diffusion term, while nonhydrostatic models solve free-surface flow directly. Generalized Padé operators improve angular dispersion accuracy.
synthesis.numerical_models: The corpus contains a generalized-[1/1]-Padé parabolic model, a phase-decoupled diffraction extension in SWAN, and a three-dimensional nonhydrostatic solver validated on flat- and sloping-bed mound benchmarks. Each trades phase detail, backscatter capability and computational cost differently.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities are irregular directional-wave benchmarks with combined diffraction, breaking and reflection; robust diffraction closures on unstructured grids; uncertainty from bathymetry and boundary reflection; field validation around reefs and structures; adaptive resolution; and separation of lateral scattering from dissipation.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent nonhydrostatic validation quantifies focusing errors across classic three-dimensional mound tests, while spatial vegetation experiments show that lateral layout controls attenuation uniformity—an engineering manifestation of diffraction and lateral redistribution absent from one-dimensional transmission metrics.
synthesis.seminal_papers: The 1989 harbor experiments established why irregular-wave diffraction-reflection transfer functions can be more stable within the energetic band. The 2003 phase-decoupled formulation made diffraction compatible with operational spectral wave modeling.
synthesis.typical_methods: Methods include regular and irregular wave-basin tests, harbor transfer functions, mild-slope finite elements, one-way parabolic marching, phase-decoupled spectral action models, three-dimensional nonhydrostatic solvers and spatial attenuation diagnostics for laterally heterogeneous vegetation or structures.
synthesis.validated_ranges: The parabolic model reports tests up to 70-degree propagation. The nonhydrostatic solver reports dimensionless wave-height RMSE of 0.070–0.165 for the flat-bed mound and 0.060–0.114 for the sloping-bed mound, with focusing to 2.2 times incident height in the latter benchmark.
synthesis.well_established: Diffraction laterally redistributes wave amplitude and direction when bathymetry or obstacles impose along-crest gradients. It interacts with refraction, shoaling and reflection; coherent phase-resolving methods capture interference, whereas spectral methods require phase-decoupled approximations for random seas.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Controls include reflection coefficient, kh, surf-similarity, relative roughness and permeability, incidence angle, structure slope and freeboard, frequency-band energy fraction, standing-wave ratio and geometry or basin length relative to wavelength.
synthesis.disagreements: Regular-wave tests reveal sharp frequency structure but may exaggerate sensitivity relative to broadband seas. Bulk height and period can hide directional reflection and multimodality, while large transfer estimates outside energetic bands may be statistically unstable yet energetically minor.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Reviewed evidence includes a 40-year multimodal outer-port/harbor spectral reconstruction for Africa basin and physical harbor-model experiments comparing regular and irregular diffraction-reflection transfer behavior.
synthesis.governing_physics: Reflection depends on impedance change, slope, roughness, porosity, structure geometry, water depth, frequency and incidence angle. Diffraction spreads reflected energy around boundaries, while nonlinear interactions and wave grouping create low-frequency components that need not be harbor resonance.
synthesis.limitations: Incident/reflected separation is ill-conditioned with poor gauge spacing, nonlinear waves, multiple directions or evanescent modes. Sparse spatial measurements, uncertain boundary spectra, diffraction, harbor resonance and changing water level complicate attribution.
synthesis.major_equations: Reflection coefficients use reflected-to-incident amplitude or energy; gauge-array methods solve incident/reflected spectral components, and momentum-flux approaches enforce force or radiation-stress balances. Mild-slope, potential-flow and phase-resolving equations represent coupled reflection and diffraction.
synthesis.numerical_models: The reviewed branch includes spectral-type reconstruction and experimental transfer coefficients. Direct third-order and momentum-flux reflection analyses remain in the lawful-full-text queue; common predictive frameworks include mild-slope, boundary-integral and phase-resolving models.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities include robust multidirectional separation, nonlinear and third-order reflection, currents, porous and overtopped structures, field-scale phase observations, reflection under changing water levels and morphology and uncertainty-aware links to loads and navigation.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent advances use dense radar/video and pressure arrays, Bayesian directional separation, high-order and fully nonlinear solvers, porous and flexible boundaries, data-assimilative harbor digital twins and spectral-type clustering that retains reflected multimodality.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Standing-wave gauge methods established laboratory reflection measurement; linear potential-flow and mild-slope theory treated structures and bathymetry, while directional spectral arrays and irregular-wave transfer functions extended analysis to realistic seas and harbors.
synthesis.typical_methods: Studies use multi-gauge arrays or directional spectra to separate incident and reflected energy, test regular and irregular seas, map harbor spatial spectra, compare frequency bands and directions, validate against structures or bathymetry and check whether low-frequency energy is bound, reflected or resonant.
synthesis.validated_ranges: Evidence is limited to the studied harbor configurations and dominant incident-energy bands. In irregular tests, coefficients varied less than regular-wave values within the main band; Africa-basin energetic patterns were linked to Reina Sofia breakwater reflection.
synthesis.well_established: Coastal wave reflection redirects energy from beaches, structures and depth transitions; reflected and incident components interfere to form standing or partial-standing patterns, alter directional spectra and redistribute harbor agitation even when bulk significant height is similar.

claims.text: Video-derived uprush/backwash asymmetry integrates surf- and swash-zone transformation and can predict shoreline wave reflection better than surf similarity, particularly on intermediate and reflective beaches where swash dissipation controls the reflected energy fraction.
claims.regime: Three microtidal natural beaches spanning upper-beach slopes 0.05-0.15, grain sizes 0.2-0.6 mm, and low-to-energetic swell conditions in Chile, Vietnam, and Benin.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Controls include kh, relative depth and bathymetric slope, incident angle, directional spread, current-to-group-speed ratio, refraction and shoaling coefficients, mound height and width relative to wavelength, focusing gain and grid or spectral resolution relative to caustic width.
synthesis.disagreements: Geometric rays are efficient away from caustics but fail where diffraction or multi-path interference matters. Spectral phase-averaged models handle broad seas but smooth coherent focusing, while phase-resolving models capture interference at higher cost and remain sensitive to boundaries and breaking.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Reviewed evidence includes Vincent–Briggs flat-bed and Berkhoff 1:50 sloping-bed mound benchmarks and a roughly 300 km by 300 km Southern California Bight comparison of refraction and refraction–diffraction spectral models.
synthesis.governing_physics: Conservation of frequency along stationary paths and of wave action in currents combines with the dispersion relation to rotate wave crests toward slower regions. Bathymetric mounds, channels, headlands and current gradients produce caustics, shadow zones and frequency-dependent focusing.
synthesis.limitations: Bathymetric resolution, boundary directional spectra, current uncertainty, caustics, diffraction closure, unresolved islands and structures, nonlinear breaking, bottom friction and sparse directional observations can dominate. Agreement at exposed sites does not prove skill in sheltered zones.
synthesis.major_equations: Linear dispersion links frequency, wavenumber and depth; Snell-type relations conserve along-crest wavenumber for parallel contours. Spectral action balance transports action through geographic and directional space, while mild-slope, Boussinesq and nonhydrostatic equations include diffraction and nonlinear transformation.
synthesis.numerical_models: The set includes a three-dimensional nonhydrostatic model for shoaling, diffraction and refraction and two regional spectral formulations with and without diffraction. Direct current-refraction and multidirectional model records remain in the lawful-full-text queue.
synthesis.open_questions: Priorities include current–depth refraction in strong shears, probabilistic caustics, rapidly changing bathymetry, spectral-to-phase coupling, breaking-limited focusing, remote directional validation, adaptive grids and uncertainty propagation into loads and sediment transport.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent advances combine unstructured high-resolution spectral models, current-coupled action balance, nonhydrostatic and dispersive solvers, satellite-derived bathymetry, data assimilation, adaptive phase-resolving nests and differentiable calibration.
synthesis.seminal_papers: Snell-law and ray theory established depth refraction; action conservation extended it to currents and spectra, while mild-slope equations introduced diffraction and reflection and later Boussinesq/nonhydrostatic solvers resolved nonlinear phase effects.
synthesis.typical_methods: Studies map directional spectra and bathymetry, ray-trace or solve spectral/phase-resolving equations, validate mound and island benchmarks, compare cross-shore wave-height sections, test frequency-direction boundary sensitivity and report focusing, sheltered-site and bias errors separately.
synthesis.validated_ranges: The Berkhoff focusing section reached 2.2 times incident wave height; the flat-bed focusing section had MAE 0.158 and MBE -0.114. Regional models improved with broader incident spectra but neither was accurate at highly sheltered sites.
synthesis.well_established: Wave refraction changes propagation direction and energy density as phase speed varies with depth or current; converging rays focus energy and diverging rays defocus it, while diffraction, reflection, breaking and spectral spreading regularize ideal ray singularities.

claims.text: In the flat-bed mound case, the largest reported MAE was 0.158 at the energy-focusing section and the MBE there was -0.114, indicating local underprediction of dimensionless wave height.
claims.regime: Vincent-Briggs flat-bed elliptical-mound benchmark and the paper's section definitions.

claims.text: In the Berkhoff 1:50 sloping-bed mound case, wave height at the focusing section reached 2.2 times the incident height.
claims.regime: Regular H=4.64 cm, T=1 s wave over the specified rotated elliptical mound on a 1:50 bed.

claims.text: Ten months of Hanalei Bay observations and modeling show that episodic long-period swells are preferentially refracted into the reef embayment and drive currents up to an order of magnitude stronger than modal trade-wind conditions.
claims.regime: Hydrodynamics of a bathymetrically complex fringing coral reef embayment: Wave climate, in situ observations, and wave prediction

claims.text: Assuming linear wave theory for waves riding on a weak current of 0(ε) compared to the wave phase speed, an approximate dispersion relation is developed to 0(ε2) for arbitrary current U(z) in water of finite depth.
claims.regime: The study system, forcing, data and methods stated in the indexed abstract.

claims.text: Abstract We apply a coupled circulation‐wave model to simulate extreme sea levels induced by tropical cyclones at the basin scale.
claims.regime: The study system, forcing, data and methods stated in the indexed abstract.

claims.text: Characteristic-based regular- and irregular-wave models reproduce current-depth refraction benchmarks, while irregular-wave height is not amplified by following or opposing currents and opposing-current cases show slight overestimation from directional energy leakage.
claims.regime: Regular and directional irregular waves refracted by one-dimensional following or opposing currents and depth gradients.

claims.text: A multidirectional random-wave action-balance model using a QUICK scheme resolves transformation, breaking, and blocking in current fields and reproduces wave-height behavior in caustics and a river-mouth application.
claims.regime: Directional random waves traveling through spatially varying following or opposing coastal currents, including river-mouth flow.

claims.text: At the Gunsan-Janghang Harbor entrance, comparison of spectral wind-wave and energy-balance models characterizes wave transformation through a changing reclaimed coastline, islands, shoals, breakwaters, and a long navigation channel.
claims.regime: Gunsan-Janghang Harbor entrance under reclamation-modified bathymetry, river-mouth shoals, coastal islands, breakwaters, and wind waves.

synthesis.dimensionless_parameters: Regime selection uses relative depth h/L or kh, deep-water steepness H0/L0, local relative height H/h, Ursell number, bed slope, breaker index, directional angle, vegetation submergence and density, and bandwidth or spectral shape.
synthesis.disagreements: No single shoaling coefficient spans all regimes. Linear theory departs at greater steepness, local H/h is not constant throughout surf zones, and depth-integrated radiation stress obscures vertical flux structure needed by 3-D circulation models.
synthesis.experimental_datasets: Reviewed benchmarks include variable-geometry and regular-wave laboratory shoaling, no-free-second-harmonic linear/cnoidal tests, exposed dissipative-beach surf-zone observations, and source-specific vegetation-force calculations or comparisons.
synthesis.governing_physics: Energy or action-flux conservation drives nondissipative height change; nonlinearity sharpens crests and transfers energy among harmonics; refraction redistributes flux directionally; reflection, bottom friction, breaking, vegetation drag, infragravity modulation, and currents add sinks or couplings.
synthesis.limitations: Common exclusions are reflection, friction, breaking, free harmonics, broad bandwidth, currents, directional spreading, flexible vegetation, rotational flow, and complex three-dimensional bathymetry. Field depth limitation mixes shoaling, breaking, setup, and infragravity variability.
synthesis.major_equations: Core descriptions include Green's law for long waves, linear energy-flux shoaling coefficients, matched linear-cnoidal theory, random-wave height distributions with breaking, depth-limited surf-zone relations, radiation-stress/momentum-flux balances, and phase-resolving nonhydrostatic equations.
synthesis.numerical_models: Model classes include linear and cnoidal transformation tables, stochastic breaking-height/vegetation-drag formulations, depth-limited surf-zone decay, 3-D momentum-flux theory, and nonhydrostatic phase-resolving models for combined shoaling, refraction, diffraction, and breaking.
synthesis.open_questions: Needs include common uncertainty-aware benchmarks across shoaling and breaking, broadband nonlinear directionality, wave-current and vegetation flexibility, consistent 3-D momentum coupling, bathymetric-history effects, and efficient model-selection criteria for engineering applications.
synthesis.recent_advances: Recent nonhydrostatic models jointly resolve shoaling, refraction, diffraction, and breaking in three dimensions, creating a route to test reduced coefficients against complex transformations while retaining computationally practical coastal domains.
synthesis.seminal_papers: The 1968 Green/linear laboratory comparison and 1977 linear-cnoidal matching study establish early engineering transformations; the 1992 field study demonstrates nonconstant surf-zone H/h, while later work extends forcing vertically and to vegetation.
synthesis.typical_methods: Studies combine analytical conservation laws and asymptotic expansions, wave-flume measurements, natural-beach arrays, stochastic transformation models, barred-beach calculations, and three-dimensional nonhydrostatic simulation.
synthesis.validated_ranges: The matched linear/cnoidal model agreed very well without free second harmonics for H0/L0 up to about 0.03-0.04, using linear theory above h/L0=0.10 and cnoidal theory below; other demonstrations cover small-amplitude variable transitions, dissipative-beach surf zones, rigid vegetation, and nondissipative barred bathymetry.
synthesis.well_established: As surface gravity waves enter decreasing depth, reduced group speed and depth-dependent kinematics transform height, wavelength, shape, energy distribution, and momentum flux before and through breaking. Linear shoaling is reliable only within restricted amplitude and bathymetric regimes.

claims.text: For regular waves without free second harmonics, a wave-height-continuous linear/cnoidal shoaling model agreed very well with experiments up to H0/L0 about 0.03-0.04, whereas linear theory failed at larger steepness in the h/L0>0.10 region.
claims.regime: Regular waves without free second-harmonic components; linear theory for h/L0>0.10, cnoidal theory for h/L0<0.10; H0/L0 up to 0.03-0.04 for very good agreement.

claims.text: For stationary narrow-band random waves over rigid vegetation, empirical regular-wave drag coefficients combined with a stochastic shoaling-and-breaking height distribution provide a practical vegetation-force estimate across different slopes.
claims.regime: Stationary narrow-band random waves in shallow water over rigid vegetation; shoaling and breaking represented by the Mendez et al. wave-height distribution.

claims.text: On an exposed dissipative beach, surf-zone wave-height-to-depth ratios decayed with both local mean water depth and distance from the breaker line, indicating an infragravity-associated decay process in addition to breaking turbulence.
claims.regime: Natural exposed dissipative beach within the surf zone; field analysis of local depth and breaker-line distance effects.

claims.text: For small-amplitude waves propagating through variable-geometry transitions, Green's law and a reflection- and friction-free linear transformation model showed fair agreement with laboratory shoaling measurements.
claims.regime: Small-amplitude waves over variable-geometry shallow-water transitions; reflection and friction omitted in the intermediate/deep-water comparison.

claims.text: For irrotational nondissipative waves over alongshore-uniform irregular bathymetry, vertically varying wave-induced momentum flux balances other vertically varying forcing terms, leaving a depth-invariant total forcing governed by wave-energy and water-depth gradients.
claims.regime: Irrotational, nondissipative three-dimensional waves over two-dimensional irregular bathymetry, illustrated for a barred beach.

claims.text: In 225 irregular-wave hydraulic-model tests on a mobile-bed beach with parallel contours, Snell refraction described turning, linear theory slightly overpredicted shoaling, bottom friction and percolation were small, and saturation-limited breaking attenuation was essential.
claims.regime: The 225 irregular-wave tests on the reported mobile-bed parallel-contour hydraulic model.

claims.text: For modeled nonbreaking regular waves, horizontal-bed stream-function theory described nonlinear shoaling and de-shoaling on a very gentle cot(beta)=1200 foreshore, whereas steeper de-shoaling released free waves that violated the constant-form approximation.
claims.regime: Nonbreaking normally incident regular waves over gentle and steep foreshores, including de-shoaling slope cot(beta)=1200.

claims.text: Stochastic and deterministic Boussinesq models reproduce observed nonlinear transformation of continuous wave spectra over a natural barred beach; shoaling depends on nonlinearity, incident spectral shape and bottom profile.
claims.regime: Nonlinear Evolution of Surface Wave Spectra on a Beach

claims.text: A 2 week field experiment was conducted to measure surface wave dissipation on a barrier reef at Kaneohe Bay, Oahu, Hawaii.
claims.regime: The study system, forcing, data and methods stated in the indexed abstract.
